en: Lakṣmīdhara’s *Kṛtyakalpataru*, Section on Judicial Procedure (*Vyavahārakāṇḍa*)
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One Vāsudeva!
Oṃ, homage to Śiva!
Established by the power of wisdom skillful in investigating the words of various scriptures...
Having heard those various eloquent words, clear in their exposition of the paths of legal procedure such as *nyāya* and so forth,
by which the wise experience horripilation at every step,
Lakṣmīdhara extends this twelfth section on legal procedure here.
In that regard, first is the king’s formal declaration, then the inspection of the legal proceedings,
and immediately after that, the instruction of the chief judge, the court officials, and the members of the assembly.
[2] The definition of legal procedure and the rule for deliberation follow from that;
thereafter, the plaint, the reply, the investigation, and the characteristics of the corrupt are declared.
The characteristic of the inferior [plaintiff] is known to be compromise and the giving of a gift;
then follow the subject matter of the legal action, witnesses, and likewise non-witnesses.
The removal of witnesses, the hearing of the defects of witnesses,
the oath, and the testimony of the witnesses— this constitutes the examination of witnesses.

Then follows the section on false testimony and the relative strength or weakness of witnesses; thereafter is the section on oral testimony, and after that, the secular edict regarding written documents.
Afterwards comes the examination of the document, such as a confession of debt;
immediately following that is the examination of a tainted document, and after that, its relative strength.
The weakness of a document [is established] by another document, and possession follows immediately after that;
in this regard, non-establishment through lack of enjoyment has been declared according to the sequence.
There shall be a loss of mutual enjoyment, and after that, defamation;
when enjoyment has been interrupted, there shall be a legal decision and a formal reprimand based on reasoning.
[3] The procedures for the balance, fire, and water have been proclaimed in succession;
next is the procedure for poison and the ordeal of the sacred jar, and after that, the procedure for rice grains.
The procedure for the heated gold coin (*taptamāṣa*), the ploughshare (*phāla*), and the oath of Dharmada;
the oaths, the certainties, the varieties, and the relative strength of the methods of decision.
The determination of what must be done, the conduct of the victorious disputant,
the re-establishment of the rules of logic, and the cessation of what has been accomplished.
And thereafter, the characteristics of the independent and the dependent [debtor] have been declared;
next shall follow the purpose of the non-payment of debt, interest, and its prohibition.
Then follow the rules for the perfection of a pledge and its owner, as well as for sureties;
and the rules regarding those who seize a debt, as well as the procedure for recovering it.
The rules regarding deposits, followed by sale without ownership, partnership, and likewise the non-delivery of what has been given;
Then follows the non-performance of service after having agreed to the terms of wages;
this is the dispute between the master and the keeper regarding the non-payment of wages.
[4] Breach of agreement, subsequent sale, and likewise non-delivery;
regret after purchasing, and the dispute over boundaries—these have been fully described.
Thereafter, verbal abuse and physical assault are described;
the thefts of open thieves and the punishments for them are proclaimed therein.
Then follow the punishments for thieves who act in secret, the search for thieves by means of their dress,
the extension of the rules for theft to other offenses, and the restitution of stolen goods when they cannot be recovered from the thief.

Following the denial of theft, there may be the commencement of an act of violence; therein follows the search for the perpetrator, as well as the defense against the charge and the handling of an assailant.
Then follow the punishments for adultery between men and women, the defilement of virgins,
intercourse with harlots and the like, and subsequently, the rules regarding the union of men and women.
In that very section, there is the determination of the merits and defects of the bride and groom;
following that, the substitutes for a wife, and the proper times for marriage.
The sequence for giving a daughter in marriage, the determination regarding the giving of gifts,
the relationship between husband and wife, and the regulation concerning vehicles.
The characteristics of marriage, the determination of their virtues and defects,
the conduct of the man toward the woman, and the entire duty of women.

Then follows the rule for their application and the rule regarding women who have had previous husbands; after that comes the partition of inheritance, and the specific time for that is also treated therein.
[5] Thereafter follows the determination of shares for those whose fathers are living,
and after that, the distribution for those whose fathers are deceased.
The statement regarding those unfit for partition, the consecration of the unconsecrated,
what is divisible and what is indivisible, and the treatment of women’s property in the division of assets.
The utilization of wealth by women who lack progeny has been proclaimed;
furthermore, the characteristics of a woman’s property and the division of that which has been lost are described.
In the case of a combination of phonemes, however, there is the determination of their division,
as well as the division of those produced by division, and this very [division] which is further subdivided.
The partition among other types of sons, as well as the definition of sons,
the investigation into the nature of sonship, and the extension of the status of sonship.
The etymologies and so forth of the word "son" have been declared, as well as those sons who are censurable;
furthermore, the partition of the wealth of one who has no son, and the property of those dwelling in the forest and others, is explained.
The classification of joint property and the determination of its partition,
the duties regarding partition, as well as gambling and prize-fighting.

From that, a distinction of ritual acts would arise; therefore, the miscellaneous matters were proclaimed, as well as the king's engagement for the sake of protecting the conduct of the castes and stages of life.
[6] And the grounds for the increase and decrease of punishments have been specified;
thereafter, the rules for verbal punishment, divine ordeals, and the determination of legal status, as well as the regulations concerning tolls, are set forth.
Then, the discernment regarding the system of punishment was set forth,
as well as the increase and decrease of penalties and the king’s fault in his actions.
From that [source], there arise the notion of punishment and the mental notion based on the conventions of common usage and so forth,
according to the order of birth and caste, whether in direct or inverse sequence.
Whatever characteristics, qualities,
and modes of conduct they possess are set forth in due order by the skilled Lakṣmīdhara.
[7] The Matrix of Legal Procedure.
The Section on Legal Procedure.
Now follows the exposition of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*).
Regarding this, Manu says:
"But the king, desiring to investigate legal cases, [should do so] together with Brāhmaṇas."
Disciplined, he should enter the assembly hall together with his ministers and counselors.
Seated there, or even standing, having raised his right hand and being modest in dress and ornaments, he shall examine the legal cases of the litigants.
Day by day, they were composed separately on eighteen topics, using arguments observed in local traditions as well as those found in the scriptures.
Having occupied the seat of justice, with his limbs properly covered and his mind composed,
he should begin the examination of legal cases after bowing to the guardians of the world.
[8] The eight kinds of persons who are not to be associated with.

‘Vyavahārāḥ’ refers to the subjects of dispute between the plaintiff and the defendant. ‘Didṛkṣuḥ’ means desiring to investigate or determine [the truth]. ‘Pārthivaḥ’ is the lord of the earth; this applies even to one who is other than a Kṣatriya. ‘Mantrajñaiḥ’ means by those skilled in determining matters appropriate to place, time, and so forth. This is an adjective qualifying the term ‘Brāhmaṇaiḥ’. For Brāhmaṇas ignorant of counsel, by hastily pronouncing even a legal rule that is inconsistent with place, time, and other factors, might bring some misfortune upon the king. ‘Mantribhiḥ’ means by the ministers of intellect. ‘Vinītaḥ’ means endowed with discipline acquired from natural teachers. ‘Pāṇim udyamya’ means having raised his hand, that is to say, having lifted up his upper garment and arranged his lower robe. ‘Paśyet’ means he should examine or decide. ‘Kāryāṇi’ refers to legal cases such as the non-payment of debts and others. ‘Deśadṛṣṭā hetavaḥ’ are the means of decision established by local custom; for example, among the Northerners and Middle-Indians, if food is given to one asking for a maiden, it is considered a betrothal even if the words “she is given to you” have not been spoken. ‘Śāstradṛṣṭāḥ’ are those prescribed by the scriptures, such as witnesses and the like.
Yājñavalkya: Free from anger and greed, the king should preside over legal proceedings together with learned Brāhmaṇas, in accordance with the Dharmaśāstras.

[9] Gautama states: "The King is the *prādvivāka*. He is called *prāṭ* because he questions the plaintiff and the defendant; he is called *vivāka* because, having been informed by them, he deliberates with the members of the court (*sabhyas*) and pronounces judgment. Kātyāyana [55, 57, 76] says:
"Dressed in modest attire, the King, having entered the court with a composed mind, shall sit facing the east and examine the legal cases of the litigants."
He, however, was joined by steadfast members of the assembly— foremost among the twice-born, rooted in wisdom,
skilled in the meaning of the treatises on dharma, and experts in the treatises on worldly affairs.
Accompanied by the chief justice, his ministers, the Brahmins and the domestic chaplain, and the members of the assembly, the king remains in heaven according to dharma as a witness.

Nārada: Having placed the treatises on Dharma before him and remaining in accordance with the opinion of the presiding judge, he should examine the legal case with a concentrated mind, following the proper sequence.
[10] Dharma is known to have the virtuous as its foundation, and the king has Dharma as his root, O lord of men;
therefore, the king should purify legal proceedings in the company of the virtuous.
"Established in the good" means situated among the virtuous. Bṛhaspati (1.49–51):
"The Brahmin is the root of the tree of Dharma; the king is its trunk and branches;
the ministers are its leaves and flowers; and protection through justice is its fruit."
Fame, wealth, the essence of fruits, enjoyments, freedom from obstruction, worship, invincibility, inclusion in the ranks of the world, and an eternal station in heaven.
Having understood these principles of justice and becoming impartial toward the litigants,
the king, having abandoned greed and other such passions, shall issue a decision in accordance with dharma.
Kātyāyana says: The king is the authority for legal disputes; he himself should investigate them according to the path seen in the scriptures, and that very practice is followed by the learned.
Therefore, one should protect the kingdom properly and with diligent effort according to justice;
from that, wealth, righteousness, and a vast sovereignty shall arise.
Yama says: "One should not deviate to another side while upholding the law of Vaivasvata;
therefore, a king, being vigilant, should constantly examine legal cases."

[11] "But he should not go to another side" means that he should not act out of partiality. Manu says: "When one perceives according to dharma, having restrained desire and anger, the subjects follow him just as rivers flow toward the ocean."
Therefore, like Yama, the Lord himself, having abandoned both the pleasant and the unpleasant,
he should conduct himself with the discipline of Yama, having conquered anger and subdued his senses.
Kātyāyana says: A king who is capable should, with effort, set aside what is contradictory;
there is no fault if he is unable to do so—this is the law remembered by the wise.
Nārada, Kātyāyana, and Yama are mentioned first [in this regard]:
"Whatever is contrary to the Śruti and Smṛti, and whatever is harmful to living beings—that the king shall not promulgate; if it has been promulgated, he shall cause it to be revoked."
Whatever has been done by another king through ignorance, even if it was in accordance with justice,
that too should be brought back into the path of justice as prescribed by the sacred tradition.

[12] Nārada: Examining the course of legal proceedings with skill, in accordance with the path that is not in conflict with the treatises on Dharma and the treatises on worldly affairs (Artha), one should guide the case.

Following the word "by the king," Gautama states: "His means of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) consists of the Veda, the Dharmaśāstras, the Arthaśāstras, the auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*), the Upavedas, and the Purāṇas. The term "legal procedure" (*vyavahāra*) means that by which one proceeds; the meaning is that the Veda and other texts are the instruments for establishing the legal order. The meaning is that they include the Upavedas and so forth. The "Upavedas" are four: Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, Gāndharvaveda, and Arthaśāstra. Again, Gautama says: "In the acquisition of justice, reasoning (*tarka*) is the means. Having deliberated by means of it, one should lead [the case] to its proper place. In the event of a conflict of opinions, having brought back [the matter] from those learned in the three Vedas, one should lead it to a final conclusion (*niṣṭhā*); for in this way, his supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) comes to be. "In the acquisition of justice" means in the determination of the meaning of justice. "Reasoning" (*tarka*) means investigation. "Having deliberated" means having determined. "One should lead to its proper place" means one should cause each person to reach that very refuge which is their basis of duty. [13] "In the event of a conflict of opinions" means when doubt does not cease even through investigation. "Having brought back" means having determined. "One should lead to a final conclusion" means one should cause it to reach a state of certainty. Yājñavalkya says:
When there is a conflict between two Smṛtis, the principle that prevails in legal practice is this:
"The Dharmaśāstra is more authoritative than the Arthaśāstra; such is the established rule."

"Conflict between two Smṛtis" means that when there is a mutual contradiction between two Dharmaśāstras, the matter must be determined by following principles such as the general rule (utsarga) and its exception (apavāda). For example: "But that which has been enjoyed without a title by three ancestors, including the father, in succession—that cannot be taken away."
But he who enjoys property that has not been transferred to him, even for many hundreds of years,
the king, as lord of the earth, should punish him with the punishment due to a thief.

Thus, regarding these two Smṛtis, Bṛhaspati [1.113] states: "The treatises of Manu and others must be upheld, but never the treatises on worldly affairs (Arthaśāstra). When there is a conflict between the two, the word proclaimed in the Dharmaśāstra must be followed."
Nārada says: Where there may be a conflict between the Dharmaśāstra and the Arthaśāstra,
one should set aside what is stated in the Arthaśāstra and act according to what is stated in the Dharmaśāstra.
But when there is a conflict with the Dharmaśāstras, a rule supported by reason is declared authoritative;
for judicial procedure is powerful, and by it the Dharma is not lost.
Even one who is not a thief incurs the state of being a thief, while a thief attains the state of being a non-thief;
through legal proceedings, Māṇḍavya—who was not a thief—was treated as a thief.
"For the Dharma, O Blessed One, is subtle, beyond the senses, and difficult to investigate;
therefore, one should lead the course of worldly affairs by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

"Consistent with reason" (*yuktiyukta*) means established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Here, "means of knowledge" refers to worldly practice (*lokapravṛtti*), which is common to both valid and invalid cognition. Without reason, the Dharma is lost through mere worldly transaction alone; therefore, the meaning is that one must follow the means of knowledge. "By means of the path of direct perception" means by way of the most firm means of knowledge, such as direct perception and the rest.
[15] Manu: Just as a hunter traces the track of a deer by drops of blood,
so should a king trace the path of dharma through inference.
In the course of legal proceedings, one should consider truth and righteousness (as well as the matter at hand), oneself, the witnesses,
the place, the time, and the specific circumstances.

"One should perceive the truth. Even if neither the plaintiff nor the defendant has stated the matter with full clarity due to boldness, nevertheless, if the king should determine from other means of proof that "this is the nature of the case," then he must not neglect that which rests upon it—this is the meaning. "The matter" (*artha*) refers to wealth such as cattle, gold, and so forth. One should perceive "oneself" as the one who partakes in the fruit of the legal proceeding. "Form" (*rūpa*) refers to the essential nature of the subject matter of the lawsuit; one should perceive its gravity or lightness. Bṛhaspati [1.114, 116]:
A final decision must not be made by relying solely on the scriptures;
for if one deliberates without logical reasoning, O Lord of Creatures, there will be a loss of Dharma.
A thief may become a non-thief, and a virtuous man an evildoer, through legal proceedings;
without investigation based on reasoning, even Māṇḍavya was reduced to the state of a thief.
In the Mahābhārata:
"The wise make even what is untrue appear as true,
just as those skilled in the art of painting make the level ground appear uneven."
Therefore, the king should always personally strive to oversee judicial proceedings. Nārada says:
However, a king especially, while protecting his own duty, [should do so].
Because of the diversity of human minds, one must examine whether something is good or bad.
Unreal things appear like the real, and real things appear like the unreal;
they are seen in various forms, therefore investigation is appropriate.
The sky appears as if level like the ground, and a firefly appears like a fire;
yet there is no level ground in the sky, nor is there fire in the firefly.
Therefore, even an object perceived through direct perception ought to be examined;
one who explains matters after having examined them does not fall away from dharma.
But a king should not tolerate a manifest deception that subverts justice;
he should pursue only what is factual, for prosperity has its root in truth.
Even that which is untrue, if spoken at the appropriate time, is examined with favor;
but that which is not spoken due to negligence, even if it be true, is lost.
"Like a palm tree," meaning like the lower part of a palm tree. [17] Yājñavalkya says:
Having set aside deception, the king should adjudicate legal cases according to the facts (*bhūta*). Even if the facts exist, they are lost in a lawsuit if they are not presented.
Bṛhaspati [9.32]: Thus, by carrying out the adjudication and protection ordained in the treatises, a king spreads his fame throughout the world and becomes a counselor to Mahendra.
In the Mahābhārata: That king who does not grant an audience to supplicants who have approached him, being attached only to his own pleasures, shall suffer like Nṛga.

In the *Rāmāyaṇa* (Uttarakāṇḍa, 53.6): "Indeed, that king who, while seated in the assembly hall, does not attend to the affairs of the citizens, will clearly be cooked in a terrible hell; of this there is no doubt."
Manu [8.174]: But that evil-minded king who, out of delusion, conducts affairs unjustly,
will soon bring himself under the control of his subjects.

Kātyāyana [44–45]: When the word of the king exists, self-made law leads away from heaven, causes the destruction of the world, brings fear from the enemy's army, and takes away the life and seed of kings.
Therefore, the king should settle legal matters in accordance with the scriptures;
however, in the absence of scriptural statements for all cases, he should decide them according to local custom.
Now, regarding local customs and so forth.

On this point, Gautama states: "The laws of regions (*deśadharma*), castes (*jātidharma*), and families (*kuladharma*), when not in conflict with the sacred traditions (*āmnāya*), are authoritative. Farmers, merchants, herdsmen, moneylenders, and artisans [are authoritative] within their respective groups. Having ascertained the matters from them according to their specific jurisdictions, the legal settlement is established. "The law of regions" refers to what is well-known in a particular place, such as the division of taxes and so forth; that which is established in a certain region is authoritative only there. "The law of castes" is, for example, the absence of teeth-blackening among the Ābhīras. "The law of families" is, for example, the practice of churning curd and so forth. "By the sacred traditions" means by the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and other authorities. "Having ascertained" means having determined [the facts].
Manu:
One who knows the law, having carefully examined the laws of castes and regions, the laws of guilds,
and the laws of families, shall establish the specific duty (svadharma).
Even when they are far away, men who perform their own duties and remain steadfast in their respective tasks become dear to the world.
[20] One should establish that which has been practiced by the virtuous and by righteous twice-born men, provided it is not in conflict with the customs of the particular region, family, or caste.

Guilds (*śreṇi*) are those engaged in a single occupation, such as merchants, farmers, laborers, and so forth. "Not contrary" means not contrary to the *śāstra*; this is the ellipsis. Kātyāyana [84.46]:
"But whatever the established tradition (*gotrasthiti*) of those [guilds] may be, which has come down through succession according to the law (*dharma*),"
They call that the family dharma; one should protect it in that very same way.
Whatever custom has been practiced for all time in a particular region,
provided it does not conflict with the Śruti and Smṛti, that is called a regional custom (deśadharma).
One should not disturb the established and righteous duty of those born in the inverse order, nor of those who dwell in difficult terrains, among the various social classes.
Bṛhaspati [1.126–127]: Likewise, those customs which were established of old for those born in the inverse order, for those dwelling in forts, and for specific regions, castes, and families;
In that very same way, those subjects must be protected; otherwise, they become agitated.
When the people are alienated, the army and the treasury perish.
[21] The daughters of maternal uncles are married by the twice-born of the South;
in the Middle Country, laborers and artisans eat beef.
In the east, men will be eaters of fish, and women will be devoted to infidelity;
in the north, women will drink liquor, and menstruating women will be touched by men.
Those born of the same lineage take the wife of a brother who is without a husband;
because of this practice, they are not worthy of being subjected to penance.
Because they constantly fail to perform what is enjoined and indulge in what is forbidden,
the king, having provided them with food and clothing, shall take their remaining property.

"‘These are not worthy of penance or punishment. This means that penance need not be performed by them, because their sins do not require atonement; nor are they to be punished, for fear of causing unrest among the subjects. Regarding the phrase ‘constantly from the non-performance of what is prescribed’ and so forth: this refers to the failure to perform the duties pertaining to one’s caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*) due to repeated negligence, even when no calamity is present. Likewise, it refers to the constant performance of forbidden acts, such as eating what is unfit to be eaten. The meaning is that the king should confiscate all wealth beyond what is necessary to provide food and clothing. And this should be understood to apply to the practice of prohibitions other than those established by local custom. It does not apply to the performance of local customs, because it has been stated therein: ‘By this act, these are not worthy of penance or punishment. Accordingly, apart from local customs, there is the general statement of Gautama (12.24): ‘In the case of failing to perform what is prescribed and practicing what is forbidden, there shall always be the confiscation of everything except a single garment and a morsel of food. [22]
Kātyāyana says:
Where an action not previously undertaken has been performed in accordance with what is approved by Śruti and Smṛti, it should not be done otherwise; one should avoid that which is devoid of justice.

"Apravṛttam" means that which has not been practiced before, such as the avoidance of touching a woman in her menses among the people of the North. "Śrutismṛtyanumoditam" means sanctioned by the Śruti and Smṛti. The reason for the statement "that should not be done otherwise" is as follows: "One should avoid what is contrary to justice," because this is characterized by injustice; such is the meaning. Bṛhaspati [1.133, 132]: Regarding shares, tolls, customary fines, monthly or six-monthly taxes, and duties, a boundary established by a document should always be maintained, even when presided over by a judge.
She must be protected with effort according to the scriptures; for she is the means of proof when there is doubt.
Having examined her, one should reach a decision in accordance with the established rules previously settled.

‘Naigamāḥ’ refers to merchants. ‘Saṃdigdhau’ means in a state of doubt. Kātyāyana [48]: “A legal settlement that has been determined with the consent of the region must always be maintained in writing, sealed with the royal seal. [23]

[It should be protected with effort as prescribed by the treatises; having examined it, one should reach a decision. But that which has been established in writing by those standing in the guild (naigama) must be carried out by them.
Therefore, that [tradition] should proceed accordingly and not otherwise;
for a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is that which is observed in a particular place and is thus determined to be "so."
‘By those residing among the *naigamas*’ means by those dwelling among the merchants, such as artisans and others.
Now, the judge (*prāḍvivāka*).

In this regard, Kātyāyana [63–64] states: When, due to the burden of business, the king is unable to personally oversee the adjudication of legal cases, he should then appoint a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the sacred scriptures.
One who is self-controlled, of noble birth, impartial, free from causing agitation,
steadfast, fearful of the next world, most righteous, diligent, and devoid of anger.
Manu:
When the king himself does not personally attend to the examination of legal cases,
then he should appoint a learned Brāhmaṇa to examine those cases.
When weary from overseeing the affairs of men, the king should appoint to that seat a chief minister who knows the dharma, is wise, self-controlled, and of noble birth.
Surrounded by exactly three members of the assembly, he should examine his legal cases,
having entered the foremost assembly hall, whether seated or standing.
— Bṛhaspati [1.65, 69].
The king, or else a learned Brahmin acting as the presiding judge, shall examine the legal cases,
placing the constituent elements of justice at the forefront and remaining steadfast in the opinion of the council and the sacred scriptures.
In a legal dispute, he asks the question as well as the counter-question;
then that judge speaks first with words of kindness.
Vyāsa says:
Having carefully questioned both the parties who have consented to the dispute, he deliberates together with the members of the court;
for this reason, he is known as the Prāḍvivāka (the judge).
Nārada and Hārīta state:
Just as a physician should extract a splinter from the body by means of an instrument,
so should the judge extract the splinter [of injustice] from the legal proceeding.
Gautama [13.31]: "Among all things, truthful speech is weightier than anything else for a judge.
[26] 3 — Now, the court.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"The assembly is declared to be of four kinds: established, unestablished, sealed, and likewise that which has witnesses; and the members of the assembly are of the same kinds."
Established in cities and villages, she is called "Moving" (Calā) and "Unestablished" (Apratiṣṭhitā);
she is sealed, joined with the overseer, conjoined with the king, and the ruler.

The king, the appointed official, and the members of the court; the legal code, the calculator, and the scribe; gold, fire, water, and one's own men—these indeed are the ten constituent elements of proof.
Of these limbs of the state, the king is made the head and the presiding judge the mouth;
the members of the court are the arms, the legal codes are the hands, and the astrologer and the scribe are the shanks.
Gold, fire, water, the eyes, the heart, and the feet, as well as one's own person—
thus for these ten, the specific function of each has been declared separately.

The king is the presiding speaker and the ruler; the court members are the examiners of the case. Smṛti (the sacred law) declares the final decision, as well as the awarding of victory and the imposition of punishment.
Gold and fire are for the purpose of an oath; water is for those who are thirsty or agitated.
The accountant shall calculate the matter, and the scribe shall record the legal judgment.
The king’s own officers shall summon the defendant, the members of the court, and the witnesses;
they shall always keep the plaintiff and the defendant under guard as sureties.
That assembly in which a king, acting as the lord of men, presides and examines legal cases by means of these ten constituent factors, is equal to a sacrificial rite.
A council where seven, five, or even three eminent Brahmins— learned in the worlds, the Vedas, and the Dharma— are seated with diligence, is equal to a sacrificial assembly.
The king should appoint as members of the assembly those who are engaged in performing virtuous deeds, devoted to truth and righteousness, free from anger and greed, and learned in the scriptures.
Manu [8.11]: "In whatever place three Brahmins learned in the Vedas sit together, and a learned minister of the king, the wise know that assembly to be a *sabhā*."
Nārada [3.4–5]:
But the king should appoint righteous assessors who have been well-tested,
who are capable of bearing the burden of legal proceedings like excellent oxen.
[28] The members of the king’s assembly should be men of noble birth, speakers of truth, and skilled in the meaning of the treatises on Dharma; they should be impartial toward both enemy and friend.

Viṣṇu [3.74]: "The members of the court (*sabhāsadaḥ*) should be appointed by the king as those endowed with noble birth, virtuous conduct, and learning; who are impartial toward both enemy and friend; and who cannot be led astray from their duty by those seeking their own ends through means such as desire, anger, fear, or greed. "Incorruptible" (*anāhāryaḥ*) means they cannot be brought under control by litigants. Kātyāyana [71, 66–67]:
"Brahmins should be appointed by kings as members of the court (*sabhyāḥ*), provided they are free from greed, wealthy, knowers of the Dharma, speakers of truth, and proficient in all the Śāstras."
One who studies only a single treatise cannot reach a definitive conclusion regarding legal matters;
therefore, kings should ensure that those most proficient in many scriptures are present in judicial disputes.
Where there may be no learned Brāhmaṇa, one should appoint a Kṣatriya there, or a Vaiśya who knows the Dharmaśāstras; one should avoid a Śūdra with great effort.
Therefore, whatever task has been performed by others in an unjust manner should be recognized as such, even if they were appointed [to the office], whether by chance or according to the scriptures.

[29] "Bahvāgama" means one who knows many treatises (bahuśāstrajña). Regarding the phrase "by others than these" (*ato 'nyaiḥ*): even if appointed by others who lack the aforementioned characteristics, if the meaning of the scripture is determined by chance, nevertheless, that must be understood as being indeed unjust. Manu [8.20–21]:
One who merely lives by his birth may, if he so desires, be called a "pseudo-Brāhmaṇa";
however, a Śūdra can never be a teacher of dharma to a king.
The kingdom of that king for whom a Śūdra performs the discernment of dharma perishes, like a cow sinking in the mud while he looks on.
Vyāsa says: He who, setting aside the twice-born, should look after affairs together with the low-born,
his kingdom becomes agitated, and his army and treasury perish.
Bṛhaspati [1.64, 81–82]: Those who are ignorant of local customs, atheists, those devoid of scriptural knowledge,
the insane, the angry, the greedy, and the afflicted— these should not be questioned in a legal determination.
The king should appoint as astrologer and scribe two men who know the true nature of words and their denotations, who are skilled in calculation, pure, and proficient in various scripts.
In matters of non-injury and protection, as well as for the testimony of plaintiffs and defendants,
one who speaks the truth and is dependent upon the members of the court must be appointed as his own representative.
Kātyāyana [58]: Those royal officers who are to be directed by the members of the court and are properly appointed—
the accountant and the scribe as well— he should appoint them all to their respective positions.
It should be presided over by a few merchants who possess noble lineage, good character, youth, proper conduct, and wealth, who are free from envy, and who are like members of one's own family.
Bṛhaspati says:
For those who wander in the forest, the performance [of the rite] should take place in the forest;
likewise for soldiers in an army and for merchants on a caravan.
Those families, guilds, assemblies, and so forth, who have been properly recognized by the king, shall carry out the legal affairs of men, excluding cases involving violence or injustice.
The heads of families, guilds, and assemblies are declared to be the makers of decisions;
the authority of a decision made before them increases progressively from one to the next.
That which has not been decided by the guilds (*śreṇi*) should be dealt with by the families (*kula*);
that which is unknown to the guilds should be dealt with by the corporations (*gaṇa*); and that which is unknown to the corporations should be dealt with by the appointed officials (*niyuktaka*).
The members of the assembly are superior to the family and other such groups; the presiding officer is declared to be superior to them;
and the king is superior to all of them—this is the righteous law determined with effort.
[31] By investigating disputes among the superior, inferior, and middling,
the cognitions of the Lord proceed higher and higher above all other cognitions.

‘Karaṇa’ means the assembly. ‘Excluding matters involving violence’ means excluding legal proceedings concerning violent acts. ‘Niyuktakāḥ’ here refers to the members of the court (sabhyas). On this point, Kātyāyana says:
“Whatever matter has been decided by the family councils should be reviewed in ascending order;
it must be finalized until it is known to have been settled by the king.”
And those who, though unappointed, should carry out the determination of legal cases— those acting contrary to the king’s conduct— the king shall prescribe punishment for them.
Ascetics, guilds, corporations, merchant associations,
and others shall always settle their disputes according to their own respective laws.

In the dealings of merchants and artisans, and among those who live by agriculture or animal husbandry, a definitive decision is indeed impossible; therefore, one should have such matters decided by those who are experts in them.
Bṛhaspati [1.84]: Farmers, artisans, craftsmen, moneylenders, guilds, dancers, those bearing religious emblems,
and thieves shall carry out judicial decisions according to their own specific laws.
‘Kīnāśas’ are plowmen; ‘śilpins’ are painters and the like. Bṛhaspati and Kātyāyana [state]:

“One should have the affairs of ascetics conducted by those learned in the three Vedas alone, and likewise those of those who know the application of magic (māyā-yoga), but not by oneself, for fear of provoking their anger.”
When twice-born men dispute among themselves regarding their duties in the various stages of life (āśramas),
a king who desires his own welfare and seeks to uphold dharma must not pronounce a judgment for one side.
Having honored these men as is fitting along with the Brahmins, the king,
having first pacified them with conciliatory words, should establish them in their own duty.

"In the stages of life" (*āśrameṣu*) refers to those such as the student (*brahmacārin*) and so forth. "He should not speak out" (*na vibrūyāt*) means he should not speak specifically, that is, he should not make a definitive determination regarding victory or defeat. "By conciliation" (*sāntvena*) means by pleasant speech. "Having pacified" (*praśamayya*) means having calmed anger and the like.
Kātyāyana [84, first section]:
One should not proceed with instruction toward one who is already fully possessed of correct understanding.
Of those of noble birth and character, pure conduct, and ascetic practitioners.
Appointed to judicial proceedings, the world proceeds according to worldly custom; yet Bhṛgu says that both the king and the assemblies should lead them solely by means of dharma.
Now, the instruction for court members;
regarding this, Bṛhaspati states [1.96–97]:
He who, by means of the ointment-stick of the scriptures, renders free from disease those afflicted by the darkness of ignorance and covered by the film of doubt.
In this world he gains fame and royal honor, and in the hereafter, he attains the heavenly realm;
therefore, a definitive resolution must be made for those who are bewildered by doubt.
Nārada [3.1–2]:
One who has not been appointed must not speak at all in a legal proceeding;
but one who has been appointed must speak words that are impartial.
Whether appointed or unappointed, one who knows the Dharma is fit to speak;
he who lives by the scriptures speaks the divine word.
"Divine" means pertaining to the scriptures, that is to say, true. [34] Bṛhaspati [1.108]:
Whether appointed or unappointed, one who knows the dharma is fit to speak;
whatever he declares in the assembly must be carried out—of this there is no doubt.
Nārada and Hārīta [Nāradasmṛti 3.14] state: "He who,
having entered the court, speaks behind one's back due to a deficiency in wealth, eats like a blind man who is indifferent to fish even when they have bones."
‘Due to a deficiency in the matter’ means due to a failure to understand the true nature of the case. Bṛhaspati [1.98, 54]:
“He who, having abandoned greed, hatred, and the like, renders a decision on a legal matter according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, shall obtain the fruit of a sacrifice.”
In brief, the gods know truth, while humans know falsehood;
he whose mind is established in truth attains divinity even in this very world.
Nārada [3.7]:
In pure legal proceedings, the members of the court attain purity;
their purity indeed arises from dharma, therefore one should speak only that which is dharma.
Kātyāyana says: When the king appoints those ignorant of the law to adjudicate the disputes of litigants,
the court member, having informed the monarch, should then properly cause him to desist.
A member of the assembly must necessarily speak words consistent with dharma and artha;
if the king does not listen, then that king would be untruthful.
[35] But having recognized that the king’s mind has strayed from the path of justice, one should speak what is pleasing to him; a member of the assembly does not thereby become guilty of sin.
But if the members of the court do not disregard an action that has proceeded contrary to the law,
they all go headlong to hell for having so disregarded it.
Those members of the assembly who follow one who intends to act unjustly share in that guilt;
therefore, they must admonish that king.

"Those ignorant of dharma" means those who follow what is contrary to dharma. Manu [8.19, 13]: "The king becomes tainted by sin, but the members of the court are released; the guilt goes to the perpetrator where one deserving of censure is censured."
In an assembly, one must not remain silent, nor should one speak improperly;
for by either remaining mute or speaking falsely, a man becomes a sinner.
Nārada [3.3]: A member of the court who speaks what is appropriate shall incur neither hatred nor guilt;
but a member of the court who speaks otherwise shall incur both of those.
Kātyāyana says: When the true nature of a matter is indeed hidden, if they should reach a decision otherwise after having understood it correctly, that is not in accordance with what is prescribed.
Where the determination of a legal case is carried out by such wicked members of the court through falsehoods according to this procedure, there truth has been destroyed by those evil-minded men.
Where the members of the court have reached a decision by overstepping the science of logic (nyāya), there dharma, being struck down by adharma, destroys [the wrongdoer]; of this there is no doubt.

Bṛhaspati says: In the case of an unjust decision, there shall arise a lack of confidence among the witnesses, the members of the court, the presiding judge, and the king; likewise, they shall fall into hell.

"Apratyayaḥ" means lack of trust. Manu, Nārada, Hārīta, and Baudhāyana state this in the first [chapter]: "One quarter of the injustice falls upon the perpetrator, one quarter falls upon the witness, one quarter falls upon all the members of the court, and one quarter falls upon the king."
When dharma, pierced by adharma, enters an assembly,
the members of that assembly do not extract the dart if they themselves remain pierced by it.
[37] For where dharma is slain by adharma, and truth by falsehood, while the members look on, there the members of the assembly are themselves slain.
Manu [8.13, 17, 15]: "For the blessed Dharma is a bull; he who treats it with contempt, the gods know him as a *vṛṣala* (outcaste). Therefore, one should not violate Dharma."
Dharma alone is the true friend who follows one even unto death;
everything else, however, perishes along with the body.
Dharma alone, when violated, destroys; Dharma, when protected, protects.
Therefore, Dharma must not be violated, lest violated Dharma slay us.
Nārada [3.11, 17]: But those members of the court who, having entered the assembly, sit silently lost in thought and do not speak as required, they are all speakers of falsehood.
[38] Where all the members of the assembly consider, "This is well done," that dispute shall be free from thorns; otherwise, it would be fraught with thorns.
Furthermore, Nārada [3.38] says:
That is not an assembly where there are no elders; those are not elders who do not speak of dharma.
That is not dharma where there is no truth; that is not truth which resorts to deceit.
Kātyāyana [80, 79, 81]:
Having properly reached a decision on the matter at hand, the member of the court (*sabhyas*) should then speak;
otherwise, he must not do so, for the speaker shall be subject to a double fine.

Whether out of affection, ignorance, delusion, or even greed, if a member of the court speaks falsely, that member is to be punished; for such a person is considered a true member of the court [only when he speaks the truth].
Whatever has been lost due to a fault of the court must then be restored by the judge;
thus, once the matter of the litigants has been settled, one should not overturn it.
[39] Bṛhaspati [1.108]: Those members of the court who speak unjustly, as well as those who live on bribes, and those who betray the trust placed in them— all of these indeed shall be banished.
Viṣṇu [5.179–80]: "The confiscation of all property shall be carried out against false witnesses; likewise for judges who live on bribes. Kātyāyana [70]:
"But if, while the matter is not yet concluded, one should converse in secret with the plaintiff..."
Then the judge and the members of the court shall also be punished; of this there is no doubt.
Bṛhaspati [1.76]: But the judge who, disregarding the opinions of the members of the court, should decide cases based on his own reasoning alone, shall incur punishment.

Thus ends the section on legal procedure (*vyavahāra-prakaraṇa*) within the section on legal affairs (*vyavahāra-kāṇḍa*) of the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, the son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara and the great minister for treaties (*mahāsandhivigrahika*).
Now, the definition of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*);
regarding this, Kātyāyana [states in verses 25–26]:
In this extensive exposition of Nyāya known as Dharma, which is to be accomplished through effort and is subject to interruption,
that discourse which has the matter to be proven as its basis is called *vyavahāra* (legal procedure).
In the sense of "diversity" (*vi*), when there is doubt, the act of removing it is called *hāra*;
because it removes diverse doubts, it is traditionally known as *vyavahāra*.

"In matters to be accomplished through effort," such as fields and the like; "when interrupted," meaning deprived of enjoyment. "The expansion of legal procedure called dharma" (*dharmākhyo yo nyāyavistaraḥ*): that in which legal procedure (*nyāya*) is expanded is the "expansion of legal procedure" (*nyāyavistara*), namely the court of justice (*dharmādhikaraṇa*). The meaning is that the dispute occurring therein is "legal procedure" (*vyavahāra*). Regarding the continuation of legal procedure, Nārada says: (1.4; 8.14, 26–29, 15–20) "It should be known to be of two kinds: with a counter-claim (*sottara*) and without a counter-claim (*anuttara*). That which is 'with a counter-claim' is superior, wherein there is a wager (*paṇa*) preceded by a written deposition (*vilekhā*)."
It is proclaimed as having four feet, four bases, and four means;
it is fourfold in its benefits, fourfold in its pervasion, and fourfold in its effects.
[41] It has three origins, two types of prosecution, two gates, and likewise two destinations;
it consists of eight limbs, eighteen points, and likewise has a hundred branches.
Dharma, judicial procedure, custom, and royal edict—
this four-legged judicial process is such that each subsequent element establishes the preceding one.
In that regard, legal procedure based on truth rests upon witnesses;
customary law rests upon witnesses and written records; and royal decree rests upon witnesses.
Because it is accomplished through the means of conciliation and the rest, it is called the "fourfold means";
because it protects all four castes, it is the "fourfold benefit."
Because it pervades the doer, the witnesses, the members of the court, and the king itself— one quarter each— it is therefore remembered as "four-pervading" (caturvyāpin).
Because he brings about these four— dharma, wealth, fame, and likewise the affection of the world—
he is proclaimed as the "performer of the four."
Since it constantly proceeds from desire, anger, and greed, it is proclaimed to have three wombs; therefore, this triad is divided into two.
A lawsuit should be understood as being of two kinds: based on suspicion and based on facts.
Suspicion arises from association with the wicked, while the facts are established by the discovery of stolen goods.
[42] Because it is connected with two sides, it is declared to have two doors:
the prior claim is one side, and the counter-claim is its opposite.
Because it follows both the truth and the deceptive, it is declared to have two courses:
the "truth" (bhūta) is that which is joined with the real meaning, while the "deception" (chala) is that which is struck down by negligence.
The king, the legal officers, the members of the court, the legal treatise, the astrologer, the scribe, gold, fire, and water— this is declared to be the eightfold constituent of the court.
Recovery of debts, deposits, partnerships,
the resumption of what has been given, and the breach of agreements after having entered into them;
Non-payment of wages, as well as sale without ownership, non-delivery after selling,
and rescission after buying;
Non-performance of agreements, disputes, and matters concerning sons born of the field; the union of men and women, partition of inheritance, and then violence.
Abuse of speech, likewise assault,
gambling, and miscellaneous matters— this is remembered as the eighteenfold system of law.
Another division of these very [categories] is recorded as one hundred and eight;
the classification of humans according to their modes of acquisition is said to have a hundred branches.

‘Vilekhā’ means a written document. ‘Śaṅkā’ (suspicion) arises from association with the good or the bad; the meaning is that through such association, there arises the suspicion of being a thief or the like. By the word ‘hoṣha’, a fallible mark is expressed.
[43] Manu [8.4–8]: Of these, the first is the non-payment of debt, followed by deposits, sale without ownership, and so forth.
Joint undertaking and the non-repayment of what has been given.
Non-payment of wages, breach of contract,
rescission of purchase and sale, and disputes between an owner and a herdsman;
The law concerning boundaries, verbal assault,
physical assault, theft, violence, and the abduction of women.
The duties of husband and wife, partition [of inheritance], gambling, and betting—
these eighteen are the topics in this world for the administration of legal procedure.
In these matters, for men who are mostly engaged in disputes,
he should carry out the decision of the case by relying upon the Dharmaśāstra.

Thus ends the section on the definition of legal procedure (*vyavahāra-lakṣaṇa-prakaraṇa*) within the section on legal procedure (*vyavahāra-kāṇḍa*) of the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara’s son.
6 – Now, the procedure for investigation. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states [1.45–47, 115, 65]:
"In the center of the fortress, he should construct a separate residence provided with water and trees."
To the east of that [hall], he should construct an auspicious assembly hall facing the east.
It should be provided with garlands, incense, and seats, endowed with seed-syllables and jewels,
joined with images, paintings, and deities, as well as fire and water.
Having occupied that [throne] in the forenoon, he should look upon it together with his aged ministers and dependents,
and likewise listen to the ancient treatises on dharma and artha.
The king, or else a Brahmin acting as the presiding judge, shall examine the cases,
having placed the constituent elements of justice at the forefront and remaining steadfast in the opinion of the legal treatises and the court members.
Kātyāyana [60, 61, 31]: In the forenoon, in the assembly halls, the king— the subduer of enemies— should reach a decision on legal cases by means of the path of the authority of the śāstras.
Having eaten during the eighth part of the day, that period which constitutes the three times [of the day] is recorded in the scriptures as the supreme time for legal proceedings.
The plaint, the reply, the assessment, and the stage of legal procedure— by these it is declared to have four feet.

In this context, the first eighth part is the half-watch (ardha-prahara). Nārada [2.36] states: "The reception [of petitioners] should be performed first, followed by the subject matter of the lawsuit, then medical treatment, and finally the decision; thus, the judicial process is fourfold."

‘Āgama’ is the recording of what has been heard from both the plaintiff and the defendant. ‘Vyavahārapada’ is the formal determination that “this is the matter” among the categories such as non-payment of debt (ṛṇādāna) and so forth. ‘Cikitsā’ is judicial deliberation. Bṛhaspati [1.16, 2–3]:
The first quarter is known as the plaint (pūrvapakṣa), and likewise the second is the reply (uttara);
the third is the quarter of legal action (kriyāpāda), and the fourth is known as the decision (nirṇaya).

In the case of a false statement, however, it consists of four parts; likewise in the case of a counter-attack (pratyavaskandana) and in the plea of prior judgment (prāṅnyāya). It should be known as consisting of two parts in cases of admission (saṃpratipatti).

Yājñavalkya [2.5]: When one who has been oppressed by others through a path deviating from the dictates of the Smṛtis and established custom brings it to the notice of the king, that indeed constitutes a matter for legal dispute.
[46] Uśanas: Whoever shall report a grievance to the king with reference to a matter to be adjudicated—
that is proclaimed as the eighteenfold division of legal disputes.

Bṛhaspati [1.169]: When litigants dispute repeatedly regarding their legal titles (*āgama*), the king should examine the claims he himself has formulated, and not those merely reported by his officials.
Kātyāyana [27]: A king, however distinguished, should not personally undertake legal cases for men who are not disputing, nor should he do so out of greed for wealth.
Manu [8.43]: The king himself shall not initiate a legal case, nor shall his official;
nor shall he ever swallow up a matter brought forward by another.
‘He should not swallow’ means he should not neglect it. Bṛhaspati [2.26–27; 1.170]:
“The legal dispute, consisting of eighteen titles, has been declared to be subject to investigation.
There are other titles here as well; the king himself should examine them.”
[47] The sixth-part tax, customs duties, breach of agreement, treasure-trove, homicide, adultery, theft, and violation of an injunction or prohibition.
When a plaintiff comes of his own accord, being oppressed, modest, and seeking redress, the judge—
or a representative— should question him slowly and gently.
"Other [fees]" refers to hand-levies (*kara*) and so forth. "He should enter" means he should look [at them]. "Modest" means not arrogant. Kātyāyana (86–87):
At the proper time, he should question the one seeking justice who stands before him with a bowed head:
"What is your business? What is your grievance? Do not fear; speak, O man!"
By whom, toward whom, when, and for what reason should one ask? Thus asks the assembly member. Uśanas says:
One who is armed, without an upper garment, with the lower garment untucked, and seated together [with others].
Or, wearing a garland, if he utters [a curse] with his left hand, he shall receive a staff as punishment.

Gautama [13.27]: "One should approach the judge"; that is to say, one should follow the judge. Regarding the title of law concerning theft, Manu [8.312–313] states: "The lord must always forgive litigants who revile him;
likewise, he should forgive children, the elderly, and the sick, if he desires his own welfare."
[48] He who, when insulted by those in distress, endures it, is exalted in heaven because of that;
but he who, out of pride in his power, does not endure it, goes to hell because of that.
[The two] hurling [insults], [the two] roaring. Nārada and Kātyāyana [Nā 2.18; Kā 129]:

"If, provoked by one [party] through passion or other [emotions], he should speak during the legal proceeding, he shall write 'Om' for all [that] upon the writing board or other [surface] for the plaintiff."
Bṛhaspati [1.134]:
"The words of the plaintiff must be acted upon, and likewise the words of the defendant;
one should proceed after careful examination, otherwise there will be hell."
"Padam" refers to matters such as the non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*). "Ādadyāt" means one should accept [the case] as a matter for adjudication.
Furthermore, Bṛhaspati [states]:
"But he who is abandoned by the king, and he who causes opposition among the citizens..."
Or likewise for the entire kingdom and its constituent elements.
Any legal proceedings that are contrary to justice and opposed by the city, the village, or the public assembly—
all such cases are declared inadmissible.
A king should avoid a case that is unestablished, defective, meaningless, purposeless, impossible to resolve, or contradictory.
That which has not been made by anyone is declared to be "unestablished" (aprasiddha).
It is proclaimed as faulty when it has a different meaning, lacks its own intended meaning, or is deficient in its own sense.
That which involves a minor offense and a very small purpose is known as "useless" (nirarthaka);
however, that which is devoid of any obstruction to the task at hand should be understood as "purposeless" (niṣprayojana).
A legal proceeding devoid of [the parties] beginning with the indolent is useless;
likewise, one involving verbal abuse and the like should be known as purposeless.
"He must give me a bow made of hare's horn"—
the wise call such a position impossible and unachievable.
When a conflict arises within the city or the kingdom regarding the side that has been presented before the judge or the king, that case is called "contradictory" (*viruddha*).

"Unestablished" (*aprasiddha*) means, for example, as stated in the *Purāṇa*, that on every full moon or new moon day, the increase of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is declared to be twofold; such a claim is "unestablished. Legal proceedings concerning usury and so forth consist of fourteen subject matters; one devoid of these is "meaningless" (*anirarthaka*). One devoid of [matters involving] verbal abuse and other forms of violence is "purposeless" (*aniṣprayojana*). Kātyāyana [136–137] states:
"A plaint that is contrary to the city or the kingdom, that which is devoid of the king's authority, and that which is confused by multiple points does not succeed."
Even a legal matter that has been decided in court proceedings on the basis of many assertions,
the king may, if he desires, take it up again out of a wish to discover the truth.

[50] "A plaint involving a confusion of multiple points (*anekapadasaṃkīrṇa*), being employed with various grounds for dispute, cannot be resolved simultaneously; likewise, even if there are multiple claims, they cannot be resolved all at once. However, the mere mention of various claims does not constitute a loss of the case. Rather, the king should have the defendant set down those points as well so that they may be examined in due order. But where various grounds for dispute are to be proven by a single cause, there the decision shall be made simultaneously.
Thus say Bṛhaspati, Kātyāyana, and again Yama: "He who either refuses to administer justice or administers injustice..."
But he who does not cause this to be written down, his position is not established.
One should avoid from afar that position in which both contradictory and non-contradictory meanings are seen to be established within a single [subject].
Bṛhaspati and Nārada [Bṛ 1.135]:
A lawsuit brought by one person against many, or against women, or against servants,
is declared by those who know the Dharma to be inadmissible.

"One against many"—a dispute concerning various matters between one person and many people together should not be investigated simultaneously; however, a single matter must indeed be investigated. "By women" means by those who are under the control of a husband or others. "By servants" means by those dependent on their master and permitted by him. Bṛhaspati [1.124, 125]:
"A teacher and a pupil, father and son, husband and wife, and master and servant—among these, when they are assembled together, no legal proceeding (vyavahāra) takes place."
[51] Having thus examined the plaintiff's case, the members of the court should cause it to be recorded in writing;
however, they shall not adjudicate a dispute that is unestablished or one that is odious to the city.

"Legal procedure does not exist" means that a dispute between teacher and pupil and others, preceded by the hearing of the plaint and the reply, should not be adjudicated by the king. Rather, having understood the matter himself by whatever means possible and having settled it correctly, he should quash the dispute; this is the meaning. Nārada [12.89]:
"But when a conflict arises from jealousy or malice, caused by passion, a husband and wife should settle their dispute among their own kinsmen, not before the king."

The meaning is that they should announce their own dispute among their kinsmen. Kātyāyana [87, 88] states: "When questioned in this manner, whatever he may say, the judges, together with the Brāhmaṇas, should deliberate upon the matter; if it is found to be just, then after this, for the purpose of summoning him..."
He should deposit a token there, or he should direct a person [to do so].
"Just" means worthy of justice. Bṛhaspati [1.144]:
"One who does not abide by the matter to be stated, and one who departs from his word..."
The plaintiff shall keep the defendant under restraint until the appearance for summons.
Confinement may be of four kinds: restricted to a place, restricted by time, restricted from travel, and restricted from work; one who is under such confinement must not violate it.

Regarding the term *vaktavye*, it means "when there is doubt. Regarding *na tiṣṭhantam*, it means one who does not return for the sake of a decision. Not only does he not return, but from that very fact, if he "departs" (*utkrāmantam*), then [the king] "should restrain him" (*āsedhayet*), meaning he should block him. Likewise, "until the appearance of the summons" (*yāvad āhvānadarśanam*) means as long as he is being summoned by the king. *Sthānāsedha* (restraint of place): "You must not move from this spot without giving [the required payment]; if you do move, then such-and-such a fine shall be yours. Similarly, *kālakṛta* (restraint of time): "If you consume [the property] without giving [the payment], then such-and-such a fine shall be yours," and so forth. *Pravāsāt* (restraint from departure): "If you go to another village without giving [the payment], then this fine shall be yours," and so forth. *Karmaṇaḥ* (restraint from activity): "If you perform study and other such acts without giving [the payment], then this fine shall be yours," and so forth. — Kātyāyana [103–108, 110].
He who commits violence or fails to give what is owed to one who begs,
due to his immoral conduct, shall be dragged away by order of the king.
But once the matter has been reported to the king and he has given his unhesitating assent,
the judge shall then issue an injunction of restraint until the appearance of the parties for trial.
If one who has been restrained while seeking to fulfill a legal obligation should violate that restraint,
he may be held back even by his own hand, provided he does not prove his innocence.
One who is subject to restraint but has not been restrained deserves punishment upon escaping;
however, one who restrains someone who is not subject to restraint must be punished by the king—this is the settled rule.

"In a matter that is undisputed, promised, reported, and determined by the king"—the meaning is that it has been declared as something to be investigated. "His restraint" (*tadāsedhaḥ*) means his confinement. Regarding the phrase "even with his own hand": the meaning is that when the plaintiff is unable to demonstrate in public the evidence (*kriyā*) that is the cause of the dispute, then the king should restrain him even by means of physical intervention with his own hand.
Nārada [1.49]:
"In cases such as crossing rivers, traversing wildernesses, difficult terrains, or times of calamity..."
One who, being unestablished, departs from that obstruction would not commit an offense.

Kātyāyana [107, 106]: Those who have ascended trees or mountains, those situated on elephants, horses, chariots, or boats, and all those in difficult positions— none of these should be restrained by those seeking to accomplish their business.
But he who, by restraining the senses through silence, breathing exercises, and so forth, should obstruct those who ought not to be obstructed, is to be punished; he is not one who has transgressed.
[54] He who denies a fact that has been established shall be censured;
indeed, he alone shall be punished if the fact is not established.
If the two parties should mutually obstruct one another regarding a disputed matter,
the king shall cause a lawful punishment to be inflicted upon both for such transgression.
"By non-restraints" means by means of breath-holding (*ucchvāsa*) and so forth, which do not constitute formal restraint. "As it occurred" means as it actually happened.
Bṛhaspati [p. 22, 26, 23]:
"One intent on studying the scriptures, one preparing for a marriage, the sick, those afflicted by grief, the insane, and children..."
One who is intoxicated, one who is excessively aged, one intent on the king's business, and one observing a vow [are disqualified].
One accompanied by soldiers in battle, or a cultivator during the harvest season,
those in a precarious position, and likewise women who have a protector, must not be arrested.
"In battle" means in combat. "In the gathering of crops" refers to the connection with beginningless grain.
One who desires to marry, one afflicted by disease, one wishing to sacrifice, or one situated in calamity...
Likewise one who is prosecuted by another, or one who is occupied with royal business.
Cowherds [are summoned] when cattle are grazing; farmers at the beginning of the sowing season;
artisans at their respective times; and those who bear arms during a conflict.
Those who have not yet attained legal capacity, an envoy, one intent on giving, one observing a vow, and those in a precarious situation must not be detained; nor should the king summon them.
Kātyāyana [111]: "The wise know that for one who is accused, one who is imprisoned, or one who remains by the king's command,
no other person may bring a charge against him."
Vyāsa says: A yogi, one desiring to speak, a madman, one seeking dharma, one in distress, one observing a vow,
or one intent on giving— such a person should not be prosecuted, nor restrained, nor summoned as a witness.
In the context of the rule "they are not to be obstructed," Kātyāyana [states]:

"One who has set out for his installation, one for whom a specific time has been fixed, a farmer engaged in his crops, and likewise one waiting for the arrival of water— none of these may be interrupted in the interim."

From the commencement until the conclusion, one should not litigate during that time; nor should one do so with those who are ill, children, the elderly, those in difficult circumstances, or those preoccupied with ritual acts.

A king should not summon servants who are negligent in their duties, those distressed by royal business, those distracted by their own affairs, or those who are intoxicated, insane, heedless, or afflicted.

One should not marry a young woman of inferior lineage, even if she is born of a noble family and has recently given birth; nor should one marry a maiden who is the best among all castes, for women do not have mastery over their own kinsmen.
Those whose wives are dependent on them, wanton women, courtesans, those of ruined families, and those who have fallen from their caste— these are worthy of being summoned.
Having learned of their resolve, even those who have gone forth as forest-dwellers and the like,
the king should summon them for weighty matters, provided he does not provoke their anger.
Having understood the time, the place, and the relative strength or weakness of the matters at hand,
the king should gradually bring even those who are unwell or otherwise unfit before him.

"Indisposed" means ill. "One who neglects his business" is one whose work perishes when it is obstructed. "Women dependent on such men" refers to the wives of cowherds, vintners, and others. Bṛhaspati [1.136]:
A merchant whose goods have been sold, a farmer once the crop has grown, and those with weapons raised and so forth—these should be made to pay once their task is completed.
Kātyāyana [100–101]:
But if one who is summoned should disregard the royal command while being capable of obeying it,
the king shall inflict upon him punishment according to the procedure prescribed by law.
For a minor offense, the fine shall be fifty; for a middling one, it shall be at least one hundred;
and for grave matters, the punishment shall always be at least five hundred.
Vyāsa says:
In a region struck by enemies, during a famine, or when afflicted by disease,
one should perform a renewed invocation [of the deity], but one should not inflict punishment.

[57] Kātyāyana [112–113]: Having accomplished the business for the messenger, one should cause him to be provided with food, taking into account whether it took one day, two days, or more, and considering the place, time, and other such factors.
The experts in the Tantras know that eating is prescribed as being dependent upon place, time, age, strength, and so forth,
for one who is the agent in all circumstances.
Yājñavalkya [2.10]: A surety capable of deciding the matter should be accepted for both parties. Kātyāyana [117]:
If, however, there is no surety for the plaintiff who is fit to plead,
he shall, being protected, pay a fee to the messenger at the end of the day.
[58] 7 — Now, regarding speech in that regard, Bṛhaspati says: [3.25]
When the plaintiff and the defendant arrive in a scramble for precedence,
the trial should be conducted according to the order of their castes, while also taking into account the relative severity of their suffering.
Manu [8.24]: Having understood both the beneficial and the harmful, as well as dharma and adharma in their entirety,
he should examine all the legal cases of the litigants according to the order of their castes.
Kātyāyana [120–121]: A king should not apply the legal principle of "taking back what has been taken";
rather, he should either restore that [property] to him, or cause them to settle the matter between themselves.
In that case, the plaintiff shall speak first, and the defendant immediately thereafter;
when both have spoken, the members of the court shall deliberate, and after that, the judge.

Regarding the term "the taking of what has been taken" (*gṛhītagrahaṇa*), what is intended here is the seizure of that wealth which has been brought by the plaintiff from the defendant for the purpose of accomplishing his own objective. [59] Nārada [2.38]:
A written order, a tablet, a royal edict, a mortgage, a deed of sale, or a deed of purchase; or...
That plaintiff who first makes his representation to the king should be known as the *pūrvavādī* (the first claimant) by those who know the law.
Or, to whomsoever the suffering is greater or the matter is more urgent, to him the plaintiff's claim should be granted; not to one who would have reported it earlier [but failed to do so].

Regarding the term *ājñālekha* (an edict): the meaning is that the "prior claim" (*pūrvavāda*) belongs to one who first makes a formal representation to the king concerning matters such as an edict. Bṛhaspati [2.36, 41, 42] states:
"The prior claim is of four kinds, and likewise the counter-claim."
The determination is said by some to be fourfold, while by others it is recorded as being eightfold.
A charge based on suspicion, a factual claim, a request when the object has been obtained, and a retrial after a case has been concluded: these are to be known as the four kinds of pleas.
Delusion is defined as doubt; truth is the perception of an object as it is seen.
Seeking after an object already obtained is delusion, as is acting again toward that which has already occurred.
Yājñavalkya [2.6]: The defendant must write down, in the presence of the plaintiff, exactly what has been stated by the plaintiff,
marked with the year, month, fortnight, day, names, caste, and other identifying characteristics.
"Before the defendant" means in the presence of the defendant. Kātyāyana [124–128]:
Having recorded the time, the year, the month, the fortnight, as well as the lunar day (tithi), the hour, the region, the district, the location, the caste, the appearance, and the age.
The goal, the means of proof, the substance, the number, and likewise the name of the self; the names of the kings in succession, their residence, and the name of the object to be accomplished.

In due order, one should state the names of the ancestors, as well as the afflictions, the acquirer, and the donor; having determined the lunar fortnight, one should also recite other signs of forgiveness.
The country, the time, as well as the location and the configuration; the caste, the name, the residence, the measurement, and the name of the field.
In disputes concerning immovable property, one should present these ten things: the ancestral lineage of the father and grandfather, and the recitation of the previous genealogy.

[61] Kātyāyana and Bṛhaspati: Those who know the subject matter (pakṣa) declare that a thesis is one that is free from defects of the proposition, endowed with valid reasons, certain, and established in the world.

It consists of few syllables yet contains abundant meaning; it is free from ambiguity and free from confusion. It is liberated from causes of contradiction and serves as a refutation of opposing views.
But when such a position has been formulated by the proponent,
then the opponent should provide a reply that connects with the conclusion of that position.
Kātyāyana [138]: A plaint that is devoid of place and time, lacking in substance and number, and deficient in the measure of the matter to be proven, is held to be inadmissible.
Bṛhaspati [2.20]: "If one causes a plaint to be written that is joined with falsehood, devoid of action, lacking substance, or confused,
there is defeat in the lawsuit, O Prajāpati."

Nārada [2.7, 17, 7]: A document that is for another's purpose, devoid of meaning, lacking authoritative sources or tradition, deficient or excessive, or corrupted— these are indeed declared to be defects of the plaint (*bhāṣā*).
If the placement of syllables is incorrect or if they deviate from their intended meaning,
the ritual gift becomes confused, and the ritual itself likewise becomes confused.
[62] As long as the defendant has not yet committed the answer to writing,
the plaintiff shall commit to writing everything that he intends to state regarding the matter.
"Document" (*lekhyam*) is the term to be qualified. "Lost" (*bhraṣṭam*) means fallen away from what was previously presented. Bṛhaspati [2.22].
The proponent shall first clear up any deficiency or excess in his initial plea;
he shall not offer a rejoinder until the defendant has been present before the assembly of judges.
Likewise:
"When the accuser, due to lack of confidence, does not dare to speak,
time should be granted to him in accordance with the requirements of the case."
Nārada [2.3]:
"Or he may obtain it by his own writing for three days or even seven days. Kātyāyana [134]:
In a dispute where the intellect of two parties who wish to speak is unable to reach a conclusion,
time for deliberation should be granted to both the plaintiff and the defendant.
[63] Likewise [131]:
Then the judge shall cause the plaintiff's own statement to be written down on a wooden board with chalk,
and once it has been refined, it shall be recorded on a leaf.
One should cut down excessive expenditures and fill up those that are deficient;
one should establish [the state] upon the ground for as long as the purpose has not been fully described.
That which has been well-considered by those established in dharma for the sake of unconfused understanding—
therefore, that which was propounded by the two litigants should be set aside if it serves another purpose.

Once it has been authorized by both disputants, he shall record the agreement of the two litigants in writing upon a leaf, together with witnesses, and set it down in its entirety upon a wooden board.
One should subtract the first term as long as the second term is not yet visible;
once the second term has been reached, the subtraction process for that term is completed.
Thus ends the section on the Plaint (*bhāṣāpāda*) in the Section on Legal Procedure (*vyavahārakāṇḍa*), composed by Bhaṭṭa Lakṣmīdhara, the son of Hṛdayadhara.
8— Then, regarding the subsequent stage, Bṛhaspati [3.2–4] states:
"When the prima facie case has been determined and distinguished as to what is admissible and what is inadmissible..."
Once the meaning of the plaint has been established, he should then cause the reply to be written.
Where an opponent, out of modesty or fear, or due to a lapse of memory,
requests a delay, he deserves to obtain that time.
Depending on one's capacity, one obtains [the fruit] for one day, three days, five days, seven days, or even a fortnight, a month, three seasons, or a year.

"Viniścita" means determined according to its own nature. "Distinguished by what is to be grasped and what is not to be grasped" means that when the plaintiff has specified the qualities of what is to be accepted and the qualities of what is to be rejected, and when the matter has been made known through this prior position (*pūrvapakṣa*) as being thus qualified, the defendant should be made to write his reply once the subject of the claim has been established. Kātyāyana [153, 145, 146, 154, 156, 147, 164, 157, 148]:
"In matters that have arisen immediately, one should litigate immediately;
or in matters that have passed some time, the master [the judge] should grant a period of time to the defendant."
Having heard the meaning as it is being written down, if the defendant departs for a valid reason, time should be requested for the dispute; it must be granted to him, without a doubt.

[65] Depending on the gravity or lightness of the matter, he may obtain repayment of debts and the like immediately, after one day, five days, three days, or within three fortnights, or within seven days.
If [the death] occurred immediately, the impurity lasts for one day; if it occurred more than a day ago, one should add a day.
For a death six years ago, it lasts three nights; for twelve years, seven days.
In the twentieth year, a man receives ten days;
when thirty years have passed, he receives one month; and beyond that, it shall be three fortnights.
For those who are not independent, the dull-witted, the insane, children, the initiated, or the sick,
[the teacher may perform initiation] himself at any time desired, even before a year has passed.
Having understood the power of time and the relative strength or weakness of the matters at hand,
the lord should grant a period of time— whether short or long— to the defendant.
