Or, whatever custom has been handed down through a succession of tradition in a particular place,
the king, having considered that according to the rule, should cause a reply to be given accordingly.
If the primary witnesses or the secondary witnesses are situated in a foreign land,
there shall be time for men to come from their own country to give testimony.
Whether it be a day, half a month, a full month, a season, or even a year,
the defendant must grant a period of time appropriate to the nature of the legal action.

[66] Regarding "of one who causes [the document] to be written," the word "plaintiff" (*arthin*) is to be supplied as the subject. The syntactical connection is "having heard the matter. Regarding "time should be granted," the word "by the king" is to be supplied. "When the year has passed" means after one year has elapsed. "In which place, family, etc. refers to the location and so forth. "The root" (*mūla*) refers to the wealth that is the subject of the dispute; it is said to be that which the defendant states was obtained from such-and-such a person. "To speak" means to state the reply (*uttara*). The syntactical connection is "time should be granted," extending up until the time of the next assembly. Likewise: [156–157] "One who is mentally deficient, an idiot, or afflicted by disease [should be granted a year]."
If one goes to other regions without having reached a definitive conclusion regarding the matter at hand.

"One year" means it is to be awaited for a year. Yājñavalkya [2.12]: "In cases of violence, theft, verbal abuse, false accusations regarding cattle, and regarding women, one should litigate immediately; in other matters, time is prescribed according to one's own wish."

"Sāhasam" refers to acts such as striking with weapons and the like. "Gauḥ" refers to a milch cow. "In cases of false accusation" (*adbhiśāpe*) means when one falsely accuses another of being a perpetrator of harm. "In cases of loss" (*atyaye*) means when there is the possibility of the destruction of the object under dispute. "In the case of women" refers to a dispute regarding the character of a woman of good family, or a dispute regarding the integrity of a female slave. In these instances, one should cause the trial to proceed immediately; that is, one should cause the defendant to provide an immediate answer. [67] Bṛhaspati and Kātyāyana state:
"In cases of violence, theft, assault, false accusation regarding a cow, and likewise in cases of loss..."
And Bṛhaspati quickly descended to the earth and to the tree, even though it was not the proper time.
"In this context, 'the wrong time' refers to a period when litigation is not appropriate, such as the time for farmers to sow or gather their seeds. Nārada [1.45] states:

'In cases of theft of cattle, land, gold, or women; in cases of assault and verbal abuse; in urgent matters; in acts of violence; and in cases of false accusation—one should institute a lawsuit immediately.'"
Kātyāyana [150, 151, 149]: In the case of a milch cow, a bull, a field, women, and likewise in procreation;
in the case of a deposit, a loan for use, a gift, and similarly in buying and selling.
In cases of violating a maiden, theft, quarrel, acts of violence, embezzlement of a deposit, fraud, and perjury, one should institute a lawsuit immediately.
When dignity departs at the time of death or through abandonment, one should not perform urgent business then; for that [time] is indeed a critical emergency.

"Procreation" here refers to marriage. "Fraud" (*upadhi*) means deception in the form of dealings with fraudulent accountants and the like. "Weightiness" (*gaurava*) means importance. Regarding the phrase "in case of ruin, there is abandonment," the meaning is that when ruin occurs, what results is simply abandonment. Nārada and Kātyāyana [Nāradasmṛti 2.2; Kātyāyanasmṛti 159]:
"But the defendant, having heard the matter stated by the plaintiff, immediately thereafter..."
One should present the counter-argument connected with the meaning of the prima facie position.
[68] "'Pratipakṣam' means the reply. Yājñavalkya [2.7]:
"Having heard the meaning, the reply should be written in the presence of the plaintiff.
Nārada and Prajāpati.
Those who know [the art of debate] recognize a reply as being that which pervades the position (*pakṣa*), is essential, free from doubt, unconfused, and not requiring further explanation.

"Comprehensive" (*vyāpaka*) means all-encompassing. "Substantial" (*sāra*) means not trivial. "Unconfused" (*anākula*) means free from internal contradictions between earlier and later parts. "Not requiring further explanation" (*avyākhyāgamya*) means having a clear meaning. Bṛhaspati [2.2]:
"False admission, as well as counter-attack (*pratyavaskandana*), and the plea of a prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*)—these four replies have been declared by those who know the treatises."
Likewise [3.17]:
If a defendant, when being charged, should make a denial,
one should know that such a plea in response is false according to the legal procedure.
Vyāsa says: "This is false; I do not know it, for I was not present there at that time;
and I was unaware during that period"—thus, a falsehood is of four kinds.
[69] Bṛhaspati and Nārada state: "If the defendant,
having been subjected to a charge based on what was heard, admits the truth of it,
that is declared by those learned in the scriptures to be 'admission' (saṃpratipatti)."
If the defendant, having admitted the matter written by the plaintiff exactly as it is,
should state a legal reason [for his defense], that is indeed a plea of "counter-attack" (pratyavaskandana).

"Tattvam" means "that-nature. "Having accepted, one should state the cause": if the defendant, having acknowledged the matter stated by the plaintiff as true, returns it by stating a reason—such as "it has been returned"—and thereby attacks the plaintiff's case, then that reply constitutes "pratyavaskandana" (an attack in return). This is the meaning. Kātyāyana [170] states:
"If the defendant, having accepted the matter exactly as it was pointed out by the plaintiff, should state a reason, Bhṛgu declared that to be *ādharyam* (a ground for dismissal)."
The term *ādharya* means that the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is unfit to be further scrutinized by means of proof. Bṛhaspati [3.21–24]:
"If one who has been defeated according to established practice is made to write again, he is declared to have been previously defeated; this is correctly termed *prāṅnyāya* (a prior judgment)."
One should apply the true to what is true, and cause the false to be recorded as false;
likewise, one should apply the grounds of proof to a case supported by grounds, and both [the plea and the proof] similarly to a plea of prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*).
[70] That which arises from fear or fault is false and is censured by those who know the scriptures;
however, that which is a truthful recognition is declared to be righteous.
A plea that is true, consistent with justice, and praiseworthy has been declared by the virtuous;
the opposite would be contrary to dharma, and the defendant shall suffer defeat.

‘By conduct’ means by the course of legal procedure. ‘Defeated’ means having fallen into one’s own ruin, that is to say, broken. ‘Should file again’ means that, having made a new accusation, he should have his plaint written down in another court. ‘That which is called “prāṅnyāya” (prior judgment), etc.’: the meaning is that where it is stated, “In this matter, I was previously defeated in this lawsuit,” that is *prāṅnyāya*. Vyāsa says: If both a plea of denial (*mithyā*) and a plea of a special cause (*kāraṇa*) should occur in one case, or even a plea of truth (*satya*) along with another, which answer should be accepted there?
Between two false pleas, the defendant's answer should be accepted which concerns a more substantial matter,
or that in which the burden of proof (kriyā) lies.
In that case, the answer should be understood as unambiguous; otherwise, it would be the opposite.

"Or in the case of *mithyā* and *kāraṇa*," and so forth. When *mithyā* and *kāraṇa* rejoinders are mixed regarding a single subject, the decision must be made by relying on the *kāraṇa* rejoinder. For example: when it is stated, "My cow was lost at such-and-such a time, and it is now found in his house," the reply is, "What you say is false; for even before that time, she was staying in my house and gave birth there. Even when *satya*, *mithyā*, and *kāraṇa* rejoinders are mixed, only the *kāraṇa* rejoinder is to be accepted. This is because the two uses of the word "or" (*vāpi*) in the phrase "or in the case of *mithyā* and *kāraṇa*" demonstrate that when all three are mixed, the *kāraṇa* alone is to be taken. An example is as follows: in a lawsuit concerning ninety [coins], the reply is, "This is false; only sixty coins were received, and of those, thirty have been cleared, so I owe only thirty. Regarding the phrase "that which concerns a large amount of matter": if, however, one rejoinder concerns a large amount of matter, then the decision must be made by adopting that one. An example is as follows: in a lawsuit concerning one hundred, the reply is, "Eighty is false; only twenty were received, and that has been paid. Here, because the portion concerning *mithyā* involves a large amount of matter, the *mithyā* rejoinder alone is to be accepted. The meaning is that the burden of proof (*kriyā*) should be placed upon the plaintiff alone. Regarding the phrase "or where the fruit of the action lies": where, in a mixture of *mithyā*, *kāraṇa*, and so forth, there exists a clear means of proof such as a document, that rejoinder is to be accepted even if it does not concern a large amount of matter. The remainder of the sense is: otherwise, the rejoinder remains mixed.
Kātyāyana [191]:
If the first ground of defeat is preceded by another that is more serious and pertains to the defendant's case,
this [first ground] shall be set aside and the latter proved.

The meaning is that if, after stating one reason first, one then states another reason that is more weighty, then the latter should be followed as the authoritative proof, not the previously stated one. Bṛhaspati [3.28]:
One should not record a rejoinder that is different from what was stated, obscure, deficient or excessive, incoherent, non-pervasive, unsubstantial, doubtful, or contrary to the opponent's position.

Kātyāyana [175, 189–190]: An answer that contains disjointed words, is non-comprehensive, has a hidden meaning, is likewise confused, requires interpretation to be understood, or is devoid of substance, does not lead to the achievement of one's own objective.
[72] That which is true in one part of the subject, but is a reason in another part,
and is false in yet another part— that immediately follows is *saṃkara* (confusion).
In a single dispute, there should not be legal action for both litigants;
there can be no establishment of the claim for both, nor can there be two actions in one case.

"And not in a single lawsuit," and so forth. In the case of two false grounds of defeat (*kāraṇa*), the legal procedure (*kriyā*) would apply to both; however, that is not logical, because there is no object to be proven (*sādhya*) for both. In the case of a plea of prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*) and a ground of defeat, a dual procedure for one party is contradictory, since there is only a single object to be proven. "In one" refers to the plaintiff. Yājñavalkya [2.9–10]: One should not bring a counter-charge against someone without first having resolved the original charge. Nor should one subject an accused person to further harassment, nor should one alter what has been stated.
And one may bring a counter-charge in cases of quarrels and acts of violence.
"Viprakṛti" means being other than one's natural state. Bṛhaspati [3.7, 8; 2.4; 1.173]:
But he who does not give a reply in accordance with the facts regarding the plaintiff’s case...
The defendant shall be made to pay by means of conciliation and other such methods.
[73] Conciliatory speech preceded by pleasant words, sowing dissension, pointing out the facts, withholding wealth, as well as punishment, beating, and imprisonment.
But he who, though being urged by various means, does not give an answer,
is considered defeated once seven nights have passed and deserves punishment.
Those who are insane or intoxicated, those defiled by mortal sins,
the mentally dull, the very aged, and children should be known as those who are exempt from being questioned.
‘Nirdhūtaḥ’ means one whose insults have been shaken off. ‘Niruttarāḥ’ means those who, because they are unfit for legal procedure, are not required to provide a reply. Kātyāyana [206, 193]:
When both parties have submitted their statements and the determination of the case has begun...
If someone should state there what has not been mentioned, he is defeated on account of that very point.
But when the investigation has been conducted according to the preceding and succeeding rules and fully entered upon,
Bhṛgu declared that the testimony of those two litigants therein must be thoroughly examined.
Whether due to delusion or through guile, that which was not stated by the proponent but is included within the reply should be accepted by both parties as well.
That which was heard, that which was written, that which was reflected upon, and that which was refined—on the very first day, the procedure for the lawsuit regarding that is declared.

(74) The term "from that meaning" (*tadarthāt*) refers to a matter not previously stated. Regarding "the plaint and the reply" (*pūrvottare*), this refers to both the initial statement (*bhāṣā*) and the defendant's response (*uttara*). "Refined" (*nirṇiktam*) means purified. If, at the time of writing the plaint, something was not stated due to confusion or deceit, yet it becomes manifest through some means during the time of deliberation, then even that must be included within the plaint. The same should be understood to apply to the reply as well.
Thus is the nature of the response [75] 9; now, the substitute.
Regarding this, Kātyāyana [89–90] states:
"The right to act belongs to the one who is accused, not to another, because of the lack of connection;
even another person, when impelled by the accused, is considered unaltered [as a representative]."
One who is presented by the plaintiff to another person acting as a judge is to be known as a *prativādī* (respondent), as is one who has come forward of his own accord.

The *prativādī* is the representative of the plaintiff (*vādī*). The *pratipanna* is one who, though not the defendant himself, has been accepted by the defendant as his representative for the purpose of pleading. Bṛhaspati [1.142]:
[The representation of] those who are not self-reliant, the dull-witted, the insane, the aged, women, children, and the sick [is permitted].
A kinsman, or another person appointed for the purpose, shall state the answer.
The "prior and subsequent" refers to the reply (*uttara*). Kātyāyana [93, 95] states:
"In cases of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, violating the teacher's wife, and other intolerable accusations, no opportunity for a defense is granted."
In the case of killing a human, theft, violating another's wife,
eating what is unfit to be eaten, and the abduction or defilement of a maiden;

In cases of harsh speech, forgery, and likewise treason against the king, the defendant shall not be compelled to plead; rather, the perpetrator himself shall litigate. (Kātyāyana and Nārada, Kātyāyana 91; Nārada 2.22)
Whether commissioned by the plaintiff or even sent by the defendant,
whoever litigates on behalf of another, the victory and defeat belong to those two [parties].
Bṛhaspati [3.30]:
When appointed to the dispute between officiating priests, both are considered equal;
yet in the sacrifice, the master obtains the merit, whereas in the dispute, he obtains either loss or victory.
Nārada and Kātyāyana [Nā. 2.23]:
He who is neither a brother, nor a father, nor a son, nor one acting by mandate, yet speaks on behalf of another, shall be punished for speaking falsely in legal proceedings.
Kātyāyana [92]:
Slaves, laborers, pupils, those appointed to service, and likewise kinsmen—these litigants shall not be subject to punishment; he who is other than these is liable to punishment.
Bṛhaspati [3.31, 32]:
Where the plaintiff or the defendant has died after the written plaint and reply have been submitted,
their son shall clear up the legal dispute on their behalf.
If a legal dispute remains undecided, a person may be deceived; there can be neither the granting of victory nor punishment. Therefore, one must reach a definitive conclusion of the case.
Thus ends the fourth quarter [77].
Now, the *pratyākalita*.

In that regard, the characteristics of the wicked are as follows. On this point, Manu [8.25–26] states: "One should discern the internal disposition of men by means of their speech, signs, tone of voice, complexion, gestures, facial expressions, eyes, and movements."
By means of physical forms, gestures, gait, movements, and speech,
as well as through changes in the eyes and face, the mind within is perceived.

One should "ascertain" (*vibhāvayet*)—that is, determine—the "intention" (*bhāva*), which is the inner purpose, "of men," such as litigants, witnesses, and others. "Appearance" (*ākāra*) refers to a modification, namely the alteration of natural qualities such as the voice and so forth. Among these, a modification of the voice includes stammering and the like; a modification of the complexion refers to a change in the appearance of the limbs; and "gestures" (*iṅgita*) include perspiration, trembling, horripilation, and so on. One should observe this "with the eyes," that is, by means of glances imbued with affection or anger, and "by movements" (*ceṣṭita*), such as the clenching of the hands or the knitting of the brows. In the world, it is well known that these qualities, beginning with the voice, possess the capacity to reveal the internal mind; thus he says, "by appearances" (*ākāraiḥ*), and so forth. "Appearances" (*ākāra*) are so called because they are "formed" (*ākriyante*) or modified; they consist of gestures and the like. Here, "gait" refers to walking that falters or deviates from its natural state. Here, "speech" refers to words that are contradictory in their preceding and succeeding parts. "Distortion of the face" (*vaktravikāra*) refers to the drying of the mouth and similar symptoms. [78]
Kātyāyana [385–386]:
One should examine his internal state through his facial expressions, gestures, and movements;
that defendant is considered defeated when he is perceived by means of such inference.
Trembling, perspiration, discoloration, dryness of the lips, touching [the ground], scratching the earth, loss of one's position, and looking sideways or upwards;
The wise say that a change in voice is a sign of one who is corrupted.

"Appearance" (*ākāra*) refers to a physical transformation produced by intense anger. The term "respondent" (*prativādī*) includes both parties, as they are mutual adversaries. "Touching" (*abhimarśanam*) means licking the corners of the lips with the tongue.
Yājñavalkya [2.13–15]:
He moves from one place to another, licks the corners of his mouth,
his forehead perspires, and his face turns pale.
With speech faltering as it dries up, he speaks much that is contradictory;
he does not honor his voice or his eyes, and he even distorts his lips.
If one departs from their natural state through actions of mind, speech, or body—
whether during a legal proceeding or while giving testimony— they are declared to be corrupt.

‘Sṛkkiṇī’ refers to the corners of the lips. ‘Vāk cakṣuḥ pūjayati no’ means that one does not honor the speech uttered by another by returning a reply, nor does one honor it with a look from the eyes. ‘Nirbhujati’ means to distort or make crooked.
As stated in the Rāmāyaṇa (Yuddhakāṇḍa, 16.64):
“Even when being concealed, one’s facial expression cannot be hidden.”
For indeed, [the body] forcibly reveals the internal state of men.
In the *Kālikāpurāṇa*: "One who is terrified does not speak; there is neither trembling nor perspiration, nor any other transformation in the limbs, nor would the mind be otherwise."

He is the victor if he remains free from anger; otherwise, indeed, he is merely the one who was there before. The word "not" (*na tu*) is connected with trembling, perspiration, and so forth. The word "nor" (*na ca*) is connected with the phrase "or any transformation. "Merely the one who was there before" means the original plaintiff himself. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "he would be the victor.
Thus is the definition of a defeated party.
Now,
in that regard, Manu [states]: [8.53–58] |
He who points out a wrong place, he who denies what he has pointed out,
and he who does not understand the contradictory meanings of what precedes and follows;
Furthermore, he who, having cited an instruction, subsequently evades it;
or who, when questioned about a matter that has been correctly resolved, does not acknowledge it.
He who converses secretly with witnesses in a place where conversation is forbidden,
he who refuses to answer when being questioned, or he who walks away;
When told "Speak," he does not speak; and what has been said, he does not clarify.
He does not understand the sequence of what precedes and follows; therefore, he fails in his case.
Having said, "There are those who know," if one who has been asked to point them out does not do so,
the judge, by these reasons, should declare that person as well to be defeated.
If he does not speak when summoned, he shall be punished with death according to the law;
if he does not speak within three fortnights regarding the matter of justice, he is defeated.

[81] ‘*Adeśaḥ*’ refers to a place where the plaintiff and the defendant are not present at that time. ‘*Nirdiśya*’—the remainder of the phrase is “having specified the place and so forth. ‘*Adharottarān arthān*’ means matters both preceding and subsequent. ‘*Vigītān*’ means contradictory. ‘*Apadiśya*’ means having set forth. ‘*Apadeśam*’ means a pretext. ‘*Apadhāvati*’ means he flees. ‘*Samyak praṇihitam artham*’ means a matter stated clearly and decisively. ‘*Pṛṣṭaḥ*’ means being addressed as follows: “Regarding what you have said, what do you say? By what evidence do you prove your own position? and so forth. ‘*Asambhāṣye*’ means in a place unfit for conversation. ‘*Niṣpatet*’ means he should depart for another village without making an announcement. The repetition of what was already established by the words “speak” (*brūhi*) and so forth is for the sake of emphasis. ‘*Dharmasthaḥ*’ means one situated in the court of justice (*dharmādhikaraṇa*).
Nārada and Kātyāyana [Nā. 3.165]:
One should not approach witnesses in private as directed by another, nor should one cause dissension among them through anyone else; he who acts in such a manner is defeated by them.
One who flees when summoned, one who remains silent, one defeated by witnesses, and one who confesses of his own accord—these are the four kinds of defeated litigants.

One who speaks inconsistently, one who hates the performance of legal acts, one who does not appear, one who fails to provide an answer, and one who flees after being summoned— these are recorded as the five kinds of defeated litigants.
The man who, having abandoned his original thesis, takes up another, should be known as one who shifts his position; indeed, that man is a debater of inferior standing.
One should not bring about a change in the meaning of the matter one has undertaken;
nor should one move to another alternative position, for by doing so, one falls away from the original position.
One who wastes time under various pretexts, one who remains silent in the assembly, or one who, when questioned, speaks inconsistently— these are the characteristics of a losing party.
He who, having been summoned, flees, or who, having arrived, does not engage in the dispute,
shall be disciplined by the king as one who has indeed lost the case.
‘Abhyupapannaḥ’ means one who has admitted defeat. ‘Āvasannaḥ’ means one who has fallen into despondency. Yājñavalkya [2.16]:
He who settles a doubtful matter on his own authority, and he who runs away;
And one who, though summoned, says nothing, is declared to be defeated and liable to punishment.
"Independent" means acting without reference to a report to the king; "if he should establish [his claim]" means if he should seize it—
however, he who proceeds regarding a disputed matter without having reported it to the king shall be punished,
and his entire claim shall not be established.
Thus, from the words of Nārada. Kātyāyana [196–197]:
"But he who, having caused it to be written, subsequently by word of mouth makes it either less or more..."
If the litigant speaks thus, he should be granted [the victory]; however, he does not deserve the formal charge.
One should not speak of a matter as having been asserted by oneself after having charged another;
one who speaks falsely in this manner should likewise be declared defeated.
[83] Bṛhaspati [3.33–39]: But he who, having designated witnesses, does not bring them to trial within thirty nights or three fortnights, incurs a loss of his case.

One who flees after being summoned, one who remains silent, one defeated by the testimony of witnesses, and one who admits the claim with his own words— these are the four kinds of litigants who have lost their case.

One who flees is defeated after three fortnights; one who maintains silence, after seven days; one whose testimony is contradicted by witnesses, at that very moment; and one who admits the claim, immediately.

Not stating what has been presented, failing to appear in court, remaining silent when the defendant is to be refuted, and silence regarding the meaning of one's own position— these are the characteristics of one who is losing the case.
If one who is accused in an assembly of a great sin, a minor sin,
or a heinous crime consents to it, people know him to be joined with that guilt.
Therefore, a wise person should diligently perform the purification of the self;
whatever task is most important, that one should first purify.
He who, accused of a great sin, wishes to escape from that transgression,
deserves punishment, for he has already been defeated by his own prior admission.
"Previously" refers to a grave offense (*mahāpātaka*). Nārada [2.25] states:
"In all disputes concerning property, one does not fail because of a verbal deception."
In cases involving cattle, women, land, or the non-payment of debts, even one who deserves punishment does not lose his property.
"Arthāt" means because [the ordeal] for animals and so forth has already been mentioned.
Bṛhaspati [3.40–42]:
Having performed the determination of the standing position (upasthāna) in the case of an ordeal involving conduct (ācārakaraṇa).
When one is not present, one should not employ deception therein.
Whatever fault may arise at that time through the agency of the king of the gods,
he shall not be defeated by virtue of his state of non-violence and renunciation.
But when an investigation has been commenced and settled between two parties,
those who first go over to the other side shall be made to pay double the fine.
[85] 12 — Now, regarding peace (*saṃdhi*),
Bṛhaspati says [3.43–45, 47–49]:
When the two opposing sides have been drawn out and the decision on the matter has begun,
a reconciliation may occur between the two heated parties, like that of two pieces of iron.
In that case, there may be a choice between witnesses and assessors;
those who are wise and remain impartial should bring about a settlement between the two parties.
Where there is equality in authority despite a difference between the scriptures and their practice, a reconciliation between both is praised by royal decree.
Through impartiality, the king shall obtain the acquisition of merit and wealth, as well as fame;
the witnesses and the members of the court do not suffer, and enmity comes to an end.
From conflict arise for men the punishment of restraint or favor, the attainment of justice or injustice, fame or infamy, and likewise, further enmity.

Therefore, whatever those presiding over the family and the assembly— who know the Dharma and possess impartial vision— should say out of freedom from hatred and greed, that must be carried out by one who understands.

[86] Regarding "the dilemma of witnesses and assessors": where there might be a dilemma concerning witnesses and assessors for both the plaintiff and the defendant—namely, wondering what they will say—and where the decision on the case is wavering and thus doubtful as to how it will turn out, the meaning is that those two who would effect a settlement (*saṃdhi*) are the wise ones. Regarding "equality" (*samatā*): where the commonality of evidence appears on the side of both the plaintiff and the defendant; and where there is a conflict between scripture and custom—meaning a contradiction with another scripture in the case of *śāstra*, and a contradiction with another legal proceeding in the case of *vyavahāra*—there a settlement by the king’s command is praised. This is the meaning. Regarding "punishment and favor" (*nigrahānugraha*): since punishments and so forth remain applicable when a dispute exists between the plaintiff and the defendant, the meaning is that a settlement is therefore better.
[87] 13— Now, regarding the gift of ritual action (*kriyādāna*),
Bṛhaspati states in [4.2]:
But for those who persist in their defense, the members of the court shall cause a proper rejoinder to be made by one of the litigants and then proceed with the investigation.
The plaintiff shall prove his claim, and likewise the defendant shall prove his defense;
the one who asserts what occurred previously shall establish his victory by means of a written judgment of victory.

"But those who remain," the ellipsis being "those who speak with perverse arguments"; "investigation" (*vibhāvanā*) means the action must be performed; the meaning is, "state the proof. "He should establish his proposition" (*pratijñāṃ sādhayet*) means he should prove the matter asserted by means of proof. And this applies in the case of a "false plea" (*mithyottara*). The meaning is that the defendant (*pratyarthī*) should establish the "cause" (*kāraṇa*); and this applies in the case of a "plea of prior judgment" (*pratyavaskandanottara*). Vyāsa states: "But in a plea of prior judgment, when the cause is stated, the defendant shall point out the proof (*kriyā*)."
But if he makes a false statement, or if he fails to prove his case when challenged, the plaintiff shall lose.
Kātyāyana [211]:
For even the plaintiff may adopt the defense for a specific reason;
therefore, the burden of proof (kriyā) is always declared to belong to the one who establishes the initial claim.
[88] Manu [8.52]: When a debtor, having been told "Pay! in the presence of an assembly, denies the debt, the plaintiff must point out the place [of the transaction] or state another reason.

When, in the "assembly"—that is, in the place of legal proceedings such as the court—the debtor denies the statement made by the creditor, then the "plaintiff," meaning the lender of the money, the creditor, "shall indicate the place," that is, he shall point out witnesses who serve as evidence; or "another ground," meaning he shall point out documents and so forth—this is the meaning.
Nārada [3.163]:
When there are two litigants and there are witnesses for both parties...
The plaintiff shall be his [the defendant's] opponent, and there shall be witnesses for him.
Yājñavalkya [2.17]:
When witnesses exist on both sides, the witnesses belong to the plaintiff;
when the initial claim has been refuted, they belong to the defendant.
"Of the plaintiff" (*pūrvavādinaḥ*) means one who asserts, "I purchased it and accepted it at an earlier time.
"That in which the priority of the plaintiff's claim arises from the force of the facts..."
In that dispute, the witnesses of the defendant shall be questioned there.

[89] But when the prima facie argument regarding the establishment of the cause has been refuted, the defendant must indeed act with diligence; he should be understood as being like the proponent of the prima facie case.

"In the case of establishing a cause" refers to a rebuttal (*pratyavaskandana*). "As in the case of the plaintiff's plea" means that just as the plaintiff establishes his own position when there is a plea of denial (*mithyottara*), so too should the defendant who asserts a cause establish his own position; this is the meaning.
Vyāsa states: "By means of a document of victory in a prior trial, and likewise by the presiding judge and others..."
The speaker of truth attains [his goal], for what has been declared does not fail him.
A "speaker of truth" is one who speaks according to reality, namely the plaintiff.
Thus ends the section on the *pratyākalita* (the defendant's response).
14 — Now begins the section on ritual action (kriyāpāda).
Regarding the subject matter of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
Bṛhaspati states [4.5]:
Having heard the plaintiff's case,
the members of the court shall direct that he who has made the assertion prove his entire claim by means of written documents and other evidence.
Kātyāyana [213, 222]:
That which is intended by the proponent to be clearly established for himself is the *sādhya* (the thesis);
that by which the *sādhya* is entirely established is the *sādhana* (the proof).
Having set aside the essential point, one might accomplish many non-essential actions; however, one should abandon whatever action is devoid of essence.
One should abandon from afar that ritual action which establishes two opposing positions;
for he who abandons a powerful action and resorts to a weak one [reaps the consequences].
Once his victory has been determined by the members of the court, he shall not undergo that legal procedure again.
But once the legal proceeding has concluded, there shall be the fruit of the means of proof.
[91] Neither a written document nor even witnesses are admissible if they were not previously presented.

Just as the qualities of the rainy season are fruitless when the grains have already ripened, so too would the means of valid cognition be useless for those whose worldly affairs have already been accomplished.
Yājñavalkya [2.78]:
Thereafter, the plaintiff shall immediately have the proof of the matter asserted written down;
upon its establishment, he attains success, but otherwise, the opposite occurs.

The term "plaintiff" (*arthin*) is used to include both types of claimants; for by the definition of being one who seeks the establishment of his own position, both are encompassed. Nārada [1.6] states:
"The plaint (*pratijñā*) is declared to be the essence of legal proceedings."
Upon its abandonment, the proponent is defeated; by surpassing it, the opponent becomes victorious.
‘Taran’ means carrying across; ‘uttaraḥ’ means victorious. Bṛhaspati [4, 6, 8] states:
"Action is said to be of two kinds: human as well as divine."
Each one has been divided into many ways by the seers who know reality.
Written testimony, witnesses, and inference constitute the threefold human means of proof;
while the divine means of proof, beginning with the balance and ending with sacred water, is recorded as being ninefold.
Oral testimony is of twelve kinds, written evidence is recorded as being of ten kinds;
inference is of two kinds, and divine proof is of nine kinds.

Kātyāyana [214, 233]: Witnesses, written documents, and possession—these they know as the threefold means of proof. Presumption based on a slight indication is reasoning (*yukti*), while poison and the like are the ordeals (*divya*) in this world.
A debt may be established by a written document, witnesses, or even a slight application of reasoning;
likewise, divine proof has been declared for the benefit of the subjects.
Yājñavalkya [2.22]: Written documents, possession, and witnesses are declared to be the means of proof.
In the absence of any one of these, one of the divine ordeals is prescribed.
Nārada and Bṛhaspati state:
"When a judicial procedure is conducted during the daytime in villages and cities,
and when witnesses are available, the method of divine ordeal (divya) is not to be employed."
If one party should propose human evidence and the other should propose divine evidence,
the king should accept the human evidence in that case, but not the divine procedure.
If even a human action that achieves only a partial result were to exist,
it would not be justifiable for men who speak of divine action to claim that even the former [human action] is superior to the latter.
[93] When witnesses are available, an ordeal is not declared to be the means of proof;
and when there is a written document in legal disputes, neither an ordeal nor witnesses shall be used.
"Ekadeśaprāptā" refers to that which pertains to only one part of what was asserted. Pitāmaha says:
"In disputes concerning immovable property, one should avoid ordeals."
One should establish these [matters] by means of witnesses, a written document, or possession.
Bṛhaspati [4.10]:
"But in matters such as debts and the like, one should employ human means of proof.
In cases of verbal abuse, land disputes, and when there is a dispute regarding what was given, what was not given, or what was taken back by the owners, one should not employ divine ordeals.
When a dispute arises concerning a sale or a gift, or when one has received wealth but does not wish to relinquish it, or in the case of a dispute involving gambling and betting; |||
For guilds, trade associations, and assemblies, it is declared that witnesses are the means of proof, neither divine ordeals nor written documents; such is the established rule proclaimed for them.
[94] However, the means of proof for that [title] is documentary evidence, and not divine ordeals nor witnesses;
this applies likewise to matters concerning doors, paths, works, possession, watercourses, and so forth.
In cases of physical injury, indeed, possession alone shall be weighty evidence, and neither ordeal nor witnesses;
likewise in a lawsuit concerning violence, verbal abuse, or threats involving punishment.
In matters arising from force, both witnesses and ordeals are admissible.

"Having given, he takes back" refers to when one has promised "it is given" but has not yet delivered it; "likewise having taken" refers to when it has been seized again after being returned. This is said "when there is a determination regarding the owners," meaning when there is a certainty as to whose property this is and whose that is. The meaning is that in disputes concerning what was given and what was not given, witnesses are the authority, and neither divine ordeal nor a written document is required. "Wealth" means in the form of its value. The word "unwilling" implies unwilling to give; this is the ellipsis. Vyāsa says: "Divine proof is said to be of two kinds: that performed in secret and that performed publicly."
An act committed in secret by divine means must be brought to light by witnesses.
"Bhāvyam" means it must be cleared up.
Bṛhaspati says: "But when a written document or the testimony of witnesses becomes subject to doubt..."
When one is confused by inference, there is the divine means of purification in that regard.
In cases of treason against the king and in acts of violence, one should employ divine proof (*daivikī kriyā*).
"In a lonely forest, at night, or within a private dwelling, in cases of violence..."
And in the case of the denial of a deposit, a divine ordeal may indeed be employed.
When no witness is found for men litigating in a dispute,
then one should examine them by means of ordeals and various kinds of oaths.
This same rule is prescribed for women in cases of an assault on their character, as well as in theft and acts of violence,
and in all instances of denial of a debt.
Kātyāyana [230, 224]:
Where a downfall is incurred—whether by the amputation of a limb or even by death—the plaintiff may propose an ordeal;
he should cause it to be administered by those who possess correct vision.
But for those who have committed secret acts of violence, examination by means of ordeals is appropriate,
as well as [examination] through subtle reasoning, hints, facial expressions, speech, the eyes, and gestures of men.
In a legal proceeding where there is no document and no witness, one should assign it to divine means;
when a matter is to be settled by divine means, one should not employ human evidence or a written document.
Bṛhaspati [4.14, 21]: A forger of gems, pearls, and coins; one who misappropriates a deposit;
a perpetrator of violence; and one who consorts with another's wife—these should always be examined by means of oaths.
In cases of grave accusations of great crimes, as well as in the misappropriation of deposits,
the king should examine the matter by means of ordeals, even when witnesses are present.
When witnesses have been silent for a long time, or when they have long since disappeared,
or when they are found to be equally corrupt, the matter must be cleared by means of ordeals.
"In those done long ago" means in those performed in the distant past and in those performed in secret. "Among equals" means among similar [persons].
Vyāsa says:
"Where the first [witnesses] differ, and the others likewise..."
And likewise, he should bring that dispute before others by means of oaths.
"They differ" means they disagree.
Kātyāyana [232, 231]:
Where there is equality among witnesses, one should verify it even by means of ordeals.
In disputes where life is at stake, even when witnesses are present.

In such cases, the litigant may resort to divine proof; however, he should not question witnesses therein. But in all cases involving the highest crimes and acts of violence, Bhṛgu maintains that one should determine the truth by means of divine proof even when competent witnesses are present.

"Where there is equality among the witnesses" means where the witnesses are equal—that is, where they possess equal status—and where they are equal in number, even for both parties, namely the plaintiff and the defendant. Vyāsa states:
"This document was not made by me; it is a forgery commissioned by him."
Having set aside that document, the decision regarding the matter shall be made by means of divine proof.
[97] Prajāpati: When a document written under certain names and lineages may be equal to another document in some respect,
but the money has not been received, a decision in that case must be made by means of an ordeal.

The meaning is that when another document, written with names and lineages identical to those in the original document, contains a contradictory sense, then having rendered that [original] invalid, a decision must be made by means of an ordeal.
Kātyāyana [238]:
"If a document containing fraud should have been presented to the king..."
There, the king, seated upon the seat of justice, should purify [the matter] by means of the divine ordeal.
"Sopādha" means accompanied by fraud.
Nārada and Kātyāyana [state]:
"The means of proof must be diligently upheld by those who know the means of proof."
For means of valid cognition collapse when they themselves are not established by means of valid cognition.

"Indeed, the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) fail. The meaning is that by operating upon what is not their proper object, the pramāṇas become unsettled; they fail and do not produce a definitive determination.
Thus ends the section on the objects of the pramāṇas in the Kriyāpāda [98].
15— Now, regarding witnesses,
Nārada says [at 4.147]:
"But in cases where there is doubt between two parties disputing..."
Because of having seen, heard, or experienced [the object], the manifestation [of it] occurs for witnesses.
Manu [8.74]: "Testimony is established through seeing in person and also through hearing.

The mention of "seeing in person" and "hearing" is for the purpose of indicating any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in general; therefore, the meaning is that he who has experienced the subject of dispute by means of any such valid cognition is a witness.
Kātyāyana says: "The testimony of witnesses must be accepted as it was experienced in the presence of both the plaintiff and the defendant; otherwise, it is not valid, according to Bṛhaspati."
"Eleven kinds of witnesses are seen in the treatises by the wise;
among them, five are said to be appointed and three unappointed."
The written witness, the reminded witness, the witness by chance,
the secret witness, and the corroborating witness— thus the witness is declared to be of five kinds.
Nārada and Kātyāyana state:
"Furthermore, others who have not been specifically designated are declared to be witnesses—
the village headman, the presiding judge, and the king for those engaged in legal proceedings."
Those who are insiders in legal matters, those sent by a litigant, and kinsmen in family disputes— these also may be witnesses.
Bṛhaspati [5.4, 13]: The written, the caused-to-be-written, the secret, the reminded, the hereditary, the messenger,
the incidental, the subsequent, and another who is involved in the midst of the matter.
The king, the official, and likewise the village headman are recorded as the twelve kinds of witnesses;
I shall explain their distinctions correctly and in due order.
He by whom one's own caste, name, paternal lineage,
and place of residence have been recorded should be known as a witness designated as "written."
That which is recorded in writing after one has performed a transaction involving money-lending and the like through various acts for the sake of a purpose,
and which is witnessed, is declared to be a "written document" (lekhita).
[100] But he who, being made to hear the debtor's statement while separated by a wall,
denies it as it truly was, is declared to be a concealed witness.
One who is summoned and made a witness in a matter such as a debt or the delivery of a deposit,
and who is repeatedly reminded, is called a "reminded" (smārita) witness.
In matters of partitioning inheritance or in trade, where a kinsman is designated who is common to both parties and is learned in the Dharma, he is proclaimed to be a *kulya*.
But he who, having been dispatched, hears the statements of both the plaintiff and the defendant,
being approved by both and being virtuous— he is declared to be a *dūtaka*.
But when a duty is being performed, whoever happens to arrive of his own accord and says, "I am a witness for us," he is called an incidental witness.
Where a witness, while departing for another direction or when about to die, causes another to hear [the testimony] exactly as it was heard,
one should know that person to be a subsequent witness (uttara-sākṣin).
Vyāsa:
That witness who gives testimony again and again,
whether by hearing it himself or by causing others to hear it, is designated as an *uttara-sākṣin* (a secondary witness).
Bṛhaspati and Kātyāyana state:
"He whose affairs or business have been entrusted by both parties,
and who likewise remains within the midst of the proceedings, should be known as a *gūḍhacārī* (secret agent)."
[101] Whatever statement of the plaintiff and the defendant has been heard by the king himself, that alone shall serve as the witness there in a dispute between the two.
But when a legal case has been decided and a retrial should take place, the presiding judge, together with the members of the court, shall act as witnesses therein; it cannot be otherwise.

"Where trust is placed in both": the meaning is that he in whom confidence has been reposed by both the plaintiff and the defendant is to be understood as a secret agent operating within the midst of the legal proceedings. Kātyāyana [355]:
"The scribe, the presiding judge, and the members of the court, in their proper order..."
When the king observes that matter, witnesses are summoned.
Bṛhaspati [5.18]: Where something has been stolen or killed within the vicinity of a boundary,
the village shall undoubtedly be considered a witness there, even if it was not formally appointed as one.
Manu [8.76]: Where one might see or hear anything that is not recorded,
even there, when questioned, one should speak it exactly as seen and exactly as heard.
Kātyāyana [352]: Where it is impossible for witnesses from foreign lands to arrive,
one should cause a document composed by those learned in the three Vedas to be read as evidence.
[102] ‘Āgama’ means coming. Manu [8.60]:
“But one who, having been questioned, denies [a debt], while his status as a debtor is established for those seeking wealth...”
The case should be decided by at least three witnesses in the presence of the king and the Brahmins.

"Questioned" by the judge; "denying," that is, making a denial; "one who has been placed under restraint," meaning one whose confinement or restriction has been established by means of legal injunctions and the like; "to be proved," meaning to be demonstrated. Bṛhaspati [5.1, 19, 2]:
There may be nine, seven, five, four, or even three [witnesses].
Or both may be learned in the Vedas and renowned; one should never consult with only one.

Two who have written [the document], as well as two who are secret witnesses, those who have written three, four, or five times, those recalled by chance, members of the same family, and likewise secondary witnesses (uttara-sākṣins).
A messenger, a scribe, one who has entered into the midst of the business,
as well as the king and the presiding official— each of these alone may be an authority.
"Two are written," meaning these two serve as witnesses, whereas others—excluding messengers and the like—must be at least three in number. Yājñavalkya [2.72]:
Even a single person may be a witness if he is approved by both parties and is a knower of the Dharma.
Vyāsa says: A witness who is pure in conduct, knows the dharma, and speaks from personal experience shall be authoritative even if he is alone, especially in cases of violent crimes.
‘Anubhūtavāk’ refers to one whose speech has been experienced as true;
[Kātyāyana 353–354]:
"But in the case of an internal deposit, even a single witness can be contradicted."
A witness sent by a plaintiff becomes competent even if he is alone and has been formally requested.
Whatever has been refined by someone, that merchandise he alone shall determine;
in a dispute concerning it, he alone is declared to be the authority.

"That by which the merchandise was refined" means that whatever merchandise, such as earrings and the like, has been fashioned by a goldsmith or similar artisan, that should be proven by that very person as a witness.
Nārada [4.167]:
"Even after a very long period of time, a written document attains validity."
One who understands his own writing may cause one who does not understand it to write.

[104] One who does not know how to write should not have it written. This is the meaning here: at the time when one is about to write, if he does not know how to write himself, but has another person who knows writing write for him, saying, "I, so-and-so, an inhabitant of such-and-such village, the son of so-and-so, am the witness," then even he shall attain success after a long time. Kātyāyana [370]:
Furthermore, if he has ascended with his own hand and stands alone, he is indeed that very person.
If he should not recognize it, then he himself should settle the matter with his own hands.
In this world, the testimony of a witness who has been reminded is valid from the eighth year onwards;
likewise, the testimony of one who has appeared spontaneously is valid up to the fifth year.
The validity of a secret witness is established up to three years;
however, they say that the validity of a subsequent witness is established for one year.
Alternatively, no fixed time limit has been observed regarding witnesses;
for those learned in the scriptures say that witnesshood depends upon memory.
He whose intellect and memory are never impaired, and whose sense of hearing remains constant even over a very long period of time, is indeed worthy to serve as a witness.
I shall fully describe the kind of witnesses who should be made by litigants in legal proceedings, and how truth must be spoken by them.

[105] "Householders, those with sons, hereditary residents, and those born of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes— having stated this, they alone are worthy to give testimony, and not just anyone, except in times of emergency."
Witnesses may be drawn from all castes for all legal matters;
they should be those who know all the laws and are free from greed, while one should avoid those who are the opposite.
‘Ṛta’ means truth. ‘Maulāḥ’ refers to those born of well-known lineages.
Yājñavalkya [2.68–69]:
Ascetics, those of a charitable disposition, those of noble birth, and speakers of truth.
Those who prioritize righteousness, who are upright, who have sons, and who are endowed with wealth—

Witnesses should be known as at least three in number, devoted to the performance of Vedic and Smṛti rites; they are traditionally held to be either according to their respective caste and class, or all may serve for all.

Gautama [13.2–4]: "There should be many blameless men who are trustworthy in their own duties toward kings, free from both affection and aversion toward either side; this applies even to Śūdras. [106] "'Trustworthy toward kings' means those who inspire confidence in kings. 'Free from affection and aversion' means those devoid of friendliness and [hostile] treatises. Kātyāyana [347–348]: "And those of renowned family and character, free from greed and delusion..."
The word of those who are authoritative, disciplined, and awakened is undoubtedly [the truth].
A witness should be examined by the litigant in such a manner that he may be cross-examined by those of equal status;
one should never examine a superior witness through inferior witnesses.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "Now, regarding witnesses: a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) who is virtuous, handsome, a youth, and of good character; likewise a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya or Śūdra who is righteous and endowed with good conduct; one who is known for his performance of ritual acts, but not one person alone. Vyāsa says:
"Or that which is bestowed through the power of jewels, mantras, or medicinal herbs, according to the prescribed rule."
A witness endowed with good qualities should not give false testimony, even regarding a divine ordeal.
Nārada [4.155]:
In guilds, members of the guild; in their own groups, those belonging to the group;
among outsiders, outsiders; and among women, women shall be witnesses.

[107] Kātyāyana [3.49–350]: Bhṛgu spoke concerning those who bear sectarian marks, guilds and corporations, those born of the merchant class, and others who stand in assemblies, as well as other groups.
The leaders of the various groups consisting of slaves, wandering performers, wrestlers, and those who live by elephants, horses, and weapons,
are known as the *vargiṇas*.
Their testimony shall be given by their own groups, and those group members are the witnesses.
Manu and Kātyāyana [M. 8.68; K.
351] state: "Women shall give testimony for women, and the best of the twice-born for the twice-born."
And those who are Śūdras among Śūdras are mortals born from mortal wombs.

Thus ends the section on Witnesses in the Section on Judicial Procedure within the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, the son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara and the Great Minister for Peace and War. [108]
16— Now, regarding those who are not witnesses,
Nārada [states in verses 4.157–158]:
"Indeed, even those who are not witnesses are seen in the treatises to be of five kinds by the learned."
Because of the statement, because of the fault, and because of the difference, there is a self-statement by another being.

Where there is a conflict among witnesses due to differences— such as those who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and others based on their testimony, or thieves and others based on the observation of their faults— in such a dispute, [the decision shall be made otherwise].
One who, being unappointed as a witness, comes of his own accord and speaks, is considered self-accused;
he is as good as dead even while the claimant is still alive, except in the case of one who has been informed by someone about to die.
Vedic scholars, ascetics, the elderly, and those men who have renounced the world are not witnesses; no reason for this has been stated here.
Thieves, violent men, the fierce, gamblers, and those who play with five dice—these are non-witnesses because of their wickedness; in them, truth is not found.
Manu [8.64]: "Neither those with a financial interest, nor friends, nor associates, nor enemies;
nor those whose guilt has been previously observed, nor those afflicted by disease, nor those who are corrupt should be appointed as witnesses."
156]: A slave, a deceitful person, one lacking faith, an old man, a woman, a child,
a deceiver, one intoxicated, insane, negligent, afflicted, a gambler, and a village priest;
Great travelers, sea-faring merchants, renunciants, and the sick;
those with missing limbs, Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*), those lacking proper conduct, eunuchs, and professional musicians.

Atheists, those who have abandoned their wives and the sacred fire, those who officiate at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, those who eat from a single vessel, companions of enemies, and those related by birth to such persons.

Actors whose faults have been previously observed, those who live by the arts of others, snake-charmers, poisoners, incendiaries, usurers, the sons of Śūdra women, and those who approach women for illicit purposes;

[110] Those who are exhausted, reckless, tireless, and utterly devoid of final resolve; those of broken conduct, those who have not returned to their vows, water-carriers, oil-pressers, and root-diggers.

Those possessed by spirits, those hostile to kings, those who predict rain or the positions of the stars, those who proclaim misfortune, those who sell themselves, and those whose limbs are deficient or whose livelihood is based on fortune-telling;

One with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one afflicted with white leprosy, a betrayer of friends, a rogue, a vintner, a magician, a hunter, a cruel person, one belonging to a guild, and one who opposes a corporate body;
A murderer, a painter, a potter, one who has fallen from his caste, a forger, a cheat, a debtor, a thief, and a royal officer;
A Brāhmaṇa who sells human beings, cattle, meat, bones, honey, milk, water, or clarified butter, as well as a twice-born man who is a usurer— [these are excluded from the Śrāddha].
[111] One who has fallen away from his own duty, a member of a guild, a slanderer, a servant of the lowly, one who disputes with his father, and a creator of dissension— these are non-witnesses.
But in guilds and other such associations, if someone should incur the state of being hated by another,
he shall not be a witness for that person, for all of them are his haters.

‘Naikṛtika’ means a deceiver. ‘Aśraddha’ means one devoid of faith. ‘Mahāpathika’ means a long-distance traveler. ‘Kuśīlava’ means one who lives by the stage (an actor). ‘Ekasthālī’ means one who eats from a single cooking-pot. ‘Aridhara’ means a bearer of weapons. ‘Āhituṇḍika’ means a snake-catcher. ‘Upapātika’ means one overcome by a mortal sin. ‘Sāhasika’ means one who acts impulsively without reflection. ‘Aśrānta’ means one who performs improper acts. ‘Nirdhūta’ means one expelled from the village, the royal court, guilds, and so forth. ‘Bhinnavṛtta’ means one who does not abide by his own duty. ‘Mūlika’ refers to one who practices deception, which is the root (*mūla*) of such conduct. ‘Śaṅkha’ means one whose habit is to wander for alms while mimicking a bull. ‘Pratyavasita’ means one who has fallen away from the life of renunciation. ‘Kulika’ means one who is excluded from being a member of a family council.
A king shall not be made a witness, nor artisans or actors;
nor a learned Brahmin (*śrotriya*), nor one who dwells in a religious order (*liṅgastha*), nor one who has withdrawn from all worldly attachments.
Neither one who is dependent on another, nor one who is censurable, nor a thief, nor one who performs forbidden acts;
neither an elder, nor a child, nor one alone, nor an outcaste, nor one with impaired faculties.
[112] Neither one who is distressed, nor intoxicated, nor insane; neither one oppressed by hunger or thirst, nor afflicted by fatigue, nor tormented by desire, nor angry, nor even a thief.
‘Ādhyadhīna’ refers to one held as a pledge.
Yājñavalkya [2.70–71]:
Women, the elderly, children, gamblers, those intoxicated, the insane, and those accused of a crime;
Those who enter the stage [of performance], heretics, deceivers, and those with impaired faculties.

Outcasts, kinsmen, those with a financial interest in the case, associates, enemies, thieves, those who have been convicted of crimes involving violence, and those previously found to be unreliable— these are non-witnesses.
Bṛhaspati [5.39–40]: A mother’s father, a paternal uncle, a wife’s brother, a maternal uncle,
a brother, a friend, and a son-in-law are not witnesses in any legal dispute.
Those addicted to other men's wives or to drinking, gamblers, those who are universally despised,
the insane, the afflicted, the rash, and atheists are not to be witnesses.
Kātyāyana [362–364]:
Those who subsist on his livelihood, those who perform services for him,
his kinsmen, friends, servants, and trusted associates— these, however, are not witnesses.
[113] Likewise, the daughters of one's mother's sisters and father's sisters,
as well as the sons of one's maternal uncle and the maternal uncles of one's uterine brothers.
These are declared to be "sapinda" (blood relations); one should not employ them as witnesses.
In this same way, those who are sapinda on the father's and mother's side are to be understood.
So too are kinsmen by marriage, relatives, and the husband of one's sister.
The father, kinsmen, paternal uncles, fathers-in-law, and likewise teachers;
as well as those appointed to positions within cities, villages, and districts.
And those royal officers, being addressed, should question the beloved ones [of the accused],
provided they are neither angry, nor socially mixed, nor seated, nor afflicted by disease.
One should not determine the case by means of witnesses who are censurable or deluded;
nor should there ever be testimony from a group if its members are mutually contradictory or excluded [from the legal assembly].

[114] Now, under the heading "those who are not witnesses," Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "The official in charge of tolls, a messenger with his head wrapped, all women, those living in the teacher's household, wandering mendicants, forest-dwellers, Nirgranthas, conch-blowers, and snake-catchers. "Official in charge of tolls" (*śulkādhikṛta*) means one who holds authority over the place where taxes are collected. "Official in charge of military outposts" (*gulmādhikṛta*) refers to a troop of foot soldiers known as a *gulma*, and one who commands such a force. "Those living in the teacher's household" (*gurukulavāsinaḥ*) are celibate students (*brahmacāriṇaḥ*). A "Nirgrantha" is a Jain ascetic (*kṣapaṇaka*). Nārada [4.160, 230, 161] states: "When witnesses have been accepted by the king for the determination of a single matter..."
In a case where their testimony differs, they shall be considered non-witnesses because of that discrepancy.
But where, in a legal dispute, an equality of memory is observed among the witnesses,
the testimony is set aside from that case because of the subtle nature of the requirements for witness-status.
But he who, not having been designated as a witness, comes of his own accord and speaks,
is called a "self-proclaimed" in the legal treatises and does not deserve the status of a witness.

"Equality with witnesses possessing mindfulness" means that those who, being equal by virtue of possessing mindfulness, are twice as many, become non-witnesses when they differ in their testimony due to a divergence of statements; however, they are not non-witnesses for us [in other respects]. Kātyāyana [404, 377] states:
"A witness who has not been designated, nor summoned, nor even exhorted..."
Whether he speaks falsely or truthfully, that lowest of men should also be punished.
[115] Where the plaintiff has perished, there a witness who died subsequently shall serve;
or where the defendant has died, one should likewise arrange it in that same manner.
When a matter that ought to be made known has no claimant, where could one exercise witnesshood? Thus, one who dies in the interval is not a witness.
Even if they are virtuous, witnesses are not authoritative after the death of the debtor,
except for that which was heard by him personally when he was near death.
For when the defendant has died, the testimony of witnesses is not the means of proof;
in that case, the determination of the truth must be based on other evidentiary grounds.

Even one who has died may be considered a witness regarding a matter connected with dharma that was heard by him in the interim; this applies also in the case of the six types of persons who maintain the sacred fires.

The meaning of the passage beginning with "the matter which was to be made known" is as follows: when a claimant (*arthin*) has died after having made a witness hear the matter, that witness—being one whose name is now "deceased" (*mṛtāntara*)—is not eligible to serve as a witness. For example, if a dying claimant, such as a father, had informed his son, saying: "This much wealth, along with this interest, was given by me to Devadatta at such a time; in this matter, these are the witnesses," then [the son cannot testify]. This is because he lacks the discernment of the details of that transaction, such as the date and so forth. The claimant must inform the witnesses: "In this matter, you are to be the witnesses. Without such notification, there is no examination of the specific details to be proven, and therefore the witness is unable to fulfill his duty of making the matter known. Thus it is said: "Where could that deceased witness state his witness-status? However, when the matter has been previously informed to him by the dying man, then even after the claimant has died, they indeed remain valid witnesses.
Kātyāyana [360]: A witness appointed by one person may not be made to dispute the case by another;
in his absence, however, a relative or one specially commissioned may dispute it.
One should prove the case by means of witnesses; however, if the claimant is deceased, a kinsman may do so.
If there is a written document, one should always prove it in the presence of the family and others.
Thus end the non-witnesses.
Now follows the rebuttal of witnesses.
Regarding this, Manu and Nārada state:
"In all cases of violence, in theft and adultery,
and in both forms of verbal and physical abuse, one should not examine the witnesses."
Kātyāyana [366–367]:
In cases of contradiction with the king’s command, in battle, in acts of violence,
and likewise in theft and verbal assault, one should not examine the witnesses.
In the case of an accusation concerning what occurred inside a house at night, or outside a village,
there is no examination of witnesses here.
Manu [8.69–70]: "But whoever, being an eyewitness, should give testimony for litigants within a house, in a forest, or even when there is danger to life;"
Or it may be performed by a woman, or by a child, or by an elderly person;
or even by a disciple, a relative, a slave, or a hired servant.
One who has experienced [something] is called an *anubhāvī*.
[Examples include] Uśanas,
a slave, a blind person, a deaf person, one afflicted with leprosy, women, children, the elderly, and so forth.
These also are considered witnesses in cases of violence, even if they have no prior connection [to the parties].
Those who have been designated as non-witnesses— such as slaves, dishonest persons, and the like—
even they may become witnesses when the gravity of the matter requires it.
Among them, neither a child, nor one who is alone, nor a woman, nor a fraudulent person,
nor a kinsman, nor an enemy shall give false testimony.
A fool lies out of ignorance; a woman, out of untruthfulness; a forger, from the habit of sin;
a kinsman, from affection; and an enemy, from the desire for revenge.
Manu [8.77]: "A single witness who is free from greed may be accepted, but not women— even if they are many and pure—
because of the instability of a woman's intellect and because others as well may be corrupted by defects."
Kātyāyana [365]: One should examine witnesses in matters such as debts and in cases involving stable transactions;
however, in cases of violence and urgent offenses, examination is prescribed only in certain instances.
[119] Manu [8.71]: One should recognize that the speech of children, the elderly, and the sick who speak falsely in witness-depositions, as well as that of those with overexcited minds, is unstable.
Thus concludes the section on the removal of witnesses (120) 18;
now follows the examination of witness defects.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati [5.21] states:
"One may refute witnesses designated by the plaintiff when actual defects exist;
however, a litigant who refutes those who are faultless deserves a fine equal to the value of the claim."
Kātyāyana [278, 275]:
One should not invalidate a means of proof through a groundless defect;
rather, one who brings a false accusation shall be punished or shall lose his case.
Indeed, those defects of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that are to be stated must be pointed out by the disputant;
however, those that are obscure should be made manifest by the members of the assembly at the proper time through the citation of authoritative treatises.

The meaning is that defects which have not been pointed out by the disputant because they were unknown to him should be made manifest by means of citing the legal treatises (*śāstra*) and then declared by the members of the court.
Bṛhaspati and Kātyāyana state:
"Whatever defects of the written document (*lekhya*) there may be, as well as those attributed to the witnesses..."
They should be stated at the time of debate; however, one may refute them after they have been spoken.
Vyāsa: Whether it be well-known among the members of the assembly or even established among the common people,
the disqualification of witnesses is to be accepted, since it cannot be remedied by the absence of fault.
[121] But if the refutation of the previous witnesses were to be established by other witnesses,
there would be the fault of infinite regress, because it would be possible for those [subsequent witnesses] to have others as well.
"Unprovable because of the absence of defects"—"unprovable" means unfit for proof; "because of the absence of defects" means because it is free from defects such as infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Bṛhaspati [5.29]:
"In a legal dispute, whether the documents or the witnesses are corrupted..."
His task shall not be accomplished as long as he does not purify that [mind].
That document and the witnesses constitute the means of proof;
likewise [5.30]:
"But when a decision has been commenced by the witnesses and the members of the court having spoken..."
If he engages in a dispute again, the king shall investigate that case.
Vyāsa states:
All defects of the witnesses must be set forth by the defendant in court;
however, those [defects] which are recorded in writing must be stated as a rebuttal.
[122] However, they are never eligible to serve as witnesses regarding the performance of the act;
therefore, they must be treated otherwise by the defendant through legal procedure.

If the defendant fails to prove his case, he must be compelled to pay; witnesses who have clearly been proven [to be false] should be excluded, as they have been disqualified by the rules governing witnesses.

If the plaintiff, remaining composed before the witnesses and the members of the court, has no further desire for the case, then the defeated party shall be made to pay a fine according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures with due decorum.
"Pratyuttaram" means "in response to each answer"; the meaning is that those faults must be stated. "Anyathā" means in the case of non-admission. Kātyāyana [407, 379]:
"By whomsoever, out of greed for a matter, false witnesses have been pointed out..."
Having confiscated his entire property, he should then banish him from the realm.
But he who, after witnesses have been cited for the matter at hand, should find fault with those previously unimpeached and yet cannot state the reason for that, shall incur the first amercement.
regarding the examination of witnesses,
Kātyāyana states [at verse 339]:
A king must not allow a delay in the testimony of witnesses;
for from such delay there arises a great fault characterized by the subversion of dharma.

Nārada [4.198]: Having summoned the witnesses and bound them firmly with oaths, he should question them individually— provided they are all present, their conduct is known, and they have understood the matter at hand.
Viṣṇu [8.19]: "Having summoned the witnesses at sunrise and having made them take oaths, he shall question them. Kātyāyana [388–390]:
"In the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant, and in the presence of the matter to be proven..."
One should present testimony when it is directly perceived, and never in any way when it is out of sight.
The meaning should be stated above [the verse], even without those two in some cases;
this rule applies to quadrupeds as well as to bipeds and immovable things.
For even in the absence of things measurable by weight, number, or quantity, one may indeed act as a witness in all formal legal proceedings; it cannot be otherwise.
‘Weighable’ refers to gold and the like; ‘countable’ refers to cowries and the like; ‘measurable’ refers to rice and the like; and ‘in transactions’ means in legal dealings.
“In the presence of the gods and Brahmins, he should question the twice-born regarding witness testimony with truth.”
Facing north or facing east, being pure himself, [he should honor] those who are pure during the forenoon.
In the midst of the assembly, the presiding judge, while consoling them, shall examine all the witnesses in the presence of both the plaintiff and the defendant according to this rule.
Whatever you two know of each other’s conduct regarding this matter, tell it all in truth; for your testimony is required here.
A witness who speaks the truth in testimony attains abundant worlds;
and in this world, he gains unsurpassed fame—this speech is honored by Brahmā.
A witness who speaks falsely while testifying shall be bound by the nooses of Varuṇa for a hundred births, rendered powerless; therefore, one should speak the truth when testifying.
A witness is purified by truth; dharma increases through truth.
Therefore, truth must indeed be spoken by witnesses among all social classes.
For the self alone is the witness of the self, and the self is likewise the refuge of the self.
Do not despise your own self; for among men, the state of being one's own witness is supreme.
Evil-doers think, "No one sees us," but the gods see them, as does the inner person within oneself.
Heaven, earth, water, the heart, the moon, sun, fire, Yama, wind, night,
the two twilights, and Dharma are the witnesses of the conduct of all embodied beings.
"In the assembly" means in the midst of the court. "He should interrogate" means he should question. "A hundred births" means a hundred lifetimes.
Yājñavalkya [2.73–74]:
The plaintiff should cause the witnesses to hear [the charges] while they are in the presence of the defendant.
Those worlds which belong to the perpetrators of minor sins, as well as those of the great sinners;
Whatever worlds belong to those who set fire to dwellings and whatever worlds belong to those who kill women and children—
all of those he attains who gives false testimony.
126] Bṛhaspati: The members of the court, who are well-versed in the treatises on dharma, must address the litigants with words praising truth and rejecting falsehood.
Whatever merit has been acquired from birth until death—
all that goes to ruin by the false accusation of another.
A corrupt judge, a false witness, and a slayer of a Brahmin are declared to be equal;
a destroyer of an embryo or a stealer of wealth is said to be no greater than these.
Having understood this, the witness should speak exactly as it is;
thereby he attains fame in this world and a blessed state in the next.
Regarding the calling of witnesses, Viṣṇu and Nārada state:
"A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were placed upon a scale;
indeed, truth alone outweighed the thousand horse-sacrifices."
One should also greatly terrify [the witness] with ancient declarations of dharma that demonstrate the greatness of truth and the censures against falsehood.
[127] He who would give false testimony would see his enemies once more when he is besieged within a city and hungry at the outer gate.
The night that a woman is wedded, the night that one is defeated at dice, and the night that one whose limbs are tormented by a heavy burden speaks wickedly— in all these, he shall dwell.
A witness who, when questioned regarding the matter at hand, behaves with the laxity of a cow’s ear,
fastens upon himself a thousand nooses of Varuṇa.
When a hundred years of that period have been completed, one noose is released;
in this manner, he is certainly liberated from that bondage in due course.
That which they call the one, without a second, the purifier of the self—
truth is the stairway to heaven, like a boat for crossing the ocean.
A single large tank is better than a hundred wells; a sacrifice is better than a hundred tanks;
a son is better than a hundred sacrifices; and truth is better than a hundred sons.
The earth supports all by means of truth; by truth the sun rises;
by truth the wind blows; and by truth the waters flow.
Truth alone is the supreme abode; truth alone is the supreme austerity;
truth alone is the supreme dharma for all worlds—thus have we heard.
In brief, O gods, truth is the mark of humans, while falsehood is traditionally held to be their nature;
yet he whose mind is established in truth attains divinity even in this very world.
There is no dharma higher than truth, and no sin greater than falsehood;
especially regarding the duty of a witness, one should therefore speak only the truth.
In this regard, two verses approved by the Purāṇas are cited here,
hearing which wise men should always speak only the truth in this world.
That lowest of men who, for the sake of another, betrays his own word—
fearless of hell, what sin would he not commit for his own sake?
Meanings are indeed fixed in speech; they have their root in speech and have issued forth from speech.
That man who steals that speech is a thief of everything.
"Acting with the looseness of a Gokarṇa" means conducting oneself as loosely as a Gokarṇa, that is, not speaking firmly. Baudhāyana says:
"He destroys three fathers and indeed three grandfathers."
A witness who speaks falsely regarding testimony concerning seven past births and those yet to come, [is reborn]...
One kills five by lying regarding cattle, one kills ten by lying regarding cows;
one kills a hundred by lying regarding horses, and one kills a thousand by lying regarding men.
