A witness who speaks falsely in testimony destroys everything pertaining to the earth.
Thus ends the hearing of witnesses [130]. Now follows the oath of the witnesses.

Regarding this, Gautama states: "Some hold that the act of establishing truth is by means of an oath; that should take place in the assembly of the King of the Gods (Indra), a Brāhmaṇa, or [the king] himself, for those who are not Brāhmaṇas.
"The act of establishing truth" (*satyakarma*) refers to the formal determination of the truth.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "Witnesses [should swear] by means of gold, silver, gems, cows, grain, the sun, fire, the shoulder of an elephant, the back of a horse, the seat of a chariot, weapons, and so forth, as well as by their sons and grandsons, according to their respective castes and specific status, in the presence of the gods, Brāhmaṇas, and the owner [of the property in dispute]."

"By touching gold and other such items, and by looking at the sun and other such objects"—the word "one should cause him to swear" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Likewise, "by sons and grandsons" means that for a minor matter, one should cause him to swear by touching the heads of his sons and grandsons. "According to the caste" means that whichever substance is prescribed for swearing by a particular caste, he should be made to swear by that very thing, according to another Smṛti text.
Nārada [4.199]:
One should cause a Brāhmaṇa to swear by truth, and a Kṣatriya by vehicles and weapons.
A Vaiśya by means of cattle, seeds, and gold; but a Śūdra by all the aforementioned sins.

The statement "one should cause a Brahmin to swear by means of truth" refers specifically to a degraded Brahmin, not to Brahmins in general; for Gautama has prohibited oaths for [ordinary] Brahmins. "One should cause to hear" (śrāvayet) means "one should cause to swear. Manu and Nārada state in the sixth [chapter]:
"One should ask a Brahmin, 'Speak!'; one should ask a king, 'Speak the truth!'"
A Vaiśya by [stealing] cows, seeds, or gold; and a Śūdra by these same [five] heinous crimes.
Whatever worlds are ordained for the slayer of a Brahmin, and those for the killers of women and children,
and for the betrayer of friends and the ungrateful— those shall be the fate of one who speaks falsely.
O Bhadra, whatever merit you have accumulated since birth—
all of that would go to a dog if you were to speak otherwise.
O virtuous one, you who think of yourself, "I am alone," this sage who observes merit and demerit dwells eternally within your heart.
[132] If you have no dispute with that god Yama Vaivasvata who resides within your heart, then do not go to the Gaṅgā, and do not go to the Kurus.
Naked, shaven-headed, carrying a skull-bowl, and tormented by hunger and thirst,
he who gives false testimony shall go to the house of his enemy in a state of rage.
Headlong into blind darkness shall the sinner go to hell,
he who, when questioned regarding the determination of dharma, speaks falsely.
Like a blind man eating fish heedlessly along with their bones, so is he who,
having entered the assembly, speaks what is inconsistent with the facts and not based on direct perception.
For the gods know no other man in this world to be superior to him, whose inner self (kṣetrajña) does not harbor suspicion when he speaks as a wise man.
Manu and Nārada say: Hear now, O gentle one, in due order and according to their number, how many kinsmen a man destroys by speaking falsely when giving testimony in that particular case.
[133] One kills five by lying about cattle; one kills ten by lying about cows;
one kills a hundred by lying about horses; one kills a thousand by lying about men.
By speaking a falsehood for the sake of gold, one destroys both those who are born and those yet unborn;
by a falsehood regarding land, one destroys everything. Therefore, do not speak a falsehood regarding land.
Manu [8.100–101]: "They say that with regard to water, sexual intercourse with women, and all aquatic gems as well as those made of stone, the rule is the same as for land."

Regarding honey and ghee, one should behave like a beast; likewise regarding vehicles, like a horse; regarding silver and clothing, like a cow; and regarding grain and indeed Brahmins, [one should behave] exactly like a cow.
Consider all these faults in speaking untruth;

‘In gems born from water’ refers to pearls, coral, and the like; ‘in the Brahman’ refers to the Veda.
“Speak the truth, having abandoned falsehood; through truth you shall attain heaven.”
Having spoken a most terrible falsehood, you shall fall into hell.
And in the hells, those powerful and cruel servants of Yama will constantly cut out their tongues and sever them with swords.
Trampling him as he cries out for help and having no refuge, they will slowly tear him apart;
lifting him up with his head hanging down, they will throw him into fires and into lakes.
Having experienced those most painful torments of hell for a long time,
you will go here to the wombs of unworthy beings, such as vultures, crows, and the like.
Having understood these faults in falsehood as well as the virtues in truths, speak the truth and uplift yourself; do not cast yourself down by your own hand.
Neither kinsmen, nor friends, nor even great riches are able to support one who is sinking into the darkness of death.
The ancestors hang upon you now that you have become their witness;
will you deliver us, or will you cause us to fall?
Truth is the self of a human being; everything is established in truth.
By every means, you should employ the self for the sake of the highest good.
The interval between the night you were born and the night you will die would be spent in vain for you, if you should speak falsely as a witness.

Whatever merit has been performed by you through actions in previous births,

yet desire the status of the twice-born— one should treat them just like Śūdras.
The meaning is that even these Brāhmaṇas, being such as they are, must have an oath administered to them in testimony just like a Śūdra.
Thus ends the section on the oath for witnesses.
21. Now, the rule regarding witnesses. On this point, Kātyāyana [387, 391] states: "Witnesses must deliver their testimony while standing within the court; it is not to be given elsewhere."
This rule applies to all types of testimony, except in cases concerning immovable property.

When something is seen correctly with an undisturbed mind, that is considered direct perception; the witness should speak of that which is to be proven as such.
"In the absence of that" means in the absence of Śiva; "in the vicinity of the mark" means in the presence of bones, hair, and so forth. Bṛhaspati [5.42]:
Having set aside his sandals and turban, he should raise his right hand.
Having taken gold, cow dung, and darbha grass, one should carry out the rite of truth.
Gautama [13.6]: "Those who are not members of the assembly shall not speak unless questioned. "Not members" means those who have not assembled. Kātyāyana [394–395]:
"But that which has been seen by those who are members of the assembly must be stated by them exactly as it was seen."
And that which has many different forms should not be spoken of as a single entity, but rather as distinct and separate.
But when a matter is learned by witnesses at different times, Bhṛgu says that one should cause each of them to testify separately; for that is what constitutes testimony given at different times.
Witnesses who have arrived at the place of legal dispute must not, unless asked or appointed, voluntarily speak the truth with effort; rather, they must testify when questioned.
"Not having a single task" means "having many tasks. "By those not appointed" means by those not presented as witnesses.
Baudhāyana [1.20.29]: "People should give testimony according to what they have seen and heard for the sake of receiving [the reward]. Manu [8.74]:

In that regard, a witness who speaks the truth does not fall away from dharma or worldly prosperity. Kātyāyana [393] states: "The testimony of those witnesses should be accepted as it was spoken spontaneously, provided it is free from defects."
Once the witnesses have been addressed by the king, they should not be questioned again and again.
Thus ends the rule regarding the testimony of witnesses [138].
22. Now follows the examination of witnesses.
Kātyāyana [340, 409]:
The king himself should examine the witnesses who have been presented;
he should examine the statement spoken by the witnesses together with the members of the court.
When pure action is to be maintained, then its verbal expression must be purified;
that which is pure because it consists of words with pure meaning is truly pure in meaning, but not otherwise.
In this context, "action" (*kriyā*) refers to the means of proof consisting of witnesses. Bṛhaspati [5.43] states:
"Those who have appeared must be examined by their voice, complexion, gestures, and so forth."
[139] In that regard, false witnesses:

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "The ministers should discern the signs of a wicked person by means of their expertise in the treatises. He casts side-long glances; he looks all around; he voids urine or excrement without cause; he moves from place to place; he squeezes one hand with the other; he bites his nails; his face becomes discolored; his forehead perspires; he does not respond to the eye or the speech [of others]; he gives gifts or offers praise without cause; he repeatedly dismisses another; he gazes outside; he touches upon the scriptures [or reflects on them]; [he describes his grief]; he scratches the ground; he shakes his head; he distorts his lips; he licks the corners of his mouth; though not surprised, he furrows his brows during great undertakings; he laughs; he meditates in silence; he speaks in a manner contradictory to what precedes or follows—such are the signs of a wicked person. And this applies to a master when he is angry, except for his natural disposition. In that regard, legal proceedings have the king as their root."

Regarding the phrase "and of one who is angry," these very same signs are to be observed by ministers even in the case of a king who is possessed by anger. "Except for his natural disposition" means that these are the characteristics of a wicked person, distinct from one who is naturally of such a character. He states the purpose for ascertaining the king's anger: "Legal proceedings have their root in the king"; the word "since" (*yat*) is to be understood as the remainder of the sentence.
But he who, because of being corrupted by his own faults, appears as if unwell,
moves from place to place and pursues each one in turn.
He coughs suddenly and violently, sighs repeatedly,
scratches the ground with his feet, and shakes his arms and clothing.
His facial complexion changes, his forehead perspires,
his lips become parched, and he looks upward and sideways.
He who speaks much without being asked, as if in haste, even though he has not witnessed the event, should be known as a false witness; one should severely punish that sinner.
He who, having caused others to hear [the testimony], then denies his status as a witness, must be punished even more severely;
for he is worse than a false witness.
‘Āviddha’ means confused.
Now, the punishment for witnesses.
In this regard, Kātyāyana [406] states:
"Those who speak otherwise than what was stated, being possessed of verbal quibbling (vākchala), shall be punished."
Manu [8.118–123]: "False testimony is given out of greed, delusion, fear, friendship, lust, anger, as well as from ignorance and childishness."
Whosoever among these, in his respective position, should give false testimony— I shall now declare the specific punishments for him in due order.
For an offense committed out of greed, the fine is one thousand; for one out of delusion, it is the first *sāhasa*;
for one out of fear, the two middle *sāhasas* are to be imposed as the fine; and for one out of friendship, four times the first *sāhasa*.
It is said that [the merit] from desire is tenfold; from anger, it is three times greater than that;
from ignorance, it is two full hundreds; and from childishness, it is exactly one hundred.
The wise have declared that these are the punishments prescribed for false testimony,
for the purpose of ensuring the non-deviation of dharma and for the restraint of adharma.
A righteous king, having punished them, shall banish members of the three [lower] castes who give false testimony, but he shall only exile Brāhmaṇas.

"Thousand" refers to *paṇas*, as is the understood remainder. "Through delusion" means through negligence; "the first *sāhasa*" is two hundred and fifty *paṇas*. "Two middle [fines]" means two *sāhasas*; thus, one thousand *paṇas* is what is expressed. One thousand *paṇas* is said to be four times the first *sāhasa*. "The highest is threefold": the highest, namely the middle *sāhasa*, when tripled in relation to the previous [fine], results in fifteen hundred. "Through ignorance" means through a misconception at the very time of the legal proceeding. "Folly" here refers merely to having reached the age of youth, not actual childhood, because a child is prohibited from being a witness. "He shall banish" means he shall expel him from his own country.
Viṣṇu [5.179]: "The confiscation of all property should be carried out for false witnesses.
Yājñavalkya [2.81–82]:
"The forger and the witnesses shall each be punished separately."
In the case of a dispute, the fine is declared to be double; however, a Brāhmaṇa is to be banished.
He who, when testimony has been heard from others, conceals it out of being shrouded in darkness, shall be made to pay an eightfold fine; but a Brāhmaṇa, however, one should banish.
[143] Manu and Nārada: If, within seven days of the testimony being given, a witness is seen to suffer from disease, fire, or the death of a kinsman, he shall be compelled to pay the debt and a fine.
Yājñavalkya [2.76]: For a man who fails to give testimony regarding a debt shall be compelled by the king to pay the entire amount, along with a tenth part as interest, on the forty-sixth day.
"With a tenfold bond" means accompanied by a tenth part. Manu [8.103]:
"A man who, being healthy, does not speak as a witness in matters such as debts within three fortnights..."
He shall incur that entire debt, along with a tenfold fine in every respect.
Viṣṇu [8.37]:
"Those who, though capable of testifying, remain silent and sit by watching,
are indeed equal to false witnesses in their sin and in their punishment."
[144] Kātyāyana [405]: If a witness does not testify to the evidence, he shall pay the debt and incur an equal fine;
for other disputes, he deserves a fine of three hundred [paṇas].
Bṛhaspati [5.45, 47]:
But a witness who, being summoned, does not come while remaining free from bias,
shall be made to pay both the debt and a fine after three fortnights have passed.
Witnesses who do not speak the truth when questioned, as well as those who fail to answer a question, should be restrained, censured, and punished according to the law.
Gautama [13.5]: "But a Brahmin is not to be restrained on the basis of the word of a non-Brahmin, provided he is unbound.
"Unbound" means not recorded on a leaf.
Kātyāyana [342].
The time for summoning witnesses should be granted when there is a full understanding of the proper procedure;
however, where the testimony is doubtful, one should adjudicate the case immediately upon questioning them.
"In order to fully understand correct action" means for the sake of knowing what ought to be done correctly.
Manu [8.75]: "A witness who, in an assembly of noble men, speaks otherwise than what was seen or heard..."
After death, he goes downward to hell and falls away from heaven.

Kātyāyana states: "False witnesses shall dwell in the Avīci hell for an eon. Gautama [13.7–8] says: "They would be at fault for failing to speak; there is heaven for truthful speech, and in the opposite case, hell."

[146] 24—Regarding the denial of truth, Vasiṣṭha [and Viṣṇu 8.14–15] state: "Witnesses are purified by truth; but where there is the execution of those belonging to the [four] castes, they are purified by falsehood."

Manu [8.104, 103]: "In cases where the death penalty would otherwise be pronounced for a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya, or a Brāhmaṇa upon their giving testimony, a falsehood should be spoken; for that is superior to the truth."
A man who speaks thus regarding matters of dharma, even though he knows otherwise, does not fall from the heavenly world; they call that the speech of the gods.

Regarding "in the case of speaking the truth" (*ṛtoktau*), Gautama states [13.24, 25]: "There is no fault in speaking untruth if life depends upon it; however, not if it is for the livelihood of a worse person.
Regarding "a worse person" (*pāpīyasaḥ*): where one's livelihood would be secured through an untruth involving a thief or the like, there one must not speak an untruth.

[147] Yājñavalkya [2.83]: Wherever there is the execution of those belonging to the [four] castes, one who is a witness may speak untruth; for the purification of that sin, a *sārasvata* oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) must be offered by the twice-born.

Viṣṇu [8.1617]: "To purify that [act], a twice-born man should offer oblations into the fire with the Kūṣmāṇḍa verses; and a Śūdra should give a morsel of food to ten cows for one day. Manu [8.105–106]:
"And they should worship Sarasvatī with sacrificial porridges (caru) dedicated to Speech (Vāk)."
Performing the supreme expiation for that sin of falsehood.
Or one should offer ghee into the fire according to the prescribed rule with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras,
or with the verse beginning "ud" addressed to Varuṇa, or with the triplet of verses addressed to the Waters.
Now, regarding the strength of witnesses, Manu [states in 8.73]:

In the event of a conflict between witnesses, O lord of men, the king should accept the majority; if they are equal in number, he should accept those distinguished by their virtues; and if there is a conflict between those equally virtuous, he should accept the best among the twice-born.

In a conflict between witnesses, those who are more numerous should be accepted; if they are equal in number, those endowed with superior qualities;
in a conflict between those of equal quality, those possessed of [corroborating] action; and if they too are equal, those most possessed of a retentive memory.

But in the event of a conflict among witnesses, the majority is the authority;
if they are equal in number, those with superior qualities are to be accepted; if they too are equal, those who possess greater memory are to be followed.

Likewise:
"Even when testimony has been given by witnesses, if others who are more virtuous,

if the defendant should then establish the matter otherwise;
Former witnesses may be many and of noble birth;
[150] 26 — Now follows the examination of witnesses.
Regarding this, Vyāsa says:
"If it is declared to be not deficient in terms of time, form, age, substance, place, caste, and measure, one should point out that the goal to be accomplished is achieved."
Viṣṇu and Yājñavalkya: He whose witnesses declare his claim to be true shall be the victor;
he whose witnesses speak otherwise shall certainly suffer defeat.
[151] Now, regarding the *anigada* [in that context], Nārada [states verses 4.232–234]:
If a witness, having been summoned to give testimony regarding the matters specified,
does not speak in accordance with the facts, that testimony is not considered validly delivered.
Regarding place, time, age, substance, quantity, appearance, and caste—
wherever there may be disagreement in these respects, even that testimony is contemptible.
Where witnesses state a matter that is either deficient or excessive, that too should be understood as unstated; this is the traditional rule regarding witnesses.
[152] 27 — Now, Bṛhaspati was written there.
This determination regarding the number and characteristics of witnesses has been declared;
now I shall state, in due order, the rules concerning written documents.
Since even after six months confusion arises,
the Creator therefore created letters long ago so that they might be fixed upon paper.
A royal edict, one executed by [an official] in his position, and likewise one written in one's own hand—
document is said to be of three kinds, and it is further divided into many types.
Secular documents are of seven kinds: those concerning shares, gifts, sales, mortgages, agreements, slaves, and debts; royal edicts are of three kinds.
Marīci: In the case of sale, pledge, partition, and even gift of immovable property,

Even a verbal pledge is established, as is one concerning immovable property after ten years;
however, in the case of a gift or a purchase, a transaction is not established without a written document.

[153] Regarding the term "immovable" (*sthāvara*): the meaning is that in matters concerning fields and the like, there is no legal validity for transactions such as sale without a written document. However, it is said that even a verbal transaction may be established; the point is that in the case of immovable property, a pledge (*ādhi*) that has been enjoyed for a period of ten years is established in that manner—even verbally—without a written document.
Kātyāyana [257, 301]: When a dispute regarding boundaries has been settled, a boundary-deed (*sīmāpatra*) is prescribed.

Documentary evidence should be known to be of two kinds: that executed by one's own hand and that executed by another;

The meaning is that for these two—the one with witnesses and the one without witnesses—there is a fixed rule based on local custom and so forth.

"Brothers who have divided among themselves by mutual consent..."

Whatever matter has been settled by mutual consent between the parties...

first, however, one should record the statements of both the accuser and the accused.
Thereafter, he should cause the decision of the Smṛti-śāstra, which is the authoritative opinion of the members of the court, the judge, or the families [of witnesses], to be recorded right there.
The wise know that a document executed according to this procedure is a *paścātkāra*;
it is one in which the opposing party's claim has been refuted by the plaintiff through evidence.
In that case, there may be a subsequent performance; it is not prescribed for all instances.
‘Paścātkāra’ is a document of victory. [161] 29 — Now, ‘sallekhya’.
Regarding this, Kātyāyana [252] states: "A document, however, should be executed with witnesses, with its sequence and letters uncorrupted,
conforming to the established customs of the region, and complete in all its matters."

Nārada [3.136]: A document that is not contrary to local customs, which clearly exhibits the characteristics of legal procedure, and whose sequence and letters are uncorrupted, is declared to be authoritative evidence.
"Wherein the characteristics of the manifest procedure are clear, and the characteristics of the deceptive means of knowledge are evident"—thus it is said. Kātyāyana [253, 267] states:
"That which is endowed with color, sentence, and action, which is unambiguous, and whose syllables are distinct."
And that document which possesses the signs of an unimpaired sequence shall attain validity.
Yājñavalkya [2.89]:
Even without witnesses, whatever document is written in one’s own hand is declared to be valid evidence in its entirety, except for that which was produced through force or fraud.
"Upadhi" means fraud.
Kātyāyana [272] states: "If it has been declared on the second day and no one should retract it..."
However, it may indeed be authoritative, provided it is not composed by one who is intoxicated or insane.
Yājñavalkya [2.91]: When a document is located in another country, is illegible, has been rubbed out,
stolen, broken, burnt, or torn, one should cause another document to be made.
Kātyāyana [312]: That document which is defiled by stains, burnt, torn, or even faded—
one should have another written, or likewise one written by oneself.
Regarding a defective document,
Kātyāyana [states as follows]: [273–274]
A document becomes invalid due to the defect of witnesses, or indeed due to that of the scribe;
likewise, it may be invalidated by the defect of fraud on the part of the creditor or the debtor.
A document written by the wicked should be declared wicked; one written by the pure should be designated as pure.
Such a document [is invalidated] by witnesses, the scribe, and the makers [of the deed] who are corrupted by fraud.
*Upadhā* is a defect of intention.
Bṛhaspati [6.30]:
By those who are about to die, by infants, by the frightened, by the afflicted, by women, and by those overcome by intoxication or addiction.
A document executed at night, under duress, or by force is not valid.
Nārada [4.137]:
That which is executed under intoxication, by one who is accused, by a woman, or by a child; and that which is done by force, as well as a document executed through fear or fraud, is invalid.
[164] Kātyāyana [281, 270]: A document written by the creditor’s own hand, even if devoid of witnesses,
shall be considered forged unless the maker can prove, "It was indeed executed by me."
That which is contrary to local custom, that which is ambiguous, that which lacks proper sequence,
that which is executed by one who is not the owner, and that which is devoid of a valid claim— all such [deeds] are defective.
Bṛhaspati [6.31–32]:
Where a single witness who is tainted or censured is produced, that is declared to be a forged document;
or it is so when the scribe is of the same character.
A document that is bright but old, soiled but recent,
or contains erased or rewritten syllables, shall be considered forged.
Kātyāyana [269]:
"But where letters are displaced from their positions, out of order, doubtful, or deviate from their characteristics—if such letters are present, the document is invalid; so too says Bhṛgu."
Vyāsa [Kātyāyana 311]:
He who forges a document regarding an immovable property, whether in sale or mortgage, shall,
when duly convicted in that matter, be deprived of his tongue, hands, and feet.
[165] 31 — Now, the examination of forged documents. On this matter, Kātyāyana [states]: [276, 323]
Just as those who act as witnesses or scribes fall into falsehood,
so too should faults be attributed to them when a document is corrupted by wicked persons.
The acquirer, even if possessed of possession, shall clear the document of its defects;
his son, however, shall clear the defects of possession, but shall not incur the defects of the document.
The "claimant" (āhartā) is one who has taken possession. Bṛhaspati [6.39] states:
"The claimant shall produce the document; his son, however, shall produce possession alone."
If one who was accused and condemned [is cleared], his son may also clear [the charge].
The meaning is that if the debtor, being accused, should die, then his son too shall discharge the debt.
Kātyāyana [266, 308]: Having summoned him by the king's command, one should investigate the case according to the law.
A document is [validated] by the conduct of writing, and witnesses by the conduct of witness-hood.
Just as a reflection in a mirror appears to exist though it is non-existent,
so do crooked men create images for the sake of painting.
Vyāsa (Bṛhaspati 6.41):
Some skillful men write a document like a painting;
therefore, it is held that success is not invariably achieved through the power of the document alone.
Bṛhaspati [6.40, 42–44]: Having heard of the time, place, and purpose, experts who are forgers produce a document that appears similar; one should examine such a document with great care.

One's own relatives may deceive women, children, the afflicted, or those ignorant of writing by having them sign a document marked with their own names; therefore, such a deed must be scrutinized through logical reasoning and legal precedents.
When an error arises in this threefold document,
one should then correct it by the hand-writing of the debtor, the witnesses, or the scribe.
[167] Ujjāma is known from its arising and its taking up; ādhāna from the gathering of the fruit; and yatnopadhi is to be understood from the abundance of the wealth of the counter-correlate.

‘Ujjāma’ means debt. ‘From lending at interest’ means from taking it back after a lapse of time. ‘Ādhāna’ means a pledge (ādhi). ‘From the collection of fruits’ means from the enjoyment of the yield. ‘The state of being a lender’ means the status of a creditor (uttamarṇa). Nārada [4.143–144]:
“In some cases, when there may be doubt regarding a document as to whether it was executed or not executed...”
One should extract that [meaning] by means of one's own manual action, signs, reasoning, and attainment.

Any document that bears another's name or was produced for some other purpose must be examined when there is a dispute, by means of the reasons for its connection and the circumstances of its acquisition.

"Action" (*kriyā*) refers to the presentation of witnesses. "Sign" (*cihna*) refers to a unique mark, such as an admission of ownership. "Attainment through reasoning" (*yuktiprāpti*) takes the form of inferring that "this person possesses this property because it was used in this place at this time," and so forth. "Disagreement" (*vipratyaya*) means a conflict of opinions. "Connection" (*saṃbandha*) here refers to a prior relationship between the plaintiff and the defendant based on mutual trust, such as the receipt of money. "Source" (*āgama*) refers to the probable origin from which one might have acquired such an amount of wealth. The meaning is that one should establish a doubtful document by means of these grounds, beginning with one's own handwriting.
Vyāsa:
Furthermore, when a document executed by one person is seen in the hands of another,
that person must necessarily explain how the document came into his possession.
[168] Kātyāyana [277, 290, 285, 286]: "When the defendant states that it was not written by the scribe, nor witnessed by the witnesses in that manner, such a document is declared to be forged."
In the case of a false statement, if a witness or a scribe does not bring the document to its true purity through their testimony, he shall be made to pay the highest fine for perjury.
Now, if the scribe together with the witnesses has met his death, he shall be cleared by means of their own handwriting and other evidence; of this there is no doubt.
When there is doubt regarding a debt due to one's own handwriting— whether the debtor is living or dead—
the determination of that document is made by means of other documents written in his own hand.
Likewise:
"Even when all those residing there have died, if they are recorded in writing upon the ocean,
that writing remains authoritative even though they are indeed dead."
Prajāpati says: A decision regarding the royal edict must be made with great care;
[its authenticity is confirmed] by seeing the seal and the letters of the scribe from the king's own hand.
Kātyāyana:
[296, 294, 296] Pure in its seal, pure in its ritual action, and approved through tradition;
untainted, touched, diverse in its performance, and fully realized.
One attains such accomplishment as this, marked by royal authority within the teaching.
That which is recorded as a subsequent deed should be examined with great care;
if it is indeed consistent with reason, then it shall be accepted as valid evidence in writing.
Otherwise, one should re-adjudicate the case from its very root.
That which was established as true when it was actually false, due to a delusion of knowledge,
must be overturned even if it was carried out with great effort by kings.
"Pure in action" means supported by witnesses. "Approved through tradition" means approved by many.
[170] 32 — Now, the force of written documents.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati [6.49] states:
"One should present the cases of families, guilds, assemblies, and so forth at the appropriate time;
one should cause them to hear and remember [the law] so that it may become more authoritative."
Nārada [4.140]: A document is established as valid in all cases— provided it was shown at the proper time, read aloud, and reminded of— even when the witnesses have died.
Kātyāyana [298–303]:
If the debtor does not point out a manifest defect in the document upon inspection,
then after twenty years have elapsed, the document shall become established as valid.
If a person enjoys property through a document in the presence of a capable owner for a period of twenty years, that document is free from defects.
Alternatively, if a pledge has been enjoyed for twenty years, it is considered certain;
its validity is established by that document, provided it is free from defects of the document itself.
When a boundary dispute has been decided, a boundary document (sīmāpatra) is prescribed;
its defects must be examined for up to twenty years.
Where a debt, together with its principal, is recorded in a document,
they know that it is established by the evidence of witnesses who have died, even through a small amount of possession.
If something has been received by him, or if a gift is specified for a purpose,
then even without a seal, a document with deceased witnesses is authoritative as evidence.
Vyāsa says:
A document written by one's own hand is more authoritative than a provincial record, and a royal edict is indeed held to be even more authoritative when it has come before a court of law.
One who knows two or three scripts should, by means of logical reasoning, make a document resembling one written by another; therefore, a local document is auspicious.
A document that is not publicly known, which is corroborated by witnesses, stamped with the letters of the scribe,
well-known to the world, inferior to one written by oneself, and executed by another, is auspicious.
A document concerning the countryside that has been executed by a provincial governor or similar official—
whether it be contemporary with the event or later— is considered valid when it bears the royal seal.
"From one's own hand" means from a document executed by one's own hand. Saṃvarta states:
"In the case of a written document, the legal act is declared to be that of writing; in the case of a verbal [transaction], it is considered to be that of speech."
But that verbal transaction which is made on the basis of a written document shall not be valid.
Testimony that is contrary to what is written on a document is called forged; since half of the matter depends upon it, the king should therefore reject such testimony.
[173] If the capacity of syllables as verbal expressions were destroyed,
there would be the total annihilation of actions and an infinite regress would arise.

"In writing, the action based on writing is declared to be more authoritative"—the word "more authoritative" is the ellipsis here. "Oral" refers to the action based on witnesses; here too, "more authoritative" is the ellipsis. "An action superior to writing"—meaning an action that contradicts the action based on writing is not a valid means of proof. Kātyāyana [306–307]:
"A written document is never invalidated by ordeals or even by witnesses."
The law of written documents is always superior; therefore, one is not defeated by any other means.
A written document may be set aside by a counter-document supported by reasoning or by one superior to it; it can never be refuted by witnesses or oaths.
— Now, regarding the weakness of documentary evidence,
Bṛhaspati states [6.51, 47, 48]:

If a person who is capable does not request a debt from a wealthy creditor standing nearby, that document— due to the suspicion that it may be a mere claim for a pure loan— will suffer in its legal validity.
A document that is more than thirty years old, and which has neither been seen nor heard of,
does not attain validity, even though witnesses may still be present.
But when a peaceful settlement has been reached, he who does not produce the written document nor demand it from the debtor shall incur doubt regarding that matter.

"By the suspicion of a pure debt" means by the suspicion that it is a debt free from [fraudulent] interest. "When the profit has ceased" means when it no longer causes oppression to the debtor. Vyāsa says:
A document that has not been seen or heard [by the court], and where the creditor or the debtor is deceased...
Furthermore, a loan without a pledge or a guarantor does not succeed even after a long period of time.
‘Free from pledges and sureties’ means devoid of both pledges (*bandha*) and sureties (*lagnaka*).
Bṛhaspati [6.51]:
“Of those who are insane, idiotic, or minor; and of those who have fled out of fear of the king...”
A document drawn up by those who are timid, fearful, or afflicted shall not be valid; it would suffer loss [of legal force].
Nārada and Kātyāyana state:
When a document has been taken to another country, burnt, poorly written, or falsified, the time for its production is equal; furthermore, witnesses who were present at the time must be produced.

[176] "Equal is the time for its production" means that if the document exists in another location, one must wait until it is brought here; and if it does not exist, one must wait until the person indicated by that document is found. Kātyāyana states:
"That document which has not been seen by the judge, nor has been acknowledged..."
When a document has been executed for a debt not yet received, how shall the creditor recover that [debt]?
Or, when a deposit has been withheld, as long as the surety remains, that period is considered authoritative;
in the absence of a written document, the testimony of witnesses is the proof.

"Whatever document," and so forth. The meaning is: if that document which was promised to be shown has not been seen by the presiding judge (*prāḍvivāka*), how can one who has not yet recovered his wealth obtain it once that [judgment] has been made?
[177] 34 — Now, possession (*bhukti*).
In this regard, Bṛhaspati [27.22–28] states:
This rule has been declared concerning witnesses and written documents;
now, the procedure regarding the possession of immovable property is being stated.
Immovable property acquired through learning, purchase, alliance, valor, marriage,
or inheritance is declared by tradition to be divided into seven parts for a sapinda who is childless.

When possession has been acquired through inheritance, purchase, or gift, or through the manifestation of one's own valor, it becomes sevenfold; such possession, when accompanied by a legal title, attains validity.
That possession which is hereditary, authorized by the teaching, and accompanied by purchase, grant, or inheritance—
such a possession shall attain validity.
Immovable property acquired through partition, by purchase, inherited from a father, or received from a king attains legal validity through possession; however, it is lost through neglect.
By one who has accepted and consumed it as soon as it was obtained, without opposition, that [mantra] attains success for him; likewise, through neglect, it incurs failure.

[178] If one has been in possession of a property for thirty years, beginning from the time of its acquisition, and that enjoyment has been uninterrupted and unchallenged, one shall not displace him from it.

‘By learning’ (vidyayā) means by way of receiving gifts and so forth. ‘Seizure’ (bandhaḥ) refers to a mortgage or pledge. ‘Acquired through valor’ (śauryāgatam) is that which is obtained through battle and the like. ‘Acquired through a wife’ (bhāryāgatam) is what is gained together with a wife. ‘Inherited’ (anvayāgatam) is what has come down through the succession of father and ancestors. ‘Marriage’ (pravedanam) refers to wedding. By the words ‘paternal’ (pitrya) and so forth, there is a restatement of the seven previously mentioned modes of acquisition. ‘Without opposition’ (aparipanthinam) means without conflict. ‘Occupancy’ (adhyāsanam) is established possession. ‘Uninterrupted’ (avighātinī) means continuous. Viṣṇu and Kātyāyana state: “But when a property has been enjoyed for a long time through possession accompanied by a legal title...”
The one who brings it back receives that [property], and it must never be taken away from him under any circumstances.

Whatever property was enjoyed by the father through lawful means of enjoyment, when he has passed away, no objection can be raised against it; for that which was acquired through enjoyment belongs to him.
But when land has been enjoyed by three persons in accordance with the law,
even in the absence of a written document, a fourth person may acquire it there through that enjoyment.
[179] "By the practice of enjoyment" means by proper enjoyment.
Nārada [4.97]: But that which was enjoyed through unlawful means by the father and three preceding ancestors cannot be taken away, having been held for three generations in succession.
Regarding the phrase "with the father and three earlier ones," the grammatical construction is: with the father and with three other earlier ones. Likewise:
"In the beginning, however, the cause is the gift; in the middle, possession is for the Sāmavedins."
The sole cause is possession alone—continuous and long-standing.
"Kāraṇa" means proof. Kātyāyana [329, 321] states:
"In the scriptures, possession that is continuous and long-standing is powerful."
But that which was previously established should be understood as being interrupted.
From the time of its acquisition until the continuous enjoyment that follows upon reaching the place of consumption,
testimony generally proceeds with respect to that [ownership].
In the period of memory, possession of land is held to be valid when accompanied by title;
in the period beyond memory, because there is no means of tracing it, it is valid when descended through three generations in succession.

"Established by predecessors" means performed by previous persons. "Uninterrupted" means that in a possession which has lasted for a short time, the evidence of witnesses proceeds once the acquirer has obtained a title such as a gift; this is the meaning. "Smārte" means within the period suitable for memory. "Kriyā" means proof. "Āgama" is the cause of ownership, such as purchase, acceptance of a gift, and so forth. "Due to the absence of *anugama*" means due to the absence of investigation or inquiry; this is the meaning. Yājñavalkya [2.27]:
"Title is superior to possession, except in the case of possession resulting from a prior succession of titles."
Kātyāyana [318]: Possession inherited from a grandfather is primary, and that from a father is also recognized as valid;
when uninterrupted by these three, it is considered stable and established for sixty years.
Vyāsa says: If one's father, grandfather, and great-grandfather are all living,
the enjoyment [of property] by these three must be informed to a single representative person.
The possession by the son of that which was enjoyed by the grandfather must also be maintained;
for one who possesses it in the absence of those two and his father, his enjoyment extends over three generations.

Possession of land that has been enjoyed for twenty years by a master without interruption is "puruṣa-possession" (pauruṣī); possession for twice that duration is "dvi-puruṣa-possession" (dvipauruṣī).
And that which extends for three pauruṣīs is tripled; there, no further scriptural authority needs to be sought.
Likewise, Bṛhaspati [8.64]:
"Possession is said to have five constituent parts: it must be accompanied by title, long-standing, uninterrupted, free from objection by others, and in the presence of the opponent."

"Without gaps" means free from interruption. "Abandoned by other sounds" means devoid of contradiction. "In the presence of the defendant" means that which occurs while the defendant is present. Bṛhaspati [7.32–35]:
If a village, field, or garden is recorded in a single edict...
Even when only one part is enjoyed, all of them are considered to have been enjoyed.
Direct perception is superior to inference; a written document is weightier than witnesses; and possession by three successive generations, when unopposed, is more authoritative than these.
Inference is effective immediately, while a witness remains so until death; a document and possession that are uncontradicted are authoritative for three generations.

"Inference [is effective] immediately. At the very time of the dispute, inference proceeds by means of signs such as facial expressions and gestures. Nārada [4.75–76]: "A written document is always more authoritative; however, witnesses are authoritative only while they are alive."
"Enjoyment [of the fruit] results from the passing of time; such is the determination in the scriptures."
Among these three types of perceived means of valid cognition, each preceding one should be known as more authoritative than the following; among these, direct experience is the most authoritative.
However, among these, possession for a long period is more significant and stronger than possession for a short time or possession supported by witnesses or documents.
Yājñavalkya [2.28]:
He who has made a formal title-deed (āgama) must, when challenged, produce it.
Neither his son nor the son of his son [has authority]; in that case, possession is more weighty.
[183] Bṛhaspati [7.39]: The possessor shall prove possession and the title in court;
his son shall prove only possession; but his grandson and the rest need prove nothing at all.
Kātyāyana [324]:
For he by whom a property was acquired must restore it when sued for;
even if possession has been enjoyed for a long time, such enjoyment is not recognized as belonging to him.
Bṛhaspati [7.38]:
When the plaintiff is challenged, then the document and the witness are the primary means of proof;
but in the absence of a document, there is circumstantial evidence (*yukti*), and possession (*bhukti*) is weightier than those two.
Likewise, Kātyāyana (verse 316) states: "Neither the seizer nor his son should employ force regarding the enjoyment of cattle, women, men, and so forth; such is the established law."
Yājñavalkya [2.29]: If one who has been accused should pass away, his heir shall clear him [of the charge];
in that case, possession is not a valid ground of proof unless it is supported by a legal title.
"In the case of a deceased litigant who had thus ascended to a lawsuit, the matter must be investigated by his son; possession shall not bar that claim."
Possession attains the status of valid proof through pure title;
possession with impure title does not achieve validity.
Likewise [Nārada 8.87–88, 92]:
"That which has been enjoyed without a legal title, one shall not acquire by virtue of that enjoyment alone;
however, this wealth goes to the possessor, it is held by those who know the law."
But the lord of the earth should punish that sinner with the punishment due to a thief, even if he enjoys [the property] for many hundreds of years without legal title.
That which is deposited, that which is taken, that which is placed down, that which is obtained by force, that which is begged,
and that which is enjoyed out of sight— these six [types of property] are acquired without a formal title.
Now, if it is argued that possession is not established without enjoyment, regarding this Yājñavalkya [2.27] states:
"Even in the case of a title deed, there is no strength at all where there is not even a slight amount of possession."
Even when a document exists and witnesses are still living,
that possession of immovable property is not secure where it has not been enjoyed for a long time.
When someone, out of delusion, neglects his own wealth while it is being enjoyed by others,
even though he is present and alive, that very enjoyment brings those riches under the control of the other.
Vyāsa says: Just as a cow, if neglected and left without a keeper, perishes,
so too land that is watched over by others while being enjoyed [by someone else] is lost through the passage of time.
If the earth has been enjoyed here by others for twenty years,
even while a capable king is present, his claim to it is not established here.
Nārada [4.42]:
Through actual use, however, the property of a master is forfeited after twenty years;
even deposits and the like are lost through such use, except in the case of women and the property of a king.
"Twelve years" means twenty years. "Except for the property of a woman or a king" means excluding the property of a woman and the property of a king.
Yājñavalkya [2.24]: "The loss of land belongs to one who looks on and does not speak; it occurs after twenty years."
In the case of property being enjoyed by another for ten years, [the owner's claim is lost].
[187] Manu and Nārada [Manu 8.143; Nārada 4.79]:
Whatever property an owner observes being enjoyed by others for ten years in his presence while remaining silent, he is not entitled to recover it.

Gautama [12.34]: "The property of one who is not an idiot (*ajaḍa*) and not a minor (*apogaṇḍa*), if enjoyed by others for ten years in the presence of the owner, belongs to the enjoyer. The meaning is that the property of one who is neither an idiot nor a minor, if enjoyed by others for a period of ten years without dispute in his presence, becomes the property of that very enjoyer. Manu [8.145]: Both a pledge (*ādhi*) and a deposit (*upanidhi*) do not suffer loss through the lapse of time.
Those two, having remained for a long time, shall be liable to be confiscated.

‘Ādhi’ means a pledge (*bandhaka*). ‘Upanidhi’ also refers to a field or similar property handed over out of affection for the purpose of enjoyment; it does not, however, refer to that defined by the Smṛti as “that which is placed in a container without being described,” because the latter is unfit for enjoyment. ‘Kālātyaya’ is the lapse of the stated time limit. It is unfit for enjoyment [once that time has passed]. ‘Kālātyaya’ is the transgression of the stated time limit. “They do not deserve the lapse of time” means that they must necessarily be redeemed at the time of redemption. He states the reason for this with the words “they would become liable to be seized,” and so forth. For if these two remain for a long period, they would become liable to be seized by the enjoyer; the meaning is that the enjoyer might even take them away.
[188] Bṛhaspati [7.40, 41]: If property is given openly by others to one person while another person subsequently enjoys it, the former does not deserve to recover it.
If a landowner sees another person giving away land and does not prevent it,
he shall not regain that land again, even though he possesses a written deed.
Likewise [7.66–67]:
Non-enjoyment of land, failure to produce a document at the proper time,
and failing to remind the witnesses are causes for the loss of one's own right.
Therefore, one must diligently maintain the authority of the means of valid cognition;
by that, all matters, both stationary and moving, are accomplished.
[189] 35— Now follows the refutation of the denial regarding the loss of another’s enjoyment;
on this point, Bṛhaspati says (7.43, 44, 46):
The enjoyment [of property] by three generations is established for others; there is no doubt in this matter.
However, as long as the sapinda relationship has not ceased, it is not established for the sakulyas.
But property such as a house, field, or shop that has been enjoyed by someone who is not the owner does not lapse through mere enjoyment in favor of a friend, relative, or kinsman.
Even after a very long period of time, that wealth does not accrue to those Śrotriyas who have married and to the king’s ministers, for they have already consumed it.

"Even while sapinda-relationship has not ceased": the meaning is that even though sapinda-relationship exists, property being enjoyed by kinsmen (sakulyas) for three generations does not become the property of the enjoyer. "One to be wedded" refers to a son-in-law. Gautama [12.34–36] states: "The wealth of one who is not mentally incapacitated or a minor, if enjoyed by others in the presence of the owner for ten years, belongs to the enjoyer—except in the case of learned Vedic scholars (śrotriya), renunciants (pravrajita), and royal officials. There is no loss of ownership through mere enjoyment in the case of cattle, land, or women. The meaning is that loss occurs only through excessive enjoyment. Kātyāyana [335] says:

That which has been enjoyed by kinsmen of the same lineage, by relatives, and likewise by one's own people—there is no success through enjoyment in that case; one should arrange for enjoyment with others.
"In others" refers to unrelated claimants. Manu and Nārada state:
"A pledge, a boundary, the property of a minor, deposits, sealed deposits, and women."
The property of a king and the property of one learned in the Vedas are not lost through adverse possession.
Bṛhaspati [7.47]: The possession by another of a document executed for those who are incapable, indolent, afflicted by disease, children, terrified,
or traveling abroad does not result in loss of title through such possession.
"Engraved on a royal edict" means inscribed on a copper plate or similar medium.
Kātyāyana [330] states: "One should not allow the enjoyment [of property] by women, nor in the case of the property of a deity or the king."
And in the wealth of a child or a Vedic scholar, [the inheritance] proceeds respectively from the mother and from the father.
[191] There shall never be enjoyment of women without a written document;
the same is held to apply to the property of enemies, Vedic scholars, kings, and minors.
Manu [8.146]: "Cows, camels, draft horses, and those animals used for training that are enjoyed with mutual consent are never lost."
"One who is being tamed" refers to one who is employed for the purpose of training;
this is [the view of] Kātyāyana. [The property] deposited with artisans, that which is pledged, that which is sent on a mission, and that which is borrowed.
One who, being base, kills another by force out of delusion, shall indeed be punished.
"Kraya" means the price. Yājñavalkya [2.26]:
One should cause the person who conceals deposits and the like to pay the wealth to the owner.
And he should pay a fine to the king equal to that [debt], or else according to his ability.
"According to his capacity" means as far as his ability allows; "he shall cause the fine to be paid.
192] 36 — Now follows the determination of interrupted possession.

Or, if he remains silent at the time of giving, that purpose is still approved.

"One of these": if even one of these grounds for proof is demonstrated, then the fundamental action is indeed established. Nārada [4.172–175]:
"But other disputes are proclaimed to be sixfold, wherein there is no reliance on witnesses."
The wise declare that these very characteristics themselves are the witnesses.
One with a torch in hand should be known as an arsonist; one with a weapon in hand is a murderer;

"In the capacity of a witness," that is, in the position of a witness.

[197] 38 — Now, the divine [qualities] (divya), categorized according to their various types.

The balance, fire, water, poison, and the fifth, the sacred libation—

For the purpose of examining those involved in a doubtful matter, these [ordeals] were proclaimed here by the high-souled Nārada for the purification of truth and falsehood.

"Ardayet" means he should cause pain. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "In a case where no witnesses have been produced, there is reliance on the person [involved], such as a formal decree, causing dissension, or flogging; or in a case where [the matter] has been abandoned or in a dispute, there is recourse to divine ordeals, such as the ordeal by sacred libation (kośa), poison, eating [hot] metal, or water.

"Asākṣipraṇihite" means when it has not been determined by witnesses. [198] Bṛhaspati [8.3–4]: “The balance, fire, water, poison, and the fifth is the sacred libation (kośa);
rice is declared as the sixth, and the seventh is the saptamāṣaka.”
The eighth is said to be Phāla, and the ninth shall be Dharmaja.
These divine dharmas were taught by the Self-Existent One.
"I shall speak by way of summary for the sake of purifying the doubtful meaning,
employing [the topics] of place, time, object, and number in their proper sequence."
According to the sequence of offenses and with the intention of declaring what is right or wrong,
these [penalties] should be administered according to the procedure prescribed in the treatises, and not otherwise.

Now follows the specific classification of divine ordeals (*divya*) according to the value of the object and other criteria. Regarding this, Viṣṇu [9.1–3] states: "Next is the procedure for oaths (*śapatha*). Here, "oath" (*śapatha*) refers to a divine ordeal (*divya*).
Following the term "divine procedure" (*daivī kriyā*), Bṛhaspati [8.7] says:
"In legal matters such as debts and the like, when there is mutual disagreement..."
Likewise, it should be given according to the number of persons, accompanied by the appropriate materials.
Kātyāyana [416]:
Where there is proof that what was given has not been received, one should determine the penalty;
in cases of theft or violence, one should cause an ordeal to be administered even when the matter is of small value.
Regarding "proof" (*pramāṇam*): one should cause divine ordeals (*divya*) and other such means of proof to be administered according to the value of the property that has been denied.
Bṛhaspati [8.27–32]:
"The scale of fines was declared by Manu to be based on the *raśmi*, the *rajas*, and the *mūla*."
In matters concerning divine ordeals and likewise in civil law, that fine shall extend up to one kārṣāpaṇa.
When a thousand [palas] have been subtracted, poison is used; at three-quarters less, fire;

In a lawsuit involving four hundred [paṇas], a heated māṣaka coin must be administered;
for three hundred, rice grains are to be given, and for half of that amount, the ordeal by sacred libation (kośa).
When a hundred [paṇas] have been stolen and denied, the purification by ordeal must be administered;
for one accused of stealing a cow, the members of the court must diligently administer the plough as the ordeal.
According to the respective numbers, it is traditionally held that for those of inferior status it is one part, for those of middling status it is double,
and for those of superior status it should be diligently calculated as fourfold.
"Raśmirojomūlā"— when the sun has reached the root of its rays, that subtle dust which is seen is called the *trasareṇu*, the first among all measurements.
And so forth. "Discipline" (*vinaya*) means punishment. "Of the lowly" refers to those inferior by birth, action, or quality; likewise for the middling and the superior.
Yājñavalkya [2.99]: One should not employ the plowshare ordeal, nor poison, nor the balance, for less than one thousand [paṇas].
Then, being pure, they shall bear the burden for the sake of the king and in cases of formal accusation.

The meaning of "not for less than a thousand" is that when the denial exceeds one thousand *paṇas*, the ordeal by plowshare (*phālādi*) and so forth shall be employed. Regarding "in matters concerning the king," this refers to acts such as treason against the sovereign. Regarding "in the case of a formal accusation," this refers to an accusation of a mortal sin (*pātaka*). "Pure" means purified by bathing and other such rites.

Viṣṇu [9.4]: "In all matters concerning wealth, one should determine the value in gold. Likewise [9.10–19]: "For a Śūdra, the ordeal of the balance (kośa) should be administered when the amount [in dispute] is half a suvarṇa; beyond that, any one of the ordeals of the water-jar, fire, or poison, according to the merit of the case. For a Vaiśya, the prescribed ordeal of the balance applies when the amount is double [that of a Śūdra]. For a Kṣatriya, it applies when the amount is triple. For a Brāhmaṇa, it applies when the amount is quadruple, with the exception of the balance ordeal. One should not administer the balance ordeal to a Brāhmaṇa, except as a formal agreement for a future time. In place of the balance ordeal, one should cause a Brāhmaṇa to swear by touching the earth ploughed by a team of oxen. If he has been previously observed to have committed offenses, even in a small matter, one should cause him to undergo any one of the divine ordeals. However, if his good character is well known, this applies even in a great matter."

"When the value is less than half a *suvarṇa*," meaning slightly below the value of half a *suvarṇa*. "When the object has become double" refers to when the object previously mentioned as being worth half a *suvarṇa* has doubled in value; the same applies to threefold values and so on. "The performance of the stipulated ordeal" refers to the drinking of the *kośa* (holy water). "Elsewhere" and so forth: the making of an agreement that "we must act together in this manner" constitutes the agreement; "elsewhere" means other than that. "One whose hand holds earth dug up by a plough" means one whose hand holds soil excavated by a plough. "Of the ordeals" refers to the *ghaṭa* (water ordeal) and others. "Known among the virtuous" means well-established among the learned. "Even in a great matter" means that one should not cause any of the ordeals, such as the *ghaṭa*, to be performed [in cases where they are prohibited].
Kātyāyana [417, first part]:
Having ascertained the value of all the property involved, one should determine the amount of gold;
then, one should employ the ordeal in accordance with that measure of gold.
In a hundred [palas], poison is used; when three-quarters remain, the fire-eater (the ordeal by fire) is seen there;
when reduced by one-third, water is used; and at fifty, the balance is prescribed.
The ordeal by sacred libation (kośapāna) is prescribed for ten, five, or seven [karṣas];

"In a hundred" refers to a hundred *suvarṇas*; this is the remainder [of the sentence]. The elder [Kātyāyana, verses 418–20] states:
"Having ascertained the number of *suvarṇas*, poison is prescribed in the case of the loss of a hundred."
Indeed, upon the destruction of eighty [years], one should offer oblations into the fire.
If the debt is lost due to sixty [māṣas], water should be known as the ordeal; if due to forty, the balance;
and if due to thirty or ten, Bṛhaspati says the ordeal of drinking from a vessel (kośapāna) shall be used.
Or, in the event of the loss of a *pañcārdhika* coin, there shall be rice-grains equal to half of that [value].
A *pañcārdhika* is "half of five," which is two and a half.
(kha) Now, regarding the specific divine times: on this matter, Pitāmaha says:
"Whatever time has been prescribed for each, whatever procedure for each, and in whatever manner,"
I shall explain that in its true nature, as well as the strengths and weaknesses of the disputant.
Caitra, Mārgaśīrṣa, and likewise Vaiśākha—

The *dhaṭa* ordeal is declared suitable for all seasons, yet one should avoid it when the wind blows;

"In autumn and summer, however, it is water; in late winter and early spring, it is poison. Nārada [4.260, 254]:
"Having deliberated with those who are skilled in dharma and proficient in the treatises on dharma..."
The maintenance of the balance by those who have gathered together is declared to be righteous and suitable for all seasons.
Fire is [the poison] during the rainy season, as is water in the winter and the cool season;

Those who are experts in the treatises on Dharma should not allow women, children,
the sick, the elderly, or men who are weak to immerse themselves in water.

One should avoid granting a treasury loan to an atheist or to one who has been observed to commit offenses.

The wise should not provide a legal deposit for those who drink liquor, for women, for gamblers, for cheats, and likewise for those who follow the ways of atheists.

[208] Kātyāyana [427–30]: For those who kill their mother, father, a twice-born, a guru, a child, a woman, or a king;

who are born of the intermixture of castes, and who persist in the habitual practice of sin—

Likewise,
[431–32] the ordeal must not be administered to those guilty of mortal sins, especially to atheists,

In matters of confidence, in all doubts, and likewise in the business of making peace—
in these instances, the treasury must always be provided for the sake of purity of mind.

The "head" (*śīrṣaka*) is the head. And that refers to the voluntary acceptance of punishment by one who employs a divine ordeal upon winning. Pitāmaha says:
One should avoid divine ordeals that lack a standing penalty for the head.
But the four [elements] beginning with earth are remembered as the sheath, while the headless one is the sword itself.
In ordeals, the plaintiff shall be placed upon the head;

Yājñavalkya [2.26]:
Or, by mutual consent, one may perform a lighter penance while the other undergoes the full course;

When there is a disagreement, a dispute, or when a charge of infamy has been brought,
the king should cause that ordeal to be administered, beginning with the test of the head.
[211] And in cases of violating another's wife where there are many disputants,
the ordeal shall be one involving decapitation for the purpose of establishing one's own purity.

"In cases of misconduct" refers to matters such as false accusations regarding another's wife; "in disputes" refers to matters such as the non-payment of debts. ["Avarṇaḥ" means defamation. The phrase "and in the case of violating another's wife" is also indicative of theft and similar offenses. Viṣṇu [9.22] states:

The Grandfather said: For those suspected by kings, for those pointed out by bandits,

Nārada [4.270]:

(Ṅa) Now, regarding the place and time, Kātyāyana [434–35] states:
"In the abode of Indra, for men who have been accused of great sins..."
One should employ those who have committed acts of treason against the king at the royal gates.
[212] For those born of inverse unions, the ordeal should be administered at a crossroads;
for other matters, the wise know that it should take place in the midst of the assembly hall.
‘Indrasthāna’ is the place for the worship of Indra’s banner.
Bṛhaspati and Kātyāyana [Bṛhad-yogayātrā 8.15–16; Kāśyapa-saṃhitā 439–440] state:
"The divine [offering] should be given according to the prescribed rule by those skilled in divine matters."
And that which is given in a manner not as stated is incapable of accomplishing what is to be accomplished.

Those [depositions] given at an improper place or time, or those made outside the presence of the opposing party, cause deviation from the truth regarding the matters at hand; of this there is no doubt.

(c) Now follows the procedure for ordeals (*divya-vidhi*), according to Bṛhaspati [8.14]:

The Grandfather said:
The king, or an appointed official,
should cause the ordeal to be administered in the presence of learned Brāhmaṇas as well as the subjects.
Viṣṇu and Yājñavalkya:
Having summoned one who has fasted since sunrise and bathed with his clothes on,
one should cause all ordeals to be performed in the presence of the king and Brāhmaṇas.
Nārada [4.268]:
For a man who has fasted for a day and night, bathed, and is wearing wet clothes,
the administration of all ordeals is prescribed for the forenoon.
The Grandfather said:
To one who has fasted for three nights, or even for one night,
divine objects should always be given, provided he is pure and dressed in clean garments.
In all divine matters,
the judge shall act like the Adhvaryu priest in sacrifices, remaining fasting by the king's command.

If there is a contradiction in the means of proof, then that which is to be proven must be established once more;

39 — Now, the procedure for the balance ordeal (*dhaṭavidhi*).

Regarding this, Viṣṇu [10.2–3] states: "Now, as for the balance: it shall be four cubits high and two cubits wide. And upon it, there shall be a scale made from a strong wood, five cubits long, with a sling on both sides. Pitāmaha says:
The balance-beam should be made four cubits long, and its two supports should be made likewise;
the distance between them should be one cubit, or indeed one and a half cubits.
Having cut the sacrificial tree like a sacrificial post according to the prescribed mantras,
and having bowed down to the guardians of the world, the wise should have the balance constructed.
One should have a staff made there from khadira wood, free of wounds and devoid of dryness;
in its absence, however, one may use a staff of śiṃśapā or sāla wood, provided it is without hollows.
Arjuna, tilaka, aśoka, timiśa, and red sandalwood—
one should prepare such kinds of wood for the balance.
The balance-beam of the *dhaṭa* should be made straight, fashioned from iron or *tinduka* wood;
it should be square and supported at three points by the *karkaṭaka* (crab-claw) and other supports.
It is prescribed that two cubits (*hasta*) of the beam should be buried for those two *muṇḍaka* (head-pieces).
The measurement of those two is declared to be six cubits in size.
The Grandfather [Manu] says:
"Likewise, two arches (toraṇa) should be constructed on both sides;
they must always be ten finger-breadths higher than the balance-beam."
And two supports should be made from clay, suspended from the two arches with their faces turned downward,
fastened by cords, and touching the top of the balance-beam.
The balance-beam (dhaṭa) should always be placed facing east, kept steady, and situated in a clean place—
either in the temple of Indra, in an assembly hall, at the king’s gate, or at a crossroads.
At the door of the assembly hall, the royal palace, a temple, or a public square,
the *nakṣatra* [the deity of the lunar mansion] should be made stationary and worshipped with perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
Having performed the auspicious rites of Vedic study with curds, unbroken grains, oblations, and fragrant perfumes,
he was presided over by the world-protectors who had been summoned for the sake of protecting the Dharma.
The Grandfather (Brahmā) should likewise station the world-protectors (Lokapālas) in all directions;
one should worship them constantly at the three junctions of the day with incense, garlands, and ointments.
Likewise, the world-protectors, the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus,
endowed with the power of worship, manifest their presence there.
One should cause a spacious, elevated, and pure weighing-chamber to be constructed,
where [the balance] stationed shall not be defiled by dogs, outcastes, or crows.
The king should ensure that it is provided with door-bolts and seeds, guarded by attendants, supplied with water and fire, and never left empty.
One should always cause a sacrificial pillar (dhaṭa) to be made, adorned with banners and flags,
accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments and drums, and provided with incense, garlands, and ointments.
Having secured two balances firmly to the hooks of the beam,
one should weigh a man on one scale and a stone on the other.
One should place a man on the northern side and a stone on the southern side;
one should fill the pit there with bricks and excellent clods of earth.
Viṣṇu [10.5]: "In that case, one should place the person on one scale and a counterweight, such as a stone, on the second.
Pitāmaha:
"Having suspended two scales on both sides..."
There, the composed Brahmin should have darbha grass blades laid down with their tips pointing eastward.
One should weigh a mortal [remains] on one side and auspicious earth on the other—
earth that is free from bricks, ashes, stones, potsherds, and bones.
Examiners skilled in weights and measures should be appointed,
as well as merchants, goldsmiths, and likewise bell-metal workers.
Likewise:
"The judges must always ensure that the balance-beam is level;
and water must be poured upon the balance by the learned."
[218] That scale upon which water does not float is to be known as even; Nārada [4.273,
275] states that at the first weighing, the measurement should be recorded by experts together.
And the archway, marked with the prescribed characteristics, should be equal in weight to the balance-beam and the stone.

having placed a leaf upon his head in a windless place free from rain.
When that very enclosure has been made, having formed a chamber within it, the twice-born should say with words concerning the various aspects of Dharma: "O Dhaṭa, you are so named."

you alone, O God, know those things which human beings do not know.

The sun and the moon, wind and fire, heaven, earth, water, and Yama;
day and night, and both twilights.

but if he remains equal or, upon being weighed again, has gained weight, he shall be the victor.

even one who remains stationary is not pure—this is declared to be purification.
In the event of the snapping of the side-arms, the breaking of the beam, or likewise the breaking of the *dhaṭa* or *karkaṭa*,
as well as the snapping of the cord or the breaking of the axle, the king shall cause the ordeal to be performed again.
Kātyāyana [440]:
In the event of a break in the sling, a fracture of the balance-beam, or likewise of the cord,
and also when there is doubt regarding purity, one should examine the man again.
[224] 40— Now follows the procedure for the fire-ritual;
regarding this, Bṛhaspati [the Grandfather] says:
I shall proclaim the procedure for the fire sacrifice exactly as it is enjoined in the scriptures;
one should cause eight mandalas to be made, and likewise a ninth in front.
The first mandala is of Agni; the second is remembered as belonging to Varuṇa;
the third has Vāyu as its deity; and the fourth has Yama as its deity.
The fifth, however, has Indra as its deity; the sixth is said to belong to Kubera;
the seventh has Soma as its deity; and the eighth belongs to all the gods.
That which is the ninth [altar] in front, they know as the Mahāpārthiva;
it should be made with cow-dung and sprinkled with water.
They say that the distance between one mandala and the next is thirty-two finger-breadths;
however, the mandala should be made according to the measure of the practitioner's own even step.
"Mahat" means having a greater dimension than the previous mandalas. "Pārthiva" means having the Earth as its presiding deity.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme rite of the fire.
They say that the distance from one mandala to the next mandala is thirty-two finger-breadths.
Thus, with eight circles, the measurement of two hundred fingers is declared; this is the conceptual arrangement of the ground.
One should make the measurement of the mandala equal to that step.

[One should not step beyond the mandala, nor should one place a step short of it. From the first mandala, another mandala measuring thirty-two finger-breadths—or even more—should likewise be made. In this way, for the ground to be traversed, the interval consisting of seven mandalas amounts to two hundred and twenty-four [finger-breadths].
Yājñavalkya [2.106]: The distance from one mandala to the next mandala should be known as sixteen aṅgulas.
Pitāmaha [226].
In every mandala, kusha grasses as prescribed by the scriptures should be offered;
the performer must always place his foot upon them—this is the established rule.
Hārīta says:
One should stand there facing the east, with the fingers of one's hands extended,
wearing wet clothes and remaining pure, having placed a leaf upon one's head.
The grandfather [Manu] says: In the western circle, the pure [accused] should stand facing east with palms joined;
the judges should observe any wounds or other marks on the hands of that performer.
Viṣṇu [11.20]: One should first examine his hands for crushed grains of rice.
Nārada [4.301]:
In all cases of wounds from hands, one should indeed apply the *ha-sa-pada* [mantras];
then one should again observe those very two hands, adorned with drops (*bindu*).
Likewise, the Grandfather [said]:
"One should place seven leaves of the *aśvattha* tree, *śamī* leaves, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*) in his hands, as well as seven threads of thread."
For fire is born from the *pippala* tree, and the *pippala* is known as the king of trees;
therefore, its leaves should be employed by the wise.
Having made it symmetrical and free from flaws, one should heat a uniform iron ball weighing fifty palas in the fire for eight finger-breadths.

"He who is a blacksmith by birth and also skilled in his craft..."

O Agni, you are the supreme purifier and the source of bliss for all the gods;

this has been declared by the Vedas and other scriptures, and you ought not to act otherwise.
By this [oath], he declares: "If he should speak this falsely, then I shall maintain the fire so that it may be false in every respect."
This man sustains you by this very truth;

Having caused him to hear [the mantra], one should place it upon his very head and bestow [the initiation] in the proper sequence.

Since you indeed purify evil, therefore you are called Pāvaka;
manifest yourself among the wicked and become radiant, O Pāvaka!
Alternatively, O Mahābala, become cool toward those of pure disposition;
one may even command him who licks with his tongue an iron [mass].

Having consecrated it with mantras, one should place that iron ball upon both hands.
O Agni, you move within all beings like a witness.

this man, accused in a legal proceeding, desires purification.

well-heated, well-prepared, and rising with sparks and flames.

Or, directed by the pincers, one should place it upon his two hands.

nor on uneven ground, nor where it is crowded with trees and stumps.

"With discharged arrows.
Viṣṇu [12:3–4]: "[One should enter the consecrated water]; and at that same moment, another person should discharge an arrow with a bow that is neither too harsh nor too soft. Bṛhaspati [8.62]:

Having entered the water, one should cause the person to discharge three arrows. Pitāmaha says: One should immerse oneself in water that is still, not in water that is turbid, nor in water that is shallow.
Free from grass and aquatic moss, and devoid of leeches and fish.
One should perform purification using water from natural reservoirs;
one should avoid water that has been drawn up, as well as that from rivers with swift currents.
"In *grāhiṇi*": possessed of creatures called crocodiles (*grāha*). Nārada [4.305]:
"In rivers that are not too swift, and in tanks and lakes..."

Viṣṇu [12.2–3]: "In water free from mud, moss, wicked crocodiles, fish, leeches, and the like, one should enter the consecrated water while holding the knees of another person who is not submerged up to the navel and is free from passion and hatred. Nārada [4.308]:
"A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya, free from passion and hatred..."
A strong man should be stationed like a pillar in water reaching up to his navel.

This man, accused in a legal dispute, is now sinking into you;

In the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"O Varuṇa, protect him from this very curse!

If a man who has been seen by a living being dives and then surfaces,

While standing facing south in the presence of the twice-born,

"O you who manifest among the wicked, become immortal for the sake of the pure!

This man, accused in a legal dispute, desires purification;

O Poison, you are the son of Brahmā, established in truth and righteousness;
protect me from this curse, and by truth become nectar for me.
Having spoken thus, one should consume the Śārṅga poison born from the snowy mountains.

once he has overcome the exhaustion from the force of the poison, Manu declared him to be purified.

as it has been declared by those learned in the treatises, and which is not in conflict with any time.

who possesses a sense of shame and is free from malice, the drinking of the ordeal-substance (kośapāna) is prescribed.

however, for the other deities, one should bathe their weapons.
