while he has bathed according to the previously mentioned procedure, remains in a wet garment, and is pure.

one should cause the accused to pay that matter with effort, as well as a fine.
If that [calamity] were to befall only one person and not all people—
such as disease, fire, the death of a kinsman, debt, or the payment of a fine— he alone would have to bear it.
Fever, dysentery, and eruptive boils arise, as well as the affliction of colic and other pains, eye disease, throat ailments, and likewise insanity.

Headaches and paralysis of the arms are divine diseases for men. "Contradiction by fate" (*daivavisaṃvāda*) refers to opposition caused by fate, consisting of illness, the death of kinsmen, and so forth. Nārada [4.331]:
If, after two weeks have passed, a very great abnormality should occur,
the wise man should not administer [the treatment], because the appointed time has elapsed.
Yājñavalkya [2.113]:
He for whom no terrible calamity—whether caused by the king or by fate—occurs within fourteen days, is purified; of this there is no doubt.
"Calamity" means misfortune; "terrible" means causing extreme suffering. Bṛhaspati [8.65]:
"If pain does not arise for one within seven days or fourteen days..."
One will undoubtedly become pure with respect to children, wife, and wealth.

In this regard, it should be understood that the rule concerning the waiting periods of two days, seven days, or twenty-one days depends on the relative degree of the place, the time, and the specific circumstances. Kātyāyana [454] states:
"Even for one who has been accused with certainty and has cleared himself through the ordeal of the water-pot (*kośa*),"
But he shall cause the accuser to pay the legal proceeding along with the fine.
Viṣṇu [14.5]:
A righteous king should honor a person who is pure by divine means. Nārada [4.333].
One should cause the five ordeals to be performed according to the prescribed rule;
therein, the king and those accused find joy both in this world and after death.
[250] 44. Now follows the procedure for rice; regarding this, Pitāmaha says:
I shall explain the rule regarding the eating and the avoidance of rice;
it is a settled conclusion that rice should be given to a Śūdra, and not elsewhere.
One who is pure should have white rice grains of *śāli*— and not of any other kind, such as iron-colored— prepared, and place them in an earthen vessel before the Sun.
One should let them remain mixed with the bathing water in that very place during the night;
at dawn, they should be given to the performer while he faces the sun.
Having eaten rice grains, one should spit them out into a leaf during the day;
it should be on a *bhūrja* leaf and not on any other, though in its absence, a *pippala* leaf may be used.
Kātyāyana [453]: One who has consumed rice grains smeared with water used for bathing or drinking a deity becomes pure by spitting it out; otherwise, he must be restrained as impure.
Bṛhaspati [8.70]: On the occasion of a solar eclipse, one who is pure and fasting should eat rice grains;
he shall be purified if the vomit is white, but if it is mixed with blood, he incurs guilt.
Bṛhaspati and Pitāmaha:
One in whom blood is seen, whose jaw-joint sinks,
and whose body trembles— him one should designate as impure.
The "jaw-cluster" (*hanujāla*) refers to the collection of the upper and lower, left and right jaws.
[252] 45 — Now, the procedure for the heated gold coin (*taptamāṣaka*).
In that regard, the Grandfather said:

"I shall describe the auspicious procedure for the ordeal of the heated gold ball (taptamāṣa) for the purpose of clearing one's innocence. One should have a vessel made of iron or copper sixteen finger-breadths in size."
Then, one should fill a circular pit dug four finger-breadths deep, made either of clay or stone, with twenty palas of ghee and oil.
One should cast a *māṣaka* of gold into that [liquid] when it is well-heated;
then, using the thumb and finger together, one should extract the heated *māṣaka*.
A "maṇḍala" is circular.
Bṛhaspati [8.72]: One should extract a heated māṣaka from oil or ghee using a ladle.
Having joined the thumb and fingers together and addressed Satya, one who is free from fear—
Having addressed the Truth with the mantra beginning "Come, come, O Blessed Dharma," one should purify the Dharma. As for the Grandfather (Brahmā) and Bṛhaspati:
he whose fingertips do not quiver nor does a blister arise [is pure].
He becomes pure by means of the Dharma, according to the word of his grandfather.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"He who does not shake the tip of his hand, from whom no blood arises,
and who is free from defects such as eruptions— he is pure."
[253] 46. Now, the procedure for ploughing; regarding this, Bṛhaspati states [8.79–80]:
An iron ploughshare, weighing twelve palas and forged,
is said to be eight finger-breadths in length and four finger-breadths in width.
The thief shall lick that [substance] while it is red-hot with his tongue once;
if he is not burned, he shall attain purification, but otherwise he is defeated.
[254] 47. Now, the procedure for the *dharmaja* [son]: regarding this, Bṛhaspati [states] (8.82–85):
On two leaves, dharma and adharma should be written in white and black [ink], respectively,
with mantras such as those for the gift of life and with Sāman chants beginning with the Gāyatrī.
Having addressed [the deity], one should worship with perfumes and white and black flowers;
then, having sprinkled them with the five products of the cow, they should be enclosed within lumps of clay.
Having made them equal and placed them in a new jar that has not been previously used for grinding,
one should then take a single lump from the jar without delay.
One who has grasped the Dharma shall be pure and worthy of worship by those who examine him,
through acts such as the gift of life and with mantras beginning with "May we not stray from the path" and "mā pragāma patho vayam.
48. Now follows the procedure for oaths.
Regarding this, Manu [8.110] states:
"Oaths were taken by the great seers and by the gods for the sake of determining legal matters."
And Vasiṣṭha also swore an oath before the king, the son of Pijavana.
For even among the gods and the high-souled sages there are oaths;
Vasiṣṭha uttered a curse when he was addressed as a "Yātudhāna."
The great seers, as well as Indra and the others, being thus requested for the purpose of the sacrificial grass,
calmly uttered an oath for mutual purification.

Viṣṇu [9.4–14]: "In all matters concerning property, one should determine the value in gold. For a debt of one *kṛṣṇala*, one should cause a Śūdra to swear by holding *dūrvā* grass; for two *kṛṣṇalas*, by holding sesame seeds; for three *kṛṣṇalas*, by holding silver; for four *kṛṣṇalas*, by holding gold; and for five *kṛṣṇalas*, by holding earth taken from a furrow. For a debt of half a *suvarṇa*, a Śūdra must provide the *kośa* ordeal. Beyond that, whichever is appropriate—such as the balance, fire, water, or poison—should be administered. For a debt of double that amount, the prescribed procedure applies to a Vaiśya; for triple the amount, to a Kṣatriya; and for quadruple the amount, to a Brāhmaṇa."
"In *kṛṣṇalona*," [it means] "by less than a *kṛṣṇala*. In this same way, "by two *kṛṣṇalas less" (*dvikṛṣṇalona*) and so forth should also be understood.
Manu [8.113–14]: One should cause a Brāhmaṇa to swear by truth, and a Kṣatriya by his vehicles and weapons.
A Vaiśya by [stealing] cattle, grain, or gold; a Śūdra by all [the aforementioned] sins.
And he should also have him touch the heads of his sons and wife individually; Bṛhaspati [8.33–34] states:
"Truth, vehicles, weapons, cattle, seeds, and gold..."
The feet of gods and brahmins, as well as the heads of one's children and wife—
These oaths have been declared as always easy to perform in matters of small value;
however, for violent acts and grave accusations, they say that divine ordeals are the means of purification.
Truth, vehicles, weapons, cattle, grain, gold,
and the offerings made to the gods and ancestors, as well as other meritorious gifts that have been bestowed.
Thus have these oaths been declared by Manu for minor matters;
the rule regarding divine ordeals is proclaimed for grave sins and formal accusations.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "One should cause him to perform sacrifices and works of public utility, as well as other types of oaths.
Manu (8.115) says: "Him whom the kindled fire does not burn, and whom the waters do not force to float,"
And he who does not quickly meet with misfortune should be known as pure in his oath.
Kātyāyana [463]: He for whom no terrible calamity caused by the king or by fate occurs until the fourteenth part of the day has passed, is to be known as pure in his oath.
Manu [8.111–12]: A wise man should not take a false oath even for a trivial matter;
for by taking a false oath, one perishes both in this world and after death.
In matters concerning women, at weddings, regarding the consumption of cattle, as well as for fuel,
in assisting a Brahmin, and in taking an oath, there is no sin.
Yama said: "But by making a false oath involving the killing of an insect,
a man becomes guilty of both falsehood and murder."
Therefore, a person should not make a false oath according to his own desire.
Thus ends the section on Procedure (*kriyāpāda*) in the *Vyavahārakāṇḍa* of the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, composed by Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, the great Sandhivigrahika and son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara.
[258] 49 — Now, the method of reaching a decision; regarding this, Vyāsa says:

The determination of a case is recorded as being of eight kinds: by means of proofs, by the application of logical reasons, by oath, by the king’s command, or by the mutual agreement of the litigants.
Written documents, witnesses, and possession are known as the threefold means of proof;
the wise understand inference to consist of logical reason and dialectical inquiry.
The ten-fold status has been previously established, and conduct has been fully described;
oaths corresponding to the purpose are recorded as the "truth-weighing" (satyadhaṭa) and others.
In their absence, the wise know that the king’s command is the final decision.
This refers to inference (*anumāna*); the meaning is that they consider reasoning (*tarka*)—which is inference—to be the cause of a definitive conclusion. Thus says Bṛhaspati (9.1).
The determination of a matter in doubt is declared to be of four kinds: by means of legal codes, by judicial procedure, by conduct, and by the king's command.
Each one is declared by the great seers to be of two kinds due to the distinction of ritual action;
however, having thoroughly investigated the task, it has been fully determined through reasoning.
But that legal decision which has been tested by oaths should be known as the determination of dharma;
where the defendant admits [the claim], that is the determination of dharma.
The second [type of purification] is declared to be that which is thoroughly purified by divine means;
[this was stated by] Kātyāyana [36]. Furthermore, whatever Smṛti treatise has been spoken by those who establish the Dharma—
For it is indeed recorded that legal procedure (vyavahāra) exists for the purpose of deciding cases.
By the term "Smṛtiśāstra" (the treatises of traditional law), the means of proof such as witnesses and others mentioned in those Smṛti texts are intended here. Bṛhaspati [9.5] states:
"A legal proceeding that is determined by means of proof is so called."
The second [type of defeat] is proclaimed as such because it lacks a response to a quibble (vākchala).
The meaning is that the second type of legal proceeding is determined as being a quibble of speech (*vākchala*) and determined as being a non-justified reply (*anuttara*). Kātyāyana [37] states:
"Whatever is practiced by someone, whether it be righteous or unrighteous..."
That which is constantly practiced by a country is proclaimed as its *caritra* (custom).
Bṛhaspati [9.6]: Conduct determined by inference is called *caritra*;
the second, however, is declared by those learned in the scriptures to be established local custom (*deśasthiti*).
Kātyāyana [38, second section]: Bhṛgu says that when matters are doubtful, they are settled with certainty by means of the scriptures;
the king shall be the authority for those cases, for the king is indeed the lord of all.
That which the king establishes as righteous, in accordance with the treatises on logic (Nyāya) and likewise according to local customs—
that is the lawful royal edict.
Without violating the Dharma, legal procedure, or established custom, the king should maintain this by means of stability; that is the righteous royal edict.
"Without abolishing," meaning even while not abandoning it; Bṛhaspati [9.7]:
"But a royal decree accompanied by authoritative means of knowledge is considered a final decision."
In contrast, another [type] has been proclaimed as being contrary to both the scriptures and the principles of refined society.

The construction is: "A royal decree accompanied by evidence is the first type of decision. Regarding the phrase "in case of conflict between the court members and the scriptures": this refers to a mutual disagreement between the members of the court and the legal treatises.
Nārada [1.11] states:
"In that regard, Dharma is established in truth, and judicial procedure rests upon witnesses."
The term *carita* refers to the act of making a manuscript, whereas *śāsana* refers to it when done by royal command.
Bṛhaspati said: When a king understands the fourfold method of legal decision in this way,
he attains fame in this world and goes to the realm of Śakra.
[261] 50— Now, regarding the relative strength and weakness of judicial decisions, Nārada [states]: [1.10]
Dharma, judicial procedure, custom, and royal edict—
this four-legged judicial process consists of these, each subsequent one superseding the preceding.
"The later [authority] sublates the earlier. This means that among the rules of dharma, legal procedures, established customs, and royal edicts, each subsequent one sublates the preceding one.
Bṛhaspati [1.19]: "Where a decision is made by relying solely upon the treatise..."
That should be understood as mere worldly litigation; by it, the Dharma is undermined.
Kātyāyana [39]: But where an action is consistent with reason and divine ordeals are avoided,
there the Dharma is sublated by the legal proceeding (vyavahāra), and not otherwise.
Bṛhaspati [1.20]: "A decision is made based on local custom, inference, and what is accepted by the community; in such a case, however, the formal legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) is set aside."
‘Naigamāḥ’ refers to citizens and merchants. The connection is: ‘by inference approved by the naigamas. Kātyāyana [40–41]:
“The same applies to those born of inverse unions (pratiloma) and likewise to those residing in forts.”
They say that which is contrary [to the law] is fixed; one should not deviate from that dharma.
But when the king shall make a decision according to that dharma, then legal procedure is superseded by custom, and by that very [custom] it is annulled.
"By that dharma," meaning by way of local custom; Bṛhaspati [1.21]:
"But whatever the king may do again, having set aside established practice..."
But that royal decree is a final decision; thus, established custom is set aside.
‘Caritācāra’ refers to the conduct practiced by predecessors. Kātyāyana [42, 43] states: “But that custom which is contrary to justice, even if it is established by kings...”
In this manner, the conduct [of the accused] should be refuted there by the command of the king.
Whatever subsequent sublation is declared according to this rule,
where there is sublation otherwise, there dharma is destroyed.
Thus is the method of determination.
Now, the duty once determined.
In this regard, Nārada [2.41] states:
"Even if he has appeared in person, even if he is established in good conduct,
and even if he has failed in his legal performance, he deserves the final determination by the court members."
Afterwards, he is to be punished by the king according to his own legal code, as determined by the members of the court (*sabhyas*).

"One who has confessed himself" (*svayam abhyupapanna*) is one who has admitted defeat on his own accord. "One defeated through good conduct" (*sucaryāvasita*) is one known to have been defeated by such signs as change of complexion, perspiration, trembling, and so forth, due to his internal state. "One defeated by evidence" (*kriyāvasanna*) is one who has reached a state of defeat through evidence such as witnesses or ordeals. "The subsequent determination by the court members" (*param sabhyāvadhāraṇam*) refers to the subsequent proclamation by the court members gathered in one place that he is defeated by this evidence.
— Yājñavalkya [2.11].
Having reached a conclusion, he should deliver the fine to the king and an equal amount to himself;
in the case of a false accusation, he shall pay double the amount of the claim.
But one who denies a debt that has been proven by evidence,
the judge shall compel him to pay the creditor’s claim and a small fine according to his ability.
Whatever amount of wealth one may conceal, or for whatever amount one may speak falsely in a lawsuit,
both of those ignorant of the Dharma shall be made by the king to pay a fine double that amount.

‘Apavyayamānam’ means denying [the debt]. ‘By means of evidence,’ such as a written document and so forth. Regarding the phrase ‘yo yāvat tau’: the meaning is that both the debtor who denies the amount and the creditor who brings a false claim for whatever amount of wealth—both of them, due to the fault of their intention (*āśayadoṣa*), when engaged in a dispute, shall be made to pay double the fine. However, in cases where the denial is due to poverty, forgetfulness, or similar reasons, rather than a fault of intention, it should be understood that they must pay a small portion of the fine according to their capacity. Vyāsa says: “But when the disputant himself admits what he had denied...”
That should be known as the practice; it is remembered as its "half-vinaya."
Nārada [2.37]:
Those of Śūdra origin who bring false accusations against the twice-born—
the king shall have their tongues cut out and impale them upon a stake.

[265] Yājñavalkya [2.20]: If a defendant denies a written document, but is proven on even a single part of it, he must be made by the king to pay the entire amount; however, that which was not previously declared should not be accepted as evidence.

When a defendant, having been charged with a claim involving gold, silver, copper, and so forth, denies it, and the plaintiff subsequently proves (*vibhāvita*) even a portion of that claim—such as the gold—by means of documents and other evidence, the king shall compel him to pay all the amounts, including the silver and the rest. Regarding this, [the rule] "but what was not previously declared is not to be accepted" means that if a matter was not urged by the plaintiff at the time of the initial plea (*pūrvabhāṣā*), then even if a portion has been proven, the plaintiff must not be made to accept that matter.
—Nārada.
When one who is accused of multiple offenses denies all charges,
yet only one part has been proven, he must pay what he was accused of.
Yājñavalkya [2.18]: If a dispute should be accompanied by a wager, he shall compel the loser to pay that which was staked,
as well as a fine equal to double that amount and the principal sum to the creditor.
Bṛhaspati [9.25]:
And this punishment has been ordained in accordance with the offense.
52. Now, the procedure for victory (*jayipratipatti*).
On this point, Bṛhaspati says (9.21): "The proponent [wins] through the substantiation of his thesis and through the honoring of the presiding judge and others."
And because he receives the document of victory, he is called the victor in the world.
Kātyāyana [262]: Having joined the plaintiff with his proven claim, the king should, after showing him respect, give him a written document bearing his own signature.
Vyāsa: Having personally observed or heard the legal proceedings, or having learned of them from the presiding judge,
the king should then issue a certificate of victory for the sake of official recognition.
Kātyāyana [264]: That written document which has been rejected should be destroyed immediately;
likewise, a subsequent plea (paścātkāra) that is rejected should also be discarded—of this there is no doubt.

But where an action has been refuted by the proponent himself through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there a subsequent rejoinder (*paścātkāra*) may occur; it is not, however, prescribed in all such cases.
In the case of defeat concerning slaves, women, land, houses, gardens, and scribes,
the kings shall issue a *paścātkāra* (a formal decree of acquittal) only in these very instances.

"Subsequent action" (*paścātkāra*) refers to legal procedures such as the issuance of a decree following a verdict. "Means of proof" (*pramāṇa*) refers to witnesses and so forth. The phrase "in these very cases" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*).
[267] 53 — Now, furthermore, the legal procedure (*nyāya*):
Regarding this, Manu [9.233] states: "Wherever a case may have been adjudicated and a decision rendered, one should know that it has been done according to dharma; one must not reverse it."

The word *tīritam* is the form of the root *tṛ* (in the sense of "crossing over" or "completion of an action") with the suffix *niṣṭhā*. Its meaning is "concluded after having been decided. *Anuśiṣṭam* means "declared by the witnesses. *Yatra kvacana* means "in any assembly," such as that of a village and so forth.
Nārada [1.65]:
"He who considers a case that has been concluded (*tīrita*) or declared (*anuśiṣṭa*) to be contrary to the law..."
Having imposed double the fine, he should restore that property once again.
Likewise:
"For those who have been defeated by witnesses, there is a further trial upon refutation; however, for those who have been defeated by their own conduct, no rule for a second trial has been stated."

"Of those who have reached exhaustion through witnesses and assessors" means those who have become despondent by way of the witnesses and assessors. "In the case of their disqualification" refers to the witnesses and the assessors; this is the grammatical connection. "Seeing" means that the trial must be observed again and again. "Defeated by his own conduct" means one who has been defeated through his own actions, such as speaking in contradiction to himself.
[268] Bṛhaspati [9.22]: "By fleeing, by failing to provide an answer, and by resorting to the other side..."
The speech of one who is inferior is accepted, but not that of one who has been defeated by his own words.
Bṛhaspati and Kātyāyana state:
Even if a matter has been determined by the family and others, if the king does not feel satisfied,
he should investigate that which was done and, if it was wrongly done, set it aside again.
Bṛhaspati [9.24]: Having reached a decision together with many Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the scriptures,
the king should punish the former members of the court along with the victorious party if they are found guilty.
Yājñavalkya [2.305]:
But if the judges have wrongly decided legal cases and they are reviewed again by the king,
they shall be fined twice the amount of the dispute, together with their fellow jurors.
"He who thinks 'I am not defeated' when he has been defeated according to the rules— having won that case again in court, one should compel him to pay double the fine.
[Nārada 2.66]
But if the legal proceeding is wrongly judged, the members of the court shall incur that same punishment;
for indeed, no one ever remains on the path of righteousness without the threat of punishment.
Manu [9.234]: "If ministers or the judge should decide a case otherwise than it ought to be,
the king himself shall decide that case and fine them one thousand [paṇas]."
Now, regarding the cessation of action, Manu and Viṣṇu state:
In whatever legal dispute false testimony has been given, that very case shall be reversed; whether it has already been decided or not yet decided, it shall be as if undone.
Nārada [1.43]: A legal transaction entered into with women, at night, outside the village, within the house, or with enemies— even if completed— must be performed again.
Manu and Nārada [Manu 8.164; Nā. 2.15]:
A statement does not become valid even if it is well-established, if it is spoken outside of the established legal procedure (*vyavahāra*).

[271] Speech concerning worldly legal matters is said to be "fixed" (*niyata*). Even though it is established and possesses evidentiary weight such as written documents, it is not true. Whatever matter is established by such speech is not to be carried out—for example, when someone says, "He has given me his entire property," and so forth.
"That which is mortgaged, sold, or purchased through fraud, or that which is given or received through fraud..."
Or wherever one perceives any form of attachment, one should completely relinquish all of that.
"Whatever is given by force, enjoyed by force, or even recorded by force—
Manu has declared all such matters done by force to be as if not done."
"Yoga" means fraud; the meaning is that the king shall nullify whatever act, such as the pledging of property, has been performed by means of it. "Upadhi" means deceit.
Likewise [in verse 8.163]:
"By one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted, dependent, a child, or an elderly person..."
Furthermore, a legal proceeding conducted without a proper connection is not established.
[272] A slave is dependent on his master.
Whatever transaction a minor performs, and likewise one who is not independent—
Those who are learned in the treatises declare that even such an act is considered unperformed according to the scriptures.
For even that effect which an independent agent might produce while not having undergone a change in nature is said to be as good as unproduced; for it is not independent by virtue of its own cause.
Those who are overcome by desire and anger, afflicted by distress, fear, and calamity,
and enveloped by passion and hatred, should be known as having fallen into an unnatural state.
Likewise, a task performed by a servant is declared to be unperformed, except when it is by the master's command;
for a servant has no authority over himself.
If a task is performed by a son against the father’s will, they say that it is as if it were not done at all; for a slave and a son are equal in this regard.
Kātyāyana [467]: The gift, mortgage, or sale of fields, houses, or slaves does not attain validity if performed by those who are not independent, nor when they have not been duly authorized.
‘Not authorized’ means not permitted; the word ‘independently’ is to be understood as the ellipsis. Nārada [2.26–27, 42]:
They say that transactions entered into by women are invalid except in times of distress.
Especially regarding the giving, mortgaging, or selling of houses and fields.
These alone are the authorities, provided the husband approves;
or, in the absence of the husband, the son; or, in the absence of both husband and son, the king.

Whatever is done by the eldest in the family, or by one who is most excellent and established in his natural state, that deed shall be considered as done; what is done by one who is not independent is not considered as done.
[274] 55 — Now, regarding the definition of independent (*svatantra*) and non-independent (*asvatantra*):
on this point, Nārada says [4.31, 33–37]:
Independence is considered the mark of seniority; seniority is determined by qualities and age.
Likewise: "All subjects are independent, and the lord of the earth is independent."
The disciple is traditionally held to be dependent, whereas the teacher possesses independence.
All women, sons, slaves, and dependents are not independent;
rather, the master of the household is independent therein, provided that the property has descended to him through succession.
A child is to be known as being like one still in the womb until the eighth year;
from that until the sixteenth year, he is called a *bāla* (boy), and thereafter he is designated a *pogaṇḍa*.
[275] One who knows legal procedure is independent with respect to others, except for his parents;
while they live, he shall not be independent, even if he is advanced in years.
Of those two as well, the father is superior, because the importance of the seed is observed;
in the absence of the progenitor, the mother [is superior], and in her absence, the elder brother.

Kātyāyana [466]: A father who lacks independence, a son whose father is still living, a brother, or even a nephew; a younger brother who has not yet divided his property, as well as a slave and a dependent—these are [not independent].
"Dependent on the father" means one who possesses a father and is not independent. "One whose property is undivided" means one whose wealth has not been partitioned. Hārīta says:
"Whether for the purpose of giving, or for the purpose of acquiring wealth, or especially for the purpose of dharma..."
Neither in taking nor in giving does a woman deserve independence.

Nārada [2.38]: All these [male relatives] are independent in every respect, yet they are always considered masters with regard to instruction, distribution, and sale concerning those who are dependent on them.
"These" refers to the king and others mentioned previously. Kātyāyana [468–69] states:
"All of these are authoritative in the buying and selling of commodities."
If they were previously approved while conducting worldly transactions, [then they are not to be blamed].
In the same way, a brother, a brother’s son, or a son [may act] on behalf of the field and so forth,
provided they have been authorized by the preceptor to perform the necessary duties when he is departing.
[276] But he who has been authorized with full power regarding a particular matter is indeed the master in that matter; his employer cannot undo the business transacted by him in any other way.
Bṛhaspati [9.29, 28]:
He who is appointed by his master to oversee income and expenditure,
as well as money-lending, agriculture, and trade, is known as one to whom authority has been delegated (nisṛṣṭārtha).
Whatever has been done by him—whether gain or loss, expenditure or income—is authoritative;
whether in his own country or abroad, the master shall not contradict that.

Kātyāyana [471]: A father has authority over his son and his son’s wife in matters of instruction; however, he has no authority over his son in matters of sale or gift. Thus, he is not the master of his son.

Thus [ends the section] in the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Mallakṣmīdhara, son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara, who served as the Great Minister for Peace and War (*mahāsāndhivigrahika*) to His Majesty the Emperor (*mahārājādhirāja*), the illustrious Govindacandradeva.
In the section on legal procedure, the summary of legal proceedings is completed.
the legal titles concerning the non-payment of debt and so forth—
56. Next, the procedure for the non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*).
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states:
"This legal procedure has been proclaimed together with its titles and constituent parts.
Now hear the titles which are the causes of litigation."
I shall now explain in due order, according to their true nature, the non-payment and payment of debts, gambling, and betting, as well as the various types of legal procedures.

Nārada [4.1, 98]: That which is to be paid and that which is not to be paid, by whom, where, and in what manner, as well as the rules regarding giving and receiving— this is known as the legal title of "Recovery of Debts" (ṛṇādāna).
That which is intended as the acceptance of a gift for the sake of obtaining a position should be known as usury; by that, the livelihood of usurers is defined.
In this context, "place" (*sthāna*) refers to the status of the principal capital; "gain" (*lābha*) refers to the acquisition of interest and so forth. Bṛhaspati [10.6, 5] states:
"It is received without hesitation from one who is contemptible and from one who is in distress."
Therefore, that which is called usury is recorded as being fourfold or eightfold [of the principal].
Having received a complete pledge or a bond with reliable guarantors,
or having recorded it in writing with witnesses, the creditor shall always cause the debt to be paid.
"In the case of one who is contemptible and one who is indolent," thus as qualifiers of the debtor; Nārada [4.117]:
"In this matter, there are two causes of confidence: the surety and the pledge."
A written document and two witnesses are the two means that make the proof manifest.
Kātyāyana [497]: One should not give anything withdrawn from the estate to women, children, or slaves;
the giver does not recover that wealth which has been given to them.
"Uddhṛtam" means the principal amount.
Now, regarding interest, Bṛhaspati [states] at 10.28:
Listen to the rule regarding interest for a moneylender as proclaimed by Vasiṣṭha:
five māṣas on twenty [kārṣāpaṇas]; thus the dharma is not violated.
"Twenty" here refers to *māṣas*. Gautama [12.26] states: "Interest on a loan is lawful at the rate of twenty-five *māṣas* per month. [279] This is from the *Smṛti*.
A māṣa is declared to be one-twentieth part of a paṇa; [Manu 8.140]:
One may employ the interest prescribed by Vasiṣṭha for the purpose of increasing wealth.
A moneylender may take an eightieth part of a hundred per month.
Yājñavalkya [2.37]: "The rate of interest shall be one-eightieth part [of the principal] month after month when there is a pledge. Bṛhaspati [10.22]: [The same].
The interest shall increase by one-eightieth part [per month] until the debt reaches double its principal;
lent for seven years less one-third, there is no doubt of this.
Vyāsa states: "In a secured loan, the share [of interest] is one-eighth; in a loan with a pledge, it is one-eighth plus one-sixteenth;
in an unsecured loan, a monthly profit of two percent is declared."
"Āśītaḥ" means the eightieth. This very [rate], when combined with its own eighth part, is "sāṣṭabhāgaḥ" (with an eighth part). "Nirādhāne" means without a pledge. Manu [8.141]:
Or he may take two percent per hundred, remembering the dharma of the virtuous.
For one who takes two percent interest does not become a sinner for the sake of wealth.

Hārīta states: "In the Purāṇapañcaviṃśati, the interest is eight *paṇas* per month. Thus, with four years and two months, having doubled, it ceases; this is lawful interest (*dharmavṛddhi*). One does not fall from righteousness by means of this. A *purāṇa* consists of sixteen *paṇas*. "Having doubled" (*dviḥparyāgatam*) means it has become twofold. "Ceases" (*saṃtiṣṭhate*) means it stops; the sense is that it does not increase further. Manu [8.142]:
One may take interest at the rate of two, three, four, five,
or ten percent per month, according to the order of the social classes.

"Dvika" refers to that principal capital upon which an interest of two [purāṇas per month] is paid; likewise for "trika" and so forth. "Sama" means not exceeding the measure [of the principal]. Yājñavalkya [2.37]:
According to the order of the castes, [the interest shall be] one hundred [per cent], two, three, four, or five [per cent]; otherwise, it is different.

‘Otherwise’ means without a pledge (*bandhaka*). Viṣṇu [6.1–2] states: “Now, the creditor may recover from the debtor the amount as it was lent, at the rate of two, three, four, or five percent per month, according to the order of the castes.
Gautama [12.27] says: “Some say that the interest shall not exceed the principal for a period of one year.”
Manu [8.153]: One should not take interest exceeding one year's duration, nor that which is not sanctioned;
likewise, compound interest, periodical interest, stipulated interest, and interest paid by labor.

[282] "Not exceeding one year"—the interest must be restricted from the month up to one year; it must not exceed beyond one year. A restriction should be made such that: "If you cause me to split [the debt] by means of interest, I shall pay exactly that.
Nārada [4.102]: "Interest is of three kinds: corporeal (kāyikā), periodical (kālikā), and stipulated (kāritā), as well as another."
But in the treatises, there is the increase of the wheel-turner; his increase is fourfold.
Bṛhaspati [10.8–9]:
Interest is said to be of four kinds, proclaimed by others as fivefold, and declared by others as sixfold; understand it according to its true nature.
The bodily [interest], the periodic, and furthermore the wheel-increasing;
the stipulated, the crest-increasing, as well as the gain of enjoyment.

Vyāsa says: That which is joined with the acts of milking and carrying is declared to be bodily (kāyika); that which constantly does not oppose the body, such as the five types of prostration and so forth, is also bodily.
That which is never inconsistent with the body, such as half a paṇa and so forth, is bodily interest.
That interest which flows month by month is considered to be periodical (kālikā).
The interest upon interest is declared to be *cakravṛddhi*;
that interest which is stipulated by the debtor himself is called *kāritā*.

‘Not inconsistent with the principal’ (*kāyāvirodhinī*) means not inconsistent with the original capital. ‘But that which is half a *paṇa* or more daily’ refers to an amount such as half a *paṇa* or similar, to be paid every day. That interest which was first agreed upon by both parties is called ‘stipulated’ (*kārikā*). Kātyāyana [498] states:
“But that interest which is stipulated by the debtor to be higher...”
But that which is performed during a time of distress must always be given as a commissioned gift.
Interest stipulated otherwise must never be paid under any circumstances.
Yājñavalkya [2.38]:
"But those traveling through forests [should pay] ten percent; those traveling by sea, twenty percent."
Or they may pay the interest agreed upon by themselves; this applies to all [debts] among all classes of people.
"But whatever interest those skilled in sea-voyages, who perceive the requirements of place, time, and profit,
may establish, that shall apply in such cases regarding the acquisition of the goods."

[284] The phrase “skilled in sea-voyages” is an illustration intended to include merchants in general. “Discerners of place, time, and profit” refers to those who perceive that in this particular time there will be such-and-such a gain, and in that other time such-and-such another. “Adhigama” means certainty. Hārīta states: “Some say that for old cloth, the interest is one *paṇa* per month; for cotton, it is double; for grain, triple—and in this manner it increases. Likewise for wool and cotton; for grass, bamboo, ghee, molasses, and salt, it is eightfold in one year.”

The phrase "he may take a paṇika per month" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Regarding the rule "in the case of cotton, grain is double," grain may be taken as double even after two, three, or more months. "In the case of cotton" refers to the arrival of new grain; however, when it is not paid at the time of the arrival of the cotton, then it becomes triple. "It does not increase further" means that it does not reach a fourfold state. "Likewise," like grain, wool and cotton increase only threefold in a year; however, when it is not paid within a year, then it becomes eightfold in a year—meaning it remains triple [until the end of the year] and then becomes eightfold.
This rule for the accumulation of interest is declared to be universally applicable;
however, there is another established local custom where it remains at half [the principal].
In one region twice the amount is to be given, in another three times, and likewise four times;
in yet another region, eight times the amount is to be paid, according to local custom.
Bṛhaspati [10.11, 13a]:
That interest which is collected daily is known as *śikhāvṛddhi* (top-knot interest);
it increases constantly like a top-knot and ceases only upon the cutting off of the head.

When the principal has been paid, this same interest is known as "interest on the balance" (*śikhāvṛddhi*). Kātyāyana [501] states: "But that which is the entire enjoyment of the pledge, and that which is calculated as interest..."
And wherever such application occurs, that is called "possession" (ādhibhoga).
Bṛhaspati [10.14, 16]: Interest arising from a house is declared to be *stoma*; that arising from a field is *bhogalābha*.
Likewise, interest on a pledge (*śikhāvṛddhi*) and bodily labor (*kāyikā*) are also considered *bhogalābha*.
The creditor shall take [the produce] as long as the principal has not been repaid;
*stoma* means rent, and *sadaḥ* means the fruit such as grain and so forth. Yājñavalkya [2.90].

The pledge (ādhi) is enjoyed only so long as it is not returned. Following the rule that "the creditor shall deliver the pledge," Viṣṇu [6.6–8] states: "Even when the interest has reached its limit, the immovable pledge is not to be surrendered except by special agreement. The phrase "except by special agreement" means that if it was not previously stated that the pledge would be surrendered once the debt has doubled.
An interest exceeding the legal rate, or one that is excessive, is not valid;
they call that the way of usury, for it deserves a fine of five percent.
Bṛhaspati [10.21]: When interest is taken at double the principal, and when compound interest (cakravṛddhi) is received,
and when the principal is later claimed with its accrued interest— that usury is censured.
(a) Now, regarding the case where interest has not been settled, Kātyāyana [50] states:
"If one who has set aside the principal (*uddhāra*) departs for another region when requested but fails to pay it,"
After three months have passed, that wealth shall accrue interest for him.
If one who has taken merchandise should depart for another region without paying the price,
that wealth shall accrue interest after the lapse of three seasons.
If one who is being asked does not repay a deposit, the remainder of interest, or what was purchased or sold, the debt increases by five percent per month.
A gift given out of affection does not increase until it has been asked for;
if it is not given when requested, it increases by five percent per month.
If one who has taken a loan should depart for another region without returning it,
that wealth shall accrue interest after the lapse of three seasons.
But he who, though residing in his own country, does not pay when asked repeatedly, shall be made to pay interest there,
even against his will.
Viṣṇu [6.3]: "All castes should pay interest as agreed upon by themselves; even if not stipulated, it shall be paid at the end of the year according to what has been declared.
"'According to what has been declared' means as stated according to the order of castes, such as two percent, three percent, and so forth.
Interest on gifts given out of affection shall never accrue if not requested;
however, even if unrequested, it increases after half a year has passed.
This rule for interest on what has been given out of affection is declared according to dharma;
however, the interest that is prescribed on grains is designated as usury (vārdhuṣya).
‘Anākāritam’ means unuttered.
(288) (ā) Now, the supreme increase.
Regarding this, Gautama [12.28] states: "In the case of long-term storage, there is a doubling of the principal. Kātyāyana [510] says:
"Of gems, pearls, corals, and of gold and silver..."
The interest on ploughshares, wool, and skins remains doubled.

"Remains" (*tiṣṭhati*) means that it does not increase even after a very long period of time. "Silk-worm products" (*kaiṭam*) refers to items such as *trasara* (silk cloth) originating from worms. "Woolen goods" (*āvikam*) refers to items such as blankets (*kambala*).
Manu [8.151] states:
"Interest on a loan, when collected at one time, shall not exceed twice the principal."
In the case of grain, salt, wool, or beasts of burden, it does not exceed five times [the value].

‘Grain’ (*dhānya*) refers to rice, barley, and so forth. ‘Wool’ (*lava*) refers to wool, yak-tail hair, and the like, derived from the etymology that it is “that which is shorn” (*lūyate*). ‘Draft animal’ (*vāhya*) refers to oxen and the like. Gautama [12.33] states: “In the case of usury involving livestock, wool, fields, houses, and draft animals, the interest shall not exceed fivefold. ‘Livestock produce’ (*paśūpaja*) refers to milk, clarified butter, and so forth. Bṛhaspati [10.17] says:
The interest on gold is declared to be double; on clothing and base metals, triple;
and on grain, as well as on draft animals and wool, it is fourfold.
Viṣṇu [6.11–15]: "The maximum interest on gold is double; on grain, triple; on cloth, fourfold; on liquids, eightfold; offspring [is the interest] for women and cattle.

Vasiṣṭha [2.44–47]: "Gold is doubled, and grain is tripled. Liquids are explained by the same rule as grain, as are flowers, roots, and fruits. Ghee measured by weight is eightfold. Bṛhaspati [10.18].
The fivefold increase is stated for vegetables; for seeds and sugarcane, it is recorded as sixfold;
for salt, fats, and liquors, an eightfold increase is recorded when they have been stored for a long time;
and this same increase is stated for molasses and honey when used after a long period.
Kātyāyana [511]: For all types of oils, as well as for liquors, clarified butter,
molasses, and salt, the increase is to be known as eightfold.
Bṛhaspati [10.23]: "In the case of grass, wood, bricks, thread, fermenting agents, stones, hides,
weapons, flowers, and fruits, interest does not cease."
‘Kiṇva’ is a specific substance that serves as the raw material for liquor. ‘Hetī’ means a weapon.
Viṣṇu [6.16–17] states: “For *kiṇva*, cotton, thread, armor, leather, weapons, bricks, and charcoal, the fine is one hundred; for those not mentioned, it is double.
(kha) Now, the prohibition of interest.
In this regard, Nārada [2.36] states: "The price of merchandise, wages, a deposit, a fine, and that which is received as a bribe— these,
as well as gifts made in vain and stakes at dice, do not increase if they are not intended to do so."
"Obtained by deception" (*ābhihārika*) means seized through fraud and the like. "The stake in gambling" (*ākṣika-paṇaḥ*) refers to wealth for the purpose of dice-play.
Kātyāyana [508] states: "In the case of hides, grain, liquor, the goods of gambling, and the price [of such items], [interest is due] at all times."
In cases involving the bride-price for a woman, as well as in matters arising from suretyship, there shall be no interest.
‘Sasya’ refers to grain-stalks and the like produced from a field; ‘āsava’ refers to honey. Saṃvarta says:
“There is no interest on woman’s property, nor on profit, nor on a deposit, provided it remains as it was.”
In a doubtful case and in the matter of suretyship, [the transaction is invalid] if it was not made by oneself.
Vyāsa states:
Interest does not accrue on a suretyship, on property already consumed, on what was not received, on what one desires to give,
on a debt for which payment has been conceded, on a fine, or on a promised bride-price.
Yājñavalkya [2.44]:
He who does not accept his own wealth when it is being offered, having been lent out, shall have it deposited with a neutral third party; beyond that point, it no longer accrues interest.
[292] (ga) Now, regarding the procedure for *adhivāsa*, Bṛhaspati states [10.38–39]:
A pledge (ādhi) is defined as a bond, and it is said to be of four kinds:
movable and immovable, as well as to be kept (gopya) and to be enjoyed (bhogya).

It is fourfold—by way of its nature (*svarūpa*), its type (*prakāra*), its time (*kāla*), and its measure (*pramāṇa*). Among these, its nature is twofold, distinguished as immovable (*sthāvara*) and movable (*jaṅgama*). Its type is twofold, distinguished as secret (*gopya*) and open (*bhogya*). Time is twofold, by way of being restricted by a fixed term (*avadhi-niyama*) or not so restricted. Measure is twofold, distinguished as documentary (*lekhya*) and testimonial (*sākṣimat*). Nārada [4.125]: *Yādṛcchikaḥ sāvadhiko lekhyārūḍho ’tha sākṣimān |* *It is fourfold: spontaneous, with a fixed term, recorded in writing, or possessing witnesses.*
In the same way, there is the gain or loss of its value through such treatment;
likewise, for a wealthy man, it happens when his property undergoes a change due to negligence.
"Upacāraḥ" means protection; "it must be performed" is the ellipsis. "Lābhahāniḥ" of "this" pledge refers to the loss of interest. "Viparyaye" means in the event of destruction. Bṛhaspati [10.39–40]:
And when the interest on the debt has ceased, as well as when the time limit for the loan has expired, the creditor...
If one consumes a pledge out of greed, that gain shall not be realized again.
[293] This [pledge] must be protected like a deposit; interest is forfeited if it is lost.
Yājñavalkya [2.59]:
No interest is due on the use of a pledge for protection, nor when it is damaged or lost, even if it was beneficial.

"In the case of one with an accessory benefit" (*sopakāra*) refers to such things as a draft ox or a copper cauldron. "When it has been impaired" (*hāpite*) means when it has been rendered incapable of being used in ordinary transactions.
"But one shall not receive interest on a loan for the use of a pledge that provides an accessory benefit."
Likewise [8.150]:
"The unwise man who enjoys a pledge without the permission of the owner must relinquish half the interest; that shall be the compensation for his enjoyment."
Likewise:
"A pledge must not be used by force; one who uses it shall forfeit the interest.
He should satisfy the owner with its value; otherwise, he becomes a thief of the pledge."

"The half-interest (ardhavṛddhi) shall be enjoyed"—this should be understood to apply when there is no modification of the pledged property that has been used. However, if a modification does occur, the meaning is that the entire interest must be relinquished.
Kātyāyana [525]: "He who causes labor to be performed on a pledge against its will and without permission..."
The enjoyer shall be made to pay the fruit of the action, or he does not receive interest.

‘Akāmam’ means that which has been pledged without the desire to perform the ritual acts, such as those performed for specific desires (*kāmya*). Viṣṇu [6.5–6] states: “In the case of the enjoyment of the pledge, there is no interest. The creditor shall restore the pledge if it is destroyed, except by the injury caused by a king or a god. Nārada [4.126] says:
If the property is destroyed except by acts of God or the king, there shall be loss of the principal; so says Bṛhaspati (10.46):
"And when the property has been used and has become worthless, the loss of the principal occurs."
Where a high-value item has been lost, one should satisfy the debtor there.
Vyāsa states: "If the pledge is lost due to the fault of the borrower, the bond becomes forfeited;
after deducting the debt along with its interest, the creditor is made to pay the value of that [pledge]."
Yājñavalkya [2.59]:
"What is lost must be made good, as well as what is destroyed, except in cases caused by fate (daiva) or the king.
Here, 'destroyed' (*vinaṣṭa*) means that which has undergone transformation (*vikṛti*)."
Kātyāyana [526]: He who, while another is performing work as a pledge-holder, should oppress him with words, physical force, or acts,
or should even revile him, shall incur the first amercement.
Bṛhaspati [10.41]:
Where a pledge is destroyed due to an act of God or by the king,
there the creditor shall cause another pledge to be given, and he shall recover the debt along with interest.
Nārada [4.130]:
Even if it is being protected, if the pledge should become worthless with the passage of time,
then another pledge must be provided, or else the debt must be paid to the creditor.
Kātyāyana [524]: If, due to the fault of the creditor, the debtor should escape or die, another pledge must be provided; thus the debtor shall be released from the debt.
Bṛhaspati [10.42, 66]:
Whatever has been agreed upon as a deposit by one who holds a pledge, whether by a specific description or by its use,
the debtor shall never be compelled to pay that deposit against his will unless the entire debt has been liquidated.
If a debtor, having paid the principal amount, should request the release of the pledge, it must be released at that very moment; otherwise, the creditor becomes liable for a fault.
[296] ‘Citra’ refers to a painting; ‘carita’ refers to witnesses and the like.
Yājñavalkya [2.62–63]:
When the debtor has appeared, the pledge must be released; otherwise, he becomes a thief.
If the employer is absent, one may obtain the pledge after depositing the money with the family.
Or, having been valued at that time, it may remain there without interest.
Regarding the phrase "if not existing," meaning if it is not present, Viṣṇu continues from the context "the creditor shall deliver the pledge": "even when the final interest has been paid."
Yājñavalkya [2.64]:
But when the debt has become doubled on the pledge,
then indeed the pledge must be released once the money produced from it has entered [the creditor's possession] and reached the amount of double the debt.

"This pledge must be released by you once this amount has been produced and twice the principal has entered [into the account]"—having said this, if this pledge is given, this refers to that case. Such a pledge is called a *kṣayādhi* (perishing pledge) in common usage. Viṣṇu [6.9]: "That immovable property which is given solely for the purpose of bringing in the received capital, one should return upon the failure to bring in that received capital. Bṛhaspati [10.67–69]:
"When land and so forth have been enjoyed, and the produce from it has increased..."
If it has entered the root [of the debt], then the debtor shall incur interest on that principal.
When a debtor, having cultivated the field, returns it to the creditor, then that debt must be released once the profit has been realized; this is the settled rule.
When the principal together with the interest has been received, it must be returned to me;
this is the righteous rule concerning loans and the like that has been fully proclaimed.

"In the case of a debt that has reached its limit" means when the debt has reached its full amount, serving as the cause for the entry of the principal together with interest; that is to say, until the time when the doubled amount is reached.
Yājñavalkya [2.58] states:
"The pledge shall be forfeited when the debt has become double, if it is not released."
When the time comes, that which is subject to time may perish; but that which is to be enjoyed as its fruit does not perish.

"‘The pledge shall perish’ means that when the debt has doubled, if the pledge is not released by the debtor, then it perishes and becomes the property of the creditor. ‘Time-bound’ means one for which a time limit has been set; the meaning is that if it is not released when that appointed time limit has arrived, then it perishes. [298] Bṛhaspati [10.49]:
"When the time limit is fulfilled and the interest has ceased, the owner of the pledge becomes the creditor."
But before ten days have passed, the debtor ought to be released.
Vyāsa states: When the gold has doubled and the stipulated time has expired,
the creditor becomes the owner of the pledge after waiting for fourteen days.
Therefore, having paid the interest in the interim, the debtor shall recover the pledge;
but in the case of a pledge for the use of its fruit, he shall recover the principal upon the expiration of the full term by paying an equivalent amount.
"Equally" means "improperly," that is, fruitless. Manu [8.143]:
But one should never incur interest on a beneficial pledge through negligence.
Furthermore, there can be neither a relinquishment nor a sale of a pledge while it remains under the restriction of time.

"Obstruction by time" (*kālasaṃrodhaḥ*) means remaining for a long duration. "Transfer" (*nisargaḥ*) means alienating the property to another; and this refers specifically to a pledge that is intended to be used (*bhogyādhi*), because that alone is the subject under discussion in the rule, "But never [should there be transfer] in the case of a beneficial pledge" (*na tv evādhau sopakāre*). The statement of Yājñavalkya, "The pledge shall be lost when the debt has doubled" (YDh 2.58), concerns a pledge that is merely to be guarded (*gopyādhi*). Therefore, there is no contradiction between these two rules. In the phrase "neither transfer nor sale," the ellipsis is that "it must not be done by the creditor" (*uttamarṇena na kartavyaḥ*). [299] Bṛhaspati [10.70, 71, 50, 85]:
Where a house or field has been pledged as security for a loan that does not provide an abundance of enjoyment,
there the debtor shall not suffer imprisonment, nor shall the creditor recover the debt [by such means].
When the full extent [of the work] has been completed, the ownership of it is declared to belong to both;
but if it is incomplete, the two should carry on the work with mutual consent.
A pledge for use (gopyādhi) that has reached double its value, as well as one for which a fixed period was stipulated according to rule,
must be released immediately after the debt has been cleared by the debtor's family.
When the debtor has disappeared or died, the creditor should present the document and cause a deed of location (sthānalekhya) to be executed,
specifying the time limit for its validity.
*Parikarṣa* means interest.
Yājñavalkya [2.61]:
One should cause the debtor to pay the wealth consisting of the pledge together with the interest.

"Conduct" (*caritra*) refers to such acts as maintaining the *agnihotra* fire or bathing in the Ganges. The meaning is that whatever has been accepted by making that very conduct a pledge must be repaid along with interest. [300] Kātyāyana [529]:
"But where there is no pledgor, the creditor shall present the pledge."
Therefore, the established opinion is that he is known as the "King to be Sold."
Having received the amount together with the interest, he should then hand over the remainder to the king.
Yājñavalkya [2.63]:
Or, even without the holder [of the deposit], he may sell it in the presence of witnesses.
(g) Now, regarding pledge (*ādhi*):
on this point Vyāsa says— "A pledge is declared to be of two kinds: namely, movable and immovable."
The accomplishment of both of these occurs if there is enjoyment; it is not otherwise.
Bṛhaspati [10.53]: A document for which the debtor does not enjoy his own property, nor pays, nor acknowledges the debt,
and which concerns a deceased witness or creditor, is useless.
House, water-stalls, grain, livestock, women, and vehicles perish through neglect, and likewise fall into a state of worthlessness.
"His own pledge" means the deposit.
Yājñavalkya [2.60]:
"The validity of a pledge arises from its acceptance; even if it is being guarded, it may reach a state of worthlessness."

[301] Kātyāyana [517]: If one should create a pledge for two persons regarding the same object, which of the two should be accepted? That which was established earlier is to be accepted; the one who created the pledge later shall receive the punishment of a thief.

The rule is as follows: the term ‘pratipat’ refers to the formal establishment; the word ‘earlier’ (pūrvataram) implies ‘the act of making’. Viṣṇu [5.181–84] states: “He who, without releasing from one person, gives land measuring at least a *gocarma* that has been pledged to another, shall be put to death; if it is less than that, he shall be fined sixteen *suvarṇas*. A man may enjoy for one year the fruit produced from that [land].”
That earth, whether small or vast, is but the size of a cow's hide.
When two men dispute over a pledge that has been deposited with them,
the one whose possession has been established by enjoyment— provided it was done without force— is the owner of its fruit.
The meaning is: "of whom there is enjoyment without force. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "that land belongs to him. Bṛhaspati [10.44–45]:
"When a single field is given as a pledge to two people at the same time..."
By whomsoever it was previously eaten, that [substance] shall bring success to him.
When two [items] are presented at the same time, the rule proclaimed for both is equal regarding their gift or sale.
A mortgage, sale, gift, or likewise what is executed by witnesses or a document—
when these are recorded in a single deed, that document is there the means of proof.
But when one has first designated all one's property and subsequently deposits it marked with a name,
how could that not be more strongly established as being marked?
When a field or even a house is marked by boundary signs,
and villages and so forth are likewise recorded, then one shall attain success.
"Kātyāyana declared that what is unstated is stated, and what is distinguished in one place is further specified; thus, that which is written with specific detail is superior."
If one were to impose a bond upon space upon a pre-existing Pradhāna whose specific nature has not been specified, that [bond] would certainly not be established.

Whatever he might possess at that time, that should be declared as directed. "By reason of a single act" means by reason of a single type of act, such as giving and so forth. As for the phrase "all his property" and so on: if one first designates all his property as a pledge and later, at the time of drafting the document, records it under a specific name, then in the event of a subsequent dispute, only that which was recorded by name shall be authoritative; the meaning is that it is not merely what was designated in general terms. "Pradhana" here means excellent wealth. [303]
(Ṅa) Now, the procedure regarding the surety (*pratibhū*):
On this matter, Kātyāyana [states] (vv. 114–116):
"Neither an owner nor an enemy, nor likewise one authorized by the owner..."
He is neither obstructed nor punished, nor does he stand in doubt anywhere.
Neither an heir nor one who is destitute, nor those who dwell in perpetual residence,
nor men appointed to royal service, nor those who have gone forth as renunciants.
One who is incapable of paying the debt to the creditor and an equivalent fine to the king should not be accepted as a surety for his obligation,
nor should one who is unknown.

Yājñavalkya [2.52]: "Indeed, among brothers, between husband and wife, and between father and son, standing as a surety, contracting debt, or acting as a witness is not prescribed when they have not yet divided their inheritance."
Nārada [16.39]: Brothers who have divided their property may act as witnesses, stand surety, give gifts, or receive them from one another; those who have not divided may not do so.
[304] Bṛhaspati [10.73, 74, 78]: "In matters of sight, of confidence, of delivery, and likewise in the handing over of a debtor's property—
the wise have observed in the treatises that there are four kinds of surety."
One said, "I alone shall show it"; another spoke, "This is a virtuous man";
one said, "I am the giver"; and another declared, "I shall hand over this wealth."

The first two [types of witnesses], if found to be false, shall be made to pay the wealth that was reported at the time [of the transaction]; the latter two, in case of contradiction, shall likewise pay it, as shall their sons in their absence.

Yājñavalkya [2.54]: Where a surety for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*) or a surety for confidence (*prātyayika*) has died, their sons shall not pay the debt; however, those who stand as heirs (*dāyāda*) shall pay it.
"Those who stand as guarantors for giving shall pay the debt. This means that the sons of one who stands as a guarantor for a gift must pay the debt. Kātyāyana [530, 531, 533]:
"And for the purpose of giving, standing surety, trust, dispute, and oath..."
In this manner, one should cause a surety to be provided, or otherwise as appropriate in the reverse case.
But a guarantor for appearance who does not produce the person at the proper place and time shall pay the debt,
except in cases caused by fate or the king.
If, when the time has elapsed, the surety does not produce that person, he shall be made to pay the debt;
and this same rule is prescribed for the case where the debtor has died.

If the surety should violate even slightly the stipulated place, time, or manner of performance, he shall be made to pay that amount once the debt has been recovered; such is the rule when the debt is realized.
One who relies on others, or is incapable, or indeed associates with the wicked; and one who, out of hatred, is intent on doing harm whenever possible.
Out of fear of that [non-payment], one should indeed have a guarantor (lagnaka) provided for the sake of assurance;
likewise, in the event of a breach of character, the surety (pratibhū) is made to pay.
In the phrases beginning with "parāśrayam," the connection is with the word "kartumanā" (intending to act). "Abhavyam" means deformed. Manu [8.160]:
When a surety for payment has died, one should compel even his heirs to pay.
Kātyāyana [534]:
Where a pledge has been taken and the son remains liable for its appearance,
that debt shall be made payable by the son once it has been proved by the plaintiff.

The meaning of this is as follows: having considered that the debtor took a pledge and appointed a guarantor for its appearance, if that person is no longer present, the son of that guarantor shall be made to pay that debt.
Manu [8.161–162]: "But if the debtor does not pay, the one who paid the debt may recover it from the son, provided his character is well known."
Afterwards, when the surety has died, by what means should one seek to recover [the debt]?

But if the surety has been assigned a specific amount of wealth and is possessed of sufficient funds, he shall pay that from his own property; such is the settled rule regarding one for whom a sum has been assigned.

"In the case of one who has not paid" (*adātari*) refers to a guarantor other than the one for whom the gift was promised. "The payer" (*dātā*) is the creditor (*uttamarṇa*). "Of known nature" (*vijñātaprakṛtiḥ*) means one whose reason for acting as a surety is known, such as the taking of a pledge or similar security. "To whom wealth has been assigned" (*nirādiṣṭadhanaḥ*) means one to whom wealth has been assigned by the debtor for the discharge of the debt. "Adequate in wealth" (*alaṃdhanaḥ*) means possessing sufficient wealth. Here, the term "assigned" (*nirādiṣṭaḥ*) refers figuratively to the son of the one to whom the wealth was assigned; the meaning is that when the father has died, he shall pay that debt. Vyāsa says:
A grandson shall pay the debt of his grandfather, and a son shall pay that which arose from a guarantee; the two grandsons [of the debtor] need not be made to pay—this is the settled rule.
"Equal" means free from any deficiency. "His sons" refers to the great-grandson and the grandson. Kātyāyana [561] states:
That which has arisen from a guarantee (prātibhāvya) must be paid by the grandsons, but never otherwise.
A paternal debt must be paid by the son as well, in all cases.
The connection is that "debt" refers to that which has arisen from suretyship.
Yājñavalkya [2.55] states: "If there be many sureties, they shall pay the debt according to their respective shares."
When these [debts] rest under a single liability, they may be paid by the creditor according to his preference.
"Resorting to the shadow of one": those who resort to the "shadow"—that is, the likeness—of a single surety are so described. Just as a single surety would pay the entire debt, so too would several.
Bṛhaspati [10.76, 84]:
"The creditor shall grant time to the surety for the search of what has been lost."
According to the suitability of the region, [one should practice] for a fortnight, a month, or even half a month.
They should not be excessively oppressed; they should be made to pay the debt gradually.
They should not be appointed as witnesses against themselves; such is the rule for sureties.
"In one's own testimony" means in one's own direct observation;
likewise [10.82]:
"But he who, being oppressed, gives a surety when required to stand as surety..."
After three fortnights have passed, he is entitled to receive double that amount as interest.
Yājñavalkya [2.56]: Whatever property of creditors a surety is compelled to pay publicly, that shall be paid back double by the debtors.

Kātyāyana [540]: He for whose sake, by whomsoever, and for whatever purpose a thing was given according to rule upon request— that surety shall receive that very thing when he has been proven by witnesses.
(c) Now, the procedure for the recovery of debts.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states [10.102, 103, 113]:
"That debt which has been received from the hand of another according to the rules of usury..."
Now it is stated by whom, where, and in what manner something is to be given or not to be given.
A debt not contracted at an improper time must be paid to one who demands it;
when the term has expired, it must be paid with the interest ceased, and in the absence of the father, it must be paid by the sons.
[309] First, that which belongs to the father must be given, and afterwards that which belongs to oneself;
between these two, that which belongs to the grandfather must be given first—thus always should a debt be paid.
‘Prakālaḥ’ means a specifically determined time or a limit. Nārada [4.2]:
When the father has passed away, the sons shall pay the debt according to their respective shares.
Whether they are divided or undivided, whoever should bear that burden.
Yājñavalkya [2.50]: When the father has gone abroad, is deceased, or is overwhelmed by calamity, the debt must be paid by the son or grandson; if it is denied, it is established by witnesses.
Kātyāyana states: That debt which was witnessed, or that which remains after a portion has been paid, or that which was incurred by a grandfather, should be repaid;
however, a debt that is defective, contested, or was incurred by the father [against his will] shall never be repaid.
Bhṛgu says that a debt which was incurred by the father, passed down in succession from the grandfather,
and which remains undisputed and unpaid by the sons, must be paid by the grandsons.
But that which was ancestral (paitāmaha) and not given away by the sons while they were living in a state of illness—
of such a kind, the ancestral property must be given equally by the grandsons.
Even when there is a lawsuit involving multiple matters, he recovers only as much wealth as he can prove with witnesses; he receives only that much wealth which has been established.
In the absence of a son, however, the debt must be paid diligently by the grandson;
that which was incurred by the fourth [descendant] should be remitted from him.

"Defective" (*sadoṣam*) means that which has been applied to gambling, intoxicants, and the like. "Contradicted" (*vyāhatam*) means that which has been disavowed by the father, who said, "This should not be given. "That which was taken by the fourth person"—meaning that which was received or acquired—one "should cause to be returned," the sense being that one should not give it. Bṛhaspati [10.114]:
A debt incurred by a father should be paid by the sons as if it were their own, provided it is acknowledged.
That which was given by the grandfather should be returned equally; however, it need not be returned to his son.
The meaning is that it should be paid "as if it were one's own," together with interest. Nārada [4.4]:
"A debt which has been cleared by sons in due order, having been obtained without obstruction—"
That which was to be given by the grandfather must be given by the grandsons; it shall cease with the fourth [generation].

Yājñavalkya [2.90]: A debt contracted by means of a written document must be paid by only three generations of persons; however, the pledge is enjoyed as long as that debt has not been made to be paid.

Regarding the statement, "The pledge (*ādhi*) is enjoyed": once a debt has been incurred by taking a pledge, that pledge is enjoyed for as long as the debt is not repaid; the meaning is that the debt does not cease with the fourth or subsequent generation. Viṣṇu [6.27–28]: "If the creditor has died, has renounced the world, or has been away for twenty years, the debt must be paid by his sons or grandsons; beyond this, they need not pay if they are unwilling. Nārada [4.24]:
If the father has gone abroad, the son shall not pay the debt before twenty years have passed;
nor [shall he pay] upon the death of the paternal uncle or even of a brother.
Kātyāyana [548–49]: Even if the father is afflicted by illness or has gone abroad from his own country,
the debt contracted by the father must be paid by the sons after twenty years have passed.
In such cases as those of the diseased, the insane, the aged, or those who have been away on long journeys,
one should cause the debt to be paid by the sons, even while the fathers are still living.
[312] Bṛhaspati [10.110–12]: Even while the father is present, the debt must be paid by the sons once it has been proven,
provided the father is blind from birth, an outcast, insane, or afflicted with consumption, leprosy, or similar diseases.
If the father is away on a journey, the son should pay all debts incurred under a single liability;
however, when the father has died, the son shall pay only his paternal share, and never any debt contracted by another.
Nārada [4.25]:
Even a single surviving member of an undivided family must pay the debt contracted by the others;
but when they have died, their son is not liable to pay that debt to others.

Viṣṇu [6.34–36]: "He who remains among those who have not divided the estate shall pay the debt contracted by them; likewise for brothers regarding a paternal debt. And those who are divided shall pay according to their respective shares. Yājñavalkya [2.45]:
"But whatever debt may have been contracted by undivided members for the sake of the family..."
The heirs shall pay that [debt] when the head of the household has died or has gone abroad.
Nārada [4.3]: Whatever debt has been incurred by an undivided paternal uncle, or by a brother, or even by a mother for the sake of the family, all that must be paid by the heirs.
[313] Manu [8.166]: "If the borrower should die and the expenditure was made for the sake of the family,
that debt must be paid by the kinsmen from their own property, even if they are divided."
Nārada [4.31]:
"Even one who is independent, if he has not attained legal capacity, is liable for debt.
Kātyāyana [552, 551]: [same as above].
But when the father has died, the inheritance must never be given by anyone to those who have not attained the age for legal capacity;
it should be bestowed at the proper time according to the rule, otherwise they shall dwell in hell.
Since fathers are liberated from their lowest debt only by means of the gifts given by the sons born to them,
for that reason fathers desire a son.
Nārada [4.5; vulgate 5.9]:
"For this reason, fathers desire sons from every quarter, thinking:
'This one will liberate me from both creditor and debtor.'"
Therefore, once a son is born, he should strive with effort to liberate his father from debt for his own sake,
so that the father does not go to hell.
If an ascetic who maintains the sacred fires dies while still burdened by debts,
both his asceticism and his fire-sacrifices shall all belong to the creditors.

"Debts to superiors" (*uttamarṇāni*) are debts owed to the superior beings—gods, sages, and ancestors. "Debts to inferiors" (*adhamarṇāni*) are debts owed by inferior beings—human beings—consisting of gold, grain, and so forth.
Bṛhaspati [10.123]: He who, having taken a loan and so forth, does not repay it to the owner...
He is born in that person's house as a slave, a servant, a woman, or a beast.
By the word *ujjāma*, debt is expressed; by the word *ādi* (and so forth), deposits and the like are expressed. Manu [8.167]:
"Even one who is dependent may conduct legal business on behalf of the family."
Whether in his own country or in a foreign land, the wise man should not cause him to waver.
"Dependent" refers to a slave and so forth.
Bṛhaspati [10.121]:
"By paternal uncles, brothers' sons, women, slaves, pupils, and dependents..."
Whatever has been taken for the sake of the family, that the householder ought to give.
Viṣṇu [6.38, 39]: "What is promised by word of mouth must be paid by the head of the household, or what was contracted for the sake of the family. Kātyāyana [542, 543, 545]:
"That which was borrowed by one who is incapable or by one who is ill for the sake of the family..."
And one should know that the sign of an impending calamity is caused by misfortune.
Whatever was done for the marriage of a daughter or for funeral rites—
all this must be paid by the family to the master.
Bhṛgu declares that a debt contracted for the sake of the family by a slave,
a wife, a mother, a pupil, or even by a son, must be paid even if the absentee has not authorized it.
Nārada [4.11]: "Whether by the father's own command, or for the sake of maintaining the family,
whatever debt was contracted in times of distress, the father shall pay that to the son."
Bṛhaspati [10.124]: A father shall discharge a debt incurred by his son if it was approved by him;
or he may pay it out of affection for his son, but he is not otherwise obliged to pay it.
Kātyāyana [544]: According to the law, a debt contracted by a son need not be paid by the father;
however, that which has been promised or that which has been formally acknowledged must be paid.
Manu [8.159, 160]: A son is not liable to pay for a suretyship, a frivolous debt, what is due for gambling, what is due for liquor, or the remainder of a fine or a tax.
But regarding a surety for appearance, the rule previously enjoined applies;
however, when a surety for payment has died, the judge shall cause even the heirs to pay.

[316] Bṛhaspati [10.118]: One should not compel a son to pay a debt incurred through gambling, a gift made in vain, that which was promised out of lust or anger, a suretyship, or the remainder of a fine or a tax.
"Sauram" refers to that caused by liquor; "ākṣikam" refers to that caused by gambling.
Vyāsa says: A fine, or the remainder of a fine, or a toll, or the remainder of that very toll.
But a son must not give that which is not fit for legal transaction.
‘Vyāvahārikam’ means that which is made by a person capable of legal transaction. Kātyāyana [564–565]:
“Whether it be a written document or one delivered orally, that which has been promised must be given.”
One should know that debt incurred for a woman who has had a previous husband is caused by lust.
For that which is said to bring satisfaction after having produced violence or destroyed property out of anger,
one should know that to be the result of anger.
"Stated" means promised.
Yājñavalkya [2.46]:
"Neither a husband nor a son [inherits] what was earned by a wife; nor does a father [inherit] what was earned by a son."
Likewise, a husband shall not pay a debt contracted by his wife, except for what was incurred for the sake of the family.
Viṣṇu (6.32): "Neither a husband nor a son is liable for a debt contracted by a woman. Kātyāyana (578):
"A debt contracted by a wife must be paid by the husband; a debt contracted by a mother must be paid by the son."
Whatever has been done for the sake of a devotee, having spoken of it, one should depart in a certain direction.
