Likewise [8.15]: "Having completed his studies and having presented the teacher's fee to the guru, he should return to his own home; this is declared to be the proper conduct for a student."

Bṛhaspati [15.7]: Skill is said to be knowledge, such as the refinement of gold, base metals, and so forth, as well as dancing and the like; training in that, one should perform service in the teacher’s house.
One who wishes to acquire his own craft, with the permission of his relatives,
shall dwell in the presence of a teacher for a well-determined period of time.
The teacher should instruct him in his own home, providing him with food;
he should not make him perform any other work, and should treat him like a son.
Kātyāyana [716]:
But he who does not cause [the pupil] to learn the craft, yet explains the tasks and causes them to be performed, shall incur the first *sāhasa* fine; from him the pupil may withdraw.
He who abandons a teacher who is instructing him and is not at fault should be forced to remain [with him] by force; he deserves both corporal punishment and imprisonment.
Even when he has been trained, the pupil should complete the work at the appointed time;
whatever labor he performs therein, its fruit belongs to the teacher alone.

"Beating" (*vadha*) here refers merely to striking with a bamboo staff or similar object. "Binding" (*bandha*) means confinement; some say it means restraint. "The fixed time" (*kṛtaṃ kālam*) refers to the established period of service. "That fruit" (*tat phalam*) is the fruit of the labor in the form of wages. Thus [it is said]:
"Having mastered the craft, at the appointed time, having circumambulated the teacher clockwise... [385] [7.20]
And having obtained his permission according to his ability, the pupil departs.
Bṛhaspati [15.8–12]:
He who enjoys another’s female slave should be known as one who maintains a woman;
he should perform that work for her master just as any other man who is maintained for wages.
One is said to be a bearer of many riches, while another is a bearer of a portion;
furthermore, the states of inferior, middling, and superior have been declared for all of them.
Likewise, one who maintains [the practice] for a day, half a month, six months, three months,
or a year shall perform the action as vowed and obtain what was promised.
[386] A hired servant should be known to be of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
Their wages, based on their work, should correspond to their capacity and devotion.
Among these, the soldier is the highest, the cultivator is the middle, and the porter is the lowest; such is the threefold classification of the hired laborer.
Bṛhaspati [15.13–14]: Among them, the best is the soldier; the middle is the plowman;
the lowest is said to be the porter, as well as the domestic laborer.
The sharecropper is recorded as being of two kinds among those who live by agriculture and cattle-rearing;
he shall receive a share from the harvested grain as well as from the milk, without any doubt.
He who is authorized over matters concerning the family is to be known as an *adhikarmakara*; he is also remembered as a *kauṭumbika*.
For these four are declared to be performers of auspicious deeds;
however, the remaining fifteen servants partake in inferior karma.
Action is also said to be of two kinds: indeed, the inauspicious and the auspicious.
The inauspicious is called the work of a slave; the auspicious is remembered as the work of a laborer.
The cleaning of house doors, impure places, streets, and refuse heaps; the touching of private parts, the handling of food remnants, and the disposal of feces and urine.
[387] Furthermore, the service rendered with one's limbs to a master who desires it should be understood as impure karma; that which is other than this is pure.
Kātyāyana [720]:
The cleansing of feces and urine, as well as the massaging of one who is naked,
and generally the tending of cattle and such, are tasks that the sons of female slaves should perform.
One born in the house, one purchased, one obtained, one received as an heir,
one supported during a time of distress, and likewise one who has been placed there by the owner.
[388] Rescued from great bondage, won at stake in battle,
and having approached you saying "I am yours," he was made to enter the life of a wandering ascetic.
One who becomes a slave through devotion, one brought [as a slave] by a mare,
a seller of himself, and one who has sold himself— these are recorded in the treatises as the fifteen kinds of slaves.
In that regard, the first four classes are not released from servitude except through the favor of their master; for them, servitude is hereditary.
That lowest of men who, being independent, sells himself—of those [servants], he is the most contemptible; even he is not released from slavery.
"Employed out of season" means employed during a time of famine.
And in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* (18.216), there is the speech of Hariścandra, who had fallen into the servitude of a Caṇḍāla and was afflicted by grief for his son:
"If I am not permitted by the Caṇḍāla, I shall enter the blazing fire."
In another future birth, I shall attain the state of being a slave to a Caṇḍāla.
Manu [8.414]: "Even if released by his master, a Śūdra is not freed from servitude;
for that is innate to him, so who can remove it from him?"
Nārada [8.36]:
A man who has fallen from the life of a renunciant shall become the slave of the king alone;
there is no release for him, nor any purification whatsoever.
Kātyāyana [721]:
Where the three castes are twice-born, a king should impose exile upon a Brāhmaṇa who has fallen from his renunciation,
but he may subject a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya to slavery.
Dakṣa [7.33]:
But having taken up the life of a wandering mendicant, he who does not abide in his own duty,
the king should brand him with the mark of a dog's foot and banish him immediately.
(a) Now, regarding the liberation from slavery, Nārada [8.40, 30–34, 36] states:
"He who, being dependent, offers himself [saying], 'I am yours'..."
He shall not obtain that object of desire; the former owner shall regain it.
Those who have been carried off by thieves, sold, or forcibly made into slaves must be released by the king; slavery is not permitted with respect to them.
And whoever might liberate their master from a life-threatening danger shall be released from slavery and receive a share equal to that of a son.
One who was hired out of season is released from slavery by giving a pair of cattle;
however, that which has been consumed during a time of distress cannot be purified by such an act.
Even if he has been adopted, if the master should give him wealth and then emancipate him,
and subsequently cause him to be approached [by another], he too is next in rank after the purchased son.
By paying back the debt along with the interest, the debtor is released from slavery;
likewise, even one who was made a slave is released when the fixed term has expired.
Having approached you saying "I am yours," and having been won at stake in battle,
one is released by the giving of a counter-head through an equal act.
By neglecting a devotee, one is immediately released from being a slave to that devotee;
and by punishing a mare, one is released from being a servant to a mare.

"Dependent" (*asvatantra*) means having no owner. "In a famine" (*durge*) means during a time of scarcity. Regarding the phrase "he should cause him to approach," etc.: if one causes that very person upon whom the status of a slave was imposed to be accepted [by another] and does not release him, then he becomes for that [new master] "one who follows after the purchased" (*krītānantara*); the meaning is that he becomes a remainder over and above what was purchased. "By the giving of a counter-head" (*pratiśīrṣapradānena*) means by the giving of an equivalent slave. "From restraint" (*nigrahāt*) means from being covered [or bound]. "Mare" (*vaḍavā*) means a female slave. Yājñavalkya [2.182]: One who has been made a slave by force, even if sold by thieves, is released.
One who restores the life of his master [is freed] from debt through the master's renunciation of him, or even by the payment of a ransom for him.
Kātyāyana [723]: But if one should have sexual intercourse with his own female slave and she subsequently gives birth, then,
having considered the seed, she and her offspring shall be made a non-slave.
He who, with a joyful heart, desires to make his own slave a non-slave,
should take from that slave's shoulder a water-pot filled with water and break it.
They should sprinkle him on the head with water containing flowers,
and having said three times, "He is no longer a slave," they should then release him while facing eastward.
From that time forward, he should be called one protected by the favor of his master;
his food may be eaten and gifts accepted from him, and he becomes esteemed by the virtuous.
Only three are said to be without property: the wife, the slave, and likewise the son;
whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they themselves belong.
‘Samadhigacchanti’ means they acquire.
Devala says: When the father has passed away, the sons shall divide the father’s wealth.
For they would lack ownership [of the property] while their faultless father remains alive.
Manu has declared that while their husband lives, women have no independence in any matter, just as slaves have none while their master remains alive.
Manu [8.147]: A Brāhmaṇa may confidently take property from a Śūdra;
for he has nothing that is his own, since his wealth is to be taken by his master.
[394] Kātyāyana [724, 725]: "Whatever wealth a slave may possess, it is traditionally held that his master is the lord thereof;
however, as for that which results from an open sale, the master is entitled to that wealth."
Likewise: "And a female slave who is married by a male slave shall also attain the status of a slave;
for her husband is her master, since the lord is dependent upon the owner."
regarding the authority over female slaves,
Nārada says there [in verse 8.39]:
Slavery is not ordained through the inverse order of the castes;
except for one who has abandoned his own duty, slavery is considered to be like marriage.
"Bhṛgu states that through the gift of an independent self, one enters into servitude like a wife;
however, servitude for a Brāhmaṇa among the three [lower] castes is to be understood as never occurring."
Servitude for the castes occurs according to the natural order and not in the inverse order;
this applies to Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who abandon their own independence.
Even one of the same caste shall never compel a Brahmin to servitude;
however, if he is deficient in character and Vedic study, he may perform such work at his own will.
Even there, the best of the twice-born should not perform any unwholesome act;
for by becoming a slave to a Brāhmaṇa, the royal splendor of the king is destroyed.
But Bṛhaspati has declared that the duties of a Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra may never, under any circumstances, cause a Brāhmaṇa of equal caste to perform the work of a slave.

Regarding the phrase "deficient in that" (*tadūnam*), the construction is as follows: a Brāhmaṇa who is deficient in conduct and study may be made to perform work by a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with conduct and study. "At will" (*kāmataḥ*) means according to his desire. "Inauspicious" (*aśubham*) refers to tasks such as cleaning excrement and urine. [397] Regarding the passage beginning with "the duty of Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras," the meaning is that Bṛhaspati maintains that the duties of the Kṣatriyas and others should not compel a Brāhmaṇa to perform the labor of a slave.
Manu [8.411–13]: "A Brāhmaṇa who is distressed for a livelihood [may employ] a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya..."
He should support them with compassion and cause them to perform their own respective duties.

[398] If a Brāhmaṇa, out of delusion, should compel initiated twice-born men to perform servitude against their will by virtue of his superior power, he shall be made to pay six hundred [paṇas] by the king.
But one may compel a Śūdra to perform service, whether he has been purchased or not;
for he was created by the Self-existent One himself solely for the purpose of servitude.
‘Because of his authority’ means because of his power.
Viṣṇu [5.151]: “He who employs a person of the highest caste in servitude shall be punished with the highest amercement. Kātyāyana [726–29]:
He who would seize a Brāhmaṇī woman, or likewise sell her, has performed an act that must be undone by the king; all of them shall be punished.
But he who, out of lust, should make a woman of good family a servant by force,
or should transfer her to another, shall be punished, and that [marriage] shall be as if it had never been performed.
He who enjoys a nurse for a child, a non-slave woman, or even a slave woman,
or the wife of an attendant, shall incur the first amercement.
He who, being capable and not in a state of distress, desires to sell a devoted female slave who is crying out [in protest], shall incur a fine of two hundred [paṇas].

Thus [ends] the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara, who served as the Great Minister for Peace and War (*mahāsāndhivigrahika*) to His Majesty, the Emperor of Emperors (*mahārājādhirāja*), the illustrious Govindacandradeva.
The Section on the Status of Slavery in the Book of Judicial Procedure.
[400] 62 — Now, regarding the non-payment of wages, Nārada [states] at 9.1–3:

The discussion regarding wages for those who have been employed, as well as in matters of gifts, pledges, and sales by one who lacks authority— the non-payment of such wages is recorded as a title of dispute.
The master of the work shall give wages to the laborer according to the work performed,
as determined at the beginning, middle, or end of the task.
But when the wages are not fixed, merchants, cowherds, and farmers shall receive a tenth part of their profits,
cattle, and crops, respectively.
‘Govīrya’ means the milk, which is the essential substance of cows. [401] Yājñavalkya [2.194–96]:
However, one should be made to pay a tenth part from the profits of trade, cattle, and crops.
But he who causes work to be performed without having fixed the wages must be dealt with by the king.

If one should neglect the place and the time, or perform the work otherwise than prescribed, then the master's will shall prevail; however, if more work has been performed, an additional wage must be given.
Whatever amount of work one performs, that much indeed is his wages;
even if both [tasks] are impossible, he should accomplish what is possible according to the instructions.
In that regard, concerning the payment of wages: "The master's *chandaḥ*" means his will. Bṛhaspati [16.1–2]:
"The plowman shall take a third part or a fifth part."
[402] Likewise:
From the sharecropper, let him take a fifth part of the crop;
from the one who receives wages for his labor, let him take a third part of the grain that has grown.
*Upadhā* is the result of the activity.

Āpastamba [2.28.2–4]: "For a laborer (*kīnāśa*) who abandons his work while departing, there shall be flogging with a staff; likewise for a herdsman (*paśupa*). And there shall be the confiscation of his cattle.
Vṛddha-Manu [Manusmṛti, Pūrvārdha, 8.157]:
Those skilled in sea voyages, who perceive the requirements of place and time, shall determine the wages;
this applies if no wage has been fixed beforehand.
Nārada [9.4]:
Whatever has been entrusted to them as an instrument for their work must be protected with a sense of trustworthiness, and never with deceit.
[403] Bṛhaspati [16.3, 5]: A hired servant must not practice deceit toward his master; he incurs a loss of wages, and from that, a dispute arises.
When a hired laborer, having received his wages, does not perform the work,
he shall, if capable, be made to pay a fine and twice the amount of those wages.
Yājñavalkya [2.193]: One who abandons work after having received wages shall pay double;
if he has not received wages, he shall be made to pay an equal amount. The tools and implements must be protected by the servants.
"By servants" means by hired laborers. "Utensils" (upaskara) refers to implements, such as the yokes and other equipment for ploughs and the like.
Nārada [9.5]:
Having promised to perform work, if one does not do it, he should be compelled to do so after having paid the wages by force.
If one who has received wages fails to perform the work, he shall pay double the amount of those wages.
Kātyāyana [657]: But he who, having undertaken a work, does not bring it to completion, must be compelled by force; if he does not do so, he deserves punishment.
[404] Bṛhaspati [16.7]: He who, having given his word, does not perform the task, may be compelled to do so by force;
if he still does not perform that work, he shall incur a fine of two hundred [paṇas].
Manu [8.215]: "A hired servant who, though not ill, does not perform the work as stipulated out of arrogance,
shall be fined eight *kṛṣṇalas* and his wages shall not be paid."

[Thus; Manu 8.217, 216: As it has been said: Whether he is afflicted or healthy, if one does not cause that work to be performed, his wages must not be given, even for work that is only slightly incomplete.
But one who, having been ill, performs the work once he has recovered, shall receive his wages exactly as stated from the beginning,
even after a very long period of time.
‘Anārtaḥ’ means not afflicted by illness. ‘Alponasya’ means of that which has little remaining.
[405] Nārada (Nāradīya Saṃhitā 7.7):
If one abandons the work when the time is complete, he shall incur the loss of his wages.
If he fails to work due to a fault of his master, he shall receive his wages for the period [he was employed].

Viṣṇu [5.153–59]: "A hired laborer who abandons his work before the agreed time is forfeited of his entire wages. He shall also pay one hundred *paṇas* to the king. Furthermore, whatever is lost through his fault must be restored to the owner, except in the case of damage caused by fate (*daiva*). If the employer abandons the laborer’s work before the time is complete, he must pay him his full wages as well as one hundred *paṇas* to the king, except in the case of the laborer’s own fault.
Nārada [9.9]: "If the goods should meet with disaster due to the fault of the carrier..."
He shall be made to pay for whatever has been lost therein, except in cases caused by fate or the king.
Vṛddha-Manu says: "If [the animal] is lost through negligence, the keeper shall be made to pay an amount equal to its value; if it is lost by being milked twice, he shall pay double.
However, he shall not be made to pay for what has been stolen by thieves, or burnt, or carried away by water."
Bṛhaspati [16.9]:
When a servant performs an act while commissioned by his master,
if that act is an evil deed for the sake of that purpose, the master shall be at fault therein.
"For that purpose" means for the sake of the owner. "Inauspicious" refers to theft and the like. "He would offend" means he would become subject to punishment and so forth.
Yājñavalkya [2.197]:
"But the carrier shall be made to pay for goods lost through no fault of the king or of fate."
And he who causes an obstruction to the departure shall be made to pay double the wages.
Vṛddha-Manu:
If a worker, when the time for work has arrived, does not perform it but instead creates an obstacle, another person should be employed; he shall be made to pay double wages.

Yājñavalkya [2.198]: If one abandons a hired servant who has set out on the road, one must pay him a seventh part of the wage at the start, a fourth part if abandoned on the way, and the entire wage if abandoned halfway; the same applies to the person who causes the abandonment.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa* (227.6):
"He who, having received payment, does not impart knowledge or craft,
shall be made to pay the full amount as a fine by the king who knows the Dharma."
Having hired carriers for goods by means of a vehicle or draft animal,
if one abandons them on the path of righteousness, he shall be made to pay a fourth part of the wages as compensation.
Likewise, even a porter would suffer a loss of wages [if he were to abandon his load].
Vṛddha-Manu states: "If a merchant, having sold that merchandise on the road, should abandon his servant..."
Even for one who has not arrived, wages should be given; he shall receive half of the fee.
Kātyāyana [661]:
Just as that merchandise might be completed or lost on the road,
he receives wages proportional to the distance traveled by him.
"Āsidhyeta" means "would be obstructed. Nārada [9.6]:
Having agreed upon a sixth part as wages, he who abandons a beast of burden on the road while it is being hired...
Having caused [the work] to be done, however, he shall pay the wages along with interest.

"Sixth part of the wages," and so forth—the meaning is that if a hired laborer, having agreed by saying "I am going," subsequently abandons a hired vehicle that was standing on the road at the start of the journey, he shall be made to pay a sixth part of the aforementioned wages.
[408] Bṛhaspati [16.11]: "If a master does not give the wages to the hired laborer after the work has been performed..."
The king should cause him to be made to pay, and [inflict] discipline in accordance with the circumstances.

Kātyāyana [660]: He who abandons a companion on the road—whether he be exhausted or afflicted by disease—shall incur the first amercement; if he fails to provide protection for three days in a village, he shall incur the same.
62 — (a) Now, the rule regarding courtesans:
In this regard, Nārada [9.19, first half] states:
"Having received the fee, if a courtesan does not wish to comply, she shall pay double."
Even one who does not desire to pay the toll shall suffer the loss of that toll.
Smṛti [Bṛhaspati 16.13]: "One who is ill, exhausted, distracted, or occupied with royal business,
and one who, having been invited, does not come— such a woman is declared in the Smṛti to be like a mare."

In the Matsya Purāṇa (227.145): "If a courtesan, having accepted her fee, goes elsewhere out of greed and does not provide the service, she should be made to pay the hire; even for one who has not yet had intercourse, the fee must be paid."

Nārada [9.18 second half, 19]: Likewise, a man who does not pay the bride-price, or who enjoys a woman by means other than the proper way, or who strikes her with teeth, nails, and so forth— [is liable for punishment].
He who approaches a woman in a place other than the womb, or causes her to dwell with many men,
shall be made to pay eightfold the nuptial fee (śulka) and an equal amount as a fine.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa* (227.146–48):
"He who, for the sake of another, leads a prostitute away with someone else in mind,
shall receive from the king a fine of one *māṣaka* of gold."
He who, having taken up goods for use, does not return them, shall be made to pay double wages;
he shall also pay a fine of double that amount to the king, so that the law is not violated.
If many people drive a single cow, they shall all pay double the fine;
each of them shall also separately pay a further double fine to the king.
Nārada says: Those courtesans who are preeminent there, and the lovers who reside in their houses—
they are known to provide a decision regarding doubts in matters arising from them.
[Thus ends the section on the rules for courtesans.
62 — (ā) Now, the rules for hiring planetary deities and other such entities.
Nārada says: He who, having built a house on another's land, should dwell there after paying the stipulated fee,
must take with him that house— its grass, wood, bricks, and so forth— upon departing.
For having stayed in another's land without a permit and without being certain [of his departure],
he should by no means take grass or wood as he departs.
If grass, wood, or bricks have been placed there by someone other than the owner,
he must hand over all of that to the lord of the land upon its removal.
Vyāsa says:
But he who, having enjoyed [the house] for a long time out of affection, makes it his own abode—for him there is no other way; the wood belongs to him who has paid the fee as he departs.
Kātyāyana [663, 662]: He who, having taken houses, enclosures, shops, and so forth on lease,
does not return them to the owner, shall be made to pay that rent for as long as he retains them.
[412] He who, having taken elephants, horses, cattle, donkeys, camels, and so forth on lease,
does not return them when his purpose has been accomplished, must be made to pay that lease-fee.
Vṛddha-Manu:
He who, having hired a cart, takes it and goes elsewhere,
yet does not pay the hire, shall be made to pay the hire even for the distance not yet traveled.
Nārada [9.22]:
One should deliver the vessels for carrying the *stoma* when they are full and their time has come.
If they are broken or lost, the liability shall fall upon the receiver, except in the case of an accident.
Thus ends the section on non-payment of wages in the Kalpataru.
[413] 63. Now follows the dispute between the owner and the herdsman.
In this regard, Manu [8.229, 231] says:
"I shall fully declare, according to the true nature of Dharma, the legal dispute between owners and herdsmen concerning cattle, in accordance with the prescribed rule."
A servant who is supported by the milk of cows may, with the consent of the cow-owner, milk the best cow out of ten; this shall be the wages for a herdsman who receives no other pay.

"Supported by milk" (*kṣīrabhṛtaḥ*) means one for whom milk itself is the wages. "He should milk the best cow out of ten" means that from among ten cows, he should milk one excellent cow; "she" refers to the form of milking a single cow. "To the herdsman" (*pāle*) means to the cowherd. "Not being supported" (*abhṛte*)—the words "with food and clothing" are to be supplied. Nārada [9.10]: "From a hundred cows, a heifer shall be the wage; from two hundred, a milch-cow."
Every year, O Gopa, the milking of the herd takes place on the eighth day.
[414] Bṛhaspati [16.14]: Likewise, a milk-cow keeper shall indeed receive all the milk on the eighth day.
A "milk-cow keeper" (*dhenubhṛt*) is a cowherd.

Āpastamba [2.28.2–4]: "If a hired laborer (*kīnāśa*) who has moved out from his work abandons his task, he shall be beaten with a staff; likewise for a herdsman. And there shall be the confiscation of his cattle. Nārada [9.11]:
"He should lead [the animals] to the forest every day at the end of the night."
When those [milk products] have been consumed and drunk, the cowherd should bring them back in the evening.
Yājñavalkya [2.164]: Just as a cowherd should return the cattle entrusted to him in the evening,
so too must one who has received wages be made to pay for those that have been lost or destroyed through negligence.
[415] Manu [8.230]: "If the loss occurs during the day, the responsibility lies with the keeper; if at night, it lies with the owner, provided the animals were in his house.
Otherwise, if the loss occurred while they were under the keeper's care, the keeper shall incur the responsibility."
Manu and Nārada [Manu 8.233; Nārada 9.16]:
"But a herdsman does not deserve punishment for cattle stolen by thieves, provided he has proclaimed it and informs his own master at the proper place and time."
Vyāsa says: In the case of a village being attacked by a wolf, or when a village is destroyed, or likewise when there is a calamity of the kingdom,
whatever may be lost or stolen therein, the herdsman is not at fault.
Bṛhaspati [16.16]:
One should protect [the cattle] from worms, thieves, tigers, and other beasts, as well as from caves and pits;
one should strive to rescue them according to one's ability, cry out for help, or inform the owner.
If that cow should meet with misfortune, he should strive to remedy it to the best of his ability;
if he is unable, he should return quickly and report it to the owner.
Without making an effort to recover it, without raising a cry for help, and without informing his master,
the cowherd must bear the loss and pay a fine to the king.
Manu and Nārada [Manu 8.232; Nārada 9.14]:
"But the herdsman alone shall deliver what is lost, devoured by worms, killed by dogs, or dead on uneven ground, provided it was devoid of human effort."
In the phrase "killed by a dog" (*śvahata*), the word "dog" (*śva*) is intended to include beasts of prey and the like.
Yājñavalkya [2.165] states:
"But when destruction occurs through the fault of the keeper, a fine is prescribed for the keeper."
The owner shall pay twelve and a half paṇas as a fine, and the property itself must be restored.

Viṣṇu [5.137–39]: "If cattle are harmed by wolves or other predators during the day while the herdsman is not in a state of distress, the fault lies with the keeper. He shall pay the value of the lost animal to the owner. If he milks a cow without permission, he shall pay twenty-five kārṣāpaṇas."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "A cowherd who has received payment for his wages, having abandoned those [cows] in a lonely forest and wandering toward a village,
is to be executed by kings like a forest-dwelling poacher."
If a cow entrusted into the hands of a cowherd dies due to his negligence,
then he alone shall be punished, but the owner of the cow shall be made to pay the compensation.
When a cow dies anywhere in the house due to a defect such as disease, then that owner of the cattle is to be fined after having paid the wages of the cowherd.
*Śalākī* means a barber. "By reason of a fault such as disease" implies, as the context suggests, except for taking measures to remedy the master's [animal]. Manu and Nārada [state]:
"But when goats and sheep are hemmed in by wolves and the keeper is not on duty..."
If a wolf should forcibly kill one, the guilt for that would fall upon the keeper.
And among those very cows kept within the herd as they graze together in the forest,
if a wolf should spring upon one and kill it, the herdsman therein incurs no guilt.
‘Mithas’ means in private.
Nārada [9.17]:
By this, the dispute among all herdsmen has been described.
And there would be purification even among the dead, because of the observation of hair, horns, and so forth.

[418] Manu [8.234, 244]: "He shall give the two ears, the hide, the tail-hairs, the bladder, the sinew, and the bile to the owner of the animal; however, if they have died, he shall show the branded marks and so forth."
A righteous lord of the earth should observe this rule in cases of transgression involving owners of cattle, the animals themselves, and their keepers.

Thus ends [the section] from the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara, who served as the Great Minister for Peace and War (*Mahāsāndhivigrahika*) to His Majesty the Emperor (*Mahārājādhirāja*), the illustrious Govindacandradeva.
The dispute between owner and keeper in the section on judicial procedure.
regarding the transference of consciousness,
Nārada says on this matter: [13.1]
The established practice of heretics, guilds, and other such groups is called a *samaya* (convention). The failure to fulfill that convention is recorded in law as a subject of dispute.
Yājñavalkya [2.185]:
Having established a residence in the city and settled Brāhmaṇas there, the king should provide for those learned in the three Vedas and say to them: "Let your own dharma be protected."

Bṛhaspati [17.2–10]: Having summoned learned Brahmins who are knowers of the Vedic sciences, śrotriyas, and performers of the agnihotra sacrifice, he should establish them there and provide for their livelihood.
The king, having recorded it in his own edict, should grant them house-sites with the right to unassailable revenue and with their future profits secured.

They should perform the daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), optional (kāmya), pacificatory (śāntika), and prospering (pauṣṭika) rites according to the Purāṇas, as well as provide a definitive decision in matters of doubt.
An agreement and the establishment of a convention for villages, guilds,
and assemblies must be made during times of distress, as well as for the performance of religious duties.
In times of fear from scoundrels and thieves, affliction is known to be common to all;
therefore, its pacification must be undertaken by everyone collectively, not by any single individual alone.
Having first established mutual trust through a sealed deposit, a written contract, or neutral mediators, they should thereafter carry out their business affairs.
Those who harbor enmity, those beset by calamities, those who fear public alarm,
the greedy, the very aged, and children should not be appointed as counselors for state affairs.
Those who are pure, knowers of the Vedic dharma, skillful, self-controlled, of noble birth,
and proficient in all tasks— such persons should be appointed as high officials.
Seven or five members should be appointed who speak for the welfare of the community;
their word must be carried out by the village, guilds, corporations, and so forth.
[421] "It must be so": this refers to a specific source of revenue for the king.
Yājñavalkya [2.188]:
The word of those who speak for the welfare of the community must be carried out.
Whoever should act contrary to that [rule] there shall be made to pay the first fine.
Kātyāyana [671]: But he who destroys what is consistent with reason, he who gives no opportunity for the speaker,
and he who speaks what is unreasonable, shall be made to pay the highest fine.
Yājñavalkya [2.192]:
This same rule applies to guilds, merchant associations, heretics, and corporations;
the king shall protect them from internal dissension and preserve their traditional livelihoods.

"Guilds" (*śreṇayaḥ*) are artisans who subsist by a common craft or trade. "Merchants" (*naigamaḥ*) is a collective term for various citizens. "Heretics" (*pākhaṇḍaḥ*) are those who have fallen away from the life of renunciation. A "group" (*gaṇaḥ*) is a collection of Brāhmaṇas.
"In the case of heretics, merchants, guilds, corporations, associations, groups, and so forth..."
The king should protect the covenant both within the fort and likewise throughout the countryside.
Whatever their dharma, whatever their code of conduct, whatever the rules for their service,
and whatever their means of livelihood— one should approve of them accordingly.

A *pūga* is a corporation of merchants and the like; a *vrāta* is a corporation of those bearing various weapons. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), guilds (*saṅgha*), military companies (*gulma*), and classes (*varga*) are meant here. Kātyāyana [668] states:
"Whatever is the law for corporations, by that law they shall always abide."
Established in their own duties, they should perform all their actions.
Yājñavalkya [2.185]: That which is conventional and does not conflict with one's own duty,
as well as that which is established by the king, must also be protected with effort as dharma.
Kātyāyana [669, 670]: The royal edict has issued in accordance with the Dharma;
its practice must first be carried out by the command of the king.
That man who does not observe the laws promulgated by the king is blameworthy and sinful; he who violates the royal decree deserves punishment.
Bṛhaspati [17.11–14]: The restoration of assembly halls, water-stations, temples, houses, tanks, and gardens,
as well as the refinement of the destitute and the poor, and the performance of sacrifices.
And the cessation of the Kulyāyanas must be partially accomplished by us;
that which is recorded in this document is the righteous formal agreement.
He who, though capable, violates those agreements that ought to be maintained by all equally,
shall be punished with the confiscation of his entire property and banishment from the city.
In that case, whatever man creates a division or shows indifference [toward the assembly],
a fine of four suvarṇas and six niṣkas is ordained for him.
Manu [8.219, 221]: "A man who, having made a covenant by oath with a village, a district, or an assembly, should break it out of greed— that man the king shall banish from the realm."
Having restrained him, the king should compel that violator of the agreement to pay four suvarṇas, six niṣkas, and one silver śatamāna.
In this manner, a righteous lord of the earth should administer the rules of punishment against those who violate established conventions within villages, castes, and assemblies.
And a *śatamāna* consists of three hundred and twenty *raktikās*. Nārada [13.6]:
"Those who divide separate groups must be especially punished."
For if they are neglected, like a disease, they will bring about terrible fear.
Yājñavalkya [2.187]: "But he who misappropriates the property of a corporation, or he who violates an agreement, the king should confiscate all his possessions and banish him from the realm."

Kātyāyana [672]: "The perpetrator of violence, the sower of dissension, and the destroyer of the community's property—all these must be executed by kings after being publicly proclaimed; thus said Bhṛgu."
Bṛhaspati [17.15–20]:
But he who injures what is common property, reviles those learned in the three Vedas, or obstructs a formal agreement or a ritual act, shall be banished from that city.
One who inflicts wounds, a slanderer, a creator of dissension, as well as one who commits acts of violence,
and one who hates guilds, corporations, or the king, shall be banished from there immediately.
The heads of clans, guilds, and assemblies, as well as those residing in cities and fortresses,
shall impose verbal censure and social exclusion upon evildoers.

Whatever punishment or favor toward men is carried out by them according to their own duty, that must also be approved by the king; for they are traditionally considered to have been delegated full authority.
When those filled with hatred cause harm to a single person,
they must be restrained by the king and likewise punished along with their followers.
When a conflict arises between the principal members and the assemblies,
the king should then investigate the matter and establish them upon their proper course.
[426] Nārada [13.5]: The king shall not tolerate their forming secret conspiracies, the unauthorized use of weapons, or mutual injury toward one another.
Kātyāyana [673]:
If one person eats from the same vessel or from the same row as another,
he who does not act accordingly and fails to point out that person's fault shall be punished in the same manner as the offender.
Bṛhaspati [17.22]: Those who, having come together and formed a single mind, seize what belongs to the king,
as well as merchants who flee, shall be made to pay eight times that amount.
Nārada [13.4, 7]:
He should cause him to desist from whatever is contrary to the king's will, whatever is despised by the subjects, and whatever is detrimental to his interests.
Whatever instrument of action is defective and not prescribed by the sacred tradition,
even if it has been set in motion, a king who desires his own welfare should cause it to be withdrawn.
"An action performed with fault" means a defective act. "Not established by tradition" means that which is not proven through lineage.
Yājñavalkya [2.189–90]:
One should dismiss those who have come for the business of the assembly once their task has been accomplished.
Having honored him with gifts, respect, and hospitality, the lord of the earth—
One who has been dispatched for the business of a collective shall hand over whatever he may obtain;
if he does not hand it over himself, he shall be compelled to pay eleven times that amount.
Bṛhaspati [17.13–15]:
Whatever may be obtained from that, all of it shall be shared equally;
it should be divided according to their respective shares, whether it be for a month or for six months.
One should give to the poor, the elderly, the blind, women, children, the afflicted, and the sick, as well as to those seeking offspring and others; this is the eternal law.
Whatever has been acquired or preserved by them for the sake of the community, or whatever debt has been contracted,
as well as what has been obtained through the favor of the king— all that belongs equally to everyone.
[428] Kātyāyana [674–76]: Whatever debt may have been consumed by those acting on behalf of a group,
or whatever has been diverted for their own personal use, that must be paid back by those very individuals.
Even those who have joined the midst of guilds, corporations,
or associations, all of them shall receive equal shares of the previous wealth and debts.
In the same way, regarding the distribution of food, the sharing of wealth, and the performance of acts of dharma,
one who remains within the group shall share in the portion, but one who has departed shall not share in the portion.

Thus ends [the section on] the Kṛtyakalpataru composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara, who served as the Great Minister for Peace and War to His Majesty the Emperor, the illustrious Govindacandradeva.
The section on the breach of agreements in the Book of Judicial Procedure.
[429] 65— Now, regarding the non-delivery after sale, Nārada [states] at [11.1–5]:
When, after selling a commodity for its price, it is not delivered to the buyer,
that is called the legal head of dispute known as "non-delivery after sale."
In this world, there are two kinds of substances: the immobile and the mobile;
all of these are called "merchandise" in the context of the laws of buying and selling.
The wise have recorded his method of giving and taking as being of six kinds:
by counting, by weighing, by measuring, by action, by form, and by splendor.
If one who has sold a commodity does not deliver it to the purchaser for its price,
he shall be made to pay the loss of value for immovable property, and the fruit of its use for movable property.
If the price should fall by half, he shall bring back the merchandise with its profit;
this is the rule for stationary traders, while those who travel in various directions receive the local profit of their respective regions.

[430] ‘Countable goods’ (*gaṇima*) refer to betel nuts and the like; ‘weighable goods’ (*tulima*) refer to saffron and the like; ‘measurable goods’ (*meyam*) refer to rice and the like; ‘by labor’ (*kriyayā*) refers to activities such as driving or milking; ‘by form’ (*rūpataḥ*) refers to women and the like; ‘by beauty’ (*śriyā*) refers to rubies and the like; ‘immovable property’ (*sthāvarasya*) refers to villages, fields, and so forth; ‘movable property’ (*jaṅgamasya*) refers to cattle, horses, and so forth; ‘loss’ (*kṣayaḥ*) refers to deterioration through damage to crops and the like; and ‘fruit’ (*phalaṃ*) refers to milk and the like. Viṣṇu [5.127–28]: “If one who has received the price does not deliver it to the buyer, he shall be made to pay it with interest, and he shall be fined one hundred *paṇas* by the king.
Manu [8.222, 223, 228]: [text follows].
If, after having purchased or sold anything here, one should have regret,
he may return that object or take it back within ten days.
But after ten days, one should neither take [the goods] nor cause them to be taken;
both he who takes them and he who causes them to be given shall be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king.
In whatever matter one has committed an act for which he feels remorse,
he should be established on the path of righteousness by means of this procedure.
Kātyāyana [683–84]: He who, having purchased and received an article, does not accept it, or he who does not deliver an undamaged item,
shall recover his own property by paying one-tenth of the price.
If the object has not been obtained and the formal act has been performed, one must certainly not cause it to be delivered;
such is the law for ten days, but beyond that, there is no rescission.
"In the case of a formal agreement (*kriyākāra*), such as a written document of witnesses and so forth," according to Nārada [11.6]:
"The merchandise may be destroyed, burnt, or stolen."
That misfortune belongs to the seller alone, who sells but does not deliver.
But he who, having shown a faultless item, delivers one that is defective,
shall be made to pay double the price as a fine, and an equal amount as a penalty.
Bṛhaspati [18.3–4]:
An unwise man who, knowing a commodity to be defective, sells it,
shall be made to pay double that very amount, as well as an equal fine as a penalty.
If a sale is made for a low price by one who is intoxicated or insane,
or by one who is not independent or is deluded, it should be rescinded and the property taken back from him.
Yājñavalkya [2.257]:
If an item sold by another person, or one that is defective, is sold as if it were non-defective,
the fine in that case shall be double its value.
Nārada [11.8]:
Likewise, he who, having sold an item into the hand of one person, delivers it to another, shall be made to pay double that amount as a fine, and an equal amount as a penalty.
Yājñavalkya [2.61]: One should cause the person who has made a *satyaṃkāra* to pay back double the value of the object.
"Satyaṃkāra" refers to that object which is given for the purpose of ensuring the truthfulness of a purchase or sale.
Vyāsa says: When a person has given a pledge of truth (satyaṃkāra) but does not appear at the appointed time,
that merchandise shall be considered relinquished if it is not accepted by the one who was being paid.
"Released" means given.
Nārada [11.9]:
"The buyer who, having purchased a commodity, does not accept it while it is being delivered..."
If he sells it elsewhere, the seller shall not be held at fault.
Yājñavalkya [2.255]: Even if it has been sold, the goods may be reclaimed from the previous buyer if he does not accept them;
for if the loss was due to the fault of the buyer, that loss shall belong to the buyer alone.
Nārada says: If a buyer does not accept merchandise being offered for sale,
the fault for the seller’s failure to deliver shall belong to him alone.
[434] Likewise, [Nārada 11.10–12]: This rule has been proclaimed regarding merchandise for which the price has been paid;
if it is not delivered, except by mutual agreement, there is no transgression on the part of the seller.
For the sake of profit, merchants engage in the buying and selling of all commodities;
yet that profit, depending on the market price, may or may not become great.
Therefore, a merchant should determine the price according to the place and the time;
he should not act with deceit, for such is the superior path of trade.

Thus, in the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Mallakṣmīdhara, the son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara, who served as the Great Minister for Peace and War (*Mahāsāndhivigrahika*) to His Majesty the Emperor (*Mahārājādhirāja*), the illustrious Govindacandradeva.
In the section on legal procedure, [the topic of] non-delivery after sale.
[435] 66— Now, regarding the remorse after having purchased,
on this matter Nārada says: [12.1–3]
When one who has purchased a commodity for a price does not value what was bought,
this is called the legal head of dispute known as "repentance after purchase."
If a buyer, having purchased a commodity for a price, considers it a bad purchase,
it must be returned to the seller on that very same day, provided it is still unblemished.
If the purchaser delivers the price on the second day, he shall incur a fine of one-thirtieth;
but on the third day, it shall be double that amount; beyond that, the loss falls upon the purchaser alone.
Kātyāyana [686,
687]: If a person, having purchased an article such as a milch cow, should later abandon it because of regret,
provided it is not defective and he returns it at the proper time, he shall pay one-tenth of the price.
If a purchaser, having bought [an article], departs with regret once it has come into his hand,
Bhṛgu says that he may abandon the purchase by paying one-sixth of its value.

[436] Yājñavalkya [2.258]: A merchant who, being ignorant of the depreciation or appreciation of commodities, has purchased them, shall not exercise the right of rescission; if he does so, he shall be liable to a fine of one-sixth.
A merchant who is skilled in merchandise should not harbor regret after having purchased;
he should know the loss and the profit of goods according to their respective nature.
A buyer should personally examine a commodity beforehand for its merits and defects;
once it has been examined and purchased as approved, it shall not be returned to the seller.
Bṛhaspati [18.9]: One should personally examine the merchandise and show it to others;
having accepted what has been examined and approved by many, one should not reject it again.
Vyāsa: Leather, wood, bricks, thread, grain,
liquor, juice, cloth, base metals, and gold must be examined immediately.
Nārada [12.5, 6]:
One should examine a milch cow for three days, but a draft animal for five days;
however, the examination of pearls, diamonds, and corals shall last for seven days.
For bipeds, the period is half a month for males, but double that for females;
for all seeds, it is ten days; and for metals and clothes, it is one day.
Having stated the time for examination according to the sequence spoken by Nārada, Bṛhaspati [18.7] says:
"If, however, a defect in the merchandise should arise at any time prior to this [period],"
That must be returned by the seller; the buyer shall recover his purchase price.

Kātyāyana [688]: But that which was purchased without being examined, and later found to be defective—that merchandise, having been purchased, must be returned to the owner at the proper time; otherwise, it need not be returned.
One thing mixed with another does not deserve to be sold;
nor that which is defective, nor that which is deficient, nor that which is far away, nor that which is concealed.
Nārada [12.7]:
But a garment that has been worn, which is soiled,
stained, and defective— even if purchased as such— it shall not belong to the seller again.

Thus [ends the section] in the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Mallakṣmīdhara, son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara, who served as the Great Minister for Peace and War (*mahāsāndhivigrahika*) to His Majesty the Emperor (*mahārājādhirāja*), the illustrious Govindacandradeva.
In the section on legal procedures, [this concerns] rescission after purchase.
[438] 67—Now follows the dispute concerning boundaries; regarding this, Bṛhaspati says: [19.1]
This rule has been declared regarding rescission in buying and selling;
now learn the law concerning disputes over boundaries of villages, fields, houses, and the like.

Nārada [14.1]: Where there is a dispute regarding the determination of a boundary, a watercourse, a limit, or land that is cultivated or uncultivated, and where there is authority over the field— that is a dispute concerning land.

The meaning of this is as follows: when it is necessary to determine the distance from or proximity to boundaries such as embankments, fields, and so forth, a dispute concerning the field itself is called "kṣetraja" (field-born). Kātyāyana [732] states:
"Excess, deficiency, a share, and even existence or non-existence."
Possession through enjoyment and boundaries are the six causes of legal disputes.
[439] "Possession through enjoyment" (*abhogabhukti*) refers to the enjoyment of land or other property that was previously non-existent.
Manu [8.245]: When a dispute regarding a boundary has arisen between two villages...
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should lead her across the well-lit bridges.
Bṛhaspati [19.2]: At the time of settling a residence, the determination of the boundaries must be made;
marked by both public and secret signs, it removes all doubt.
And they should establish boundary trees— *nyagrodha*, *aśvattha*, and *kiṃśuka* trees, as well as *śālmali*,
*sāla*, and *tāla* trees, and other milky-sap trees (*kṣīrin*).
By means of thickets, various types of bamboos, *śamī* trees, creepers, and plateaus,
as well as reeds and *kubjaka* shrubs, the boundary is not lost.
Reservoirs, wells, rivers, and springs,
as well as temples, should be constructed at the junctions of boundaries.
Bṛhaspati [19.8–9]: "Reservoirs, wells, and ponds; sacred shrines, groves, and temples;
level ground, depressions, river currents, reeds, thickets, and heaps of stones."
One should always cause these visible marks to be made at the boundary,
as well as others that are buried, so that the earth may not consume them.
And he should cause other boundary marks to be made that are concealed,
having observed the constant confusion among men in this world regarding the knowledge of boundaries.
Stones, bones, cow-hair, as well as ashes and potsherds, dried cow-dung, bricks, charcoal, gravel, and sand.
Furthermore, those [mines] of this kind that the earth would not consume due to their [inappropriate] time,
he should cause to be established in secret at junctions and boundaries.
Bṛhaspati [19.20–21]: Dried cow dung, husks, charcoal, gravel, stones, potsherds,
sand, bricks, cow hair, cotton seeds, bones, and ashes.
Having cast these into jars, one should have them deposited at the boundaries of the boundary;
thereafter, one should carefully show them to children of tender age.
And likewise, they should show [the boundary] to children when they have reached old age;
thus, when knowledge is handed down in succession, no confusion regarding the boundary arises.
Manu [8.252]: By these signs, as well as by long-standing possession and the constant flow of water, the king should determine the boundary for men who are disputing it.
Nārada [14.6], following the phrase "they should determine the boundary," states:
"In cases where lands have had their marks removed by the waters of a river, or have been abandoned, or lost,
[the boundary shall be determined] by inferences from those locations, by measurements, and by the observation of signs."
[442] Manu [8.253]: "If there should be doubt even when signs are observed,
the determination of the boundary in a dispute shall depend solely upon the testimony of witnesses."
Kātyāyana [733]:
In that case, the enjoyment [of the property] must be established; and that rests upon witnesses.
Whether it is recorded in writing or otherwise, the witness follows both paths.
"The witnesses to the boundary marks of the villages and families must be questioned in the presence of both disputants regarding the boundary signs."
Once they have been questioned, he should record their collective decision regarding the boundary exactly as they declare it, as well as the names of all those present.
In the absence of witnesses, however, four villages situated on the boundary shall,
being purified, determine the boundary in the presence of the king.
‘Grāmeyaka’ means a villager. Yājñavalkya [2.152]:
“Or four, eight, or even ten neighboring villagers from the entire village.”
Wearing red garlands and garments, those who uphold the earth should lead the boundary.

Kātyāyana says: In their absence, the neighbors—the original inhabitants, the elders, and those who have been evicted—must be made witnesses even in the case of the six types of immovable property; there is no doubt in this matter.
In disputes between two parties concerning fields, buildings, tanks, wells, groves, or embankments, as well as all other matters, the decision shall be reached through the testimony of the neighbors.
One should determine the boundaries of a field by means of the neighboring landowners because of their proximity;
and likewise for village boundaries, as well as for cities and districts.
When neighboring vassals have become corrupt in the pursuit of their own interests due to the weight of material gain, one must effect their removal through those associated with them;
of this there is no doubt.
Those who are attached to, or associated with, those who are corrupt are proclaimed as "associated with them.
However, a king who understands the Dharma must not tolerate those who are actually corrupt.
Having set aside wicked vassals and having associated with others who are hereditary and so forth, he should have the boundary established; thus do those who know the Dharma understand it.
The neighboring kings are considered to possess one unit of merit when they have previously failed to state their objections;
those further away are known to possess two units, and others beyond them are held to possess three units.

‘Those closely associated with them’ means those situated in the vicinity of the neighbors. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “In a dispute concerning a house or a field, the testimony of the neighbors is decisive. In a dispute among neighbors, the testimony of written records is decisive. In a dispute concerning written records, the testimony of the elders and guilds of the village or city is decisive. In a dispute among the elders and guilds of the village or city, the possession for ten years is decisive, except in the case of the property of the king or a Brahmin. Nārada [14.2, 3].
In the case of a dispute regarding the boundary of a field, the decision shall be made by the neighbors,
as well as by the heads of cities, villages, and guilds, and those men who are the most venerable.
And those who live by agriculture outside the village boundaries—
cowherds, fowlers, hunters, and others who dwell in the forest.
Manu [8.259–60]: In the absence of neighboring villagers who are original witnesses to the boundary,
he should also interrogate these men who dwell in the forests.
Hunters, fowlers, cowherds, fishermen, root-diggers,
snake-catchers, gleaners, and others who dwell in the forest.
Nārada [14.4–5]:
They should mark out the boundary, clearly indicated by signs such as husks,
charcoal, potsherds, bones, wells, temples, and trees.
And by means of anthills with distinct signs, by the depressions and elevations of the ground,
and likewise by ancient fields, groves, paths, and embankments;
Manu [8.261]: "Whatever marks they may declare when questioned regarding the boundaries between two villages, the king shall establish them accordingly in accordance with dharma."
Bṛhaspati [19.31]: Bound by their respective oaths, they shall declare the decision regarding the boundary;
they shall point out hidden deposits, for that is the established rule of evidence.
"Placing their heads upon the earth, wearing garlands and red garments,
and being sworn by their respective good deeds, they shall lead the case justly."
A man, even if he be trustworthy, should not determine a boundary alone;
because of the gravity of this matter, this procedure is established upon many.
If there is only one person, he should establish the boundary while fasting;
wearing red garlands and garments, he should place the earth upon his head and then establish it.
Bṛhaspati says:
Even when the identifying marks of the cognizers have perished, a single person approved by both parties,
wearing red garlands and garments and carrying earth upon his head, [shall act as the witness].
A man who is devoted to truth and has observed a fast should point out the boundary.
Manu (8.257, 263): Those who lead [the boundary] as prescribed become purified; they are witnesses of truth.
But those who lead them astray shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred.
If the neighbors should speak falsely when men are disputing over a boundary,
they shall all be punished individually by the king with the middle amercement.
"At the boundary" means at the limit.
Katyayana [750, 741]:
"But if, among many who have been summoned, not all reach a decision..."
If they do so out of fear or greed, they shall be made to pay the highest fine.
For neighboring lords are not released from liability by claiming ignorance regarding the decision;
if they speak out of ignorance, the king should fine them and then re-examine the boundary.
If a dispute should arise regarding what has been proclaimed, those responsible shall be punished with the highest fine.
Nārada says:
If the remaining witnesses, though appointed for the legal proceeding, should speak falsely,
even those of lower status must each be punished with the first amercement.
But others, such as the elders of the guild and so forth, shall each pay a fine individually;
those who persist in falsehood are to be punished with the first amercement.
But those bordering regions that are contiguous, and those further beyond them, ending with those contiguous to the contiguous—
these are proclaimed to be shaped like a lotus.
A village is declared to be the neighbor of a village; a field is the neighbor of a field;
and a house is specified as the neighbor of a house, embracing it on all sides.
Those who were formerly neighbors there but later went to another country are proclaimed by the sages as "original" (maula) because they are rooted in that very place.

"A village is the neighbor of a village. This means that in a dispute between the inhabitants of one village and the inhabitants of another, the neighbor is not merely someone from that same village; rather, the meaning is that the neighbor is one from a different village. The same applies to "field" and so forth. By the words "field" and "house," their respective owners are indicated. Bṛhaspati [19.38–39]:
"And those neighbors born of that [place], as well as others residing in other regions..."
But those original [witnesses] who have been designated should be questioned for the determination of the case.
Whatever those who are free from malice might say, being impartial and of steady conduct, that must be accepted as authoritative; in this way, dharma is not lost.
[448] Kātyāyana [744–45]: Those by whom the work being executed is seen, and who are endowed with human virtues—
whether they be old or not old— they are proclaimed to be "elders" (vṛddha).
Because they rescue [beings] from that [suffering], being characterized by hearing, enjoyment, activity,
and narration, they are therefore known as "Uddhṛtas" (the Rescuers).
‘Upaśravaṇa’ is hearsay established by tradition. ‘Saṃbhoga’ is enjoyment. ‘Kāryākhyāna’ is news concerning the receipt of its fruit.
Nārada says: [The boundary is] that marked by a banner (dhvajinī), that which is joined (sandhinī), that which is based on a deposit (naidhānī), and that which is free from fear (bhayavarjitā).
And the boundary established by royal decree is recorded as being of five kinds.
Vyāsa says:

A boundary made by kings is of five kinds—low-lying, elevated, marked by banners, consisting of fire-pits (naidhānī), and stable; however, that which is marked by fish (matsyinī) is considered deceptive.
Where there is a depression between two villages that serves as the indicator of the boundary,
that is declared by those learned in the scriptures to be a "depressed" boundary marker (*nimna*).
Where reed-thickets, ant-hills, temples,
and heaps of stones are seen, that [ground] should be known as "elevated" (samunnatā).
Where trees stand tall at the boundary of both villages,
rising high like banners, that is proclaimed as the *dhvajinī* boundary.
That [ground] where bricks, charcoal, sand, gravel, bones,
and potsherds are seen to have been deposited is proclaimed as *naidhānī*.
Where there is an absence of witnesses and the boundary has been determined by the lord with the consent of the neighbors, that boundary is to be known as "established by the king."
Kātyāyana [747]:
"When all else is absent, it may be made by oneself, provided the king is free from fear.
Nārada [14.11].
But when there are no witnesses to the boundary and no defining marks,
then the king himself shall determine the boundary between the two parties as he deems fit.
Vyāsa says: Where the boundary is a river that flows freely, possesses abundant water, is filled with fish and tortoises, and flows perpetually, it is considered to be Matsyinī.
Manu [8.265]: "When a boundary is impossible to determine, the king himself, who knows the dharma, shall assign land to these [villages] based on what is beneficial; such is the settled rule."
Bṛhaspati and Vyāsa [in the first section of the Bṛhat-vaṃśa, verse 19.40]:
"When land has been granted by a king to one person after having been taken from another village,
or from a great river, how should the legal decision be made in that case?"
Land that is overflowed by a river or granted by a king belongs to him alone;
otherwise, men would have no gain from causes pertaining to kings or fate.
The decline, prosperity, and livelihood of men are subject to fate and the king.

Therefore, in all matters, one should not overturn what has been done by him. Where a river has been established as the boundary between two villages, if it becomes diminished due to depletion or rise, he who alters it deserves punishment.
By the power of fortune or misfortune, a river effects the loss of what was given or the acquisition of what was not by men;
it causes the collapse of a bank in one place while leaving another situated elsewhere on its shore—it does not displace that [other] part. 9–11.
When a field with standing crops is crossed and the ground becomes divided,
the original owner shall regain it by means of the flow of the river's current.
That which was seized by a king through anger, greed, or through fraud and injustice [shall be restored].
But if it has been given by one who is satisfied, she shall not obtain [the land];
nor shall one who enjoys land that lacks a formal title, or land that was seized from someone else, or land given to one of superior merit, be dispossessed of it. || 15–17 ||
regarding the extended applications (*atideśa*),
on this point Kātyāyana says:
The king shall establish provinces consisting of ten villages, a hundred villages, a thousand villages, or a hundred thousand villages, with their boundaries clearly determined by fixed markers.
Yājñavalkya [2.154]: This same rule is to be understood as applicable to groves, temples, villages, water-reservoirs, gardens, houses, and to places where rainwater flows away and so forth.
This very procedure, characterized by the testimony of neighbors and so forth, is to be understood.
Manu [8.262]: "In the case of fields, wells, tanks, groves, and houses..."
The determination of a boundary between two villages should be known as dependent upon the testimony of neighboring witnesses.
Kātyāyana [749]: Regarding fields, wells, and tanks, as well as rice-fields and groves,
and likewise houses, palaces, dwellings, and temples.

Bṛhaspati [19.45–46]: From the time of settling in, whatever house, water, shop, or other property has been used by someone to a certain extent and in a certain manner, that person shall not be deprived of it.
One should not disturb the windows, the drainage channels, as well as the turrets and the altars, nor the four-sided halls and the water-channels already established there.

A *niryūha* is a specific type of wooden structure projecting from a door. A *vedikā* is a raised ground surface constructed in places such as at a gateway (*pratolī*). A *catuḥśālam* is a house with four doors. A *syandanikā* is the edge of a roof-covering. Kātyāyana [752–53] states:
"One should not obstruct the girdle-path, the drainage channel, or the window."
One who obstructs a water-channel or a house-site shall be liable to punishment.
After the time of settling [the house], these [rites] should never be performed again;
one should not cast a glance or create a water-channel upon the dwellings of others.

The *mekhalā* is the foundation binding at the base of a wall. The *bhrama* is the outlet for water. The *niṣkāsa* is a place for sitting constructed of wood or other materials, not touching the ground, protruding from the walls of a palace or similar structure. "One should not obstruct" means one should not block it. The *gṛhavāstu* is the dwelling site. The *dṛṣṭipāta* is a window. Bṛhaspati [19.49]:
"The place for excrement, the fire-pit, the trench, and the pouring out of leftover water..."
One should never, under any circumstances, build even slightly beyond the neighboring wall.
‘Atyārāt’ means very near.
[454] Kātyāyana [754]:
And a receptacle for excrement, urine, and water, as well as a dwelling with no opening above, [should be constructed].
Having left a space of two cubits, one should construct the neighboring walls.
Bṛhaspati [19.51]:
"That path by which people and even animals go and come without obstruction is called *saṃsaraṇa* (the thoroughfare); it must not be blocked by anyone."
Nārada [14.15]: One should not obstruct crossroads, temples, carriage roads, or paths with refuse heaps, mounds of earth, pits, ditches, drains, and the like.

A *rathyā* is a crossroads. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "Discharging [waste] on a road, in a field, or on a path; turning a chariot on a royal highway; establishing a former boundary; [discharging waste] three steps within a gateway, a house, or a street; and as one pleases in the temples of the gods or the king."

‘On the field of the road’ means on that field which is situated on the road. ‘Relinquishing the path’ means the way must not be obstructed; this is the meaning. ‘Turning the chariot on the royal highway’ means that as much space as is required for the chariot to turn around must be cleared on the royal highway; this is the meaning. ‘Three paces within the arches, houses, and streets’ means one should leave a space measuring three paces near the arches, houses, and streets; this is the meaning. [455] Kātyāyana [655–57]: That place where all people always pass is a crossroads (catuṣpatha).
That which is not prohibited at the proper time is called the royal road.
One should not plant anything there, nor should one cause any harm by any means;
however, for obstructing the path of the guru, the teacher, the king, and others, one incurs punishment.
Whoever there should willfully deposit refuse in pits, ravines, or even plant trees, his fine shall be one māṣaka.
"Saṅkara" means refuse.
Manu [9.282–83]: "But he who, except in an emergency, should discard impure matter on the royal highway..."
He shall pay two kārṣāpaṇas and he shall also clean the impurity.
One who has fallen into calamity, as well as an elderly person, a pregnant woman, or even a child, deserve only a verbal reprimand; and that [offense] must be cleared away—this is the settled rule.
In the context of the term "shall be punished," Viṣṇu [5.105] states: "For the abandonment of filth near a path, a garden, or water, the fine is one hundred paṇas. Kātyāyana [758–59] says:
"He who destroys tanks, gardens, or sacred bathing places with impure matter..."
But having cleansed an impure substance, one should be punished with the first amercement.
He who defiles established sacred fords (tīrtha) founded by great souls—
ancient and purifying sites— shall incur the punishment for the first degree of violence (pūrvasāhasa).
Manu [8.264]: "One who seizes a house, a pond, a garden, or a field by means of intimidation shall be fined five hundred [paṇas]; if it was done through ignorance, the fine shall be two hundred."
‘By means of intimidation’ means by producing fear.
Vṛddha Manu says:
“And likewise, a boundary established between two villages...”
Those wicked ones who transgress [this rule] shall be punished with a fine of two hundred [paṇas].
Yājñavalkya [2.155]: "But for the breaking of a boundary-mark, as well as for the transgression of a boundary,
and for the seizure of a field, the punishments are the lowest, the highest, and the middle."

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "For breaking the boundary of a field, the fine is eight hundred; for overstepping the boundary, eight thousand; and for diverting the water of a field, eight hundred. Viṣṇu [5.172] says: "Having punished the breaker of a boundary with the highest amercement, one should have the boundary re-established. Kātyāyana [760–61] states:
In the case of trees grown within the boundary of two fields,
one should declare that their fruits and flowers belong in common to the owners of both fields.

[457] One should recognize the owner of those trees that have grown in another field but whose branches are situated elsewhere; rather, one should recognize the owner in whichever field they are established.

Thus ends the section titled "Disputes over Boundaries" in the *Vyavahārakāṇḍa* of the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, the son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara, the Great Minister for Peace and War (Mahāsāndhivigrahika) along with his family.
67 — (b) Now, regarding the embankment,
Nārada says [14.17]:
"An embankment in the middle of another's field is not prohibited."
If there is great merit and little harm, then increase is desired even when there is loss.

The meaning of this is as follows: if a dam being constructed by one person on another's field is of great benefit and causes only slight damage to the owner of that field, then it should not be removed; for even when there is a small loss, an increase characterized by the growth of crops and the like is desired by everyone. Yājñavalkya [2.156–57] states:
"A dam that brings about prosperity and causes only slight damage should not be prohibited."
A well that draws water from another's land is a small field with abundant water.
If one constructs an irrigation channel on a field without having informed the owner, the produce belongs to the owner once it has arisen;
in his absence, it belongs to the king.
[458] Nārada [14.20–22]: But he who should initiate a dam that was previously commenced but abandoned, without having asked the owner, shall not partake in its fruit.
But when the owner has died, or even when a descendant of his lineage is a human being,
one should then proceed with the construction of the stūpa after having consulted the king.
Otherwise, one would be subject to affliction, as seen in the case of the deer-hunter;
for him who shoots again at what has already been pierced, his arrows are wasted.
"‘The master’ means the owner of the bridge.
Kātyāyana [762–63]: "But he who performs a consecration without the consent of the owner..."
One who repairs houses, gardens, and ponds does not [attain that merit].
If the master has arrived and the king has not been informed, the gift should not be given;
however, if it is employed after having been reported, one recovers the expenditure incurred for that purpose.

A dam is said to be of two kinds: that which is to be dug out (kheya) and likewise that which is to be built up (bandhya). It is "to be dug out" by causing water to flow through it, and it is "to be built up" by stopping the flow.
Without water there is no crop, yet when it is excessive there is destruction;
the very same fault that exists in the absence of water occurs when there is too much water.

Thus ends the section on the Setu (Bridge) in the Vivādakāṇḍa of the Kṛtyakalpataru, composed by Bhaṭṭa Lakṣmīdhara, son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara, who was accompanied by the great minister for peace and war (Mahāsāndhivigrahika).
— Now, regarding that which is drawn away and not drawn away, Nārada says [in verses 14.23–24]:
If someone should cultivate a field when the owners are incapacitated, deceased,
or lost, he shall enjoy the fruit of that field without being hindered.
If a field is being drawn for cultivation, the original owner may return;
having provided all the expenses for clearing the fallow land, he shall regain possession of the field.
Kātyāyana [764]: If, due to incapacity, he does not pay [the share],
then the cultivator shall receive the fruit of the harvest diminished by one-eighth of whatever expenses were incurred for the purpose of clearing the fallow land.
He shall be the enjoyer for eight years; thereafter, however, it belongs to the owner.
"In one year, half of a fallow field becomes [the property of] the tiller; a fallow field becomes [his] after three years."
But a field that has been neglected for five years becomes equal to a wilderness.
Whether it be a field that has passed through three generations or a house inherited by succession,
other than by royal favor, one should not transfer its enjoyment to another.
House and field are seen as the two causes for the residence of householders;
therefore, the king should not confiscate them, for they are indeed the root of householders.
When the population increases, the king’s righteousness and treasury increase;
when it declines, they too decline. Therefore, he should resort to the causes of growth.
Yājñavalkya [2.158]:

If one neither cultivates nor causes to be cultivated a field that has been tilled with a plough, the king shall compel him to pay the value of the crop that could have been harvested and cause the field to be cultivated by another.

Regarding the term *akṛṣṭasadam*: it means the fruit of the harvest and so forth from unplowed land (*akṛṣṭasya kṣetrasya sadam*), having caused [the tenant] to pay in accordance with the nature of the plowed field (*kṛṣṭakṣetra*). Bṛhaspati says:
"Having taken [the grain], he should transport it at the proper time for the sake of sowing, guarding, and storing."
But he who does not cultivate [the field] shall be made to pay the owner half of the produce of the cultivated land.
"Madhyam kṛṣṭasadam" means that he should be made to pay in accordance with the yield of the cultivated field, which is neither superior nor inferior; such is the meaning according to Vyāsa:
"He who, having taken a field, neither cultivates it himself nor causes it to be cultivated..."
He shall always be made to pay it to the owner by the king and be fined an equal amount.
If [the time] has long passed, the tenth [part] should be taken; likewise, if it is being drawn out, the eighth;
but if it is well-prepared, the sixth should be assigned according to the established rule.
[Thus ends the section on "Ploughing and Not Ploughing," 67]
(gha) Now, regarding the protection of crops, Yājñavalkya states [at 2.166]:
The pasture for cattle may be established according to the will of the village or by royal decree;
likewise,
[2.167] the distance from a village to its fields should be one hundred bows in circumference.

[471] 68— Now, regarding verbal abuse,
Nārada says [at 18.1]:
Speech that consists of insults or slanders regarding one's country, birth, family, and so forth,
and which has a disagreeable meaning, is called verbal abuse.

‘Ākrośa’ means censure. Among these, ‘censure of place’ (*deśākrośa*) is, for example, regarding Gauḍas: “Gauḍas are fond of quarreling. ‘Censure of caste’ (*jātyākrośa*) is, for example, regarding a Brahmin: “Brahmins are exceedingly greedy. ‘Censure of family’ (*kulākrośa*) is, for example: “The descendants of Viśvāmitra are of cruel conduct. By the word ‘etcetera’ (*ādi*), learning and so forth are included. ‘Nyaṅga’ refers to that which is indecorous or vulgar. Kātyāyana [768] states:
“A grunt, a cough, and whatever else is censured in the world...”
To imitate or to speak in such a manner is called verbal abuse.

Because of its harshness, abusiveness, and severity, that [abuse] is also remembered as being of three kinds.
According to the sequence of their gravity, the punishment for each is appropriately more severe in turn.

That which is accompanied by reproach and is harsh should be known as *aślīla* (indecorous), while that termed *nyaṅga* (defamatory) consists of insults involving grounds for expulsion; the wise call such speech *tīvra* (severe).
"By way of the sequence of gravity": because of their increasing weight in successive order.

Whether based on what is untrue or even on what is true, that which is harsh speech is known as such.

[473] Speaking of a sister, a mother, or their relatives, as well as proclaiming their minor offenses (upapātaka),
