The discourse on what is unfit to be eaten or drunk, the defilement by a mortal sin,
and harshness that strikes at the vital points intensely— this is declared to be the highest [degree of verbal abuse].

In the phrase "without substance" (*dravyaṃ vinā*), the word *dravya* refers to the subject matter (*abhidheya*). Thus, the meaning is that verbal abuse (*vākpāruṣya*) consists of such speech that is distinct from the actual facts being expressed. Kātyāyana [773–74]:
He who, out of anger, proclaims non-existent defects, or who perceives virtues in one who is devoid of them...

If one swears, "I shall violate your sister and your mother," the king should cause him to pay a fine of twenty-five [paṇas].

A Brahmin shall be fined fifty [paṇas] for defaming a Kṣatriya;

Kātyāyana [states]: "But for merely raising the hand [to strike], a fine of twelve [paṇas] should be imposed."
That same [penance] is declared to be double in the case of causing the downfall of those belonging to the same caste.
Bṛhaspati [21.8]: When a stone, a slab, or a piece of wood is raised [in assault], the first fine shall be imposed;
likewise, for striking one another with hands or feet, the fine is twenty-five [paṇas].

In the context of the term "one who is to be punished" (*daṇḍya*), Viṣṇu states [5.60–62, 64]: "One who threatens with the hand shall be fined ten *kārṣāpaṇas*; with the foot, twenty; with a piece of wood, the first amercement (*prathamasāhasa*); with a weapon, the highest amercement (*uttamasāhasa*). The meaning is that when a person of lower status threatens a person of higher status with a weapon, he is to be punished with the highest amercement. Yājñavalkya [2.216] states:
If hands or feet are raised [in a threatening manner], the fines shall be ten and twenty [paṇas] respectively;
for all [such acts] against one another with a weapon, the middle amercement applies.

And this should be understood to apply to those of the same class (*samānajātīya*), since other punishments are heard for those of different classes. Regarding the continuation of the term *paṇa*, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "In the case of raising a blow, the fine is fifty-six *paṇas*; in the case of actually striking, it is double that. Bṛhaspati [21.9–10] states:
When two people are enraged and weapons are drawn, the middle fine should be applied;
however, when a wound has been inflicted, the wise should determine a punishment corresponding to the injury at the time of the blow.
For striking with bricks, stones, or wood, the fine shall be two māṣakas;
for drawing blood, the wise should impose double that penalty.
Viṣṇu [5.66, 67]: "One who inflicts pain without drawing blood shall be fined thirty-two *paṇas*; if with blood, sixty-four. Manu [8.284]:
"One who breaks the skin shall be fined one hundred, as shall one who causes blood to flow."
But one who cuts flesh shall be fined six niṣkas, while one who breaks a bone shall be banished.

Bṛhaspati [21.11–12]: For piercing the skin, the first amercement is the punishment; for piercing the flesh, however, the middle amercement; for piercing the bone, the highest amercement; and for causing death, the penalty is execution.

For the cutting off of the ears, nose, or hands, for breaking the teeth, or for breaking the feet, the middle amercement shall be imposed; and it shall be double in the case of those who have committed mortal sins.
Kātyāyana [781]:
For the cutting off of the ears, lips, nose, feet, eyes, tongue, penis, or hand, the highest fine is prescribed; for the piercing or mutilating of these, Bṛhaspati says the middle fine applies.
Yājñavalkya [2.219–20]: For breaking a hand, a foot, or a tooth; for cutting off the ears or the nose;
for piercing a wound; and likewise for striking someone who is as good as dead—the middle amercement is the punishment.
In cases of obstructing movement, food, or speech; piercing the eyes or other [senses];
and breaking the neck, arms, or thighs, the middle amercement shall be imposed.

While the term "punishment" (*daṇḍa*) continues to apply, Viṣṇu [5.70–72] states: "In the case of breaking the eye, neck, arm, thigh, or shoulder, the highest [amercement]; one who pierces both eyes, the king shall not release from bondage for as long as he lives, or he may inflict a similar [punishment]. Yājñavalkya [2.308] says:
"One who pierces two eyes, as well as one who gives commands hostile to the king..."
But for a Śūdra living by means of the status of a Brāhmaṇa, the fine shall be eight hundred.
Manu [8.286]: When a blow is struck against humans or animals for the purpose of causing pain,
the king shall inflict a punishment in proportion to the severity of the suffering caused.

Hārīta states: "In cases of verbal abuse, intimidation, or assault against those of lower caste by those of higher caste, the fine is eight *purāṇas*. For seizing the neck, throat, breasts, hair, or face, it is thirty. For plucking out body hair, threatening, or brandishing a weapon, it is sixty-three. For breaking or cutting the crest-lock, ears, or limbs, it is two hundred. For kicking with the foot or making a false accusation, there shall be amputation of that same limb, or a fine of five hundred. Or, in the first cases, the fine may be reduced by one-quarter. Because of his lordship and because he belongs to the highest caste, the Brāhmaṇa is the supreme master over those of the higher castes. Yājñavalkya [2.215] says:
Any limb of a non-Brāhmaṇa that causes pain to a Brāhmaṇa should be cut off;
however, if he merely raised his weapon, the first amercement is the punishment, and if he merely touched him, half of that.
"In contact" means touching weapons or other implements for the purpose of attempting a killing. Nārada [18.25, 31]:
"By whichever limb a lower caste person might offend a Brāhmaṇa..."
then that limb of his must be cut off; in this way, he shall attain purification.
But that evil-minded man who would strike a king, even though the latter has committed an offense, should be cooked on a spit over fire; his sin exceeds even that of killing a Brahmin.
[491] "Against one who has committed an offense" means against one who has committed a transgression. That which is prepared after being impaled on a stake is called "śūlya.
Manu [8.279–80]: "If an outcaste should injure a superior person with any limb whatsoever..."
Whatever is to be cut away, that very thing must be cut away; such is the instruction for his mind.
Raising his hand or his staff, he deserves the cutting off of his hand;
striking with his foot out of anger, he deserves the cutting off of his foot.
Manu and Nārada (Ma. 8.281–83):
A person of lower birth who seeks to sit upon the same seat as one of superior birth shall be branded on the buttocks and banished; or, he shall have his buttock cut off.
The king shall cause the two lips of one who spits out of arrogance to be cut off;
likewise, he shall cause the penis of one who urinates [upon him] to be cut off, and the anus of one who passes wind [upon him].
One who seizes him by the hair should have both hands cut off without hesitation; likewise for seizing him by the feet, the beard, the neck, or the testicles.

"One who seeks a shared seat" (*sahāsanam abhiprepsuḥ*) means one who desires to sit on the same seat. According to the statement of Viṣṇu: "One who sits on the same seat shall be branded on the hip and banished. "Dāḍhikā" refers to the beard. [492] Gautama [12.5] states: "One who seeks equality in respect to seat, bed, speech, or the road shall be fined.
Following the phrase "of a Śūdra," Āpastamba [2.27.15] says: "For one who seeks equality in speech, on the road, on a bed, or on a seat, there is flogging with a rod."
Kātyāyana [786]:
Just as the punishments for verbal abuse have been declared according to the inverse and direct order of castes,
so too shall the punishments be inflicted in the case of physical assault, in their proper sequence.

Viṣṇu [5.73–74]: "In this manner, the punishment prescribed for each of many who strike has been stated; however, for those standing nearby who do not run to assist one crying out, as well as for those who look on with indifference, it shall be double. Yājñavalkya [2.221]:
"But for many who strike a single person, the fine is double that which was prescribed."
That which was taken away during a quarrel must be restored, and a fine double that amount shall be imposed.
Kātyāyana [788]:

Those against whom verbal censure or physical assault has been prescribed for their offenses shall be made to restore what was taken or destroyed; however, those who possess no wealth shall be purified by means of labor.
By "to be purified" through labor, the meaning is that his wealth must be made whole again. Bṛhaspati [21.15]:
"In the case of crushing a limb, as well as in breaking or cutting [it]," [the same applies].
He shall be made to pay the expenses of the undertaking and whatever was done for the sake of the quarrel.
Yājñavalkya [2.222]:
He who causes pain shall be made to pay the expenses incurred for its removal,
as well as the fine prescribed for that particular quarrel.
Manu [8.287]: "In cases of crushing a limb, as well as in the case of life or blood,
the offender shall be made to pay the expenses of recovery, or else the full penalty."

"In the case of injury to the limbs" means in the case of injury to the limbs such as the hands and feet. "And in the case of injury to the vital breath and blood": when such injury has occurred, he must be made to pay the "expenses of recovery"—that is, whatever expenditure is incurred for food, medicine, and so forth during the period required to become capable of rising again. Now, if he does not wish to pay those expenses, then the meaning is that he must be made to pay both the expenses of recovery and the fine as a single penalty. —Kātyāyana [787].
But when there is destruction of the body or the senses,
the wise should impose a fine and likewise provide for his satisfaction and his recovery.
He shall also pay for the expenses of treatment until the wound is healed.
Viṣṇu [5.75–76]: "And all those who cause injury to a person shall pay the expenses arising from that [injury]; as shall those who cause injury to domestic animals. Manu [8.299–300]:
"A wife, a son, a slave, a pupil, and a uterine brother..."
Those who have committed an offense should be beaten with a rope or a split bamboo cane.
But one must strike on the back of the body and never on the head;
for striking otherwise than this, one incurs the guilt of a thief.
Yama says: A wife, a son, a male slave, a female slave, and a pupil as the fifth—
when they have committed an offense, these may be struck with a rope or a split bamboo cane.
One must strike below [the navel], and never at the head;
however, one who acts otherwise deserves the punishment as previously stated.
Regarding the term "celibate student" (*brahmacārī*), Nārada [8.13–14] states:
"If he does not comply after being instructed by his teacher,
he should be disciplined without causing physical injury, using either a thin rope or a split bamboo cane."
One should not strike him excessively, nor on the head or the chest;
having instructed him and inspired confidence, he is as praiseworthy as a teacher to the king.

‘Without corporal punishment’ means without beating. Gautama [2.49–51] states: “The correction of a pupil is to be done without beating; if that is impossible, with a thin rope or a split bamboo cane. One who strikes him with anything else shall be punished by the king. Regarding obedience toward the pupil, Āpastamba [1.8.29] says: “And one should constantly reprove him for his offenses. Threatening, fasting, sprinkling with water, and exclusion from sight are the punishments, applied according to the gravity of the fault, until he desists.”
The meaning is that the infliction of punishment must be commensurate with the offense and continue until the cessation of the offense. Nārada [18.32]:
"In the case of an offense committed by a son, neither the father nor the horse nor the dog shall be subject to punishment."
Nor [is it stolen] by a monkey, unless its owner has sent it for that very purpose.
Yājñavalkya [2.300]: A master who is capable, yet fails to restrain fanged or horned animals, shall pay the first *sāhasa* fine; likewise, if he has been called out for help, he shall pay double.
"Vikruṣṭe" means when a cry has been repeatedly raised, such as "Move away your horned beast! Bṛhaspati [21.16–17] states:
"But he who is beaten in a secluded place, or who may have been killed by an invisible assailant..."
Indeed, that [offender] is to be identified either through inference or by means of an oath.
In a house or in a forest, at night, where [the victim] was struck,
or wherever blood may be seen— there one should not question witnesses.
"By one who is invisible" means by a small pot that is not being seen.
[496] Nārada and Bṛhaspati [Nā. 4.176; Bṛ. 21.18]:
"Someone, having made a mark upon himself, might attack another out of malice."
In that regard, an examination based on the reason, the meaning, and the capacity for comprehension is appropriate.
Yājñavalkya [2.212]: A legal case involving a person killed without witnesses must be investigated by means of physical marks, circumstantial reasoning, or traditional testimony,
out of fear that false evidence might be fabricated.
Kātyāyana [779]:
If one does not perceive the grounds for physical assault through reasons and other such means,
then that case being unestablished by witnesses, one should employ divine proof (*divya*) therein.
Now, regarding the section on verbal and physical assault,
Nārada says: "The rule for both of these has been stated to be fivefold."
In that case, both purification and the liability to punishment are connected accordingly.
When harshness arises from fury between two agitated parties,
he who forgives is honored, while he who transgresses incurs the penalty.
If no distinction were seen between those two who are simultaneously engaged, being both obscured by the fault of harshness, then discipline would apply equally to both.
Furthermore, he who persists in the same manner against two parties who have both committed an offense incurs the punishment for both of them, whether he was the first or the second.
He who first insults another will certainly incur the fault;
he who does so afterwards is also a wrongdoer, yet the discipline for the former is more severe.
"Equal for both who have committed the offense" means that they act equally regarding harshness; thus says Kātyāyana:
"That man who strikes with a terrifying weapon..."
Whether he was previously oppressed or not, he is declared to be subject to punishment.
Bṛhaspati [21.19, 5]:
A man who reviles in return when he has been reviled, or strikes back when he has been struck,
or even kills an assailant, shall not be considered guilty.
If a base person should insult a virtuous man with harsh words and the like, it is that very person whom the king should strike; he must not seek out the victim.
"He himself" means he who is superior. "Beating him"—that is, inflicting a beating upon that low-born person—he "need not be sought out for punishment by the king"; this is the meaning.
Regarding dog-cookers, animals, Cāṇḍālas, prostitutes, and those who live like herons...
And toward elephant-drivers, outcasts, slaves, and those who transgress against their gurus and teachers.
When a transgression of the established rule occurs, immediate killing itself is the prescribed punishment;
and the wise say that there is no fault in such severity of punishment.
For if these [ministers] should transgress against a virtuous person among men, that very person should administer the discipline; the king does not share in the responsibility for that discipline.
For these are the stains of men, and their wealth is of the nature of stain;
the king should have them executed, but he should not punish them with a fine of money.
"Sadyoghātaḥ" means immediate striking. Bṛhaspati [21.20]:
"Those born in the inverse order (pratiloma), as well as the lowest castes, are remembered as the impurities of men."
One who has committed an offense against a Brahmin should not be executed, nor should a fine ever be imposed upon him.
Kātyāyana [783]: For untouchables, rogues, slaves, Mlecchas, evildoers, and those born of inverse unions (prātilomya), beating is the punishment; there is no fine for their offenses.
Yājñavalkya [2.225–26]:
In the case of causing pain, drawing blood, or likewise cutting off a limb or a member of small animals,
the fine shall be double two paṇas (four paṇas) respectively.
In the case of cutting off the male organ or killing [the animal], the middle amercement shall be imposed, as well as its value;
for these great animals, the fine in these instances is double.
In this context, ‘branch’ refers to the horns and so forth; ‘limb’ refers to the feet and so forth. ‘Double’ means that the fine shall be doubled in successive order, beginning from two paṇas.
Viṣṇu [5.119], following the recurring phrase “the fine shall be one hundred kārṣāpaṇas,” states: “One who destroys the virility of animals.”

Furthermore, Viṣṇu [5.48–54] states: "A killer of elephants, horses, camels, or cows shall have one hand and one foot amputated; so too a seller of forbidden meat (vimāṃsa). A killer of domestic animals shall be fined one hundred kārṣāpaṇas and must pay the value of that animal to its owner. A killer of wild animals shall be fined fifty kārṣāpaṇas; a killer of birds or fish, ten kārṣāpaṇas; and a destroyer of insects, one kārṣāpaṇa. "Forbidden meat" (vimāṃsa) refers to the flesh of dogs, jackals, and the like. Kātyāyana [790] says:
For the killing of wild animals or birds, the fine is three paṇas; for the killing of snakes, cats, mongooses, dogs, or pigs, it is twelve paṇas for men.
Manu:
"For driving a cow, a heifer, a deity’s animal, a steer, or likewise a bull, one shall incur the first amercement; for killing [any of these], the highest."
Regarding the management of dogs and bulls, Bṛhaspati states [21.21]:
"He who yokes animals that are exhausted, afflicted by hunger, or thirsty at an improper time shall be made to perform the expiation for killing a cow, or shall be made to pay the first fine."
Kātyāyana [789]: A man who yokes animals such as donkeys, cows, buffaloes, or camels when they are exhausted, afflicted by thirst, or hungry, or at an improper time, shall incur the first amercement.
Manu [8.290–92]: They say there are ten exemptions for the vehicle, the driver, and the owner of the vehicle; in other cases, punishment is prescribed.
When the nose-rope is severed, when the yoke is broken, when the vehicle turns sideways or faces backward,
and likewise when there is a breakage of the axle or the wheels of the vehicle.
Manu has declared that there is no punishment for the breaking of a yoke, nor likewise for the snapping of a thong or a rein, nor for a cry of "Get away! uttered while being startled.
‘Yantuḥ’ means of the charioteer. ‘Ativartanāni’ refers to those with broken noses and so forth, based on the etymological derivation that they proceed by transgressing the staff (of control).
Yājñavalkya [2.298]:
“There is no fault regarding a four-footed animal if one says, ‘Go away.’”
Likewise, it is made with wood, clods of earth, bricks, stones, or by means of a pair of arms.

The meaning is this: the fault characterized by deserving punishment for injuring another—which arises from using wood, clods of earth, stones, or one's arms for the purpose of practice—does not apply to one who speaks "Go away" at the very outset.
Likewise [2.299]:
"By means of a vehicle with its nose-rope cut, or likewise one with a broken yoke and so forth..."
Furthermore, when those who are retreating are killed, the master does not incur guilt.
Manu [8.293–98]: "If a vehicle turns off course due to the negligence of the driver, the owner shall be liable for the damage; the fine in such a case is two hundred panas."
The driver must be trustworthy; an untrustworthy driver deserves punishment.
If the driver is untrustworthy, all those seated in the vehicle shall each be fined one hundred [paṇas].
But if, being obstructed on the road by cattle or by a chariot,
he should cause the death of a living being, his punishment shall be without hesitation.
In the case of killing a human being, the guilt is immediate and equal to that of a thief;
for large living beings such as cows, elephants, camels, horses, and the like, it is half [the guilt].
For the killing of small animals, the fine shall be two hundred;
but for auspicious beasts and birds, the punishment shall be fifty.
For donkeys, goats, and sheep, the fine shall be five māṣakas;
however, the fine for killing a dog or a pig shall be one māṣaka.

The *prājaka* is the driver, such as a charioteer and the like. An *āpta* in this context is one who is skilled. Regarding the phrase "but if he": even if that driver has his path obstructed by cattle or other animals, if he causes them to be killed by driving the chariot forward, then the meaning is that he shall be punished for that act without hesitation. Kātyāyana [792] states:
"In the case of killing living beings, however, he should be made to pay compensation equal to their value."
"Or he should be made to pay its equivalent value," so Manu declared.
Manu [8.285]: "In the case of injury to any of the forest trees, a fine shall be imposed in proportion to their utility; this is the settled rule."
Yājñavalkya [2.227–29]:
For the cutting of branches, trunks, or joints of trees that put forth shoots,
and for trees that provide livelihood, the fines are double those prescribed for twenty [trees].
In the vicinity of a shrine, a cemetery, a boundary, a sacred site, or a temple, the fine for cutting down trees that have grown there is doubled; the same applies to a tree renowned for its fame.
For cutting bushes, clusters, shrubs, creepers, spreading plants, medicinal herbs,
or climbing vines in the places previously mentioned, the fine shall be half of that prescribed for the first offense.

‘Prarohi-śākhinām’ refers to trees such as the *vaṭa* (banyan) from which branches grow. ‘Skandhaḥ’ is that part from which the branches originate. ‘Upajīvyadrumāṇām’ refers to fruit-bearing trees such as the mango. Regarding the phrase ‘viṃśater dviguṇā damāḥ’: for cutting branches, cutting the trunk, and cutting down the tree with its roots, the meaning is that starting from a fine of twenty *paṇas*, each subsequent punishment is double the preceding one, respectively. ‘Gumāḥ’ are plants such as the *mālatī*. ‘Gucchāḥ’ are those in the form of clusters, such as the *kuraṇṭaka*. ‘Kṣupāḥ’ are shrubs such as the *karavīra*. ‘Latāḥ’ are creepers such as the grapevine (*drākṣā*). ‘Pratānāḥ’ are those that grow straight without lateral shoots, such as the *sārivā*. ‘Oṣadhayaḥ’ are plants that end with the ripening of their fruit, such as rice (*śāli*). ‘Vīrudhaḥ’ are those that sprout in various ways even when cut, such as the *guḍūcī*.

In the continuation of the term *daṇḍa* (punishment), Viṣṇu [5.65–69] states: "One who cuts down a tree that bears fruit shall pay the highest amercement; one who cuts down a tree that bears flowers, the middle amercement; one who cuts down a creeper, shrub, or climbing vine, one *kārṣāpaṇa*; and one who cuts grass, one [kārṣāpaṇa]. And all [those offenders] shall give the produce thereof to its owners. The word "shall give" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

Vasiṣṭha [19.11–13] says: "One should not harm trees that bear fruit or flowers; however, one may cut them for the purpose of cultivation and for the sake of domestic life. Thus ends the section on assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*).
[505] 70— Now, regarding theft, Manu says [8.301–02]:
Thus has the determination of punishment for assault been declared in its entirety;
now I shall proclaim the rule for the determination of punishment regarding theft.
An act committed by force, provided it involves some connection [to the owner], is *sāhasa* (violence);
whereas that which is done without such connection and where one denies having committed it after the theft is *steya* (theft).
"Anvayavat" means in the presence of the guardian official. "Prasabham" means by force; the meaning is that the act is committed along with its consequences. Kātyāyana [796]:
"That which is an appropriation accompanied by its consequences, and that which is done by force..."
In such a case, it would indeed constitute violence; what has been described as theft is actually a denial [of ownership].
Nārada states that there is an interval between these two; indeed, theft (steya) is a specific variety of that very same [sāhasa], and its distinction is stated therein:
"Sāhasa is the taking by force, while theft is the taking by fraud. [506]
That too is declared by the wise to be threefold, depending on the substances,
through the extraction of inferior, middling, and superior materials.
Earthenware vessels, seats, beds, bones, wood, skins, grass, and the like; pulses, prepared food, and anything that is not a base substance—these are declared to be [acceptable] goods.
Clothing, with the exception of silk; likewise cattle, with the exception of cows;
metal, with the exception of gold; liquor; and even rice and barley.
Gold, jewels, silk garments, women, men, elephants, and horses—
these should be known as the most excellent property belonging to gods, Brahmins, and kings.
The wise declare that theft consists in the removal of these [goods] by deceiving them through various means while they are asleep, intoxicated, or heedless.

[507] ‘Ādhi’ means pain; that which is committed by transgressing it is ‘sāhasa’. However, when it is done through deception, it is theft (*caurya*). Thus ends the section on theft (70). (ka) Now, the thieves:
In this regard, Manu [9.256] says: "The king, whose eyes are his spies, should know that there are two kinds of thieves who steal the property of others: those who are open and those who are secret."
Vyāsa says:
Thieves are recorded as being of two kinds—those who act openly and those who act in secret.
They are to be identified by their clear marks, by spies, and by those who know the ways of thieves.
Bṛhaspati [22.1–3]:
Thieves are recorded as being of two kinds: those who act openly and those who act in secret.
Through their intelligence, skill, and guile, they are divided into a thousand varieties.
Local merchants, physicians, gamblers, those who extort immediate bribes, deceivers,
those who claim to know the omens of fate, fortune-tellers, craftsmen, and counterfeiters;
Those who do not perform their duties, those who remain indifferent, false witnesses, open thieves, and those who live by deception— these indeed are the manifest robbers.
Nārada [21.2–3]:
In that regard, there are open swindlers who rely on false measures and scales;
there are those who take bribes, those who use fraudulent means, swindlers, and courtesans.
Those who act as proxies for others, those who subsist on the practice of prescribing auspicious rites,
and others such as these are to be known as thieves who openly operate upon the earth.
Vyāsa says: Those who reside in open markets and subsist on various kinds of merchandise,
as well as others such as physicians and the like, are to be known as open cheats.
An *āpaṇa* is one who lives by trade. Manu [9.258–60]:
Bribe-takers, those who use fraudulent means, gamblers, and deceivers likewise...
And those who were auspicious in their appearance and conduct, together with the fortune-tellers, were all favorable.
Likewise, high officials who act improperly, physicians,
those skilled in the practice of arts and crafts, and clever courtesans [should be avoided].
One should recognize such individuals as manifest thorns in the world,
as well as others who move in secret— ignoble men wearing the outward marks of the noble.
Likewise [9.257]:
"Those such as thieves and forest-dwellers who act as secret deceivers are to be known [as such].
Nārada [Nāradasmṛti, Prakīrṇaka, 56].
But those men who, having attacked, rob people while they are asleep, intoxicated, or heedless— whether they reside outside or within— are to be known as unmanifest thieves.
Bṛhaspati [22.4]: Those who break into houses, those who rob travelers, those who steal bipeds and quadrupeds,
those who lift up [goods from storage], and those who steal crops— these should be known as secret thieves.
Vyāsa says: Those who move about at night equipped with the means of their craft, remaining unobserved and whose specific identities are unknown, should be known as "concealed deceivers."

The one who carries off by force, the breaker of locks, the plunderer of travelers, the cutter of knots, the stealer of women, men, or horses, and the thief— thus the thief is remembered as being of nine kinds.

"Equipped with the instruments for theft" means being provided with tools such as shovels, weapons, and so forth. "Whose specific [entry] is unknown" means whose mode of entry is not recognized. Regarding the term "one who picks up" (*utkṣepaka*): he is called one who steals by deceiving the sight of someone who is right before him and not paying attention, by picking up [the object].
After the discussion on thieves, Nārada says:
"But having identified them through skillful spies who know their modus operandi..."
But having ascertained [the facts], he should seize [the offender] by means of men secretly dispatched.
And regarding thieves, Manu [9.261–62] says:
"Having identified them through secret conduct and by means of spies who know their deeds and are stationed in various disguises, he should incite them and bring them under his control."

Having publicly proclaimed their fault according to the truth in relation to each of their respective duties, the king should duly administer punishment based on the gravity of the offense and the essential nature of the act.
Bṛhaspati [22.5]:
Those identified by royal officers through their association, physical signs,
or the stolen goods themselves shall be compelled to restore what was taken and shall be punished with penalties prescribed by the scriptures.
Manu says: Indeed, without punishment, it is impossible to effect the restraint of justice for thieves of evil intent who move about secretly upon the earth.
A king should exert the utmost effort in the suppression of thieves;
through the suppression of thieves, his fame and his kingdom increase.
For that king who is a giver of fearlessness is always worthy of worship;
indeed, his sacrificial session (satra) is ever-increasing, with the gift of fearlessness as its sacrificial fee.
Or, if one's kingdom is fearless and relies upon the strength of its arms,
it will increase constantly like a tree being watered.
Āpastamba [2.25.15]: "The king is a creator of security for him in whose realm—whether in a village or in the forest—there is no fear of thieves. Manu [7.143]:
"From whose kingdom the subjects are carried off by bandits while crying out..."

Regarding the passage beginning with "with equals, the unequal," etc.: one who deals with "equals"—that is, those who pay equal prices—by giving superior or inferior goods that are unequal, incurs the first *sāhasa* (fine). Nārada [21.34]:
"With whichever limb a thief acts against men, that very limb of his shall be cut off; such is the ordinance of Manu."
Bṛhaspati [22.25]: Whether it be grass, or wood, or a flower, or a fruit—
one who takes any of these without having asked permission deserves the amputation of the hand.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "A Brāhmaṇa who forcibly or secretly steals from another Brāhmaṇa fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial wood, firewood, grass, *ulapa* reeds, flowers, fruits, or roots, shall suffer the amputation of his hand. For one who steals *kuśa* grass, water-pots, nets, or other such articles, there shall be the amputation of a limb in the presence of witnesses. When it is known that this Brāhmaṇa is a criminal, though not in the presence of witnesses, he shall be made to ride upon a donkey. For others [who steal these items], there shall be shaving of the head and riding upon a donkey."

Regarding the section on theft, Gautama [12.43–45] states: "There is no corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa. [The penalties are] deprivation of his occupation, public proclamation of the crime, banishment, and branding. If he does not adopt a [new] mode of life, he must perform penance."

"Corporal" (*śārīra*) punishment consists of such things as beating or the amputation of limbs. If one asks, "What then is [the nature of] punishment? he says: "The deprivation of activity," and so forth. "Deprivation of activity" (*karmaviyoga*) means the non-commencement of any action whatsoever with that person. "Public proclamation" (*vikhyāpana*) is wandering about with a drum (*ḍiṇḍimaka*) for the purpose of making known his character as a thief. "Banishment" (*vivāsana*) is expulsion from the country. "Branding" (*aṅkakaraṇa*) is marking him with the foot of a dog. Regarding the phrase "he is subject to penance if there is no livelihood": the meaning is that if he commits theft because there is no other way to subsist, then he is subject only to penance (*prāyaścitta*) and not to punishment.

Āpastamba [2.27.16–17]: "In the case of killing a person, theft, or seizing land, one who has taken what belongs to another should be put to death; and for a Brāhmaṇa in these cases, there shall be the blinding of the eyes. "'His own' refers to his property. Bṛhaspati [22.26]: [text follows]"
One who has committed theft, even if he possesses good conduct and Vedic study, suffers for a long time in bondage;
he must be made to restore that wealth to its owner and undergo penance.
Yājñavalkya [2.270]:
Having compelled the thief to restore what was stolen, the king shall have him executed by various means of death;
however, having branded a Brāhmaṇa, he shall banish him from his own kingdom.
Viṣṇu [5.89–90]: "All thieves, having been caught, must be made to restore the property to the owner; thereafter, the prescribed punishment shall be inflicted upon them. Nārada [21.6]:
"But thieves who have not been caught and have no means of identification should not be executed by the king."
The king should swiftly execute those caught in the act with their stolen goods and their implements.
‘Hoḍha’ refers to the signs of a thief, such as stolen goods and the like.
‘Vṛddha’:
because their wealth is acquired through unjust means, their riches are of a defiled nature.
Therefore, the king should have them executed; he should not punish them with a monetary fine.
Kātyāyana [823–26]: The followers of Manu declare that those caught in adultery (sahoḍha) should be banished immediately;
for the followers of Gautama, that is undesirable, as it is censured as being equivalent to the taking of life.
Whether he was caught in the act or not,
once his violent deed has been established by evidence, he shall be seized, the crime announced, and deprived of all his property.
But those who are secured by iron chains, though receiving meager rations, yet endowed with strength, shall perform services for the king until death; so says Kauśika.
When property has been seized from a foreign land by a foreigner, the king,
having recovered that property, should release him without punishment.

‘*Tattvāgamitasāhasaḥ*’ means one for whom the act of violence has been made known according to its true nature. ‘*Ayaḥsandānaguptāḥ*’ means those bound with iron chains. The construction is as follows: those who are ‘*balānvitāḥ*’ (endowed with strength), being bound in chains and receiving meager food, shall perform the king’s labor for the duration of their lives. Vasiṣṭha [19.38–39] states: “A thief does not incur guilt by entering [the house]; likewise one who carries weapons, one who was caught in the act (*sahoḍha*), and one who is covered in wounds—though according to some, these are exceptions.”

The meaning of this is: one does not become a thief merely by entering; rather, without the cause of bearing a weapon, one becomes tainted as a "co-seized" thief (*sahoḍha*) and one who has received a wound only if he is a bearer of a weapon. [543] 70 — (gha) Now, the search for thieves.
In this regard, Nārada says:

"Theft is established by the inclusion of the term *sahoḍha* (one caught with the stolen goods), or by enjoyment when there is no such possession; furthermore, it is established by the fact that the person is of bad character, and likewise by the absence of income and expenditure."
One should investigate those caught with stolen goods as potential thieves through various stratagems and tests, so that they may speak the truth.
Having restrained them, they should be questioned regarding their country, village, direction, name, caste, residence, lodging, the task they have accomplished, and their accomplices.
Because of differences in complexion, voice, and appearance; because of the report being given with uncertainty;
because of the residence being seen at an improper place and time; and because of the purification [of the accused].

[One should be followed] even by slight traces, not merely by the stolen goods (*hoḍha*) alone. (544) ‘*Hoḍhaḥ*’ means the plundered object. ‘By means of consumption (*upabhogataḥ*)’: when there are no stolen goods, theft is to be known through the observation of the consumption of items such as camphor, which cannot otherwise be obtained except through the acquisition of stolen property. ‘From association with the wicked (*asajjanaikārthyāt*)’: because of engaging in the same activities as those who are wicked—those addicted to gambling, drinking liquor, and so forth. ‘By various stratagems (*upādhibhiḥ citrābhiḥ*’): by means of diverse methods and various expedients.
Yājñavalkya [2.226–28]:
A thief is apprehended by pursuers either through stolen property or by a footprint;
likewise, one who has committed a prior offense and one who resides in an impure dwelling.
Others also should be apprehended with suspicion on account of their denial of name, caste, and so forth,
as well as those addicted to gambling, women, and liquor, and those whose mouths and voices appear parched and dry.

Those who inquire about the property and houses of others while moving about in secret, those who have no income yet have many expenditures, and those who sell goods that have been lost— these are thieves.

"By the apprehenders, the thief is seized. This means that once the thief has been identified by the apprehenders as "this is the thief," he is to be captured. "By the footprint" means by following the footprints of the thief and others, starting from the place where [the theft] was destroyed. "One whose dwelling is impure" refers to one whose place of residence is unknown. "Sellers of lost property" refers to those who sell broken items such as earrings and the like. Nārada [17.22–26]: When cows and other animals have gone astray, or when goods have been damaged...
Those who know [the matter] should investigate it from the very root, following the trail step by step.
In a village, a cow-pen, or a pasture, wherever that footprint falls, it must be carried by him; unless he should carry it elsewhere.
If the foot becomes paralyzed or broken due to uneven ground near a village,
one should cause it to fall toward whichever village or cow-pen is nearest.

In the same way, where there are two [types of] sounds, that which is characterized by thieves, impure people, those corrupted by prior offenses, or those associated with evil-minded persons is considered base.
The Dasyus do not emerge from the intermediate space, nor from heaven, nor from the ocean, nor from anywhere else; therefore, one should conceive of them in this way.
The Caṇḍālas, executioners, and others should conduct their search within the villages,
while those who roam outside and wander abroad should conduct it outside.
"In the same *adhvan*," meaning on the same path; "of two" villages; "abounding in thieves" means full of robbers. Manu [9.234–36]:
"Assembly halls, water-stations, pastry shops, brothels, and taverns or food-sellers..."
Crossroads, sacred trees, assemblies, and spectacles.
Dilapidated gardens, forests, the workshops of artisans,
as well as empty houses, groves, and pleasure parks.
The king should cause such types of dwellings to be patrolled by both stationary and mobile military units, as well as by spies, for the purpose of suppressing thieves.

‘Apūpaśālā’ means a bakery. ‘Veśaḥ’ means a brothel. ‘Kārukāveśanāni’ means workshops for artisans. ‘Gulmaiḥ’ means by groups of infantry. ‘Sthāvarajaṅgamaiḥ’ means those stationed in one place and those on patrol. Nārada says:
“He should employ various spies who are intent on apprehending thieves.”
Likewise, others who are intent upon it, trustworthy, and speakers of varied [doctrines] [should be examined].
For spies, as well as former thieves, should incite those criminals by means of great gifts of food and drink, and by showing them social gatherings and festivals.
Likewise, under the pretext of valor, they should bring about a meeting with them at a place where those enemies cannot approach even by means of dispatched spies.
They too, along with their sons, kinsmen, and relatives, should be gathered;
and those thieves whom one might seize there, having beaten and bound them, [should be dealt with].
Having made a proclamation everywhere, he should execute them by various methods of death;
for even those who are not thieves are seen in the company of thieves.
But the king should not touch them with punishment without due consideration. Kātyāyana [811]:
That which has fallen from another's hand and been picked up on the ground unintentionally...
Or, if it has been surrounded by a thief, one should carefully examine the stolen property.
Nārada says: If there should be suspicion against a man who follows the way of bandits, or even against a thief,
and if he should be touched by even a slight [taint], then an oath must be administered.
‘By a slight indication’ means by a trace of reasoning, such as the condition of his mouth or ears.
Yājñavalkya [2.269]: “If one who has been apprehended on suspicion of theft does not purify himself...”
Having caused the stolen property to be restored, he shall punish [the thief] with the punishment prescribed for a thief.

Kātyāyana [821]: When property that was not stolen by thieves has been recovered by those intent on searching for the thieves, they shall receive it; in that case, the king should cause double the value to be paid to them.
[548] 70 — (ṅa) Now, the extension of the rules regarding theft;
therein, Manu [9.271, 278]:
Furthermore, whoever in the villages provide food for thieves or give them space to store their goods— all of those he shall cause to be executed.
The lord should punish like thieves those who provide fire, food, weapons, or shelter, as well as those who facilitate the theft.
‘Of the stolen’: of the property that has been taken away.
Yājñavalkya [2.276]: Food, shelter, fire, water, sacred mantras, and the expenses for implements...
And having committed [theft], whether he be a thief or a killer, if he is caught in the act, the highest fine shall be imposed.

‘Food’ means sustenance. ‘Shelter’ means a place of residence. ‘Fire’ is for the purpose of dispelling cold and so forth. ‘Water’ is for one who is thirsty. ‘Instruction’ means teaching the methods of theft. ‘Equipment’ means the tools for committing theft. ‘Expenditure’ refers to provisions for travel when going to another country for the purpose of plundering.
Nārada [17.19; 21.14]: “Those who provide food and shelter to thieves who have been apprehended...”
And those who, though capable, remain indifferent, they too partake in that fault.
All those who conceal them are declared to be equally punishable.
Kātyāyana [827] states: Those who provide food for thieves, as well as those who supply fire and water, [are likewise liable].
As well as the buyers of goods and their very acceptance [of them].
For these are remembered as those who wield equal punishment, as well as those who conceal them.
In the context of the phrase "he shall kill," Viṣṇu (5.16–17) states: "[The king shall punish] those who forcibly provide shelter or food to thieves, except when the king is incapable [of doing so].
Manu (8.340; 9.272, 274) states: "A Brāhmaṇa who shall receive wealth from the hand of one who takes what is not given..."
Even by officiating at sacrifices or teaching, he is exactly like a thief.

In the various kingdoms, he should certainly treat provincial governors and vassals who have been incited [to rebellion] as if they were disciples turned into thieves when they remain neutral during times of calamity.

Those who do not run to the aid of others to the best of their ability when a village is being plundered, a water-tank is being destroyed, or when they witness a robbery on the road, shall be banished along with their belongings.

‘Of one who takes what is not given’ refers to a thief. Regarding the phrase “in the kingdom” and so forth—the meaning is that when harm is being inflicted upon the subjects by thieves and others, the king should punish those officials of the state and village-dwellers who remain indifferent or look on, treating them as if they were thieves themselves. Medhātithi explains that ‘destruction of profit’ (hilābhaṅga) means ‘the destruction of crops grown in another’s field. ‘Upon seeing a theft and so forth’ means upon seeing stolen property. [551] Now follows the specific classification of theft according to the social classes (varṇa).
Regarding this, Manu states (8.337–38):
"The guilt for theft incurred by a Śūdra is eightfold;
that of a Vaiśya is sixteenfold, and that of a Kṣatriya is thirty-twofold."
For a Brahmin, it may be sixty-four, or even one hundred,
or double that sixty-four, for one who hates the faults and virtues of those [others].

Kātyāyana [485]: By whatever penalty a Śūdra incurs according to dharma for a particular offense, that same penalty shall be doubled for a Vaiśya, tripled for a Kṣatriya, and quadrupled for a Brāhmaṇa.

70 — (c) Now, regarding the restitution of stolen property when the thief cannot be apprehended, Āpastamba [2.26.4–8] states: “In villages and cities, the king should appoint noble, pure, and truthful men for the protection of the subjects. Their attendants should likewise possess those same qualities. A city must be protected from thieves for a radius of one *yojana*, and a village for a *krośa*. Whatever is lost therein shall be made good by them. Kātyāyana and Nārada [Kā. 813; Nā. 21.18] state:

If property has been stolen from houses, the king should compel the thieves' catchers to pay restitution; however, if the thief is not apprehended, he should make the guards or the local district officials pay.
Yājñavalkya [2.271–72]:
If cattle are killed or stolen, the guilt falls upon the village headman if they have not yet left the village;
but on the way, it falls upon the superintendent of the pasture-lands, and in a place without such lands, upon the one who captures the thieves.
A village shall grant land within its own boundaries, or wherever it happens to go;
or else, five villages from the cultivated area outside, or even ten villages.

‘Of the thief-catcher’ means of one appointed for the protection against thieves. ‘In a non-pasture’ (avītake) means in a field or similar place other than a pasture. ‘Outside of the cultivated area’ (bahiḥ kṛṣṭāt) means elsewhere than the area under cultivation; whatever has been stolen there, the five villages combined shall pay for it. Depending on proximity, there is an alternative that the ten villages shall pay. Nārada [21.16–17]:
“If a theft occurs within the range of someone’s watch, he must diligently pursue the thief.”
He must be made to pay for the loss, unless the track [of the stolen goods] has been lost.
But if it has not fallen elsewhere after leaving this [boundary],
one should cause the neighbors, the guardians of the road, and the guardians of the quarters to pay it.
[553] Kātyāyana [814]: Property stolen within a village boundary shall be made to be restored by the village headman;
in a pasture (*vivīta*), it must be given by the owner; and in a non-pasture (*avivītaka*), by the thief-catcher.

Viṣṇu [3.66–67]: “Having recovered property stolen by thieves, he shall restore it all to all the social classes (varṇas). If he has not recovered it, he shall restore it from his own treasury. Kātyāyana [815]:
Whatever has been stolen in one’s own country, that must be restored by the king.
The king himself should take that which was lost and subsequently recovered after being sought.
Nārada and Kātyāyana [Nā. 21.21; Kā. 816]:
One should restore the exact form of an object stolen by thieves with due effort;
in its absence, however, its value shall be paid, otherwise the king becomes a sinner.
Kātyāyana [817]: But if the thief has been caught and yet the stolen property is not recovered from him,
he should either pay that value himself or cause the thief to be made to pay it as desired.
Vṛddha-Manu says:
"If, while those being made to pay are in doubt as to whether the theft actually occurred,
the victim is made to swear an oath, or he may clear himself through his kinsmen."
Since the owner has recovered only a small portion of the property taken away,
he shall receive the remainder from that [stolen] object once the owner has provided proof [of ownership].
Yājñavalkya [2.173–74]:
When property that has been lost or stolen is recovered by customs officials or local guards, the owner shall take it back within half a year; after that, the king shall take it.
One should pay one paṇa for a single-hoofed animal, four or five for a human,
two each for buffaloes, camels, and cows, and one-quarter each for goats and sheep.
In the case of a single-hoofed animal such as a horse that has been lost and recovered, the owner shall pay four *paṇas* to the king for the purpose of its protection.

Gautama [10.35–37] states: “Having found property that was lost and without an owner, they should announce it to the king. After proclaiming it, it should be guarded by the king for one year. After that period, the finder shall receive a fourth part, and the remainder belongs to the king. Manu [8.31–34] says: “Property that has been lost and found should be guarded by the king for three years; after that time, he may take it for himself. He must not allow a man of noble birth who has lost his property to fall into distress. If a man of low birth recovers the property of a high-born person, the king should cause him to be branded with a dog’s foot and banished. If a man of low birth recovers the property of a Brahmin, he should be put to death. If a man of high birth recovers the property of a low-born person, he should restore it to the owner or surrender it to the king.”
He who says, "This is mine," shall be questioned according to the rule;
having verified the form, number, and other details, the owner deserves that property.
But one who does not truly report the place, time,
color, appearance, and size of the lost item deserves a fine equal to its value.
Then, remembering the duty of the virtuous, the king should take a sixth, a tenth, or even a twelfth part of property lost and then found.
Property that has been lost and found shall remain under the supervision of appointed officials;
any thieves the king may catch therein, he shall cause to be executed by means of an elephant.
‘Ibhena’ means by an elephant.

Āpastamba [2.28.8–10] states: “If, through negligence, one brings cattle that were released in the forest back to the village, one should return them to their owners. If this negligence occurs again, one should pen them up once; after that, one need not care for them.
‘Na sūrkṣyet’ means one should not take them back.
Thus ends the section on Theft (steya) in the Vyavahārakāṇḍa of the Kṛtyakalpataru.
[556] 71— Now, Violence (sāhasa).
In that regard, Nārada says:
"Killing a human being, theft, violating another's wife,
and the two kinds of harshness— this is declared to be the fivefold *sāhasa* (violent crime)."
Whatever action is performed impulsively by those arrogant in their strength is called *sāhasa*; here, *saha* is said to mean strength.
Theft is indeed a variety of that [appropriation], for a distinction is observed therein:
seizure by force is *sāhasa*, whereas theft is seizure by means of deception.
Furthermore, that is declared to be threefold— namely, the inferior, the middling, and the superior— and its specific characteristics have been explained separately in the treatises.
The first degree of *sāhasa* (violence) is declared to consist of the breaking, throwing down, or trampling of fruits, roots, water, and other such items that serve as agricultural implements.
[557] For clothing, cattle, food and drink, and household utensils—
by this very same method, the middle amercement is prescribed.
Malice, attacking others with poison, weapons, and the like, violating another's wife, and whatever else is said to endanger life— these constitute the highest degree of violence (uttamasāhasa).
"But *sāhasa* (violence) shall be that act which is committed forcibly against one who is related.
Bṛhaspati [23.3; 8–8??]: [text fragment].
That [self-restraint] is proclaimed to be threefold—inferior, middling, and superior.
Among these, self-restraint with regard to material things is the first; it is inferior, middling, and superior.
One who destroys or steals the implements of a field, an embankment, or flowers, roots, and fruits, shall be fined one hundred panas or more, according to the circumstances.
One who destroys livestock, clothing, food, drink,
or household utensils shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred panas and more, like a thief.
For women, men, gold, gems, the property of gods or Brahmins,
silk, and other such superior articles, the fine shall be equal to their value.
Or rather, kings should determine double the fine in consideration of the status of the person;
and the killer should be executed in order to prevent a recurrence of such incidents.
Regarding the persistence in acts of violence, Nārada states (17.7–8):
"The punishment for the first offender shall depend on the nature of the act and be at least one hundred [paṇas];
for the second, it is seen by those learned in the scriptures to be at least five hundred."
Killing, confiscation of all property, banishment from the city, branding,
and the amputation of limbs— this is declared to be the punishment of the highest fine (uttama-sāhasa).
Yājñavalkya [2.230, 223]:
"Theft by force of common property is declared to be *sāhasa* (violence).
The fine for that is double its value; and if there is denial, it is fourfold."
In cases of striking, piercing, cutting, or causing a wall to collapse,
one shall be made to pay fifteen, twenty, or thirty paṇas, as well as the cost of the damage.
“Common property” (*sāmānya*) refers to an object (*dravya*) belonging to multiple owners. Manu [8.288–89]:
“If one should damage the goods of another, whether intentionally or even unintentionally...”
He should cause satisfaction for that [theft], and he shall be punished by the king with a fine equal to its value.
[559] For articles made of leather or leather-work, as well as those made of wood or clay,
and for flowers, roots, and fruits, the fine shall be five times their value.
Kātyāyana [807]: A man who makes a hundred cuts or similar marks upon goods shall incur the first *sāhasa* fine; he who possesses the goods is declared to be the owner.
Yājñavalkya [2.224]:
One who casts into the house an object that causes pain, or likewise one that is life-threatening,
shall be made to pay sixteen paṇas for the first offense, and for the second, the middle amercement.
‘Causing the arising of suffering’ refers to thorns and the like; ‘taking life’ refers to snakes and the like.

Under the heading "Punishment," Viṣṇu states (5.108–19): "One who breaks the walls or other parts of a house shall pay the middle amercement and shall repair that damage. One who throws a harmful substance into a house shall pay one hundred *paṇas*. So too shall one who denies a common property, one who fails to deliver what has been sent, and one who abandons—without being an outcast—one of his father, son, teacher, patron, or officiating priest; nor should he ever abandon them. Also, one who feeds *śūdras* or renunciants at a rite for the gods or ancestors, one who performs unsuitable work, one who breaks a sealed house, one who administers an oath without authorization, and one who destroys the virility of animals."

Furthermore, Viṣṇu [5.104–05] states: “One who intentionally touches something that should not be touched with those things that are untouchable is to be executed; one who touches a menstruating woman should be flogged with *śiphās*.
Here, “*śiphās*” refers to the roots or fibers of trees.
Yājñavalkya [2.232–37] says:
One who offers an insult or transgresses against the guest-offering (arghya), one who strikes his brother’s wife,
one who fails to deliver a entrusted message, and one who breaks down a house situated by the sea;
For one who commits an injury against neighbors, guild members, and others,
the settled rule is that their fine shall be fifty paṇas.

One who approaches his wife against her will, one who does not run to the aid of someone crying out for help, one who raises a cry for help without cause, and a Cāṇḍāla who touches those of the highest caste; [these are all equal to a killer of a Brahmin].
One who feeds those who have renounced the world from among the Śūdras at rites for the gods or the ancestors,
one who makes an improper oath, and one who performs the duties of an unworthy person— [these are excluded].
One who obstructs the virility of bulls or small animals,
one who denies a common property, and one who causes the destruction of a maidservant’s fetus;
A father, son, sister, brother, husband, wife, teacher, and student—
among these, one who abandons another who has not fallen from their status shall be subject to a fine of one hundred [paṇas].
Manu [8.389]: Neither a mother, nor a father, nor a wife, nor a son deserves to be abandoned.
One who abandons these when they have not fallen from their status shall be compelled by the king to pay six hundred [paṇas].

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “A son should not go between his mother and father; he may follow the mother alone, for she is both the one who bore him and the one who nourished him. A son is not released from his debt to his mother, except through the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice while still living. Thus, a mother is not to be abandoned. The same applies to the father. All virtuous sapindas are likewise not to be abandoned. He who abandons those who have not fallen [from their caste] out of lust shall incur a fine of two hundred [paṇas]. One must not transgress against one’s mother or father, nor against one’s teacher. For the transgression of these three, there shall be amputation of a limb.”

Viṣṇu [5.91–97]: “He who does not give way to those to whom way should be given shall be fined twenty-five kārṣāpaṇas; likewise, he who does not give a seat to one worthy of a seat; he who fails to honor one entitled to prior honor; he who neglects to invite a neighboring Brāhmaṇa; he who, having invited someone, does not provide food; and those who, having accepted an invitation by saying ‘so be it,’ do not eat, shall each be fined one suvarṇamāṣaka. Furthermore, the host shall provide double the amount of food. Manu [8.392–93]:
“The neighbor and the next-door neighbor, when there is a festive occasion involving twenty Brāhmaṇas...”
One who fails to feed two Arhat Brahmins deserves a fine of one māṣa.
If a learned Vedic scholar does not feed another virtuous learned scholar during auspicious rites,
he shall be made to pay double the value of that food and a masha of gold.
Regarding the phrase “in a virtuous [house] with twenty twice-born men” (*kalyāṇe viṃśatidvije*), it refers to a place where twenty twice-born men are eating.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa* (227.8):
“A twice-born man who, having been invited, is currently engaged in receiving gifts...”
But if he goes without a valid reason, he shall be made to pay a fine of eight hundred.
[563] Yājñavalkya [2.263]: A ferryman who collects a land-toll shall be made to pay ten *paṇas*;
likewise, a Brāhmaṇa who fails to invite his neighbors [to a feast].
A *tarika* is one authorized to collect tolls for crossing rivers and the like.

Viṣṇu [5.120–21] states: “In a dispute between a father and a son, the fine for witnesses is ten *paṇas*; but for whoever stands as an intermediary between them, the punishment is the highest amercement. Yājñavalkya [2.239] says:
In a dispute between father and son, the fine for witnesses is three paṇas;
but for anyone who stands as an intermediary between the two, the fine shall be eight hundred [paṇas].

In continuation of the term "punishment" (*daṇḍa*), Viṣṇu states (5.98–103): "Having defiled a Brāhmaṇa with something unfit for consumption, one shall pay sixteen *suvarṇas*; if with something that causes loss of caste, a hundred; if with liquor, he is to be executed. For defiling a Kṣatriya, half of that [fine]; for defiling a Vaiśya, half of that as well; for defiling a Śūdra, the first amercement. Regarding "something unfit for consumption," this refers to excrement and the like. Regarding "something that causes loss of caste," this refers to garlic and other such items unfit for consumption. For a Śūdra, items unfit for consumption include the meat of five-toed animals and so forth. Yājñavalkya (2.296) states:
Having defiled a twice-born man with forbidden food, he shall be fined the highest amercement;
for a Kṣatriya, the middle amercement; for a Vaiśya, the first amercement; and for a Śūdra, half of that.
Manu says:
By feeding twice-born men who are low, middling, or superior with food that is unfit to be eaten or unfit to be drunk,
one should incur fines in the order of low, middling, and high.
The fine for a Śūdra shall be five *paṇas*;
however, those who have swallowed [the coin] themselves must be deprived of their territory by the king.

Viṣṇu [5.173]: “One who eats forbidden food that causes loss of caste shall be banished. Yājñavalkya [2.301, 303]: “One who addresses an adulterer as a ‘thief’ shall be made to pay a fine of five hundred [paṇas].”
Having used wealth for one's livelihood, if one relinquishes it, that very same wealth becomes eightfold.
The punishment for one who sells the limbs of a corpse, for one who strikes his teacher, and likewise for one who mounts the royal vehicle or throne, is the middle amercement.

[565] Speaking of his paramour as a thief out of fear of bringing disgrace upon his own lineage, he conceals the fault of his wife by saying, "This thief, who is her paramour, is escaping. Taking the wealth and abandoning the paramour whom he had been supporting—Manu [9.290, 286] states:
"In all cases of malevolent magic (abhicāra), a fine of two hundred [paṇas] shall be imposed."
And in the case of root-rites performed by those who are untrustworthy, as well as in various types of sorcery.
For the adulteration of unadulterated goods,
as well as for their breaking or the damaging of gems, the punishment is the first amercement.
Likewise [10.96]:
"If one who is low by birth should live by superior occupations out of greed,
the king, having deprived him of his wealth, should banish him immediately."
Yājñavalkya [2.304]:
But for a Śūdra who lives by means of the status of a Brāhmaṇa, the fine is eight hundred [paṇas].
Manu [9.285]: "One who breaks down bridges, flagstaffs, or sacrificial posts, or destroys images,
shall repair all of that and pay five hundred [paṇas]."
Kātyāyana says: If one should steal, break, or burn an image of the gods,
or likewise destroy its temple, he shall incur the first amercement.

Viṣṇu [5.174]: “One who sells what is unfit for consumption or what is not to be sold, and one who breaks an image of a deity, shall be punished with the highest amercement. Nārada [4.67]: “A Brāhmaṇa who sells things that ought not to be sold falls away from his path.”
Furthermore, he should be restored to the path by the king with severe punishment.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "In the case of the destruction of an image, a grove, a well, a bridge, a flagstaff, a dam, a water-trough, or a temple of the twice-born, the restoration of that [structure] and a fine of one hundred [paṇas] shall be imposed.
"But he who diverts the water of a tank already established..."
And he who should also breach a watercourse shall be made to pay the first amercement.
One who destroys a tank should be executed by drowning in water or by some other pure form of killing; or he may repair that very tank and pay the highest fine.

In continuation of the phrase "he shall kill," Viṣṇu [5.15] states: "And one who destroys a dam. The punishment is "corporal or the amputation of a limb. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "For the destruction of a step-well, a tank, a well, or a watercourse; for the defilement of water or substances; and for making a non-slave into a slave."

Yājñavalkya [2.279]: A woman who administers poison or sets fire [to a house], one who kills a man, or one who destroys a bridge— provided she is not pregnant— one should cause her to enter the water bound with a stone.

One who has given poison or fire, or one who has caused the death of her husband, her teacher, or her own child, should have her ears, hands, nose, and lips cut off and then be put to death by oxen. A woman who has killed a man—if she is not pregnant—should be cast into water, and not otherwise.
Yama says: "Thieves who set fire with torches, murderers, and those who cause injury..."
Manu, the Lord of Creatures, has declared that they should be punished with their own bodies.
Yājñavalkya [2.282]: Those who set fire to fields, houses, villages, forests, pastures, or threshing floors,
as well as one who approaches the wife of a king, shall be burned by a fire of straw mats (kaṭāgni).
Kātyāyana [809]: He who should break down a wall, or cause it to fall, or likewise demolish it,
or block the course of water, shall incur the first amercement.
Manu [9.289, 275, 272]: "One who breaks down a wall, fills up a moat,
or breaks open a gate, one should have executed immediately."
He should have executed with various punishments those who steal from the king's treasury, those who stand in opposition to him, and those who instigate his enemies.
In kingdoms, servants appointed to protect are generally deceitful and seize the property of others; one should therefore guard these subjects from them.
Likewise [7.124]:
"Those of evil intent who would thus seize wealth from their duties—
the king, having confiscated all their property, shall banish them."
Likewise: "But those who, having been appointed to official duties, ruin the affairs of the litigants while being consumed by the heat of wealth— the king should deprive them of their property."
Yājñavalkya [1.338–39]:
Having learned through spies the conduct of those appointed to oversee the kingdom,
the king should honor the virtuous but put to death those who are the opposite.
Having deprived those who live by bribery of their wealth, he should banish them;
but he should always settle Śrotriyas there, providing them with gifts, honor, and hospitality.

[569] Likewise [2.243]: He who imprisons one who should not be imprisoned, or releases one who should be imprisoned, and he who interferes with legal proceedings, shall be made to pay the highest fine.
Viṣṇu [5.195]: One who releases a person liable to punishment shall incur a fine double that of the punishment itself;
and one appointed [to oversee justice] who inflicts punishment on those who should not be punished is the lowest of men.
Kātyāyana [955–56]: "Those who are skilled in royal amusements and subsist on the king's service— whoever speaks unpleasantly to them, for them he should ordain the death penalty."
Those who manufacture counterfeit coins, those who examine them,
those who distribute them, and those who steal for the sake of the king shall receive various forms of capital punishment.
In continuation of the phrase "he shall kill," Viṣṇu [5.18] states: "And those who are of low birth who might covet the kingdom. Yājñavalkya [2.295] says:
"One who writes a royal edict either deficient or excessive..."
The punishment for one who releases an adulterer or a thief is the highest.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "In the employment of forged edicts, in the subversion of royal decrees, and in dealings with false weights, measures, and balances, corporal punishment or the amputation of limbs shall be imposed.
Kātyāyana [954] says:
"By means of a forged document, or even by a forged seal..."
But he who indeed accomplishes the task shall be made to pay the highest fine.
"And those who forge royal edicts, those who corrupt the ministers,
those who kill women, children, or Brahmins, and likewise those who serve his enemies— he shall put them to death."

Viṣṇu [3.33–35, 37]: “The sovereign, the ministers, the fort, the treasury, the army, the realm, and allies are the constituent elements [of sovereignty]. He should put to death those who corrupt them. He should have spies as his eyes regarding both his own kingdom and the kingdoms of others, and he should put to death those who are wicked.”

Furthermore, Viṣṇu [5.9–11] states: "The king shall put to death those who forge edicts, those who write fraudulent documents, poisoners, arsonists, violent thieves, and those who kill women, children, or men. Yājñavalkya [2.277] says:
"For causing an abortion by striking with a weapon, the highest fine is prescribed."
Uśanas says: For causing an abortion by means of affliction, the first [amercement] shall apply; for by means of medicine, the middle;
but for by means of a blow, the highest fine is the punishment for causing the miscarriage of the fetus.
Kātyāyana [799]: But one who commits murder shall suffer various forms of capital punishment.
Bṛhaspati [23.9–12]:

Sāhasa (violent crime) is declared to be of five kinds; among these, killing is considered the most serious. Those who commit such acts should not be punished with fines or penances, but must be executed with diligence.
Those who kill openly, as well as those who kill secretly,
having been properly identified and their wealth confiscated, shall be executed by various means of death.
Whether out of a desire to gain friends or out of greed, a king who seeks the welfare of the world must strive with great effort not to release those who bring fear to all living beings.
If a king, out of greed or fear, does not punish evildoers,
his kingdom becomes agitated and he is deprived of his sovereignty.
Likewise [23.13]: "A man who, through motives such as anger and the like, causes the death of others by means of binding, fire, poison, or weapons— he is a perpetrator of *sāhasa* (a violent crime)."

Baudhāyana says: "In the case of killing a Brāhmaṇa by Kṣatriyas and others, the punishment is death and the confiscation of all property. For killing their equals or those of lower status, one should prescribe a corresponding punishment according to one's power. Upon killing a Kṣatriya, one should release to the king a thousand cows with an additional bull for the purpose of avenging the enmity. One hundred cows [should be released] for a Vaiśya, and ten for a Śūdra, with a bull added in each case. Killing a woman, a cow, or a bull is explained by the rule for killing a Śūdra, except in the case of killing an Ātreyī woman, a milch-cow, or a draft-ox. For killing a milch-cow or a draft-ox, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance at the end of the period. Killing an Ātreyī woman is explained by the rule for killing a Kṣatriya. For killing a swan, a vulture, a peacock, a ruddy goose, a crane, an owl, a frog, a water-snake, a mongoose, a cat, a dog, a babhru, a mongoose, and so forth, the punishment is the same as for a Śūdra."
Bṛhaspati and Kātyāyana state:
"Where many people, filled with rage, strike at one person,
he who delivers the blow to a vital organ is declared to be the killer."
But he who strikes at their vital points shall be made to pay the fine as previously stated;
the instigator and the accomplice shall each be liable for half of that amount.

Having ascertained through signs the smallness or greatness of the wound, the location of the vital points (marmans), the strength [of the patient], and the complications, one should treat it with diligence.
This rule of punishment is ordained for all without distinction;
except for the case of a Brāhmaṇa, a Brāhmaṇa does not deserve death.
Shaving the head is his punishment, as is banishment from the city;
furthermore, he shall have a mark of infamy branded upon his forehead and be made to travel on a donkey.
There is a restriction regarding the two types of association:
"A corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa shall never take place;
however, having bound him in secret confinement, the king shall cause food to be provided."
Alternatively, the king, having ascertained the matter in its true nature, may cause the offender to be bound with a rope or made to perform labor for half a month or a full month.
According to the offense, one may compel even a Brahmin to perform forbidden acts;
if he speaks evil of the king, it is ordained that his punishment shall be banishment from the realm.
"Brahmins and cows are not to be slain; such is the Vedic revelation in this world.
The meaning is that the punishment which has departed from its proper object (*viṣaya*)—that is, the punishment which is applied where it does not belong—is what must be avoided. Yājñavalkya [2.231]:
He who causes a rash act to be committed shall be made to pay double the fine;
and he who, having said "I will give," then causes it to be done, shall pay four times the fine.
[574] “I am the giver. Having declared, “I shall give you wealth; you do the work,” he who causes it to be done is to be fined fourfold—this is the meaning. Kātyāyana [832–34]:
“The instigator, the assistant, as well as the one who points out the way...”
The one who provides shelter, the giver of weapons, and the giver of food to those who perform forbidden acts [are all liable].
One who instructs in war, one who demonstrates its destruction,
one who is indifferent, one who is not appointed [to the task], one who speaks of faults, and one who approves [of the act].
Those who are unable to prevent [a crime] but are capable [of witnessing it] shall all perform the duty [of reporting it];
however, the king should impose a punishment upon them according to their respective capacities.

‘One who demonstrates its destruction’ means one who teaches the means for its destruction. ‘And one who speaks of a fault without being appointed’ refers to one who, not having been commissioned by the king, speaks of a fault.
“He who, having committed an improper act of violence, seeks to establish a close connection [with the victim]...”
Or if he should speak himself in the assembly, his punishment is likewise ordained.
But if that wicked man lives while concealing his immorality,
the members of the assembly are not satisfied with him, and a severe punishment is inflicted.
[575] 71 — (ka) Now, the search for the slayer;
on this point, Yājñavalkya [2.280–81]:
The sons and kinsmen of one who has been killed while unobserved should quickly investigate the quarrel;
they should also separately question his women who were devoted to other men.
Or, desiring his wife, wealth, or livelihood, with whom did he go?
Or he should slowly question people in the vicinity of that place.
Where a person is seen killed but the killer is not seen,
he should be identified by the king through inference based on prior enmity.
His neighbors, both those living nearby and those further away, as well as his friends, enemies, and kinsmen,
should be questioned by the king’s officers using conciliation and other such means.
He is to be identified by men through association with the wicked, or by signs, or by stolen goods;
thus has been declared the method for investigating murderers and thieves.
But he who, having been seized on suspicion, does not proceed to perform that act, must be cleared by means of oaths; this is the rule in all legal disputes.
Vyāsa says:
Having thoroughly identified the slayer along with his accomplices and kinsmen,
the king should put them to death by various means of execution that cause terror.
Bṛhaspati [23.26]: One who is purified by divine ordeals should be released; one who is impure deserves execution. Through the king’s acts of restraint and favor, his fame and righteousness increase.
Thus ends the Sāhasaparvan [577],
section 72— now follows the Strīsaṃgrahaṇa (On the Seduction of Women).
In this regard, Bṛhaspati [24.1–5] states:
"Harshness is declared to be of two kinds, and violence is of two characteristics;
understand that adultery, which is rooted in evil, is of three types."
Two types are produced through force and inducement, while the third arises from passion;
that [third] is further said to be of three kinds: inferior, middling, and superior.
That which is done against her will by one who is asleep, intoxicated, or distracted,
or while she is speaking incoherently in private— that indeed is an act committed by force.
When a union is brought about by leading a woman to one's house under false pretenses or by administering intoxicants or magical charms, they know that as "induced by fraud" (*upādhikṛta*).
That which is produced by mutual passion for each other's eyes, by the dispatching of female messengers,
and by greed for beauty and wealth, should be known as love born of attachment.
Vyāsa says: "The compendium is declared to be threefold— namely, the inferior, the middling,
and the superior— and its characteristics have been stated separately in the scriptures."
Conversation with another's wife in an improper place or time,
gazing at her from the corner of the eye, laughing with her, and previous intimate association— these are recorded as "seduction."
[578] Bṛhaspati [24.6]: Gazing with sidelong glances, laughter, sending female messengers,
as well as touching ornaments and garments— this is recorded as the first stage of courtship.
Nārada [15.63]: When a man and a woman meet at the confluence of rivers, at sacred fords (tīrthas), in groves, or in forests— that is recorded as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse).
Bṛhaspati [24.10]:
The sending of perfumes, garlands, fruits, food, drink, and new clothes,
as well as private conversation, they know to be the middle form of solicitation.
Vyāsa says:
The sending of perfumes, garlands, incense, ornaments, and garments,
as well as the enticing with food and drink, is recorded as the middling form of recruitment.
Bṛhaspati [24.8]:
"Sharing a bed and a seat, as well as playing, kissing, and embracing—
this is declared by those who know the scriptures to be the highest form of *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual misconduct)."
Vyāsa says: On a secluded bed or seat, mutual embracing,
and even pulling each other's hair should be known as the highest form of sexual union.
According to Nārada and Manu, the first two [types] are as follows:
"Providing assistance, playful dalliance, touching ornaments and garments,
and sharing a bed or seat— all this is recorded in the Smṛti as *saṃgrahaṇa* (seduction)."
If a man touches a woman in an improper place, or if he, being touched by her, consents to it,
it is all recorded in the legal tradition as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse), provided there is mutual consent between them.
