Nārada [15.39, 37]: "Whether out of pride, or through delusion, or out of a desire for self-glorification, if one should say of one's own accord,
'This woman was enjoyed by me previously,' that is recorded as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse)."
If one should seize another by the hand, or by the braid of hair, or even by the hem of the garment, or say "Stay! Stay!", all such acts are recorded as *saṅgrahaṇa* (sexual assault).
Yājñavalkya [2.283–84]:
A man shall be apprehended for adultery when he is caught by the hair with another’s wife,
or immediately by signs born of passion, or likewise when there is mutual consent between the two.
[580] Uncovering the knot of her garment or her breasts, touching her thighs or her hair, conversing at an improper place or time, and staying together in private;
In passages such as "sahāvasthānam," the word "kurvāṇaḥ" (performing) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Kātyāyana says:
"Whatever actions a man performs at any time while desiring them..."
But those undertakings you have described are censurable, as they accomplish only sensual desires.
If he employs the conduct of a messenger but stands at an improper time or place,
seizing her by the throat, hair, or garment, or by the ears, nose, hands, and so forth;
Dwelling in one place, sitting in one place, and eating in one place—this is known as the ninefold gathering. One who acts otherwise should not be accepted; such a recipient deserves punishment.
The miscarriage of a fetus, the appearance of fingernails, the retention of a fetus,
and the wearing of another's clothes, ornaments, or weapons;
By these signs women devoted to infidelity are always to be known:
by their use of perfumes, garlands, and garments, as well as by their sending of letters and messages.
Indeed, everything would be a grasper, for that is the act of initiating [an action];
therefore, the wise know "grasping" (graha) as a seizing resulting from this connection with what is not its effect.
But when one who is lustful remains engaged in an undertaking that accomplishes desire,
they call that his "seizing" (grahaṇa), because it is from that [engagement] that "sexual intercourse" (saṃgrahaṇa) arises.
Bṛhaspati [24.11]: Among these three as well, the first, the middle, and the highest [penalties] should be prescribed;
the discipline should be greater when the wealth is greater.
Manu [8.358]: A man who engages in private conversation with another's wife,
having previously been accused of such offenses, shall incur the first amercement.

"Previously" means by "faults," such as soliciting her women and so forth; "accused" means charged. Āpastamba [2.26.18–19] states: "One who, though not intentionally, enters another's wife's quarters or a maiden while being adorned and young, shall be restrained by word only; but one who does so intentionally, being of wicked intent, shall be punished. The *Matsyapurāṇa* [227.119–20, 125–26] states:
Whether it be a mendicant, a woman,
or even a professional actor who enters [the assembly] in violation of a prohibition, he shall incur a fine of two hundred [paṇas].
The man who acts as a go-between there shall be punished in that same manner;
and he who provides lodging for an adulterer shall be punished like an adulterer himself.
Manu [8.355]: But he who, having previously been unaccused, speaks out on account of a cause,
shall incur no fault whatsoever, for there is no transgression on his part.

[582] Nārada [15.67]: When a woman who has a protector is seen joined with a man in another's house, that is considered adultery by those who know the law; it is not so when she has come to his own house of her own accord.
Kātyāyana states regarding following [the husband] after approaching him:
"If she proceeds in any manner other than this, there would be an act of taking her captive;
however, if she has come of her own accord to the man's house, he incurs no fault."
Nārada and Kātyāyana [Nā. 15.61]:

"In the case of one who has abandoned his wife because she is not virtuous, or who is impotent, or incapable, there shall be no offense for the violence committed against her if he approaches her according to his own will."

The meaning of this is as follows: for one by whom his own wives—who were previously faultless—have become corrupted and have been abandoned; if he approaches wives who are corrupt, or the wives of eunuchs or those unable to endure [sexual intercourse], solely by the consent of those wives, he is not to be punished. Manu [8.360–61]:
"Beggars, bards, those initiated for sacrifice, and likewise artisans..."
They may converse with women in the house without being restrained.
One who has been forbidden should not engage in conversation with the wives of others;
however, one who converses despite being forbidden deserves a fine of one suvarṇa.
Yājñavalkya [2.285]: When a woman prevents [a man from approaching her], she shall be fined one hundred [paṇas]; but a man shall be fined two hundred.
In the case of their mutual prevention, the punishment shall be the same as that for adultery (saṃgrahaṇa).

The meaning of this is as follows: if a woman proceeds to engage in conversation and so forth when such activities have been forbidden by her husband, father, or others, she shall be fined one hundred *paṇas*. A man, however, proceeding in this manner when thus forbidden, shall be fined two hundred *paṇas*. But for both a woman and a man who proceed to converse despite being forbidden, the fine shall be the same as that prescribed according to their respective castes (*varṇa*).
"This rule does not apply to the wives of performers (*cāraṇa*), nor to those who live off their own labor."
For those women prepare themselves and move about in disguise.
But he who engages in conversation with such women,
or with female slaves who have a single master, or with female ascetics in secret, shall be made to pay a small fine.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "For all, the restriction to one's own wife and the performance of one's own duties constitute *dharma*. With whichever limb one commits an offense, that very limb of his shall be cut off; or else, the fine shall be eight thousand [paṇas], except in the case of a Brāhmaṇa. For a Brāhmaṇa is exempt from punishment. Manu [8.352–53, 359]: "The king should punish those men who are intent on violating the wives of others..."
Having branded them with punishments that cause terror, he should banish them.
For from that arises the intermixture of castes among the people,
by which unrighteousness, which destroys the very root, leads to total ruin.
A non-Brāhmaṇa deserves the death penalty for adultery;
the wives of all four castes are declared to be most worthy of protection.
In the rule “An *abrāhmaṇa* [is liable to punishment] for adultery,” the word “of a Brāhmaṇī” is to be understood as the ellipsis.
(ka) Now, the punishments for sexual intercourse:
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati [24.13] states:
"But he who should lust after her by force, one shall confiscate his entire wealth;
having cut off his penis and testicles, one shall cause him to be paraded on a donkey."

Āpastamba [2.26.10]: “When sexual intercourse has occurred, there shall be the excision of the penis together with the testicles. Kātyāyana [830]: When a man forcibly enjoys women who have been protected.
In that case, execution would proceed, for that constitutes a transgression of one's duty.
Bṛhaspati [24.14–15]:
But he who should desire her by means of deception shall suffer a fine that takes away all his property;
having been branded with the mark of a female organ, he shall then be banished from the city.

In the case of equal status, the punishment is the final amercement; in the case of inferior status, it is half of that. However, in the case of approaching a woman of superior status, the man shall be put to death.

Yājñavalkya [2.286]: "In the case of those of equal caste, the highest fine shall be imposed; in the case of a woman of a lower caste, the middle fine; but in the case of a man of a higher caste, there shall be death for the male and the cutting off of the ears and so forth for the female."

Viṣṇu [5.40–43]: “One who commits adultery with a woman of his own caste shall be fined the highest amercement; for approaching a woman of a lower caste, the middle amercement; likewise for approaching a cow; and for approaching a woman of the lowest caste, he shall be put to death; as also for approaching a woman of the highest caste. Śaṅkha and Likhita: “For entering the houses of women without prior announcement, the highest amercement applies if she is of the highest caste; in the reverse case, the middle amercement. For violating a woman of a lower caste by force when she is alone, the confiscation of all property or death shall be the penalty; in the reverse case, imprisonment and the confiscation of all property.”

The meaning of this is as follows: for a Brāhmaṇa who enters the house of a woman without prior announcement and approaches an *uttamā*—that is, a woman of the Brāhmaṇa caste or higher—the punishment is the highest fine (*uttama-sāhasa*). However, in the "reverse case" (*viparyaye*)—that is, when a Brāhmaṇa approaches a woman of the Kṣatriya or lower caste—the punishment is the middle fine (*madhyama-sāhasa*). For one of the inverse order (*pratiloma*), such as a Śūdra, approaching a woman of the twice-born castes separated by one degree, the punishment is death accompanied by the confiscation of all property. The word "or" (*vā*) is used in a cumulative sense. This is based on the statement of Gautama: "For approaching an Ārya woman, there shall be excision of the organ and confiscation of his property; if she was protected, the punishment is additionally death" (GDh 12.2–3). Regarding the "reverse case," Manu states: "In the case of approaching an unprotected wife of a Brāhmaṇa, the Vaiśya shall be imprisoned for one year and then have all his property confiscated" (MDh 8.375). Thus, the punishment for a Vaiśya is the confiscation of all property following one year of confinement.
[587] Regarding the section on pride, Manu [8.372] states: "One should cause the wicked man to be burned upon a heated iron bed;
they should pile wood upon it, and there the evildoer shall be consumed by fire."

Nārada [15.73–75]: A mother, a maternal aunt, a mother-in-law, a maternal uncle’s wife, a paternal aunt, the wife of a paternal uncle, a friend, a female disciple, a sister, her female friend, and a daughter-in-law.
A daughter, a teacher’s wife, one of the same lineage, one who has sought refuge,
a queen, one who has gone forth, a nurse, a virtuous woman, and one of the highest caste.
Having approached any one of these women, one is called a violator of the Guru's bed;
in that case, the cutting off of the penis is ordained as the punishment, and no other.

Yājñavalkya [3.232–33]: [One who has sexual intercourse with] his father’s sister, his mother’s sister, his maternal uncle’s wife, or even his daughter-in-law; likewise, his mother’s co-wife, his sister, or the daughter of his teacher—[these are women with whom intercourse is forbidden].
But he who approaches the wife of his teacher or his own daughter is a violator of the guru's bed;
having cut off his penis, he shall be executed, as shall the woman if she was willing.
Vyāsa says:

The punishment for the abduction of a guarded woman has been declared as previously stated; however, for one who approaches a woman who desires him and comes to him of her own accord, the fine is recorded as half.
A Brāhmaṇa who approaches a protected Brāhmaṇa woman by force shall be fined one thousand [paṇas];
he who has sexual intercourse with a willing woman shall be fined five hundred.
Shaving the head is prescribed as the punishment for a Brāhmaṇa;
however, for the other castes, the punishment shall be one that ends in death.
If a Vaiśya should approach a guarded Kṣatriya woman, or a Kṣatriya a guarded Vaiśya woman,
they deserve the same punishment as one who approaches an unguarded Brāhmaṇa woman.
A Brāhmaṇa, however, committing adultery with guarded women of those two castes, must be made to pay a fine of one thousand;
for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya committing it with a Śūdra woman, the punishment shall indeed be one thousand.
Āpastamba [2.27.8]: “An Ārya shall be expelled for discharging semen into a Śūdra woman.

Here, “Ārya” refers to a Brāhmaṇa or others; “in a Śūdra woman” means having discharged semen into one who has not previously belonged to another; “shall be expelled” (nāśya) means he is to be banished from the territory. Manu [8.385, 373].

A Brāhmaṇa who approaches an unprotected Kṣatriya woman, a Vaiśya woman, or a Śūdra woman shall be fined five hundred paṇas; however, if he approaches a woman of the lowest caste (antyaja), the fine shall be one thousand.
For a wicked man who has been accused for a year, the fine is double;
likewise for one who has lived with a *vrātyā* or a *caṇḍālī*.

Regarding the phrase “of a wicked man accused for a year”: one who is accused that “this woman, the wife of another, has been enjoyed by him for a year” is called “accused for a year. The meaning is that the punishment prescribed for enjoying her for a year shall be doubled for him. “*Vrātyās*” are those of extremely wicked conduct, such as those who subsist on killing or imprisonment, and so forth; they are of seven kinds, according to the statement of Hārīta: “Those who perform censurable acts that characterize a *vrātya* are censured,” and so on. Yājñavalkya [2.294] states:
“But upon approaching a woman of the lowest caste (*antyā*), he should be branded with the mark of a headless trunk (*kabandha*) and banished.”
A Śūdra likewise shall become an outcaste; for an outcaste, there is death upon the arrival of an Ārya.
‘He is to be marked with a headless trunk’: having branded him with the form of a human body devoid of a head and shoulders.
Baudhāyana [2.3.53, 2.4.1–3]: “One should burn a Śūdra with a fire of straw mats (kaṭāgni). Furthermore, they cite this: ‘For one who is not a Brāhmaṇa, there shall be corporal punishment;
for one who is not a Brāhmaṇa, there shall be corporal punishment in the case of adultery.’”
For all social classes alike, one's wife is more worthy of protection than wealth.
But there is no killing among the wives of wandering performers, nor on the stage;
for they cause these men to disport themselves, even when they are well-guarded.

Regarding the case of a Śūdra, Gautama [12.2–3] states: “For approaching an Ārya woman, there shall be the excision of his organ and the confiscation of all his property; if she has a protector, death is the additional penalty. Āpastamba [2.27.9–10] says: “Death for a Śūdra who approaches an Ārya woman, and he shall also cause her to be emaciated as a wife.
Yama, in the context of the rule “if a Brāhmaṇī should serve a Vṛṣala,” states:
But the king shall cause a Śūdra who has committed such an act to be executed on a bed of heated iron;
there he shall burn that evildoer with wood, leaves, and likewise with straw.
A Śūdra who has sexual intercourse with a woman of the twice-born castes, whether she be protected or unprotected, shall have all his limbs cut off if she is unprotected;
if she is protected, he is deprived of everything.
A Vaiśya should be fined his entire property after being imprisoned for one year;
a Kṣatriya should be fined one thousand [paṇas] and deserves to have his head shaved with urine.
If they should have intercourse with an unprotected Brāhmaṇa woman, such is the established rule:
one should fine the Vaiśya five hundred [paṇas] and the Kṣatriya one thousand.
But both of them, having violated a guarded Brahmin woman,
are to be punished like Shudras or burned in a fire of straw.

"Living with a woman of the twice-born caste who belongs to another" means having sexual intercourse with a woman of the twice-born caste belonging to someone else. "Unprotected" means unguarded. "With his limb and all his property" means together with his limb and all his property; the meaning is that he is deprived of that specific limb by which he committed the offense, and he is also deprived of all his property. However, approaching one who is protected, the meaning is that he is deprived of "every limb.
Likewise [Yājñavalkya 2.284]: "For an unprotected Kṣatriya woman, the fine is five hundred; for a Vaiśya woman, the fine is five hundred."
A Kṣatriya, however, should desire tonsure with urine, or else a staff [as punishment].

Hārīta: “The king, having bound him who has sexual intercourse with a superior woman while she is lying on her bed, shall have her devoured by dogs; he shall also have her burned with wood. Here, “superior” (*śreyas*) refers to one of the highest class, such as a Brāhmaṇa; “lying on her bed” (*śayanaśāyin*) means one who approaches a woman; “her” (*enām*) refers to the woman of the higher class. Gautama [23.14–16]: “The king shall have a woman publicly devoured by dogs for approaching a man of a lower caste; he shall cause the man to be executed, or [punish him] as prescribed.”

[492] Vasiṣṭha [21.1–5]: “If a Śūdra should have intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should wrap the Śūdra in *vīraṇa* grass and throw him into the fire. Having shaved the head of the Brāhmaṇī woman and sprinkled her with clarified butter, one should place her naked upon a donkey and cause her to be led along the high road (*mahāpatha*). It is declared that she becomes purified. If a Vaiśya should have intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should wrap the Vaiśya in red *darbha* grass and throw him into the fire. Having shaved the head of the Brāhmaṇī woman and sprinkled her with clarified butter, one should place her naked upon a donkey and cause her to be led along the high road. It is declared that she becomes purified. If a Kṣatriya should have intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should wrap the Kṣatriya in *śara* reeds and throw him into the fire. Having shaved the head of the Brāhmaṇī woman and sprinkled her with clarified butter, one should place her naked upon a donkey and cause her to be led along the high road. It is declared that she becomes purified. In the same way, a Vaiśya who practices sexual intercourse with a Kṣatriya woman [is punished]; but a Śūdra who does so with a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya woman [is punished as above].”
Now, as for Yama: "But that Brāhmaṇa woman who, deluded by intoxication, serves a low-caste man (vṛṣala),
the king shall have her devoured by dogs at the place of executioners."
If a Brāhmaṇī woman serves either a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya,
her punishment shall be the shaving of her head and her departure on a donkey.
‘In the place of executioners’ means in the station of those such as Caṇḍālas who cause the execution of those condemned to death. Bṛhaspati [24.16–17]:
“A woman who, having come to a man’s house, entices him through touch and other means...”
If she desires it there, she shall be punished; for the man, half the fine is prescribed.
Having cut off her nose, lips, and ears, one should cause her to wander and drown in water,
or have her devoured by dogs in a place where many people are gathered.
‘Bahusaṃsthite’: where many people are assembled, such as at a crossroads and the like.
Manu [8.371]: "But that woman who, arrogant on account of her kinsmen or her virtues, transgresses against her husband..."
The king should have her devoured by dogs at a public execution ground where many people are assembled.

Viṣṇu (5.18) states in the context of the repetition [of the offense]: "A woman who is unattached to her husband and one who transgresses him. Yājñavalkya (3.233) says: "In that case, for a woman who is willing, there shall be the cutting off of her organ and execution."
[594] Bṛhaspati [24.18–19]: But she who has been released against her will should be made to dwell in the house under guard;
with soiled limbs, sleeping on the ground, and subsisting on a mere morsel of food.
If she has had intercourse with an equal, he should cause her to perform an expiation consisting of a *kṛcchra* or a *parāka*.
But if she has been enjoyed by one of a lower caste, she should be abandoned or even put to death.
“*Same gatām*” means one who has had sexual intercourse with a man of the same caste.
Kātyāyana [488–79] states: “Women who are not independent are not to be held liable; in such a case, it is the man who commits the offense.”
Those women are to be disciplined by the lord; however, the king should lead the man [to justice].
If a woman whose husband is away is apprehended,
she shall be kept in confinement until her lord has returned.
‘He should lead the man’ means he should cause the man who is the husband of the woman to come forward.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa* [227.127–29]: “If a man should anywhere defile another’s wife by force...”
The punishment for him shall be death; there shall be no offense on the part of the woman.
One who takes charge of a deceased wife who possesses no property does not commit an offense;
however, by taking her [into his household], he deserves a fine equal to his entire estate.
In the *Vyavahārakāṇḍa* of the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, [the section on] Punishment for Unauthorized Visitation [595].
72 — (b) Now, regarding the violation of a maiden, Manu [8.364] states:
"He who violates a maiden against her will deserves immediate execution."
A man who defiles a willing woman shall not suffer the same punishment as one who violates a woman against her will.
In the Matsya Purāṇa (227.124–25): "He who violates an unwilling maiden deserves immediate execution;
but he who violates one who is willing incurs the highest amercement."
In the continuation of the phrase "when the union has occurred," Āpastamba [2.26.21] states: "But in the case of a maiden, having taken her own [belongings], he should be banished.
Manu [8.366] states: "But a man of lower caste who cohabits with a woman of the highest caste deserves the death penalty."
If the father so desires, he may accept a fee when the daughter reaches her marriageable age while being courted by a suitor.
If the girl is unwilling, there shall be the cutting off of two fingers;
if she is of the highest caste, there shall indeed be execution as well as the confiscation of all her property.
But if the maiden is willing and he is of the same caste, there is no offense;
rather, having adorned her and honored her, he himself shall marry her.

Now, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "If the maiden is unwilling, the punishment is the cutting off of two fingers; however, in the case of a woman of the highest caste, there is death for the lowest caste man. With a woman of equal caste, one should take her after giving the nuptial fee (śulka), her ornaments, and double the amount of her woman's property (strīdhana). Yājñavalkya [2.287–88] says:
"For abducting an adorned maiden of the highest caste, the penalty is the highest amercement; otherwise, it is the lowest."
One should impose a fine for offenses against women of the same caste; however, in cases of the reverse order (prātilomya), death is ordained by tradition.
There is no offense when she is willing and compliant; otherwise, there is punishment. But for defilement, the hand shall be cut off, and likewise death in the case of a woman of the highest caste.
"Uttamam" means the highest fine (uttama-sāhasa). "Adhamam" means the lowest fine (adhama-sāhasa).
"But that man who, out of arrogance, violates a maiden after having promised her [to another]..."
For that offense, his two fingers shall be immediately cut off, and he deserves a fine of six hundred [paṇas].
But one who defiles a willing woman shall not suffer the amputation of a finger;
rather, he should be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas] in order to prevent a recurrence.
If a maiden should defile another maiden, she shall be fined two hundred panas;
she must also pay three times the bride-price and receive ten lashes with a rod.
But a woman who violates a maiden deserves immediate shaving of the head,
or else the cutting off of two fingers, as well as being led away on a donkey.
One should not cause a maiden who is consorting with a superior man to pay anything at all;
however, one should keep her confined in the house if she is consorting with an inferior man.

‘Abhiṣajya’ means having overcome. ‘Kuryāt’ means he should act; that is to say, he should violate or defile. ‘Kalpye’ means in that which is fit to be cut. ‘Śiphā’ here refers to a blow with a rope made of matted hair and the like. [598] 72 — (ga) Now, approaching a harlot.
In that regard, Yama states: "For adultery with women of the same caste, they should be fined five *kṛṣṇalas*;
for women of a different caste when the act is in the natural order (*ānulomya*), a fine of twelve [paṇas] is prescribed."
Vyāsa says:
That lowest of men who approaches a woman who has already been enjoyed by many incurs a punishment like that for a prostitute, and not like that for one's own wife.
Kātyāyana [831]: A wanton woman who, afflicted by desire, seeks him out of her own accord,
may be enjoyed by the king's command after she has been publicly proclaimed in the presence of people.

Nārada [15.78–79]: A woman who is self-willed, a non-Brāhmaṇa woman, a courtesan, a female slave, and one who has left her husband— these women may be approached in the direct order of castes, but not in the inverse order.

But with these very female slaves, there would be a fault similar to that regarding the wives of others; for even though they are approachable, one should not have intercourse with them, since they belong to another.
Yājñavalkya [2.290]: "A man who has intercourse with female slaves kept in the household, or likewise with female servants,
even though they are women with whom one may lawfully go, shall be made to pay a fine of fifty paṇas."
Vyāsa states: For approaching a woman who has been restrained by another, the fine is fifty paṇas;
for forcibly approaching a prostitute, the punishment is ordained as ten paṇas.
Yājñavalkya [2.291]:
For approaching a female slave by force, a fine of ten paṇas is prescribed;
if many men do so against her will, the fine is twenty-four [paṇas] for each individually.
Likewise [2.293]:
"One who has intercourse with female animals shall be made to pay a hundred [paṇas]; and for a low-caste cow, the middle amercement.
Nārada [15.76].
One who causes [an animal] to stray while it is in the womb of a beast is to be disciplined with one hundred [paṇas];
for cows, the fine is the middle amercement; and the same applies to those of the lowest castes.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa* (227.143–44): "He who indulges in sexual intercourse with an animal, excluding a cow, shall receive a fine of one paṇa, and fodder and water shall be forfeited to her."
A man of the highest caste who wanders about with a cow should be fined gold;
a twice-born man who goes to a prostitute should be fined a paṇa equal to the prostitute's fee.
Nārada [15.77]:
Punishment prescribed by the king is for those who approach women who should not be approached;
however, the prescription of penance serves as the purification for such sins.
Manu [8.386–87]: That king in whose city there is no thief, no adulterer, no speaker of evil words, and no perpetrator of violence or one who evades punishment, shares the world of Śakra.
The suppression of these five within his own realm by a king brings him imperial power over his kinsmen and confers glory upon him in the world.
Yama said:
That king in whose kingdom there are no wicked men, no violent men, no fierce men, no gamblers, and no deceivers here, shares in the world of Śakra.
Thus ends the Section on the Seduction of Women (Strīsaṃgrahaparva).
73 — Now begins the Section on the Union of Men and Women (Strīpuṃyoga).
In this regard, Bṛhaspati [25.1] says:
"The rules for seduction and likewise the methods of discipline have been declared; now hear from me as I speak the means for regulating the conduct of women and men."
Nārada [15.2]:
That legal topic in which the rules for the marriage and other rites of women and men are proclaimed is called *strīpuṃsayoga* (the union of woman and man).

The procedure for marriage is described there in the section on marriage (vivāhakāṇḍa). Now, regarding the duties of husband and wife, in that context— under the heading "the conduct of a man toward a woman"— it is said:
Manu [9.1–2]: For the man and the woman who abide in the path of dharma,
whether in union or in separation, I shall declare the eternal laws.
Women must be kept under control day and night by their own men; and if they become attached to sensual pleasures, they must be established under one's own authority.
Nārada [16.30]:
Even women born into noble families fall away through independence;
therefore, Prajāpati ordained their lack of independence.
Manu [9.3]: "The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth, and the sons protect her in old age; a woman does not deserve independence."
Yājñavalkya [1.85]: A father shall protect a maiden; her husband, once she is married; and her sons in old age. In their absence, her kinsmen shall do so; a woman never has independence.

Hārīta says: "Due to the failure of their vows and being corrupted by the senses of others, those who cause the confusion of lineages become objects of compassion. While the husband lives, the son born of an adulterer is a *kuṇḍa*; when the husband is dead, he is a *golaka*. Therefore, one should protect the wife from the corruption of semen. With the destruction of the wife comes the destruction of the lineage; with the destruction of the lineage comes the destruction of the family thread (*tantu*); with the destruction of the family thread comes the destruction of the sacrifices to the gods and ancestors; with the destruction of dharma comes the destruction of the self; and with the destruction of the self comes the destruction of everything."

‘From the failure of the single vow (*ekavrataskannabhāvāt*)’—the meaning is: from the transgression of that rule of conduct (*vrata-niyama*) which holds that there is only one husband. ‘The thread (*tantuḥ*)’ refers to the lineage consisting of sons, grandsons, and so forth. Manu [9.5–7]:
“Women must be guarded with great effort even against the slightest opportunities for misconduct.”
For if they are not protected, they will bring grief to both families.
For seeing this supreme dharma common to all castes,
husbands— even those who are weak— strive to protect their wives.
By diligently protecting his wife, a man indeed protects his own progeny, his conduct, his lineage, himself, and his own dharma.

Following the discussion on the intermixture of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*), Paiṭhīnasi states: “Therefore, one should protect one’s wife in every respect; let there be no intermixture of castes—so he says.
Guard this lineage with vigilance; let not the seeds of another be sown in your field. Protect your maiden wife, fearing the seed of others.”
Bṛhaspati [25.2]: A woman must be kept away from even the slightest opportunities for misconduct by her own kinsmen;
she should be protected day and night by her mother-in-law and other elder women.
Upon the death of her husband, the male kin of the husband is the master of a woman who has no son;
he is the authority over her employment and protection, while he is the lord over her maintenance.
When the husband's family has perished, is devoid of men, and lacks support,
and when his paternal kinsmen are no longer present, the father’s side becomes the authority over the woman.
At the conclusion of both [the husband's] life-stages, the king is declared to be the woman's protector;
he should provide for her protection and restrain her if she deviates from the path.
Manu [9.4]:
A father who does not give [his daughter] at the proper time is censurable; a husband who does not approach her is censurable;
and when the husband has died, a son who does not protect his mother is censurable.
Bṛhaspati [25.5]: A father who does not give [his daughter in marriage] at the proper time, a husband who does not approach his wife during her season,
and a son who does not provide for his mother— these are censurable and, according to dharma, subject to punishment.
These women do not examine appearance, nor is there any certainty regarding their age;
whether he is ugly or handsome, they enjoy him simply because he is a man.
Due to their proclivity for men, their fickle-mindedness, and their natural lack of affection,
these women act perversely toward their husbands even when guarded with great effort in this world.
Manu assigned to women the bed, the seat, ornaments, lust, anger, dishonesty, a malicious disposition, and bad conduct.
[605] It is established as the law that women have no ritual action with mantras;
for it is the settled rule that women are devoid of sensory power (*indriya*), lack mantras, and are untruthful.
For indeed, many Vedic verses have been sung even in the Nigamas;
listen to their definitive resolution for the purpose of examining their specific characteristics.
"Whatever my mother, wandering about unfaithful, lusted after,
may my father take that seed of mine"— this is the illustration for this [rule].
Whatever undesirable thing she contemplates in her mind for the sake of her husband,
this is rightly called the concealment of such transgression.
Having thus understood their nature, which arises from the creation of Prajāpati,
a man should exert the greatest effort toward their protection.

‘Without sense-faculties’ (*nirindriyāḥ*) means devoid of vigor, fortitude, wisdom, strength, and so forth. ‘Women are falsehood’ is said because they generally have a disposition for speaking untruths. ‘The *śrutis*’ refers to the sentences of the Vedas. ‘In the *nigamas*’ means in the Vedas. ‘*Svālakṣaṇyam*’ means their own essential nature. Regarding the phrase “of them,” etc.—among those *śrutis*, those which are in the form of expiation (*niṣkṛti*), serving as atonement for mental transgression, listen to those *śrutis* for the purpose of understanding the nature inherent in women. “*Tan me retaḥ pitā vṛṅktām*” means: “May my father’s seed remove that sin produced by my mother’s longing for another man. Here, the nominative case in “father” (*pitā*) is used in the sense of the genitive. “*Prajāpatinisragajam*” means born at the time of non-emanation (*anisarga*), i.e., during the period of creation (*sṛṣṭikāla*), belonging to Prajāpati Hiraṇyagarbha.
Dakṣa says:
Like leeches, all women, though constantly well-supported with ornaments, clothing, and food,
nevertheless draw a man down.
The leech draws out only blood, whereas that wretched woman [the wife] takes away wealth,
property, flesh, virility, strength, and happiness.
Full of apprehension during childhood, she becomes devoted in youth;
yet in old age, a woman regards her own husband as no more than a blade of grass.
Remaining under her own control, she was not restrained by affection;
yet she would later become harmful, like a neglected disease.
‘In accordance with her own desire’ means according to her will. Manu (9.9) states: “For whatever kind of man a woman devotes herself to, she gives birth to offspring of that same kind.”
Therefore, for the sake of the purity of offspring, one should protect women with great effort.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “Women give birth to a son corresponding to the disposition (bhāva) in which they are intent during their menses; just as from a dark-blue bull a dark-blue calf is produced, and from a white one a white one is born. Thus, the womb itself is powerful, because of it the castes become intermingled. In the Rāmāyaṇa:
“Among women, there is no one who is either beloved or hated.”
They cling to everything, like creepers growing in a dense thicket.
In the Mahābhārata: "Women who are of noble birth, beautiful, and have protectors do not abide by the bounds of propriety; that is the fault in women, O Nārada."
Because men do not desire them and out of fear of their kinsmen,
women— who are otherwise unrestrained— remain within the bounds of propriety toward their husbands.
Women of noble family envy those women who, being in the prime of youth, adorned with polished ornaments and fine garments, live according to their own will.
O Brahmin, if the destiny of men cannot be fulfilled in any way,
they will even turn against one another and will not remain faithful to their husbands.
Indeed, due to the lack of men, out of fear of their own attendants,
and for the sake of avoiding execution or imprisonment, they protect themselves.
Fire is never satiated with wood, nor the great ocean with rivers; Death is never satiated with all living beings, nor is a beautiful-eyed woman ever satiated with men.
Those women always strive diligently not to tolerate even one who gives them sensual pleasures, who offers them mental comfort, or who protects them.
73 — (a) Now, the method of protection.
Regarding this, Manu [9.10–12] says:
"No one is able to guard women by force."
However, by means of these applications of skillful methods, they can be protected.
He should employ her in the collection of wealth and in its expenditure,
as well as in cleanliness, religious duty, the cooking of food, and the supervision of household goods.
Women who are confined at home by trustworthy male guardians are not truly protected;
those who protect themselves by their own efforts are well-protected.
‘Pāriṇāhya’ refers to items such as earrings, bracelets, and so forth. Bṛhaspati [25.6] states:
"In income and expenditure, in the refinement of wealth, and in the protection of household utensils..."
This protection for women is traditionally prescribed: they should be engaged in purification and fire-rituals.
[609] Manu [9.22–24, 26–28, 8]: With whatever qualities a woman is united with her husband according to the prescribed rule,
she becomes possessed of those same qualities, just as a river is by the ocean.
Akṣamālā, though born of a low womb, attained venerability through her union with Vasiṣṭha;
Śāraṅgī likewise reached a state of honor through Mandapāla.
These and other women in this world, though born of lowly origin,
have attained eminence through their own respective auspicious qualities as wives.
Worthy of procreation, highly fortunate, deserving of honor, and the lights of the home—
there is no difference whatsoever between prosperity and women within households.
The procreation of offspring, the nurturing of those born,
and the daily conduct of worldly life— all these are directly dependent upon women.
Offspring, religious duties, service, and supreme pleasure depend upon the wife;
likewise, heaven for one's ancestors and for oneself is dependent upon her.
The husband, having entered his wife, becomes an embryo and is born here;
for that indeed is the "wifehood" (jāyātva) of the wife, because he is born again from her.
In the Mahābhārata (Ānuśāsana Parva 81.15):
"These women are indeed the personifications of prosperity; they should be honored by one who desires well-being.
O Bhārata, when a woman is both cherished and restrained, she becomes true prosperity."
Where women are honored, there the gods rejoice;
where they are not honored, there all rites are fruitless.
Where female relatives grieve, that family quickly perishes;
but where they do not grieve, that family indeed prospers forever.
Those houses which female relatives, when not properly honored, curse,
perish on all sides as if struck by a magical spell (kṛtyā).
Therefore, those who desire prosperity should always worship these [goddesses] with ornaments, clothing, and food, constantly with due honor, and especially during festivals.
"Kinswomen" (*jāmayaḥ*) refers to women of the family, such as sisters, daughters-in-law, and so forth. Yājñavalkya [1.82] states:
"By the husband, brothers, father, paternal kinsmen, mother-in-law, father-in-law, and brother-in-law..."
And women should be honored by their kinsmen with ornaments, clothing, and food.
Likewise [3.79]:
By failing to provide the milk of her udder, the fetus may incur harm;
it may result in deformity or even death. Therefore, one should do what is pleasing to the woman.
[611] Manu [9.74, 95–96]: A man who has business abroad should depart after providing for his wife’s maintenance;
for a woman, even one of steadfast character, may become corrupt when distressed by a lack of livelihood.
A husband obtains his wife as a gift from the gods, not by his own will;
doing what is pleasing to the gods, he should always support that virtuous woman.
Women were created for procreation, and men for the sake of progeny;
therefore, in the Veda, religious duty is declared to be common to both husband and wife.
‘Sthitimatī’ means endowed with the perfection of family conduct. ‘Prajana’ is the conception of a fetus. ‘Santāna’ is the impregnation.
Thus [it is said]: “If twice-born men should marry women who are their own [caste] or even lower castes... (9.85–87).
Among them, seniority, honor, and residence are determined solely according to the order of their castes.
The wife alone, and no woman of another caste under any circumstances, shall perform the service of her husband’s body and his daily religious duties for all [the deceased husbands].
But he who, out of delusion, causes it to be performed otherwise than by one established in his own caste—
just as a "Brāhmaṇa-Caṇḍāla" was seen before— so indeed is he.

Yājñavalkya [1.88]: When there is another wife of the same caste, one should not have religious duties performed by her. Among wives of the same caste, according to the rule of dharma, no other may act except the eldest.

Viṣṇu [27.1–4]: "When many wives of the same caste are present, one should perform religious duties together with the eldest alone; when they are of mixed castes, even with the youngest who is of the same caste as oneself. In her absence, however, one may do so with the next in order, except in times of distress; but never with a Śūdra wife. Kātyāyana in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*:
"A man with many wives should have service to the sacred fire performed by a wife of the same caste."
In the same way, one should cause [the rites] to be performed if there is plurality [of wives], provided that the eldest is not censured.
Or she who has borne heroic sons, who carries out his commands,
who is skillful, sweet-spoken, and pure— one such as this he should employ here.
Or, according to the sequence of their days, they should divide the work according to seniority and their respective capacities,
and perform it either together or individually, according to their knowledge and without deceit.
The seniority of women arises from their good fortune, just as that of the twice-born arises from learning alone;
for a husband is not satisfied with women by means of mere asceticism.
Wherever a woman, abiding by her husband’s command, serves the sacred fire with many vows, that woman shall attain good fortune.
Dakṣa said:
"The first is the lawful wife, while the second increases pleasure;
the fruit there is indeed visible, for no invisible [result] occurs."
She is declared to be the lawful wife provided she be faultless; if a fault exists, there shall be no [marital] defect, and another woman endowed with virtues should be taken.
With the word "Śūdrā" understood [from the previous context], Manu and Viṣṇu state:
"In that family where the husband is always content with his wife, and likewise the wife with her husband,
there indeed prosperity is certain."
For if a woman does not find pleasure, she will not delight the man; and from the lack of delight on the part of the man, procreation does not proceed.
When a woman is radiant, the entire family shines;
when she is not radiant, nothing at all shines.
Mutual fidelity until death—
this should be known as the supreme duty of husband and wife in brief.
Likewise, once they have performed their rites, the woman and the man should always strive so that,
even when separated from one another, they do not transgress against each other.
Yājñavalkya [1.74]:
Where there is mutual harmony between husband and wife, there the three aims of life flourish.
Dakṣa:
For household life has happiness as its purpose, and that happiness is rooted in the wife;
she is a true wife who understands her husband’s mind and remains under his control.
But she who is compliant, free from verbal faults, skillful, virtuous, and blessed with offspring—endowed with these very qualities, she is indeed the Goddess Śrī herself; of this there is no doubt.
She who is always joyful in mind, discerning in her conduct and status, and who brings delight to her husband—she is a true wife; any other is merely old age.
Vyāsa says:
A woman who rises before [her husband], is skillful, lies on a lower seat,
and is not verbally abusive, is indeed the wife of one who performs meritorious deeds.
Now, Dakṣa says:
For one with two wives, there is undoubtedly constant misery, strife, discord, mutual injury, and suffering.
[615] Manu [9.77–79]: A husband shall wait for one year for a wife who shows him hostility;
after a year has passed, he may give her her property and no longer live with her.
She who transgresses against one who is negligent, intoxicated, or afflicted by disease shall be abandoned for three months, divested of her ornaments and belongings.

There is no abandonment permitted for one who is insane, fallen [from caste], impotent, seedless, or afflicted with a foul disease; nor is there any revocation of the inheritance from such a wife, provided she is not hostile.
Now Nārada [15.95]: He who abandons a wife who is compliant, not wicked in speech, capable, virtuous, and a mother of children, shall be restrained by the king with a heavy punishment.
In the continuation of the phrase "he should punish him like a thief," Viṣṇu [5.162–63] states: "and abandoning a wife who is faultless. Yājñavalkya [1.76] says:
"One who carries out his commands, who is skillful, who gives birth to heroes, and who speaks kindly..."
If he abandons her, he shall be made to pay a third part [of his property]; if he is destitute of wealth, he must provide maintenance for the woman.
Devala says: For a man who, out of delusion, abandons his own wife, who acts unjustly,
and who forsakes the lineage of dharma, no atonement is prescribed.

One may abandon a wife who is afflicted with leprosy, outcaste, barren, insane, or devoid of menses, provided she is not otherwise corrupt; however, one must never abandon her on account of [the husband's] own ritual actions.
‘Anyāyamocinaḥ’: one who releases by means of injustice. ‘Tīrtāt’: from the womb. ‘Karmaṇaḥ’: from evil deeds and the like.
“There would be a fault for two who mutually abandon each other while being opposed to one another.”
In the case of a man and a woman, [the husband may punish her] for adultery, except when it is concealed from the woman.
A woman who has squandered her husband's wealth or her entire property, one who causes a miscarriage,
or one who desires the death of her husband, shall be expelled from the home.
A woman who is habitually intent on what is harmful, likewise one who speaks unpleasantly,
and she who eats before her husband— such a woman he should expel from the home.

One should not, out of desire, take pleasure in a barren woman, one who has given birth [only] to daughters, one who is censurable, or one who is always hostile; by acting in this manner, one incurs no fault.

‘Āgaḥ’ means sin. ‘Nigūḍhā’ means guarded or concealed. ‘Strīdhanabhraṣṭasarvasvām’ refers to one by whom all her possessions have been lost or deprived through [the forfeiture of] woman’s property; here, the root *bhraṃś* (to fall) carries an implied causative sense (*bhraṃśita*).
Yama says: “A woman who, having bathed after her menses, does not approach her husband...”
Having proclaimed her as a killer of an embryo in the midst of the village, one should banish her.
But that woman who, by refusing her husband, passes her fertile seasons in vain,
he shall proclaim among her kinsmen as a killer of the embryo and banish her.
‘With hostility’ means with excessive hatred. Baudhāyana says:
[One should avoid] a woman who is disobedient, barren, unchaste, or harmful.
Wise men quickly abandon a woman who speaks unpleasantly.
One should abandon a wife who bears no children in the tenth year, one whose children are all daughters in the twelfth year,
one whose children die in the fifteenth year, but one who speaks unpleasantly immediately.

Vasiṣṭha [21.9–10]: In cases of sexual intercourse, going on pilgrimages, or turning away from religious duties, four women must be abandoned: she who goes to a disciple and she who goes to her teacher.
And she who is particularly hostile, as well as she who has approached a degraded man;
Yājñavalkya [1.72]: "Purification occurs through her misconduct during her season, but if a child is conceived, abandonment is ordained."
In the case of the murder of their fetus or husband, as well as in other such great sins, for them...

Hārīta: "One should avoid a woman who causes abortion, one who approaches a man of lower caste, one who goes to the son of a disciple, one who is addicted to vices such as gambling, and one who causes the depletion of wealth and grain.
Yama: "And for a woman who acts according to her own will, abandonment is ordained."
One must not commit the murder of a woman, nor indeed the mutilation of a limb.
Vivasvān declared that one should practice renunciation toward a woman who acts according to her own will and is unfaithful; one should avoid imprisoning, disfiguring, or killing women.
[619] Then Yājñavalkya [1.70]: He shall cause her who has been unfaithful twice to dwell deprived of her rights, defiled, subsisting on mere alms, humiliated, and sleeping on the ground.
Nārada [15.91]: In the event of infidelity, women shall undergo shaving of the head, sleeping on the ground,
coarse food, wretched clothing, and the labor of clearing refuse heaps.
73— (b) Now, regarding the duties of women, Manu [5.147–49] states: "By a woman—
whether she be a child, a young woman, or even an aged one— "
One should not perform any action independently, even within one's own home.
In childhood she should remain under the control of her father, in youth under the control of her husband;
when her husband has died, she should not exercise independence even regarding her sons.
A woman should not desire separation from her father, her husband, or even her sons;
for through separation from these, she brings reproach upon both families.
Bṛhaspati [25.9]: A woman should not live in another's house separated from her husband, father, or sons;
especially by associating with the wicked, she certainly incurs reproach.
Yājñavalkya [1.86]:
She must not be deprived of her father, mother, son, brother, mother-in-law, father-in-law, or maternal uncles;
she should not be without her husband, otherwise she would become censurable.
[620] Manu [5.150]: She should always be cheerful, skillful in household duties, keep the utensils well-maintained, and be not wasteful in expenditure.
Yājñavalkya [1.83]: Restraining the household utensils, being skillful, cheerful, and averse to wasteful expenditure,
she should perform the salutation of the feet of her parents-in-law, remaining entirely devoted to her husband.
Bṛhaspati [25.10]: Rising before [the teacher], eating and anointing after him,
and occupying a lower seat or bed— this is declared to be the duty toward women.

Devala states: “Lack of independence, service to the husband, performing religious duties together with him, honoring those whom he honors, hating those whom he hates, being free from malice, constant conformity to his will, and devotion to his affairs—this is the duty of a woman. Viṣṇu [25.2–8] states: “Conducting herself in a manner consistent with her husband’s character; honoring her mother-in-law, father-in-law, elders, deities, and guests; keeping household utensils well-maintained; not being wasteful with her hands; keeping the vessels well-secured; having no delight in gambling and similar base activities; and being devoted to auspicious customs. The Mahābhārata [621] states:
As soon as a husband recognizes his wife as being devoted to spells and roots, he should tremble before her, like one who has entered a house containing a snake.
Regarding the Earth, Viṣṇu spoke these words to Lakṣmī [99.21.22]:
"Among women who are eternally pure, adorned, devoted to their husbands, sweet-spoken, open-handed, possessed of offspring, whose wombs are well-guarded, and who delight in making offerings."

I, the creator of the worlds, abide eternally among those women whose dwellings are well-ordered, who have conquered their senses, who are free from strife, who are devoid of greed, who regard righteousness, and who are endowed with compassion.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "Day after day, she should perform the smearing of the cooking vessels, the thorough sweeping and plastering of the house and its door, and the offering of oblations (*bali*) consisting of curds, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), *dūrvā* grass, sprouts, and flowers—having performed these acts of purification and favor. Following the salutation of her mother-in-law and father-in-law, she should attend to the necessary duties of the household. She should not eat before the gods, servants, or guests. She should not provide any remedy or medicine for anyone other than her husband. Regarding the phrase "day after day, of the cooking vessels": the meaning is that the smearing of the "cooking vessels," such as pots and the like, must be performed on each successive day. [622] Ṛṣyaśṛṅga states:
A householder should always wear ornaments and honor them;
she should worship her braid with holy garments, having performed her daily bath.
One should go into seclusion beforehand, before anyone else has awakened;
there one should perform the propitiation of the deity and offer incense, flowers, and a bali-oblation.
‘Gṛhamedhā’ means one who is intent on household duties. ‘And she should honor the ornaments’ means she should purify the ornaments by cleaning them and so forth.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “A woman shall not go outside unaccompanied; she shall not run about uncovered. She shall not wear perfumes, garlands, ornaments, or discolored garments except on festive occasions. She shall not converse with a stranger, except with merchants, renunciants, or the elderly. She shall not expose her navel. A woman of good family shall wear her garment down to the ankles. She shall not reveal her breasts. She shall not laugh without covering [her mouth], nor in the presence of a large crowd. Regarding the term “uncovered,” it means without covering the mouth with both hands. Vyāsa says:
Constant attendance at the doorway, peering out from the window,
idle chatter, and laughter are the vices that corrupt women of noble family.
Manu [9.13]: Drinking [intoxicants], association with wicked people, separation from her husband, wandering about,
sleeping [at improper times], and dwelling in the company of others— these are the six things that corrupt women.
Bṛhaspati [25.11]: "Drinking, wandering about, sleeping during the day, neglect of duties, and addiction to women.
"Neglect of duties" (*akriyā*) refers to the non-performance of household tasks.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “She should not stay together with courtesans, rogues, female wanderers, female fortune-tellers, deceitful women, those of fraudulent character, or those who have violated their conduct. For through such association, her character may become corrupted. She should not act in opposition to her husband. She should not leave household utensils, vessels, furniture, and goods scattered about, nor should she remain without rising from her bed, seat, or sandals. *Īkṣiṇikā* refers to a female astrologer.

Hārīta says: "Now we shall describe the conduct of the wife. The household belongs to the wife; indeed, one should not know a house as being without a wife. Therefore, the wife should be devoted to the duties of the household. She should keep the house well-swept, well-cleaned, well-prepared with purificatory rites, well-smeared, and honored; she should repair what has fallen into disrepair. She should guard what is unprotected. She should avoid looking at other men, speaking of wicked talk and the like, and associating with wicked ascetics or women. She should not go to the houses of others, to streets, crossroads, market-alleys, or the dwellings of ascetics. She should avoid standing near wells or paths and wandering at the junctions of time (sandhi-velā). She should not, even in thought, set her mind upon the beds, seats, clothes, or ornaments of others until they have been purified again. Likewise, she should avoid sharing a single vessel, liquor, meat, food-leavings, and discarded flower-garlands—except in the case of her teacher, her husband, or her son. She should avoid useless pursuits that involve longing for another man, as well as quarreling, laziness, despondency, and fickleness. She should not enter a temple while impure from food-leavings. She should not cook without sprinkling [the grain], without examining it, or without performing the rite of carrying fire around it (paryagnikaraṇa). She should not take barley-gruel, water for purification, milk, or curdled milk without having washed her hands. Having washed the covers of the pots and the ladles, she should put away the utensils in a secure place. On the following day, after washing them again, she should prepare them for cooking. She should take the milk products and grains according to his instructions. After boiling [the milk], she should wash, smear, and wipe the metallic vessels, and having performed the sweeping and smearing of the house, she should urge him toward the time for the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice for the sake of bathing. Having bathed, put on two white garments, washed her hands and feet, stepped out and sipped water (ācamana), she should enter the temple, pay homage, kindle the fire in the sanctuary, bring the fuel, darbha grass, flowers, offerings (bali), and the vessels for the propitiatory rite (śānti-pātra), sprinkle the food and other daily requirements. When the offering has been made to the gods in the marriage-fire, she should, by the husband's direction, offer a bali to the wives of the gods. After the rites for the gods and guests have been performed, and the householders have been satisfied according to their rank, she should satisfy the disciples, friends, and the husband; then, permitted by him, the wife eats the remainder in a secluded place. Having touched water with the respective parts of her body, and having washed and rinsed the remaining vessels, she should cast them outside in the north-eastern direction, saying, 'Salutation to Rudra, the Lord of Beings and the Protector of the Dwelling. In this same way, she should attend to the evening boiled rice and so forth. According to the purpose, she should close the door with ashes, saying, 'Salutation to the Blessed Rudra who dwells in the ashes; I provide protection with ashes,' and she should touch the master, her sons, and herself, as well as anything else that needs protection. She should not go to bed without having washed her hands and feet; nor naked; nor while still impure from food-leavings; nor without having bowed; nor without having bowed to her husband’s feet; nor without knowing when he has risen. She should rise before him. She should attend to the water-jar. She should follow him and honor the house. She should circumambulate him. She should be peaceful and pleasant in her speech. She should speak kindly to her husband. She should not sit above him. She should not look at him from a high place, nor in a place of deliberation, nor repeatedly. Having surrounded him and massaged him, she should wait upon him. In the heat, she should fan him; in the rain, she should wipe the sweat from his limbs. She should arrange his hair if it is disheveled. When he returns from another village, having crossed over heavy loads, she should approach him with a joyful heart and honor him with the guest-offering (arghya). The observance of vows, religious rites for the gods, or bathing should be performed by her only when permitted."

‘*Kūpapathasthānam*’: standing on a path leading to a well. ‘*Aikapātryam*’: eating together from the same vessel. ‘*Guravaḥ*’: elders such as fathers-in-law and others. ‘*Lolupā*’: longing or desire. ‘*Anarthaḥ*’: useless expenditure of wealth. ‘*Pratyudvadanam*’: speaking in opposition or contrary words. Regarding ‘*taulyam*’, Jayasvāmin says it refers to dress, speech, and so forth that are unsuitable for one’s own family. ‘*Avimṛśya*’: without examining whether there are hair, insects, or other impurities. ‘*Yāvakaḥ*’: a sieve or strainer. ‘*Utpavanam*’: a winnowing fan or sifter. ‘*Asya nirdeśe*’: with the permission of the husband. ‘*Snānahetoḥ*’: for the purpose of bathing; the word “quickly” (*pātu*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. ‘*Yac cānyat*’: “and whatever else,” meaning other items such as *maṇḍakas* (sweet cakes) and so forth. ‘*Āhnikam*’: the food for that day; the ellipsis is that she should stand by after having sprinkled it, with the husband’s permission. ‘*Śeṣam*’: the remainder of the daily meal, even if uneaten. ‘*Prasvābhiḥ*’: with water prepared for her own use. ‘*Upaspṛśya*’: having sipped water (*ācamya*). ‘*Nirṇijya*’: having removed the stains from the food. ‘*Śṛtādi*’: beginning with the boiled milk-rice—having washed and smeared it, and so on, up to the *rudrabali* offering. ‘*Ālabhet*’: she should touch it with her hand smeared with ashes. ‘*Anupasthāyodakadhānā*’: not leaving the water-vessel empty. ‘*Pradakṣiṇā*’: full of enthusiasm. ‘*Vitarkasthānam*’: a place of doubt where people wonder, “Who is she looking at? ‘*Parimṛjya*’: having wiped the dust from her feet. ‘*Saṃvāhayitvā*’: having massaged her limbs. ‘*Vyajanenoṣṇe*’: she should attend to him with a fan during the hot season. ‘*Anavasthitasya*’: of one whose mind is agitated or unsettled.

Kātyāyana in the *Chāndogyapariśiṣṭa* states: "Even toward her husband, a disciplined wife who desires good fortune and freedom from widowhood should serve the sacred fire with devotion to her husband."

[627] "Even by a wife who is constantly assailed by her husband with excessive force, the sacred fire must be served. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "She should not hate her husband, even if he is impotent, fallen from his caste, deformed, or diseased; for the husband is the deity of women. Neither vows, fasts, religious observances, sacrifices, nor the duty of giving are beneficial to women apart from service to the husband. However, the practice of vows, fasts, observances, sacrifices, and so forth, is the duty of a woman when she is permitted by her husband."
Patiṭhīnasi says: “Women are the deities of the household. For them there is no ritual purity, no vow, and no fasting. By service to their husband, they attain the supreme goal. Manu [5.153–54]:
“But when the time for conception has arrived, the husband, having performed the consecration with mantras...”
A wife is the constant giver of happiness both in this world and in the next.
Whether he is lacking in virtue, intoxicated by passion, or devoid of good qualities,
a husband must always be served like a god by a virtuous wife.
Manu and Viṣṇu [Manu 5.155; Viṣṇu 25.15]:
"For women there is no separate sacrifice, no vow, nor even fasting;
by that through which she serves her husband, she is exalted in heaven."
[628] Viṣṇu [25.16]: "That woman who observes a fast or a vow while her husband is still living takes away his life-span and goes to hell."
Yājñavalkya [1.77]:
Women must carry out the word of their husbands; this is the supreme duty established.
For one defiled by a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) is to be awaited until purification.

Gautama [18.1–3]: “A woman is not independent in matters of dharma; she must not transgress against her husband; she should be restrained in speech, sight, and action. Hārīta: “She who is pure in conduct, whose mind is fixed on her husband, is a virtuous wife. For thus it is said: ‘He whose wife is submissive, virtuous, and always speaks kindly...’”
Pure in conduct and with her mind fixed on her husband, she is proclaimed a goddess.”
Manu [5.151, 153]: To whomsoever her father or her brother— by the father’s consent— may give her,
she shall serve him while he lives, and once he has passed away, she must not transgress against him.
A virtuous wife, desiring the world of her husband, should do nothing displeasing to him who took her hand, whether he be living or dead.
‘Saṃsthita’ means dead. Yājñavalkya [1.75, 87]:
She who does not approach another man, whether her husband is dead or alive...
Through this, one attains fame and rejoices together with Umā.
Devoted to what is pleasing and beneficial to her husband, well-conducted, and having conquered her senses,
she attains fame in this world and the unsurpassed state after death.
Manu [5.154, 165, 166]: But she who, from the time of the giving away [in marriage] until the end of her life, remains devoted to her husband,
does not leave the world of her husband, just as Arundhatī did.
She who does not deceive her husband, being restrained in mind, speech, and body,
attains the world of her husband and is called a virtuous woman by the righteous.
By this conduct of a woman, being restrained in mind, speech, and body,
she attains fame in this world and the world of her husband in the next.
‘Patiloka’: the world acquired through sacrifices and other rites performed jointly with the husband.
Kātyāyana states in the *Chāndogyapariśiṣṭa*:
"By service to her husband alone, a woman attains all worlds."
Having returned here from heaven once more, that shall be the limit of her happiness.

[630] Bṛhaspati [25.12]: She who is distressed when her husband is distressed, joyful when he is joyful, dejected and emaciated when he is away from home, and who would die when her husband dies— she is to be known as a woman devoted to her husband (*pativratā*).

Vasiṣṭha [21.14]: For those women who are devoted to their husbands, who are householders, and who are pure in their vows of truth—those worlds are equal to their husbands; but for those who are unchaste, they are the worlds of jackals.
Manu [9.30]: "But by infidelity toward her husband, a woman incurs reproach in this world;
she enters the womb of a jackal and is tormented by foul diseases."
Kātyāyana, in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*, states:
"By transgressing against her husband out of delusion, what various hells might a woman not enter?
Having attained human status through arduous penances, what various sufferings does she not behold?"

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “One should avoid liquor, garlic, onions, leeks, mushrooms, and other such forbidden foods. The body consists of food; because of its being composed of that, a Brahmin is defiled. For the embryo arises from what the mother has eaten and drunk. Manu [9.184]:
“But she who drinks forbidden liquor, even at festive celebrations...”
Or if she goes to a public assembly, she shall be fined six *kṛṣṇalas*.
[631] Vasiṣṭha [21.11]: "The gods do not lead that Brahmin woman who drinks liquor in this world to the world of her husband.
Having exhausted her merit, she wanders right here, having become a female dog, a female donkey, and a female pig."
Now, regarding the wife whose husband has gone abroad, Manu [9.75] says:
"When her husband has gone abroad, she should maintain herself by providing for his livelihood, remaining steadfast in her observances."
But if he has gone abroad, she may live even without his authorization by means of blameless crafts.
Yājñavalkya [1.74]: A woman whose husband is away from home should abandon play, bodily adornment, social gatherings, witnessing festivals, laughter, and traveling to the houses of others.

Bṛhaspati [25.13]: While her husband is away on a journey, she should not engage in personal adornment, nor attend dances, songs, social gatherings, or festivals, nor should she indulge in meat or liquor.
Viṣṇu [25.9–11]: “When her husband has gone abroad, she should not apply cosmetics; she should not visit the houses of others; and she should not linger at doorways or windows.”

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “When her husband has gone abroad, a Brāhmaṇī woman must protect her virtue; for others, it is the mother and father, or next, the king. For noble women whose husbands are away, who are not independent, there shall be no engagement in swinging, dancing, strolling, viewing spectacles, applying cosmetics, visiting gardens, sleeping in open beds, excessive drinking and eating, playing with balls, using incense, perfumes, garlands, ornaments, tooth-cleansing sticks, collyrium, looking in mirrors, or adorning themselves.”

Regarding the phrase “of all,” and so forth: among all women whose husbands are away, the Brāhmaṇī woman herself must protect her own character; however, for other women whose husbands are away, their mother and father shall protect them. And in the absence of those two, the King shall protect them. This is stated with reference to women who have but one husband. A *preṅkhā* is a swing. Hārīta says: “She should not adorn herself while her husband is away, nor should she loosen her braid. Now, regarding the woman whose husband has died:
In this regard, Aṅgiras says:
"The woman who, upon the death of her husband, ascends the funeral fire,
is equal in conduct to Arundhatī and is glorified in the heavenly world."
As many as there are hairs on a human being— thirty million and half a million—
for that many years she who follows her husband goes to heaven.
Just as a snake-catcher forcibly drags a serpent out from its hole,
even so, having seized her husband, she goes away with him.
A woman who follows her husband purifies three lineages: that of her mother, that of her father, and that of the one to whom she is given as a bride.
There, devoted solely to her husband and intensely longing for him, she sported with her lord for as long as fourteen Indras [reigned].
"Whether a man be a slayer of a Brahmin, ungrateful, or even a slayer of a friend, that woman indeed purifies him; so it was spoken by Aṅgiras."
For virtuous women alone,
when their husband has died, no other duty is ever to be recognized here except for entering the fire.
As long as a devoted wife does not burn her body in the fire upon the death of her husband,
so long shall she not be released from the female body by any means whatsoever.
For those women whose husbands have been entrusted to the care of virtuous conduct, and who are distressed by the wounds of separation—
when their power has faded, what path remains for them other than entering the fire?

‘*Sadvṛttāḥ*’: *vṛtta* means conduct; *bhāva* means intention. Those women by whom these two are beautifully maintained are so described. ‘*Viyogakṣatakātarāṇām*’: *viyoga* (separation) itself is the ‘*kṣata*’ (wound), a festering sore; those who are distressed (*kātarāṇām*) by that. ‘*Prabhau*’: in the husband. ‘*Kaṃ*’: heaven. Vyāsa says:
“The devoted wife who, having heard that her beloved is dead while staying in another land...”
Understand her power as she swiftly ascends into the fire.
If he has entered hell, bound by most dreadful nooses,
arrived at the place of torment, and seized by the servants of Yama;
Helpless and miserable, he stands writhing under the power of his own past actions,
just as a snake-catcher fearlessly seizes a serpent by force.
In that same way, taking her husband with her, she goes to heaven by the power of her asceticism;
there, devoted supremely to her husband, she is praised by hosts of Apsarases.
She sports with her husband as long as fourteen Indras [endure].
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"When her husband has died, there is no other destination for virtuous women."
Nowhere else is there any remedy for the burning caused by the fire of separation from one's husband.
If he has died in another land, the virtuous wife, having placed his two sandals upon her breast and being purified,
may enter the fire.
According to the teaching of the Ṛgveda, a virtuous woman shall not be considered a suicide;
rather, once the three-day period of impurity has passed, she receives the funeral rites (śrāddha) in accordance with the scriptures.

[635] “From the teaching of the *Ṛgveda*”—that is, from such mantras as “These women are not widows,” and so forth. Thus, by considering all the scriptural statements, the entitlement to either simultaneous death (*sahamaraṇa*) or following in death (*anumaraṇa*) belongs to all wives of Brahmins and others—provided they desire specific fruits pertaining to themselves or their husbands—excluding those who are pregnant or have young children. Bṛhaspati says:
“A woman is declared to be half the body [of her husband], equal in the fruits of merit and demerit.”
Whether she ascends after him while still living or dies with him, that virtuous wife acts for the welfare of her husband.
Viṣṇu [25.14]: “When her husband has died, she shall observe celibacy or follow him by ascending the funeral pyre.”

Hārīta says: "If one who has maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni) should die, she should take the embers of the *aupāsana* fire, perform the *sūtrasvana* sacrifice with oblations of clarified butter (*sarpirājyā*), and not remain [without a fire]. If he was not an *āhitāgni*, she should take another fire; or, having taken the public fire (*janāgni*), avoiding the houses of her husband’s father or her own kin, with her speech, hands, feet, and senses controlled, virtuous in conduct, and mourning her husband day and night, she—through vows and fasts, with her life-span exhausted—conquers the world of her husband at the end and does not again suffer separation from her husband. For thus it is said:"
But that virtuous woman who is devoted to her husband reaches steadfastness when her lord has died;
having abandoned all sins, she shall attain the world of her husband.

‘*Avakṣāṇam*’ refers to a half-burnt log or a firebrand. ‘*Āyaṃ gauḥ*’: these are the three verses beginning with *āyaṃ gauḥ*, which have clarified butter as their subject. One should take another domestic fire according to the procedure for the formal establishment (*ādhāna*). ‘*Janāgni*’ is the social or assembly fire. Bṛhaspati [25.15]: “Devoted to vows and fasting, established in celibacy (*brahmacarya*).”
One who is constantly devoted to self-restraint and charity shall go to heaven, even if she is childless.
She may indeed emaciate her body with pure flowers, roots, and fruits;
but she must not even utter the name of another man once her husband has died.
Until death she remained patient, self-controlled, and chaste,
longing for that unsurpassed Dharma which belongs to women devoted to a single husband.
Many thousands of brahmins who practiced celibacy from their youth have gone to heaven without producing offspring to continue their lineage.
When her husband has died, a virtuous woman who remains steadfast in celibacy goes to heaven even if she is childless, just like those who are lifelong celibates.
But that woman who, out of greed for offspring, transgresses against her husband,
incurs reproach in this world and is excluded from the world of her husband.
No offspring born here belongs to anyone other than the father, nor does it belong to another's possession;
for virtuous women, a second husband is nowhere prescribed.
[638] After the husband's death, Yama says:
"As long as she lives, she should remain constantly seated, self-controlled, and chaste,
desiring that dharma which belongs to women who have only one husband."
Neither in the Veda nor in the Śāstra is renunciation prescribed for a woman;
for her own duty is procreation through a man of her own caste—this is the settled rule.
Eighty-eight thousand sages,
brahmins of sublimated vital energy, have gone to heaven without having established a lineage for their families.
In the same way, a maiden who has turned away from worldly life and remains established in celibacy shall attain heaven even without sons, just like those lifelong celibates.
Whether she is childless or has given birth to a son, a maiden who remains devoted to her husband shall attain heaven alone; so said Manu, the son of Svayambhū.
‘Ekapatnīnām’ means of those who have had only one husband. ‘Kanyā’ here refers to a married woman. Kātyāyana [837] states:
“Even when the husband has died, though he was tainted by many defects, or at any time...”
She should abide in virtuous conduct, devoted to the service of her elders.
That virtuous woman who, upon the death of her husband,
remains established in celibacy and conducts herself like Arundhatī, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
[ga] Now, regarding the formal injunction (*niyoga*), Manu [states in 9.59]:
When the lineage is on the verge of extinction, a woman who has been duly authorized by her husband or by a sapinda relative may, with the desire for offspring, obtain progeny.
Commissioned by her elders, she may approach her brother-in-law out of a desire for a son;
and he, being likewise childless and single-minded, should accept her.
Upon the birth of a son, he should return; otherwise, there would be calamity.
Having anointed his limbs with clarified butter or with unrefined oil, he should depart.
Avoiding face-to-face contact and not touching limb to limb,
he did so because that family was the last remaining one and for the sake of progeny, not out of lust.
Authorized by his elders, he may approach the wife of his younger brother;
however, if no elder is present, the destruction of the family must be reported to the king.
Then, at her word, he should go and instruct his wife;
being pure, he should do so during the *puṃsavana* rite according to the previously mentioned procedure for a woman who has bathed.
Once the embryo has been conceived, she remains so until the rite of impregnation (garbhadhāna) is performed;
otherwise, if one acts differently out of desire, whether a man or a woman, [one incurs sin].
The two should be strictly disciplined by the king; otherwise, there would be disorder.
Yama says: "But when she has bathed after her menses, he, restrained in speech, [should approach her] at night during the dark fortnight."
They experienced the smell and touch of their own beards, nails, and body hair.
Clad in a single garment, his limbs smeared with clarified butter, foul-smelling, sorrowful and dejected,
he avoided face-to-face encounters and did not touch limb to limb.
One who has restrained himself may take up the embryo; once the embryo is conceived, however, he should depart.
He should not approach a woman who has already borne a child, nor likewise once a son has been born.
Those who desire the continuation of their paternal lineage for their deceased ancestors should have all the rites performed, beginning with the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana).

Yājñavalkya [1.68–69]: Having been authorized by his elder, a brother-in-law, a sapinda, or one of the same lineage (gotra), being anointed with clarified butter and desiring a son, may approach a childless woman during her fertile period.
He may approach [the wife] until conception occurs; otherwise, he would become fallen.
By this rule, the son born is his *kṣetraja* (son of the soil).

Devala says: A husband who has disappeared, one who has renounced the world, one who is impotent, one who has fallen from his caste, one who has committed an offense against the king, or even one who has gone to another world, must be abandoned by his wife.
Whether her husband is dead or alive, a woman may take another husband for the sake of not destroying the lineage; women possess no independence.
