A Brāhmaṇa woman whose husband has gone abroad should wait for eight years if she is childless; but if she has borne children, she should wait for four years. Beyond that period, she may take another husband.

A Kṣatriya woman who has not borne children may wait for six years; one who has borne children may wait for three years. A Vaiśya woman who has borne children may wait for four years, while one who has not borne children may wait for two years.
No specific time is prescribed for a Śūdra woman, nor is there any transgression of dharma; especially for one who has not yet borne a child, her period of waiting lasts for one year.
This period is prescribed for women whose husbands have gone abroad when there is no news of them;
however, if they are heard to be living, this rule shall be doubled.
This is the conduct of women regarding the procreation of offspring, ordained by Prajāpati;
therefore, no fault is found in women for approaching another man for this purpose.
Now, regarding the section on the *sapinda* relationship with a brother-in-law, Manu [9.64–67] states:
"A widow must not be appointed to another man by members of the twice-born classes;
for those who appoint her to another would destroy the eternal Dharma."
Nowhere in the mantras pertaining to marriage is the practice of *niyoga* (appointment) mentioned;
nor is the remarriage of a widow prescribed in the rules for the wedding ceremony.
Indeed, this practice of treating humans like cattle was condemned by learned brahmins when Vena was ruling the kingdom.
In former times, while ruling over the entire earth, that most excellent of royal sages,
his mind overcome by lust, brought about the intermixture of the social orders.
From that time forward, virtuous men censure anyone who, out of delusion, employs a woman whose husband has died for the sake of obtaining offspring.

Regarding the case of a woman whose husband has died, Vasiṣṭha [17.64–66] states: “If there should be two persons authorized for *niyoga*, there is no *niyoga* if it arises from greed for inheritance; or some say that one may authorize her after prescribing an expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
Kātyāyana says: “One should perform the purification prescribed for *niyoga* for the sake of her spiritual cleansing.”
This is the duty regarding the wives of the twice-born; some maintain that it is always the refuge for the Śūdra as well.
Bṛhaspati [Saṃskāra 267–69]: The practice of *niyoga* was indeed mentioned by Manu, but he himself prohibited it;
due to the decline of the age, this cannot be performed by mortals according to the prescribed rules.
In the Kṛta and Tretā Yugas, men were endowed with austerity and knowledge;
however, in the Dvāpara and Kali Yugas, a decline in the power of men has been ordained.
The sons who were produced in manifold ways by the ancient seers cannot be produced now by us moderns, who lack such power.
73 — (gha) Now, regarding women who have had previous husbands, Nārada says [15.45–53]: "Other women who have had previous husbands are said to be sevenfold, in their respective order."
A remarried woman is of three kinds, and a wanton woman is of four kinds.
A maiden who, though her virginity remains intact, has been defiled by the taking of the hand in marriage,
is declared the first type of *punarbhū* (a remarried woman) by virtue of the rite of re-consecration.
She who, having abandoned her husband from childhood, resorts to another man and then returns again to her husband's house, is proclaimed as the second [type].
When no suitable bridegrooms are available, a woman may be given by her kinsmen to a sapinda of the same caste; this is proclaimed as the third [form of marriage].
A woman, whether she has borne children or not,
who out of lust resorts to another man while her husband is still alive, is indeed the first type of *svairiṇī* (an unchaste woman).
But that woman who, upon the death of her husband, sets aside her brother-in-law and others and follows him out of lust, she is proclaimed as the second [type of remarried woman].
She who has been abducted from her country or sold, and who, afflicted by the calamities of hunger and thirst,
approaches you saying "I am yours"— she is proclaimed as the third type.
When a woman, having disregarded the local customs, is given by her elders to another man out of impulsive passion,
she is declared to be a *svairiṇī* (an unchaste woman).
This rule for women who have remarried and for those who live according to their own will has been proclaimed;
among them, each preceding one is inferior, while each succeeding one is superior.
Manu says: She who, abandoning her own inferior husband, serves one who is superior,
becomes censurable in the world and is called "one who has had a previous husband."

Having stated, "There are three types of *punarbhūs* and four types of *svairiṇīs*," Śaṅkha and Likhita say: "Among them, each preceding one is superior to the following; regarding the inheritance, the funeral rice-ball (*piṇḍa*), and the water-offerings (*udaka-yajña*) for their offspring, whatever variation exists is explained as being due solely to the mother's qualities. Yājñavalkya [1.67] says:
"The *akṣatā* and the *kṣatā*, as well as the *punarbhū* who has been consecrated again..."
She who, having abandoned her husband of equal caste, resorts to another out of desire is a wanton woman (svairiṇī).
Hārīta says: "The wanton woman, the remarried woman, the woman who bears seed [to another], the woman who acts according to her own will,
and the woman who eats all things— these five are to be known as those born from the womb of a Śūdra."
Whatever offspring may ever be born of these women, one should not admit them into the rows [of diners]; they are recorded as being unworthy of the row.
A "retodhā" is the mother of a *kuṇḍa*. A "kāmacāriṇī" is one who goes to another man after [the husband] has passed four years [of marriage]. A "sarvabhakṣyā" is a drinker of *surā*. Kātyāyana says:
"A woman who engages [in intercourse] for her own pleasure, and not with the desire for a son for her husband..."
She may indeed give birth to a son, but she is considered blameworthy and sinful.
If a woman, having abandoned the family name of her husband, takes refuge with another,
she is censured in the world and is called one who has had a previous husband.
Wherever a woman previously married to another may reside, her husband is no longer her master;
yet, according to this law, she shall belong to him who wins her by succession or by capture.
She who has committed an offense against another should be restrained and beaten;
however, one who beats her while disregarding her lack of forbearance deserves punishment.
Having rescued [her] from the hands of thieves, from the current of a river, from famine, and from the upheaval of the country;
having found her in a wilderness dwelling, and having abandoned her after she was obtained through traditional succession.
"There shall be no fault in their enjoyment [of property]," such is the settled conclusion of the scriptures;
however, she may take what is given by her husband, but not otherwise than that.
If a woman does not consent when she is being given away, she should neither be given nor accepted; this is the rule remembered by Bhṛgu.
One should not sell a woman who is excellent, nor one who is unwilling, nor likewise one who has sons;
however, such a woman may be released by means of an appropriate ransom.

Thus ends the section on the Union of Men and Women in the *Vyavahārakāṇḍa* (Section on Judicial Procedure) of the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Mallakṣmīdhara, son of Bhaṭṭa Śrī Hṛdayadhara, who served as the Great Minister for Peace and War (*Mahāsāndhivigrahika*) to His Majesty, the Emperor of Emperors (*Mahārājādhirāja*), the illustrious Govindacandradeva.
[648] 74—Now, the division of inheritance;
regarding this, Nārada [says]: [26.2]
Where the partition of paternal property is effected by sons,
that is declared by the wise to be the legal subject of dispute known as "Inheritance" (dāyabhāga).

Manu [9.104]: After the death of both the father and the mother, the brothers, having assembled, shall divide the paternal inheritance equally; for they have no power over it while the parents are alive.
Devala says: When the father has passed away, the sons shall divide the father’s wealth;
for as long as the father remains free from defect, they would have no ownership over it.
‘Without fault’ means being free from such things as causing loss of caste (*pātitya*).
Nārada [16.2]:
“When the father has passed away, the sons shall divide the father’s wealth.”
In the absence of the mother, [the inheritance goes to] the daughters; in the absence of the daughters, their offspring.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “From this point forward is the division of inheritance. They should not divide the inheritance while the father is alive. Even if it should be acquired by them later, the sons are indeed unworthy [of such a share], because they lack independence in matters of wealth and dharma. Regarding the phrase “even if acquired later,” this refers to property obtained subsequently by sons who were previously incapable but later became capable through learning and other means, without depending on the management of the paternal estate. Manu [9.105–110]:
The eldest alone shall take the paternal wealth in its entirety;
the remaining brothers shall depend upon him, just as they did upon their father.
[650] By the mere birth of a firstborn son, a man becomes a father of a son;
he is indeed freed from his debt to the ancestors, and for that reason, he deserves everything.
He upon whom one pays off a debt, and through whom one attains infinity—he alone is known as the son born of dharma; others they know as born of desire.
The eldest brother should protect his younger brothers like a father protects his sons; and they, in accordance with dharma, should behave toward their eldest brother as sons do toward their father.
The eldest son causes the family to prosper or, conversely, brings it to ruin;
the eldest is most worthy of honor in the world, and the eldest is not censured by the virtuous.
He who is the eldest and behaves as an elder, like a mother and like a father, should be honored; but he who does not behave as an elder should be treated with respect only as a kinsman.
Likewise [9.214]:
"And the elder brother shall not make a *yautuka* (separate property) for himself without having given [a share] to the younger brothers.
"*Yautuka*" refers to separate property, such as cattle and so forth.
Nārada [16.5]:
Or, if they so desire, the eldest brother may support all like a father;
or a capable younger brother may do so. In the family, the maintenance depends upon one's capacity.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "They may certainly live together in a group and declare their mutual prosperity.
Manu (9.111) says: "In this manner they may live together or separately, out of a desire for dharma."
The dharma increases separately; therefore, the ritual action pertaining to the dharma is performed separately.
Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 26.5]:
For those living together in a single household, the worship of the ancestors, the gods, and the twice-born shall be one;
for those who are divided, that same worship shall be performed in each individual house.

Hārīta states: "While the father is alive, sons have no independence regarding the receipt, expenditure, or disposal of wealth; however, if the father is away on a journey or afflicted by illness, the eldest son alone shall manage the affairs of the estate."

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "If the father is incapable, the eldest son, or the next younger brother who understands the affairs, shall manage the family business with his permission. However, there is no division of the inheritance while the father is unwilling. If he is aged, mentally deranged, or chronically ill, the eldest alone shall protect the assets for the others like a father; for the family is rooted in the inheritance. Sons are dependent as long as their father lives. The same applies when the mother is in such a state. [652] 'Anantara' means the younger brother. 'With his permission' means with the permission of the eldest. The connection is that "sons" are "dependent."
Now, the division of property while the father is still living.
Regarding this, Manu and Viṣṇu state:
"But whatever paternal wealth one may acquire without having received it from the paternal estate..."
One who has no desire for it should not share with his sons that which was acquired by himself.
‘Inaccessible’ (*anavāpyam*): that which was neglected by a father due to incapacity or other reasons cannot be acquired by another.
Yājñavalkya [2.121]: Land acquired by a grandfather, or a leasehold (*nibandha*), or even property itself...
In that case, the ownership of both father and son would be equal.
‘Nibandha’ refers to a fixed income granted by a king or others from mines and so forth. Bṛhaspati [26.14, 58, 59] states:
“In the case of property acquired by a grandfather, whether immovable or movable...”
For it has indeed been declared that the father and the son have equal shares.
Regarding that which was seized from the grandfather, that which was acquired by the father through his own power,
or that obtained by means of learning, valor, and so forth— the father’s ownership over that is declared in the Smṛti.
One may make a gift at one's own will and take a portion from that wealth;
in the absence of such [a gift], the sons are declared to be entitled to equal shares.
Regarding the entitlement to partition, Nārada [13.3] states:
"When the mother’s menses have ceased, when the sisters have been given away in marriage,
and when the father has ceased from sexual pleasure and his desire has subsided, then the sons shall divide [the estate]."
‘When the pleasure has ceased’: when the power of sexual enjoyment has ceased.
Bṛhaspati [26.9]:
"The partition among brothers in the absence of the parents has been fully demonstrated."
It is also commended when the mother’s menses have ceased, even while both parents are still living.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “The division of the inheritance is permitted while the father is alive, whether openly or privately, in accordance with dharma.

Hārīta states: “Or, while still living, he may divide [the estate] and retire to the forest; or he may enter the stage of a recluse (vṛddhāśrama); or, having divided it into small portions, he may live taking the greater share for himself. If that [share] should diminish, he may take more from them; and he should divide [the remainder] when they have become impoverished. [654] The word *upadaśyet* means “it should diminish.”
Viṣṇu [17.1]: "If the father divides the property among his sons, he may do so according to his own will regarding wealth acquired by himself.
Yājñavalkya [2.114–15]:
"If the father makes a partition, he may divide the sons according to his own will."
Either the eldest shall receive the best portion, or all may be equal sharers.
If he should divide the shares equally,
the wives whose property (strīdhana) has not been given by their husband or by their father-in-law must be made equal sharers.

Nārada [16.12]: When dividing his own property, a father shall take two shares for himself. Regarding the father’s authority, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “If he has only one son, he should set aside two shares for himself; among bipeds and quadrupeds, he should take an extra form. A bull is for the eldest; a house is for the youngest. This applies except in the case of the father’s own residence.”
Baudhāyana [2.3.6–7]: “The eldest shall set aside one from ten; the others shall divide the remainder equally.
“Of ten” refers to ten items consisting of cattle, horses, and so forth.

Āpastamba [2.13.12; 2.14.1]: “Having satisfied the eldest with a single choice portion (*ekadhana*), he shall divide the rest among his sons equally, excluding the impotent, the insane, and the outcaste.”
‘With a single asset’ means with one asset, such as a cow or the like.
Manu [9.215]: “If there should be a joint effort among brothers who are undivided...”
In that case, the father must by no means allot an unequal share.
Nārada [16.15]:
But for those who have been divided by the father himself with shares of wealth that are equal, less, or more, that very same rule shall apply; for the father alone is the master of all.
Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 26.15]:
Those shares which have been assigned by the father, whether equal, deficient, or excessive, must be maintained exactly as they were; otherwise, those sons should be disciplined.
Now follows the partition among those whose father has died;
therein is the special portion (*uddhāra*).
On this point, Manu says (9.112–14):
The eldest shall receive a twentieth part as his preferential share, and whatever is the best among all the property;
half of that shall be the share of the middlemost, and a fourth for the youngest.
Both the eldest and the youngest shall take their shares as prescribed;
those others who are between the eldest and the youngest shall receive that which constitutes the middle portion of the wealth.
The first-born shall take the best of all kinds of wealth;
furthermore, he shall receive as his special portion whatever is most excellent among ten [shares].

"‘A twentieth part as an extra share for the eldest,’ and so forth—meaning that from the middle portion of the wealth, a twentieth part should be set aside and taken as an additional share for the eldest. And the ‘half and a quarter’ parts are likewise in relation to that twentieth part. Therefore, from the middle portion of the wealth, a fortieth part should be set aside and taken as an additional share for the middle son. It is thus stated that for the youngest, it is an eightieth part. Furthermore, this extra share applies specifically to an eldest son and others who possess virtuous qualities."

Gautama [28.5–8]: “A twentieth part of the best share consists of a pair of animals, a chariot yoked on both sides, and a bull. For the middle son, there may be several [of these], including those that are one-eyed, lame, hornless, or tailless. For the youngest, there is a sheep, an iron implement, a house, a yoked cart, and one of each type of four-footed animal. All else shall be divided equally. ‘Kūṭaḥ’ means one deficient in horns. ‘Vaṇḍaḥ’ means a young ram that has not yet been castrated. ‘Anaḥ’ means a cart.

Hārīta says: "When a herd of cattle is to be divided, they should give one bull—either as the *ekadhana* (the singular prize) or as the most excellent prize—to the eldest; and likewise the temple of the deity. The others should go outside and perform [the division]. Or, in a single [herd], the right [bull] belongs to the eldest, and the others follow in order."

‘Ekadhanam’ means the most excellent wealth. ‘Devatāḥ’ refers to images of Viṣṇu and other deities worthy of worship. ‘Gṛham’ means the paternal home. Regarding the phrase “having gone out, they should [make]...”, the ellipsis is to be supplied as “other houses for the purpose of their own residence. The meaning of the passage beginning with “in one alone” is this: when, having gone out, it is impossible to construct other houses, then the “southern”—meaning the principal or best—should belong “to the eldest,” that is, for the sake of the eldest son.
Āpastamba [2.14.7–8]: “In a specific region, gold, black cows, and black land belong to the eldest; a chariot and household utensils belong to the father.

‘Land-born’ (*bhauma*) refers to things produced from the earth, such as sesame and beans. ‘Utensils’ (*paribhāṇḍa*) refers to items such as eating vessels. Baudhāyana [2.2.9]: “In the absence of the father, cattle, horses, goats, and sheep constitute the share of the eldest among the four castes.”
Devala says:
Among sons of equal status, an equal inheritance is desired for all;
however, one should assign a tenth part to the eldest who has conducted himself according to the law.
‘The middle inheritance’ refers to the middle wealth, which is the twentieth part.
[658] This concerns the division of brothers born of multiple mothers.

Now, Manu [9.122–24]: "If a doubt should arise as to how the division of property should be made in a case where the younger son was born of the elder wife and the elder son was born of the younger wife— "
The eldest son shall take one bull as his preferential share;
the others shall have bulls inferior to that, according to their respective mothers.
But the son born of the eldest wife shall take a bull and sixteen shares;
thereafter, the remaining sons shall divide [the estate] according to their mothers—this is the settled rule.

‘He’ is one born from the first [wife]. ‘The elder-born’ (*pūrvajaḥ*) refers to the younger son of the eldest wife (*jyaiṣṭhineya*). Regarding the phrase ‘those others than him’: ‘than him’ means than the most excellent bull; the meaning is that those other bulls belong to those who are younger in age but older by virtue of their mothers. ‘Sixteen bulls’ means those cows which have sixteen bulls. ‘The remainder’ refers to the other cows. Gautama [28.14–16] states: “An extra bull belongs to the eldest. Sixteen bulls belong to the son of the eldest wife (*jyaiṣṭhineya*). The younger brothers share equally with the son of the eldest wife. ‘Equally’ (*samadhā*) means in an equal manner.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "The bull is the additional share for the eldest; the house belongs to the youngest, except for the father's residence. Bṛhaspati [26.24–25] says:
"If many are born of one [father], equal in terms of caste and number..."
From that, it should be divided among the co-wives according to their respective shares of the mother, in accordance with the law.
When there are sons of the same caste but of different numbers, the preferential share (*uddhāra*) among them is recommended; as Manu [9.115] states:
"There is no preferential share for those who are all equally accomplished in their own duties."
Whatever may be given to one's superior should be such as increases one's merit.
"In ten," the remainder is "among cows and so forth. Likewise [9.125–26]:
"For sons born of wives of equal status, there is no distinction."
There is no seniority by reason of the mother; seniority is said to be by reason of birth.
In the Subrahmaṇyā formulas, it is traditionally taught that the invocation is made according to birth-order;
and even in the case of twins conceived together, seniority is determined by birth.
A specific mantra called the *Subrahmaṇyā*, beginning with “O Indra, come! (*indra āgaccha*), is sung by the Chandogas during the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. Devala says:
“Because of their conduct among the outcaste classes and because they were twins from a previous birth...”
Of whomsoever, as soon as he is born, they see the face first among twins.
The lineage and the ancestral offerings depend upon him; in him seniority is established.
Manu [9.213]: "If an eldest brother, out of greed, should defraud his younger brothers..."
Thus he would be deprived of his seniority and his share, and must be restrained by the kings.
‘Vinikurvīta’ means he should deceive. Manu [9.116–17]:
“In this way, when the preferential share has been set aside, one should assign equal shares.”
But if their extraction has not been performed, this shall be the calculation of shares.
The eldest son shall take one share more than the others; the next younger shall take one and a half shares;
and each younger brother shall take one share—thus is the law established.

Gautama [28.9–13]: “Or the first-born shall receive two shares; each of the others shall receive one share. Or, the eldest may receive one desirable item of property for each preceding [brother]. This applies to livestock in groups of ten, but not to single-hoofed animals or bipeds. Regarding the phrase “of livestock in groups of ten”: the meaning is that he receives ten head of livestock.

Vasiṣṭha [17.40, 42–45]: “Now, regarding the division of inheritance among brothers: the eldest shall take two shares; from the cattle and horses, he shall take one out of every ten; the goats, sheep, and the house belong to the youngest; and the iron implements and household utensils belong to the middlemost. Regarding the phrase “one out of every ten of the cattle and horses”: the meaning is that having set aside one from each group of ten cattle and horses, the eldest shall take them.
An additional share for the eldest is to be given, and a smaller share is prescribed for the youngest;
the remaining [sons] shall have equal shares, as shall an unmarried sister.
And likewise among sons born of the field, who are begotten according to the law.

‘Among those born of the field (kṣetraja) who are born according to dharma,’ ‘in the same manner’ means that the allotment of shares should be made just as for the legitimate son of the body (aurasa).
Nārada [13.3]: ‘When the mother’s menses have ceased and the sisters have been given away in marriage...’
And when his father had desisted from pleasure and his desires had ceased, [he remained there].
[662] Bṛhaspati (Vyavahāra 26.21): "The eldest by birth, learning, or virtue shall receive two shares of the inheritance;
the others, however, shall share equally, for he is equal to the father."
Uśanas:
This division of the castes born in the direct order has been proclaimed;
now, however, the division of those born from equal [unions] is prescribed.
Yājñavalkya [2.117]: Sons shall divide the inheritance and the debt equally after the death of both parents.
Likewise [2.120]:
When the property arises as a common whole, however, an equal division is made;
but for those who have more than one father, the allotment of shares is according to the fathers.

Regarding the phrase “in the case of the joint production of wealth”: when there is a proper increase or growth of common property through agriculture and other means, then the division shall be equal. The meaning is that in such a case, one should not take into account whether more was acquired by one person than by another. Regarding the phrase “of those who have multiple fathers”: this refers to the sons of several brothers; even if their number is equal or unequal, when the grandfather’s wealth is being divided, whatever share belonged to their respective fathers becomes theirs alone. The meaning is that there is no further apportionment of shares for each individual son. Bṛhaspati [26.18]:

But whatever is acquired by those who are united, all of them are entitled to equal shares therein; their sons, whether of unequal or equal status, are declared to be the heirs to their father's share.
[663] Kātyāyana [855–56]: When a paternal kinsman has died while undivided, one should provide for his son with that means of livelihood which was not obtained from the grandfather.
He shall receive his paternal share from his uncle or from that uncle’s son;
for according to justice, that very share belongs equally to all the brothers.
Or his son may obtain it; thereafter, there shall be cessation [of rebirth].
Devala says:

For kinsmen who live together, whether they were previously undivided or have become divided, there may be a further partition of the inheritance up to the fourth generation; such is the settled rule.
Until then, the kinsmen shall be sapinda; immediately thereafter, however, there is a division of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa).
They desire an equal distribution of the funeral cakes as well as of the inheritance.
This rule has been declared for many [sons] of the same caste;
there shall be only one [representative] of the same caste, and the inheritance in this case is not divided.
‘Of those both undivided and divided’: that is, of those who are undivided and those who are divided.

Vasiṣṭha [17.40–41] states: “Now follows the division of inheritance among brothers; and as for those women who are childless, [the division continues] until the acquisition of sons. Here, ‘women’ refers to the wives of the brothers. Regarding the phrase ‘until the acquisition of sons’—if it is possible for them to obtain sons, then a share must also be given to them. However, if no son is born, then that share belongs to the brothers, while for those women there is merely maintenance.
[664] Yājñavalkya [2.123]: "When dividing after the father's death, the mother also shall take an equal share.
Regarding the word "father," Bṛhaspati [26] continues:
In her absence, however, the mother is entitled to an equal share with the sons;
likewise: "The mothers shall have equal shares with them, and the daughter shall have a fourth part."

A "fourth part" (*turīyāṃśaḥ*) means that, in relation to the share of a brother of the same caste, a fourth portion of the paternal estate should be assigned for the sake of the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*). As for the statement of Viṣṇu (18.34–35): "Mothers are entitled to shares according to the portions of their sons, as are unmarried daughters," even that, in accordance with the present rule, refers only to a fourth share for the daughters. Vyāsa states:
"The childless wives of the father are declared to have equal shares."
And all those paternal grandmothers are proclaimed to be equal to one's own mothers.
Now Bṛhaspati [26.19]:
"All sons are indeed heirs to the paternal estate according to their respective shares;
among them, one who is endowed with learning and virtuous conduct deserves to receive a larger portion."
He whose fame is celebrated here for his learning, discernment, valor, knowledge of meaning, generosity, and action— by him his ancestors truly possess a son.
[665] Nārada [16.35]: He who is engaged in the affairs of the family and performs that work must be supported by his brothers with food, clothing, and transport.
Manu [9.207]: But among brothers, he who, though capable by his own labor, does not desire the wealth,
shall be excluded from his share after being given something for his subsistence.

Āpastamba [2.14.14–15]: “For all who are endowed with righteousness are entitled to shares. But even the eldest, if he disposes of property unrighteously, one should exclude him from his share. Now, regarding those unworthy of a share, Gautama [28.41] states: “According to some, even the son of a wife of the same caste does not receive a share if he is of improper conduct.”
Manu [9.214]: "All brothers who persist in improper occupations do not deserve the inheritance.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "Brothers do not deserve the wealth of one who has been excluded from the community, nor his funeral oblations, nor the rice-ball offerings, nor the water libations."
Bṛhaspati [26.34–37]:
Even one born of a wife of the same caste is not entitled to paternal wealth if he lacks good qualities;
that [wealth] is declared to belong to those Śrotriyas who offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) for him.
A son protects his father from creditors;
therefore, there is no purpose in one who acts contrary to that.
What is the use of that cow which is neither a milch-cow nor pregnant?
And what is the purpose of that son who is neither learned nor righteous?
A son who is devoid of learning, heroism, and wealth, lacking in austerity and knowledge,
and bereft of proper conduct, is equal to urine and excrement.

Manu [9.201–03]: Eunuchs, outcasts, those blind from birth, and the deaf likewise; as well as the insane, the idiotic, the mute, and whoever else is devoid of sense organs—these shall not receive a share.
It is right for a wise person to give to all of them according to his ability;
however, one who fails to provide food and clothing indefinitely would indeed be fallen.
[667] But if, in any way, there should be a desire for wives on the part of eunuchs and the like,
their offspring— provided they have produced a lineage— is entitled to the inheritance.
‘Those lacking sense organs’ refers to the lame and others. The term ‘of the impotent and so forth’ is a *bahuvrīhi* compound that does not include the quality itself (*atadguṇasaṃvijñāna*).
Yājñavalkya [2.140–42]:
An outcast, his son, the impotent, the lame, the insane, and the idiot;
But those who are blind or afflicted by incurable diseases and the like should be maintained, though they shall receive no share of the inheritance.
Among them, those born of the wife (aurasa) and those born of the field (kṣetraja) are entitled to inherit shares provided they are free from defects;
furthermore, their daughters must be maintained until they are given away to husbands.
Women who are childless but of virtuous conduct must be maintained;
however, those who are unfaithful or hostile may be banished.

Nārada [16.21]: One who hates his father, a eunuch, and one who has been excluded from the community—even these, though they be legitimate sons (aurasa), shall not receive a share; how much less so those born of the wife (kṣetraja)?
‘Apapātritaḥ’: one whose exclusion from the family vessel has been performed by his relatives due to a fault such as the killing of a king, and so forth. Devala states:
“When the father has died, [the inheritance does not go to] the impotent, the leper, the insane, the idiotic, or the blind.”
An outcast, the offspring of an outcast, and one who bears the sectarian marks (liṅgin) are not entitled to a share of the inheritance.
To them, food and clothing are given, excluding those who have fallen from their caste;
their sons, being free from fault, shall receive their paternal inheritance.

‘When the father has died. The connection is that when the father has died, eunuchs and others do not receive shares. Viṣṇu [15.32–39]: “Those who are outcasts, eunuchs, those with incurable diseases, and the deformed are non-partakers of inheritance; they must be maintained by those who take the estate. Their legitimate sons (*aurasa*) are partakers of shares, but not the son of an outcast. Those born after an act causing loss of caste has been committed, as well as those born of women in the inverse order (*pratiloma*), are non-partakers; their sons are likewise non-partakers even regarding the grandfather’s property. They must be maintained by those who take the shares.”

Gautama [28.44–46]: “The idiotic and the impotent are to be maintained. The offspring of the idiot is entitled to a share. Regarding those born of women in the inverse order of castes (*pratiloma*), they are like the son of a Śūdra.

As for the phrase “like the son of a Śūdra regarding those born of women in the inverse order,” even the son of a Śūdra, if he is capable of serving his childless [parents], shall receive a livelihood according to the rule for a pupil (*antevāsin*), in the manner prescribed for that son. Just as the son of a Śūdra receives merely a means of subsistence, so too does the son born of a woman in the inverse order.
Kātyāyana [862–65].
The son born of a woman married out of order, one born of a woman of the same lineage (sagotra),
and one who has fallen from the religious life— among these, there is never any inheritance.
But a son born of a wife married out of order inherits the estate if he is of the same caste as his father;
however, this applies when there is also a son born of a wife of a different caste who was married in the proper order.
The son of a woman born in the inverse order of castes does not inherit property;
it is ordained that his kinsmen shall provide him with food and clothing for as long as he lives.
But in the absence of even kinsmen, he shall obtain that paternal property;
however, if that wealth was not inherited from the father, he should not be compelled by his relatives to pay it back.

‘Born of a woman married out of order’: here, one born of a woman married out of order (*akramoḍhā*)—that is, of a woman of a different caste—is not an heir. Likewise, one born of a woman married in the proper order (*kramoḍhā*) by a man of the same caste is a sharer of the inheritance. Regarding the phrase ‘and he who is born from a woman of the same lineage (*sagotra*)’: the meaning is that he who is born from a woman of the same lineage who has been married is not a sharer of the inheritance. ‘She is not to be made to pay by the kinsmen’: the grammatical connection is that she should not even be compelled to provide food and clothing. Now, concerning the performance of sacramental rites for those not yet consecrated, Nārada says [16.33–34]:
And for those whose purificatory rites have not been performed in due order by their father,
they must be performed by their brothers from that paternal wealth itself.
If paternal wealth is not available,
the sacramental rites that must necessarily be performed for brothers by those already consecrated should be carried out by taking [funds] from one's own share.
Devala says: The paternal property and the wealth given at marriage must be given to the daughters.
For one who has no son, a daughter born according to dharma shall inherit like a son.
Yājñavalkya [2.124]: But those who have not been consecrated should be consecrated by their brothers who have already been consecrated;
and the sisters, having set aside a fourth part from their own shares, [should be so consecrated].
Viṣṇu [15.31]: "One should perform the sacramental rite for an unmarried girl according to one's own means.
Manu [9.118]: "But the brothers should each separately give [ornaments] to their respective sisters."
If they refuse to give, they shall fall [from their caste], forfeiting one-fourth share from each of their respective portions.
Kātyāyana [858]:
For unmarried daughters, a fourth part is prescribed;
for sons, three parts are prescribed. Ownership over even a small amount of wealth is thus ordained.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “When the inheritance is being divided, the daughter shall receive her ornaments, her wedding gifts, and her woman’s property.

Baudhāyana [2.3.44] says: “The daughters shall receive their mother’s ornaments, whether they were inherited from their mother or otherwise. Regarding the recurring phrase, “A woman does not deserve a share of the inheritance,” Baudhāyana further states: “Women are considered to be devoid of virility and excluded from inheritance; such is the Vedic revelation.”
Now, regarding what is to be divided, Kātyāyana [states]:
"The paternal grandfather's property, the father's property, and whatever else has been acquired by oneself."
But in the division among heirs, all of this is divided.
Having given away the inheritance and what was bestowed out of affection, one should divide the remainder;
that [inheritance] should indeed be received by the sons in due order up to the fourth generation.
"Up to the fourth generation," says Nārada [16.32]:
"Whatever remains from the paternal inheritance, and whatever debt was contracted by the father."
That [property] must be divided by the brothers; otherwise, the father would be a debtor.
Kātyāyana [846–49, 841–42]: Debt contracted by a brother, a paternal uncle,
or a mother for the sake of the family must be paid in its entirety by the debtors at the time of partition.
That debt must be paid with wealth; one should not cause it to be paid otherwise.
If it has been proven by evidence, then, because of contradiction, it may be contested later.
Debt of this kind— whether ancestral, connected to an ancestor's debt, or one's own personal debt contracted by oneself— must be cleared by the kinsmen together during the partition of the estate.

A debt contracted for the sake of dharma, or given out of affection, or one for which one has personally engaged in labor—such a debt shall be divided while it is still visible; however, no gift from the paternal estate shall be divided.
A visible object may be divided, such as a house, a field, or a quadruped;
however, when there is suspicion of hidden property, the means of proof in this case is declared to be testimony.
Household utensils, draft animals, milch cattle, ornaments, and those engaged in work are divided while being visible; regarding hidden property, Bhṛgu has declared that it goes to the treasury.

The meaning of the passage beginning with “that debt is to be paid from the wealth” (*tad ṛṇaṃ dhane deyam*) is as follows: at the time of partition, if there is a “dispute” (*virodhāt*), meaning a mutual disagreement, regarding that which was not given, then “that debt,” when it becomes payable at a “later time” (*parataḥ*), should be paid provided it is “established by proof” (*pramāṇena cet vibhāvitam*); otherwise, it is not to be paid. “Connected with paternal debt” (*pitryarṇasaṃbaddham*) means: that which was “incurred” for the sake of clearing a father’s debt; and even that which was incurred by another for the sake of one’s own family, or even that which was “incurred by oneself” (*ātmanā kṛtam*) solely for the sake of the family. Regarding the phrase “given for religious duty or out of affection” (*dharmārthaṃ prītidattam*): wealth that is common property was given by oneself independently “for religious duty” (*dharmārtham*), as well as what was given out of affection. Furthermore, “whatever debt” (*ṛṇaṃ yat*) was given by oneself to another in the capacity of a creditor—that being known—must be divided. This is because it is not proper to give independently from ancestral wealth that has already been partitioned.
Manu [9.119]: One should never divide goats, sheep, and single-hoofed animals unequally;
however, it is ordained that goats, sheep, and single-hoofed animals shall belong to the eldest alone.
Now, regarding what is not subject to partition, Manu [9.206] states:
"But whatever is the wealth of learning belonging to him, that shall be his alone."
That which is given out of friendship, that which is given for marriage, and likewise that which is given with the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
‘Mādhuparkika’ refers to that which is obtained as an object of honor at the time of the *madhuparka* offering.
Yājñavalkya [2.119] states: "If one recovers property that was stolen, it belongs to him according to the order of succession."
And that which was obtained through learning, he should not give to his heirs.
Vyāsa: Whatever wealth may have been acquired through learning, whatever consists of valor, and whatever is a gift from a wife's family (saudāyika),
that shall not be sought back by the heirs at the time of partition.

"Saudāyika" is thus defined by Kātyāyana [971]: "Whatever is obtained by a married woman or even by an unmarried girl from her husband’s father’s house, or from her brother, or from her parents, is known as saudāyika."
Gautama [28.31]: “A learned man may, at his own discretion, not give what he has earned himself to those who are unlearned. Here, “learned man” (*vaidya*) means one who possesses knowledge.
Kātyāyana [875].
A physician should never give any portion of his medical wealth to those who are ignorant;
however, that wealth may be given by the physician to those whose knowledge is equal to or superior to his own.
Nārada [16.11]: A physician shall not, against his will, give a share from his own wealth to one who is unlearned in medicine,
unless that wealth was acquired by him while relying upon ancestral property.

In the continuation of the phrase "one should divide," Nārada further states (16.5–7): "Excluding the wealth acquired through valor and the wealth consisting of a wife, that which is the wealth of learning— these three are indivisible, as is the favor granted by a father."
And for one to whom his own mother has given property out of affection, this same rule is seen to apply; for the mother is as beloved as the father.
Vyāsa:
That which was given by the grandfather or by the father out of affection,
as well as that which may have been given by the mother, must not be taken away from him.
Yājñavalkya [2.115]:
That which is acquired by oneself without using paternal property,
as well as what is obtained from a friend or received at marriage, shall not belong to the heirs.
Manu and Viṣṇu [Manu 9.208; Vi 18.42]:
"What one acquires by one's own labor without depleting the paternal estate, and what is obtained through one's own exertion—one need not give that against one's will."
Vyāsa says: Whatever wealth one acquires by one's own effort without depending on paternal property,
as well as that which is obtained through learning, one need not give that to the heirs.
Kātyāyana:

When one has acquired knowledge from another by providing food for others, and that knowledge is obtained according to the prescribed rule, it is called "knowledge acquired through [the provision of] food."
What is obtained when [property] has been offered, and what is obtained through study—these they call "learning-wealth" (vidyādhana); anything other than this is common property.
That which is obtained from a disciple, from officiating as a priest, from answering questions, from resolving doubtful inquiries,
from praising one's own knowledge, from debate, and from the study of the Vedas;
They say that the wealth acquired through learning is not to be divided at a partition;
for this same rule applies even among artisans regarding what exceeds their wages.
That which is acquired by teaching, as well as from officiating at sacrifices or from a pupil—this they call the property of learning;
whatever is other than this is common property.
Bṛhaspati declares that what is obtained by means of learning after excluding others, having previously made a wager, is "learning-wealth" (vidyādhanam); he states that this is not to be divided.

That which is obtained through a promise for instruction, that which is received from a pupil, and that which is obtained according to the rule of the officiating priest— Bhṛgu declares this to be "wealth acquired through learning."
When they have boldly undertaken a risky venture and performed the task therein,
their master, being pleased, has bestowed his favor upon them.
Whatever wealth is obtained there through valor shall belong [to the king];
that which is brought by the standard (dhvajāhṛta) is declared not to be divisible at all.
That which is brought back from battle after routing the enemy forces,
having sacrificed one's life for the sake of the master, is called "brought under the banner" (dhvajāhṛta).
Whatever is obtained at the time of acquisition together with a maiden of one's own caste,
that wealth situated in the maiden is traditionally known as the *śulka* (bride-price), which causes increase.
One should know that wealth acquired by a wife through her husband is matrimonial; all such property is to be understood as being for the purpose of performing religious rites.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "Prajāpati has declared that there is no division of the dwelling site, nor of water-jars, ornaments, women, clothes, or the paths for the flow of water.
Manu and Viṣṇu [Manu 9.219; Viṣṇu 18.44] say:
"Clothing, vehicles, ornaments, prepared food, water, and women..."
And they declare that the management of security and protection is not to be divided.

‘Clothing’ refers to that which is worn on the body and has a fixed value. The word ‘document’ (*patra*) here refers to wealth recorded in writing, in accordance with the statement of Kātyāyana: “But that which is distinguished by a document of debt” (*dhanapatraviśiṣṭaṃ tu*). ‘Women’ refers to those who are married, according to the statement of Gautama: “There is no partition among women who are married” (*avibhāgaḥ strīṣu saṃyuktāsu* [GDh 28.48]). ‘Security and welfare’ (*yogakṣema*) refers to ministers, priests, and so forth, because they are the cause of security and welfare. ‘Pasture-ground’ (*pracāra*) is the path for the grazing of cattle and other animals. Vyāsa says:
“That which belongs to those of the same lineage (*sagotra*) is indivisible, even up to a thousand families.”
The person for whom one sacrifices, a field, a worthy recipient, cooked food, water, and women.
‘Field’ refers to a building site. Kātyāyana [882–84]: But wealth that has been recorded in writing and designated for the sake of dharma...
Water and wives, as well as any property inherited through succession, are not subject to partition.
The garment or ornament that is appropriate,
as well as whatever else may be suitable for the occasion, should be provided by the kinsmen.
According to Bṛhaspati, pasture land for cattle, a public road, clothing that has been worn on the body, and tools for a craft shall not be divided after they have been put to use.
Whatever law has been proclaimed for a country, a caste, a guild, or a village by Bhṛgu,
one should determine the law of inheritance according to that very same rule.
Those who stated that clothing and such items are indivisible have not reflected that wealth belonging to the prosperous may consist of garments and ornaments.
That which stands in the middle and cannot sustain life cannot be given to a single person;
it must be divided by means of a proper method, otherwise it would become useless.
Having sold clothing and ornaments, having recovered a debt by means of a written document,
and having exchanged prepared food for unprepared food, the property is then divided.
Just as water from a well or a pond is drawn out according to its depth,
so too is an irrigation channel divided among fields according to their respective shares.
One should have a single woman perform work in each house according to her share; many women should be assigned equal shares. This same rule applies even to male slaves.
The acquisition of property for security and well-being shall be divided equally;
and its management must be carried out by the debtors in proportion to their respective shares.

‘For the sake of security and prosperity (*yogakṣemavataḥ*): that is, for the purpose of securing and maintaining prosperity. And here it has been stated that clothing and other such items are divisible according to their specific types. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the statements of Manu and others regarding the indivisibility of clothing and so forth; those texts are intended to prohibit divisibility in terms of their physical form (*svarūpataḥ*). Kātyāyana [874]: Among brothers who have been trained in learning within the family, or even by their father...
But whatever wealth has been acquired through valor, that is to be divided; so says Bṛhaspati.

The meaning of this is as follows: regarding the phrase "in the family" (*kule*), when brothers have acquired learning from their own family—whether from paternal grandfathers, paternal uncles, and so forth, or from the father himself—the wealth obtained through that learning and valor must indeed be divided at the time of partition. Nārada [16.10] states:
"He who supports the family of a brother who is pursuing his studies..."
Therefore, one who possesses the wealth of knowledge shall receive a share from that, even if he has not studied.
‘Unlearned’ here means ignorant.
Manu [9.204–05]: Whatever property the eldest son acquires after the father has died—
In that case, the younger brothers shall receive a share if they are observant of their learning.
But if all the unlearned [sons] should acquire wealth through their own efforts, the division therein shall be equal; this is the settled rule regarding what is not ancestral property.

Regarding the phrase "whatever," and so forth: even without conflict with the paternal estate, since the eldest acquires wealth, a division of that wealth also occurs for the younger brothers, provided they are devoted to the study of knowledge. "From exertion" means from activities such as agriculture and the like.
Vasiṣṭha [17.51] states: "And whatever among these may have been produced by one himself, he shall take two shares of that. Vyāsa says:
Whatever wealth one acquires through valor or other means by relying on common property, such as a vehicle or a weapon, the brothers are entitled to a share therein.
Two shares shall be allotted to him, while the remainder are to be divided equally.
Now, regarding the disposition of a woman's property, Manu [9.199] states:
Women should not carry out any productive work from the midst of the large household,
nor even from their own wealth, without the permission of their husband.

‘Nirhāram’ means taking away after having extracted it. By the word ‘kuṭumba’, the wealth of the family is meant here due to its association with that term. ‘From her own’ means from her own husband’s exclusive property. Manu and Viṣṇu [Manu 9.200; Viṣṇu 17.22]:
“Whatever ornament may have been worn by women while their husbands were alive...”
The heirs shall not divide that property; those who do divide it fall.
Āpastamba [2.14.9]: “Some say that ornaments and the wealth of her kinsmen belong to the wife.
Nārada [4.28; *Nāradasmṛti* 2.24]:
“That which was given by a pleased husband to his wife remains hers even after he has died.”
She may eat as she pleases, or give [food] away, with the exception of immovable property.
Vyāsa says: A gift of two thousand paṇas of wealth should be given to a woman;
and whatever wealth has been given by her husband, she may enjoy it according to her desire.
Kātyāyana [901, 905–07, 921]: Whether by a married woman or by an unmarried maiden, what is obtained from the husband, from the father’s house,
or from a brother or from the parents, is declared to be *saudāyika* (a woman’s property).
Women are held to have independence regarding the property they receive as a dowry (*saudāyika*),
because that was given by their [relatives] for the sake of kindness and as a means of their subsistence.
Women's independence over property received as a dowry is always proclaimed;
they may dispose of it as they wish, even in the case of immovable property, whether by sale or by gift.
Upon the death of her husband, a woman may dispose of her husband’s inheritance as she pleases;
however, while he is still living, she must preserve it, otherwise she shall forfeit it to his family.
A childless widow, remaining faithful to her elders and protecting her husband’s bed, may live until death with self-restraint; after that, the heirs shall receive the inheritance.

The connection is with the phrase “in the husband’s house. The mention of “or from a brother or parents” is illustrative; by this, it includes others as well. That wealth which is obtained from the families of one’s own mother and father is called *saudāyika* (gift of affection). In that regard, even concerning immovable property (*sthāvara*), a woman has independence regarding its donation and other such acts. However, regarding gifts bestowed by her husband, she has the right to dispose of them as she pleases, provided they are other than immovable property. In the context of the rule that “the king shall protect the inheritance,” Manu [8.28–29] states: “The same protection should be afforded to women who are barren, those who have no sons, and those whose families are extinct.”
And toward women who are devoted to their husbands, as well as those who are widowed or afflicted by illness.
But if their own kinsmen should seize that property while those women are still living,
the righteous lord of the earth shall punish them with the punishment prescribed for thieves.

‘Vaśā’ means barren; ‘aputrā’ means one whose sons have died; ‘niṣkulā’ means one whose maternal and paternal families have perished. Devala says: Maintenance, what is brought [as a gift], the nuptial fee (śulka), and profits constitute a woman’s property (strīdhana).
And she herself alone is the enjoyer of this; the husband ought not [to consume it] except in times of distress.
She may spend her husband’s property on false pretenses for the sake of liberation, for pleasure, or for a woman;
she may also use it to maintain her sons, and she is entitled to enjoy the woman’s own property.
Kātyāyana [911–14]: Neither the husband, nor the son, nor the father, nor the brothers have authority over a woman’s property, whether in its acquisition or its disposal.
If indeed one among them should seize the woman's property by force,
he shall be compelled to restore it along with interest and shall also incur a fine.
If he should eat that very thing after having obtained permission and with a sense of pleasure,
he should be made to pay the full amount as a fine when he possesses wealth.
Having learned that [the debtor] is diseased, in distress, or oppressed by creditors, he may, out of affection and according to his own will, give what has been released [by the creditor].
Yājñavalkya [2.147]: In times of famine, for the sake of religious duties, during illness, or when there is imprisonment,
the husband is not required to return to the wife the property she received from him.
Kātyāyana [908–10]: If he has two wives and does not favor her again,
even if she has been released by him out of affection, he must be compelled to give her back that property by force.
Wherever a woman is deprived of food, clothing, and shelter,
she may take for herself her own property, as well as a share from the heirs.
This is the law regarding one who has been written [in the legal document]: she shall reside in the husband's family when [he] is alive;
but when he is diseased or deceased, she may then go to her own kinsmen's family.
Wealth has arisen for the sake of sacrifice; therefore, one should employ that wealth in purposes sanctioned by dharma, and not among women, fools, or those who act contrary to dharma.
[688] The sons must repay the woman’s property as a debt, just as it was promised by her husband;
she who remains in her husband’s house shall not dwell in her father’s family.
Now, the division of a woman’s property.
Regarding this, Manu says (9.192–93, 195):
"But when the mother has passed away, all the uterine brothers [shall divide it] equally."
The uterine sisters shall share in the inheritance of their mother's estate.
Whatever daughters they may have, to them also something should be given from the maternal grandmother's wealth, according to their merit and with affection.
The property given as an *anvādheya* gift, as well as that which was given by the husband out of affection—
this shall be the wealth of the offspring of a woman who has passed away while her husband is still living.

“*Sanābhayaḥ*” here refers to uterine siblings. “*Yathārhatas*” means according to their fitness, such as the quantity of property, the number of offspring, and so forth. “*Anvādheyam*” is the wealth obtained after marriage from the husband’s family or the father’s family. Bṛhaspati [26.31] states:
“The woman’s property shall belong to the children, and the daughter is entitled to a share of it.”
But if she is married without a son, she receives only her maintenance.

"But that which may be the mother's *yautaka* (separate property), that is indeed the portion of the unmarried daughter. "*Yautaka*" refers to the wealth given to a woman by her father and others at the time of marriage.

Gautama [28.25]: “The property of a woman belongs to her daughters who are unmarried and unsettled. ‘Unsettled’ refers to those who, though married, have husbands who are destitute, or who are unfortunate or childless. Vasiṣṭha [17.46]: “The women shall divide the mother’s dowry.”
‘Pāriṇāhya’ refers to personal belongings such as mirrors, bracelets, and so forth.
Yājñavalkya [2.117], following the rule that they “should divide” after [the father’s death], states:
“The daughters shall take the remainder of the mother’s property after her debts; in their absence, the heirs.”

‘Anvaya’ refers to his sons, grandsons, and so forth. Regarding those who are eligible for marriage, Viṣṇu (17.20) states, continuing from the previous context: “Among all those born [of the same father], that wealth goes to the daughters. Manu (9.198) says:

Whatever property may belong to a woman, having been given by her father in any manner whatsoever, that a Brāhmaṇī wife shall take; or it shall belong to her daughter, or to the offspring of that daughter.

The meaning of this is as follows: for women who are without husbands and without offspring, that daughter of a co-wife who is a Brāhmaṇa shall take what was given by the father; and if she has offspring, they [the children] shall also take it. Kātyāyana [918, 917] states:
"In the absence of daughters, however, that inheritance shall belong to the sons."
But that which was given by a kinsman goes to the husband in the absence of kinsmen.
Sisters, together with their kinsmen, shall share [the inheritance] along with their husbands;
this is the law regarding women's property, and thus the division has been ordained.
Now, regarding the property of a childless woman, Manu says (9.196–97):
"The wealth that belongs to those sons born of the Brahma, Daiva, Ārṣa, Gāndharva, and Prājāpatya forms of marriage..."
If she dies childless, it is ordained that this [property] belongs to the husband alone.
Whatever wealth may have been given to her in marriages such as the Āsura and others,
that is held to belong to the mother and father when she has passed away without offspring.
[691] Devala says:
The property of a woman is common to her sons and daughters;
however, if she dies without issue, the husband, the mother, the brother, and the father shall take it.
Gautama [28.26–27]: “The sister’s dowry belongs to the uterine brothers after the mother; some say it belongs to them even before.
‘Sister’s dowry’ (*bhaginīśulka*) refers to the wealth of a sister married through the Āsura or other such forms of marriage. ‘After the mother’ (*ūrdhvaṃ mātuḥ*) means when the mother has died.
Yājñavalkya [2.144]:
Likewise, the property given by kinsmen, the nuptial fee, and the subsequent gift—
when she dies childless, her relatives shall obtain that.
Manu [9.135]: "But if a daughter appointed as a son (putrikā) should somehow die without a son,
her husband shall take that wealth without hesitation."
Paiṭhīnasi: "If a *putrikā* (appointed daughter) dies, her husband does not deserve that property; it should be taken by her childless sister or her maiden sister. Yājñavalkya [2.146]:
"One who, having given away a girl in marriage, takes her back, shall be fined and must pay the expenses along with interest."
If she dies, he shall take all, after having cleared both types of expenses.

The meaning of this is as follows: having himself given her verbally, he becomes liable to punishment for "taking"—that is, for abducting the girl—without a valid cause. Furthermore, regarding the gold and other items given by the groom, he should return them along with the interest that has accrued; such is the instruction for the giver of the girl. Now, if the girl betrothed by word should somehow die, then "when she is dead, one should take everything. Having first deducted the expenses incurred by both parties, one should take the remainder after calculating both what was given by the girl's father—such as goods and so forth—for the entertainment of the relatives, and what was given by the relatives for their auspicious rites, such as rings and the like. One should take whatever remains after this total is accounted for.
In the continuation [of the discussion] regarding who is entitled [to the inheritance], Śaṅkha states: "She who herself pays the bride-price. Baudhāyana says:
"The uterine brothers themselves shall take the estate of a deceased maiden."
In her absence, it shall belong to the mother; in her absence, it shall belong to the father.
[693] Bṛhaspati (Vyavahāra 26.32–33): A mother’s sister, a maternal uncle’s wife, a paternal uncle’s wife, a father’s sister, a mother-in-law,
and the wife of an elder brother are declared to be equal to a mother.
If these women have neither a son born of their own body nor a daughter's son,
nor the son of such a daughter, then their wealth shall be inherited by their sister's sons and the others.
Now, regarding the characteristics of a woman’s property (strīdhana), Manu and Kātyāyana state [Manu 9.194; Kātyāyana 894]:
"That which is given before the fire, that which is given at the bridal procession, and what is given to her out of affection..."
The sixfold property of a woman is traditionally defined as that which is obtained from her brother, mother, or father.

Nārada [16.8]: That which was received in the presence of the sacred fire, that which was received in the presence of the *āhavanīya* fire, as well as the inheritance from her husband, that which was given by her brothers, and that which was given by her parents— this is declared to be the sixfold property of a woman (*strīdhana*).

Viṣṇu [17.18]: "That which is given by the father, mother, son, or brother; that which is received at the nuptial fire; that given upon supersession; that given by a kinsman; the bride-price (śulka); and the subsequent gift (anvādheya)—these constitute the woman's property (strīdhana).
Devala: "Livelihood, ornaments, the bride-price, and acquisitions shall constitute the woman's property."
Kātyāyana [904]:
Whatever wealth has been acquired through crafts, or whatever else obtained through affection, the husband always has ownership over that; the remainder, however, shall be the woman’s property.
[Verse 895–97] That which is given to women at the time of marriage in the presence of the fire is proclaimed by the virtuous as *adhyagnikṛta*, a type of woman’s property (*strīdhana*).
Furthermore, whatever a woman acquires when being led away from her father's house is declared to be the woman's property known as *adhyāhavanika*.
Whatever is given out of affection by a mother-in-law or a father-in-law,
such as that which is offered at the salutation of their feet, is said to be acquired through personal charm.
[Verse 899–900] That which is obtained by a woman from her husband’s family after marriage is called *anvādheya*; however,
that which she obtains from her own family is also so designated.
Whatever is obtained by a woman from her husband, her parents, or others, subsequent to the marriage ceremony and out of affection, Bhṛgu declares that to be *anvādheya*.
[695] [Kā. 898] Whatever price is obtained for household goods, implements, vehicles, milch animals, ornaments, or articles of craftsmanship, that is proclaimed as *śulka* (toll/duty).
Now, regarding the division of shares, Manu [9.218] states:
"When all debts and assets have been divided according to rule..."
Whatever may be seen hereafter, one should bring all of that to a state of equanimity.
Kātyāyana [885–88]:
But that which was concealed by someone, if it is brought back again and is of equal value, shall be divided together with the brothers; for in the absence of the father, the sons [shall divide it].
Bhṛgu says that property which has been taken from one another or which was improperly divided shall be redistributed according to what is appropriate, in equal shares.
Whatever wealth is obtained by one who is already divided shall belong to him alone;
likewise, what is recovered, lost and found again, or previously mentioned, shall revert to him.
One must not forcibly cause property taken by kinsmen to be returned;
nor should one initiate the enjoyment of property belonging to undivided kinsmen.
Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 26.141–42]:
When there is a denial of a common debt or a deposit, or when one has employed fraud in a transaction that causes loss to a partner,
the judge should subsequently compel the defendant to pay the remainder.
Those men who are deceitful, wealthy, cruel,
and greedy should be won over through friendship, or else by the loss of their own interests and through guile.
Now follows the analysis of the combination of various castes;
regarding that, Manu says (9.148–54):
"This division of those born from a single source is to be understood."
And among many wives born of the same caste, one should cause [the eldest] to be recognized as the principal.
If a Brāhmaṇa has four wives in the direct order [of castes],
this rule for the division [of the estate] among the sons born of them is recorded in the tradition.
A ploughman, a bull, a vehicle, ornaments, and a house—
these are to be given as a debt-recovery gift (uddhāraka) to a Brahmin, along with one share as the principal portion.
From the inheritance, the son of a Brāhmaṇa shall take three shares; the son of a Kṣatriya woman, two shares;
the son born of a Vaiśya woman, one and a half shares; and the son born of a Śūdra woman shall take one share.
Or, having divided the entire collection of inherited property into ten parts,
one who knows the Dharma should make a righteous partition according to this rule.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa shall take four shares; the son of a Kṣatriya wife, three shares;
the son of a Vaiśya wife shall take two shares; and the son of a Śūdra wife shall take one share.

‘Among women of one womb’ means among women of the same caste; ‘among various women’ means among women of different castes. ‘And one share primarily’: of the three shares belonging to the Brāhmaṇa, one share is to be made the primary [portion], consisting of the best property. Nārada [16.14]:
“In the case of those born from wives married in the inferior castes, there is a reduction of shares in successive order.”
[698] In the Mahābhārata (Anuśāsana-parvan, 42.48–56): Bhīṣma said:
"O joy of the Kurus, even for a Kṣatriya, two wives are ordained."
Or she may be a Śūdra woman as the third [wife], but she is not recorded in the traditional examples.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, the property of a Kṣatriya should be divided into eight parts;
the son of a Kṣatriya wife shall take four shares from the father’s wealth.
Whatever was intended for the funeral rites of the father, that he shall take;
the son of the Vaiśya wife shall take three shares, and the son of the Śūdra wife likewise an eighth.
He may take the wealth of his parents, but he ought not to take what has not been given;
for a Vaiśya, O joy of the Kurus, should have only one wife.
Or it may be a Śūdra woman as the second wife, but she is not recorded [as such] by way of scriptural precedent.
O bull among the Bharatas, the property of a Vaiśya may likewise be divided fivefold.
O lord of men, I shall now describe the division between those two offspring:
four shares from the father's wealth are to be taken by the son of the Vaiśya wife.
But the fifth share, O Bhārata, shall belong to the son of the Śūdra wife;
he may take what is given by the father, but he does not deserve to take what is not given.
In this context, the "example" is the Veda; "pertaining to battle" refers to the equipment for battle.

Viṣṇu [18.1–27]: “If a Brāhmaṇa should have sons from [wives of] the four castes, they shall divide the paternal inheritance into ten parts. Of these, the son of the Brāhmaṇa wife shall take four shares; the son of the Kṣatriya wife, three; the son of the Vaiśya wife, two shares; and the son of the Śūdra wife, one. Now, if a Brāhmaṇa should have only three sons, excluding the son of a Śūdra wife, they shall divide the wealth into nine parts. They shall give them shares divided according to the order of the castes: four, three, and two parts respectively. Or, excluding the Vaiśya, having divided it into eight parts, they shall take four, three, and one. Or, excluding the Kṣatriya, having divided it into seven parts, they shall take four, two, and one. Or, excluding the Brāhmaṇa, having divided it into six parts, they shall take three, two, and one. This same division applies when a Kṣatriya has sons by Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra wives. Now, if a Brāhmaṇa should have two sons, a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya, then from the wealth divided into seven parts, the Brāhmaṇa shall take four shares and the Kṣatriya three. If a Brāhmaṇa should have two sons, a Brāhmaṇa and a Vaiśya, then from that wealth divided into six parts, the Brāhmaṇa alone shall take four shares and the Vaiśya two. If a Brāhmaṇa should have two sons, a Brāhmaṇa and a Śūdra, then they shall divide that wealth into five parts; the Brāhmaṇa shall take four shares and the Śūdra one. If a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya should have two sons, a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, then they shall divide that wealth into five parts; the Kṣatriya shall take three shares and the Vaiśya two. If a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya should have two sons, a Kṣatriya and a Śūdra, then they shall divide that wealth into four parts; the Kṣatriya shall take three shares and the Śūdra one. If a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya should have two sons, a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, then they shall divide that wealth into three parts; the Vaiśya shall take two shares and the Śūdra one.”
Now, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "For those born of women of other castes, the inheritance is reduced by half for each successive caste in order."

Viṣṇu [18.38–40]: “If there should be two sons of a Brāhmaṇī wife and one son of a Śūdrā wife, then, from wealth divided into nine parts, the two sons of the Brāhmaṇī wife shall take eight shares and the son of the Śūdrā wife one share. If there should be two sons of a Śūdrā wife and one son of a Brāhmaṇī wife, then, from wealth divided into six parts, the Brāhmaṇa shall take four shares and the two sons of the Śūdrā wife two shares. By this same method, the allotment of shares is determined in other cases as well.”

Furthermore, Viṣṇu [18.28–31] states: “Now, for a Brāhmaṇa, sons born of a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya wife take the entire inheritance; for a Kṣatriya, sons born of a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya wife; for a Vaiśya, a son born of a Vaiśya wife; and for a Śūdra, a son born of a Śūdra wife. Vasiṣṭha [17.47, 50] says: “If a Brāhmaṇa has sons by wives of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya castes, then the son of the Brāhmaṇa wife shall take three shares, the son of the Kṣatriya wife two shares, and the others shall divide the remainder equally. Manu [9.156–57] states: [The text continues with the verses of Manu.]
Or, sons born of wives of equal caste to twice-born men shall,
after giving a preferential share to the eldest, divide the remainder equally among themselves.
For a Śūdra, however, only a wife of his own caste is ordained, and no other;
those born of her shall share equal portions, even if there should be a hundred sons.

Baudhāyana [2.3.12–13]: "Between the son of a wife of equal caste and the son of a wife of the next lower caste, if the son of the next lower caste is virtuous, he shall take the share of the eldest; being virtuous, he shall be the supporter of all. Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 26.120]:
"A son born to a Brāhmaṇa from a Kṣatriya woman, though junior by birth, if endowed with virtues..."
Likewise, one born from a Vaiśya woman by a Brāhmaṇa shall have an equal share with that Brāhmaṇa.

Gautama [28.36–39]: “The eldest son of a Brāhmaṇa by a Kṣatriya wife, if endowed with good qualities, shares equally [in the estate]. He receives everything except the special share due to the eldest. In the case of the coexistence of sons by a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya wife, it is the same as in the case of the son of a Brāhmaṇa wife. And if he is born of a Kṣatriya father, he shares equally.”

The phrase “by the son of the Brāhmaṇī” implies that he is the younger brother. “The rest, minus the senior’s share” means that the remaining property—excluding that portion consisting of the twentieth part which constitutes the senior’s preferential share (*uddhāra*)—is to be divided equally; this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase “just as he [was] with the son of the Brāhmaṇī”: just as that eldest son of the Kṣatriyā is to have an equal share with the younger son of the Brāhmaṇī, so too the son of the Vaiśyā, even if born of a Brāhmaṇī, has an equal share with the younger son of the Kṣatriyā. As for the phrase “if from a Kṣatriyā”: if there are two sons, one from a Kṣatriyā and one from a Vaiśyā, then even in that case, the eldest son of the Vaiśyā has an equal share with the younger son of the Kṣatriyā; this is the meaning.
Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 26.121]:
Land received as a gift must not be given to a son who is a Kṣatriya;
even if his father might have given it, once he is dead, the son born of a Brāhmaṇa woman shall take it.
Vṛddha-Manu: Sons born of Brāhmaṇa wives shall inherit land acquired through a gift from a Brāhmaṇa;
all twice-born sons [shall inherit] the house, just as the field is inherited according to the order of succession.

‘Obtained as a gift from a Brāhmaṇa’ means acquired through receiving gifts, officiating at sacrifices, and so forth. Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 26.122] states: “One born of a Śūdra woman by twice-born men is not entitled to a share of land.”
Devala [Bṛhadvyākhyāna 26.123–24]: "One shall obtain everything from one of equal birth; thus the dharma is established."
But the Niṣāda, who is the only son of a Brāhmaṇa woman, shall receive the third share;
then two others—either a sapinda or a sakulya—shall take the inheritance as the giver of the svadhā offering.
In the absence of a kinsman, the teacher or even the disciple who offers the *svadhā* shall,
in all calamities, ensure that those of the same caste maintain their own lineage.

A *niṣāda* is one born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Śūdra mother. The word "two" implies "two shares. A "giver of *svadhā*" is one who offers the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*). "In all calamities" means in the absence of all [heirs], such as *sapiṇḍas* and others. "Those castes" refers to the castes of the *niṣāda* and his paternal kin. Viṣṇu [18.32–33] states: "Among the twice-born, a Śūdra son alone is the heir to half [the estate]. The destiny that awaits the inheritance of one who has no sons applies here to the second half.
Regarding "among the twice-born," this refers to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas—those other than Brāhmaṇas—since Devala has stated that a Śūdra son of a Brāhmaṇa caste is entitled to a third share.
[Manu 9.154–55] Even if he has a legitimate son or even no son at all,
one should not, according to the law, give more than a tenth part to the son of a Śūdra woman.
The son of a Śūdra woman born to Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, or Vaiśyas does not inherit property;
whatever his father may give to him, that alone shall be his wealth.
The meaning is that when a father, being pleased, gives to the son of a Śūdra woman, he should give only the tenth part. Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 26.125]:
"One born of a Śūdra womb who is virtuous and devoted to service for a childless man..."
The sapinda relatives shall obtain the remainder of his livelihood.
Gautama (28.40): “Even the son of a Śūdra woman, if he is devoted to service, may receive a means of subsistence according to the rule for a pupil (*antevāsin*), provided the [father] is childless.
This refers to the case of a son born of an unmarried woman, because of the governing context [of Gautama’s sūtra], which specifies “among those not formally wedded.

Śaṅkha and Likhita: “The son of a Śūdra woman does not share in the inheritance. Whatever his father might give him, that alone is his share. [The father] should also give him a pair of cattle or another [gift]; [he may give] black iron and black grain, excluding sesame.”
Gautama [28.46]: “[The offspring] born of women in the inverse order of castes are like the son of a Śūdra woman. Manu [9.179]:
“The son who may be born to a Śūdra from a female slave, or from the female slave of his slave,”
Thus, it is established as the law that he may take his share once he has been permitted.
‘Dāsadāsī’ refers to a female servant. Yājñavalkya [2.133–34]:
Even one born of a Śūdra man and a female slave shall, if born of his own will, be a sharer of the inheritance.
When the father has died, the brothers shall make him a recipient of half a share.
Now, regarding the partition of property acquired after division, Manu and Nārada state [Manu 9.216; Nārada 16.44]:
"But a son born after the partition shall take only the paternal wealth."
Or, those who may be associated with him, he shall divide together with them.
Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 16.54–55]:
Those who have been divided from their father, whether they be stepbrothers or uterine brothers,
