as well as those born later, they are the ones who shall take the paternal share.

The first-born son has no authority over his paternal share once he has been divided; likewise, the son born after partition has no authority over the share of his brothers. Furthermore, whatever was acquired by the father himself after he had been divided from his sons—*Yājñavalkyasmṛti* 2.116–117.
It is recorded that all those earlier-born ancestors have no authority over that which has been partitioned.
[706] Just as with wealth, so too with a debt, in matters of giving, pledging, and buying, they have no authority over one another, except for the performance of purification rites with water.
Yājñavalkya [2.122]: A son born after the partition from a wife of the same caste is entitled to a share;
or his share may be determined from what is visible, after deducting the income and expenses.
This is its meaning: he who was not known to be in the womb at the time of partition, but is born afterwards, shall receive his own share, equal to the shares of all the other heirs.
As Viṣṇu [17.3] says: “Those divided by their father shall give a share to one born after the partition.”

And after the time of partition, he whose conception (garbhādhāna) occurs receives only his paternal share (*pitrya-aṃśa*), and not even a share from that of his elder brother. This is because of the statement of Bṛhaspati: "The elder brother has no authority over the paternal estate; the one born after partition has no authority over the brother's share" (Vyavahāra 26.55). Or rather, he receives his own share from whatever wealth is found existing at the time of the father’s partition, having been adjusted for income and expenditure. [707] Now follows the partition of property acquired after partition.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states (Vyavahāra 26.63–67,
39): "Whether the partition has been made or not, if an heir appears and establishes that the property was common, he shall indeed receive a share."
Regarding debt, documents, houses, and fields that belong to one's grandfather,
even if he has been away for a long time, he shall receive his share upon returning.
Having abandoned what is common to the lineage, he who has settled in another region must,
without doubt, be given a share when a member of that lineage arrives.
Whether it be the third, the fifth, or even the seventh [in the lineage],
if the names of the births are not fully known, one shall receive the portion that has come down by succession.
The land should be given by the kinsmen to one who has come from that lineage whom the original lords and their neighbors have traditionally known as their master.
Those humans who have been born, those yet to be born, and those dwelling in the womb—all desire that livelihood; therefore, it must not be interrupted.
[708] Now, the division among other sons; regarding this, Manu [9.130] says:
But if a son is born after the *paitṛkā* (the ancestral estate) has been divided,
the division there shall be equal, for there is no status of primogeniture for a woman.
‘Anujāyate’ means it arises subsequently. Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 26.70]:
“The legitimate son of the body alone is declared to be the owner of the paternal estate.”
A daughter is declared to be equal to that [son], while others are remembered as those who must be maintained.
"The legitimate son of the body alone is the master of the paternal wealth;
however, for the sake of avoiding cruelty, he should provide a livelihood for the rest."
[9.120–21] If a younger brother should procreate a son upon the wife of the elder brother,
the division of the inheritance there shall be equal; such is the established law.
It is not logically consistent for the subordinate to take the place of the principal according to dharma;
since the father is the principal in procreation, one should therefore honor him in accordance with dharma.
[9.146] He who takes charge of the wealth and the wife of his deceased brother shall procreate an offspring for that brother and hand over that very wealth to him alone.
[9.162] Likewise:
If there should be two sons, one legitimate (aurasa) and one born of the wife (kṣetraja), who are joint heirs—
if there is paternal property, he alone shall take it, not the other.

‘Of wealth’ means of property. ‘Of the others’ refers to those other than the *kṣetraja* son. ‘Subsidiary’ here means the state of being subsidiary. The *kṣetraja* is one born of a woman not formally authorized (*aniyuktā*).
“But for those who have multiple fathers, the allotment of shares is according to the father.”
Whoever possesses ancestral property shall take that, and no one else.
‘Of those having many fathers’ refers to those born of a woman who has had union with many men. Manu (9.164–65):
“But one should give a sixth share of the paternal wealth to the *kṣetraja* son.”
The legitimate son, when dividing the paternal inheritance, shall take exactly one-fifth.
The two sons, the legitimate son of the body (aurasa) and the son born of the wife (kṣetraja), are sharers of the father's inheritance;
but ten others, in their respective order, are sharers of the lineage, the inheritance, and a portion.

The distinction between the sixth and fifth [categories] is established by their being endowed with or devoid of good qualities. "The other ten" refers to the *dattaka* (given son) and the rest. "In due order" means that each subsequent one takes the place of the preceding one in the absence of that predecessor. "Partakers of the family name, the inheritance, and the share" means they become partakers of the family name (*gotrabhāj*) and partakers of the inheritance (*rikthabhāj*). Regarding the phrase "intending to adopt a son," Vasiṣṭha [15.9–10] states in continuation: "If, after he has been adopted, a legitimate son (*aurasa*) is born, that [adopted son] shall receive a fourth share, provided that [the estate] has not already been employed for auspicious rites."
Kātyāyana [857]:
But when a legitimate son of the body has been born, those of the same caste are declared by tradition to be entitled to one-third share;
however, those of a different caste are entitled only to food and clothing.
Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 26.71]:
"The other sons, beginning with the *kṣetraja*, are entitled to five, six, seven, or eight shares.

Hārīta states: "When dividing the inheritance, they should give twenty-one parts to the maiden-born son (*kānīna*), twenty to the son of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*), nineteen to the son of two fathers (*dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*), eighteen to the *kṣetraja* son, seventeen to the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*); the remaining portions they should give to the legitimate son (*aurasa*)."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Even the son born of the wife (aurasa), though born later, shall be the enjoyer of the entire estate;
the son born of the wife (kṣetraja) enjoys one-third, and the son of the appointed daughter (putrikāsuta) enjoys one-fourth."
The son made (kṛtrima) receives a fifth part, the son born in secret (gūḍhasambhava) a sixth part,
the son cast off (apaviddha) a seventh part, and the son of an unmarried girl (kānīna) an eighth part.
The son taken with the bride (sahoḍha) receives a ninth part, and the purchased son (krīta) receives a tenth;
the son of a remarried woman (paunarbhava), however, receives more than that, while the son who came of his own accord (svayamāgata) receives a twelfth.
A Śūdra, however, consumes the thirteenth share from the father’s wealth;
or else, one born of that same lineage who is most righteous, or even a celibate student (brahmacārī).

"From another" (*parataḥ*) means that one receives the eleventh share after the tenth; such is the meaning. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "There is an option among the six heirs: the legitimate son (*aurasa*), the son begotten on the wife (*kṣetraja*), the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*), the son of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*), the son of an unmarried girl (*kānīna*), and the son secretly born (*gūḍhotpanna*). There are six kinds of kinsmen who are heirs, because they share the same lineage (*gotra*) as the father and grandfather, and share in the inheritance, the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*), and the water offering. One should divide their property into ten shares: two shares for the father, two for the legitimate son, three for the son begotten on the wife and the son of the appointed daughter, and one each for the others."

Furthermore, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "The bull is the additional share for the eldest. In his absence, [it goes] to the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*) and the son of the appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*). In their absence, to the other three. In their absence, to the six non-heirs: the abandoned (*apaviddha*), the one born together (*sahoḍha*), the given (*datta*), the purchased (*krītaka*), the son of a Śūdra woman, and the one who has come of his own accord (*upanata*); these are the six non-heirs. To them, a maintenance shall be given according to their worth and having regard for the wealth [of the estate]."

Gautama [25.33]: “The legitimate son (*aurasa*), the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*), the adopted son (*datta*), the made son (*kṛtrima*), the son secretly born (*gūḍhotpanna*), and the cast-off son (*apaviddha*) are heirs to the estate (*rikthabhāj*). The maiden-born son (*kānīna*), the son received with the bride (*sahoḍha*), the son of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*), the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*), the self-given son (*svayaṃdatta*), and the bought son (*krīta*) are members of the lineage (*gotrabhāj*); they receive a fourth share in the absence of a legitimate son. “Members of the lineage” (*gotrabhāj*) means those who belong to the lineage; they are so called because they perform the duties of a son through rites such as the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and water (*udaka*). And this statement regarding the maiden-born sons and others being members of the lineage is for the purpose of prohibiting their right to inherit a share if even one of the heirs to the estate, such as the legitimate son and the rest, is present.

Having enumerated the *aurasa*, *kṣetraja*, *putrikāputra*, *paunarbhava*, *kānīna*, and *gūḍhotpanna* sons, Vasiṣṭha states (17.25–26): “These, they say, are heirs, kinsmen, and saviors from great danger; whereas among those who are neither heirs nor kinsmen, the *sahoḍha* is the first. This statement regarding the *paunarbhava* and *kānīna* receiving shares refers to cases where the *paunarbhava* and *kānīna* possess the same caste (*varṇa*) as their father. And Gautama’s prohibition of these two from inheriting shares refers to cases where they are of a different caste (*asavarṇa*). However, when a legitimate son (*aurasa*) has been born, the other sons are entitled to a third share.
Those of the same caste shall receive shares; however, those of a different caste are entitled only to food and clothing.

Thus, from the statement of Kātyāyana [857]. After mentioning the son born of a pregnant bride (*sahoḍha*), the given son (*datta*), the bought son (*krīta*), the self-offered son (*svayamupagata*), the abandoned son (*apaviddha*), and the son of a Śūdra woman, and then referring to the legitimate son (*aurasa*) and the others, Vasiṣṭha [17.39] says again: "If among the first six [types of sons] no one should be an heir, these [other sons] shall take his inheritance."

Hārīta states: "There are six heirs who are kinsmen and six heirs who are not kinsmen. Those born of a virtuous wife by oneself, the *kṣetraja*, the son of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*), the maiden-born (*kānīna*), the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*), and one secretly born in the house—these are the heirs who are kinsmen. The given (*datta*), the bought (*krīta*), the abandoned (*apaviddha*), the one received with a pregnant bride (*sahoḍha*), the one who has come of his own accord (*svayamupāgata*), and the one found by chance (*sahasā dṛṣṭa*)—these are the heirs who are not kinsmen."

[714] "In a *sādhvī*," meaning one who has been consecrated by the marriage sacrament, "self-produced" means a son born of her own body (*aurasa*). "Suddenly seen" refers to one who, being destitute of mother, father, and so forth, is unexpectedly encountered by someone and, without being prompted, accepts the statement, "You are my son," saying, "So be it. "Without kinsmen or heirs" means those who do not receive the inheritance from kinsmen; thus they are described. Yama says: "Twelve kinds of sons have been declared by the sages who perceive the truth."
Of these, six are kinsmen and heirs; six are not kinsmen and do not inherit.
Two [sons] are produced, and one is considered the second, the *kṣetraja*;
the third is known as the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*)—so the knowers of Dharma understand.
The son born of a remarried woman is the fourth, and the son of an unmarried girl is the fifth;
the son secretly born in the house is the sixth—these six sons are the offerers of the funeral cake (piṇḍa).
The abandoned son, the son received with a pregnant bride, the given son, the adopted son, the fifth, the purchased son, and he who initiates himself; these are the sons.
Thus, these six, born of intermixture, are non-heirs and non-relatives. [715] Manu [9.158–60]:
"The twelve sons of men whom Svāyambhuva Manu has declared—"
Among them, six are kinsmen and heirs, while six are kinsmen but not heirs.
The legitimate son of the body, the son begotten on the wife, the adopted son, the made son, the son secretly born, and the cast-off son— these six are both heirs and kinsmen.
The son of an unmarried woman, the son received with a bride, the purchased son, the son of a remarried woman,
the self-given son, and the Śūdra-born son— these six are kinsmen who do not inherit.

Baudhāyana [2.3.31–32]: They declare that the legitimate son, the son of an appointed daughter, the son begotten on the wife, the adopted son, the made son, the son secretly born, and the cast-off son are the heirs to the estate.

The son born of an unmarried girl (kānīna), the son received with a bride (sahoḍha), the purchased son (krīta), the son of a remarried woman (paunarbhava), the self-given son (svayaṃdatta), and the Niṣāda— these they declare to be sharers of the family name (gotrabhāj).

Having enumerated the son of the body (*aurasa*), the son of the appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*), the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*), the maiden-born son (*kānīna*), the secretly born son (*gūḍhotpanna*), the cast-off son (*apaviddha*), the son taken with the bride (*sahoḍha*), the son of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*), the adopted son (*dattaka*), the son received from two [families] (*dvayamupāgata*), the made son (*kṛtrima*), and the bought son (*krīta*), Devala says:
"These twelve sons have been declared for the sake of continuity, whether they be one's own offspring, the offspring of another, or those obtained by chance."
Of these, six are kinsmen and heirs; the other six belong to the father alone.
Furthermore, among the sons, the distinction is determined by their specific order of precedence.
[716] For all these sons of one who has no legitimate son (aurasa) are declared to be heirs;
however, once a legitimate son is born, seniority does not remain among them.
Those sons of theirs who are of the same caste as they are entitled to a third share;
those of lower caste shall live with him, provided with food and clothing.

Having enumerated the *aurasa* (legitimate), *kṣetraja* (born of the wife), *putrikāputra* (son of an appointed daughter), *paunarbhava* (born of a remarried woman), *kānīna* (maiden-born), *gūḍhotpanna* (secretly born), *sahoḍha* (born with the bride), *datta* (given), *krīta* (bought), *svayamupāgata* (self-offered), and *apaviddha* (cast off) sons—those born anywhere at all—Viṣṇu [15.28–30] states: “Among these, each preceding one is superior; he alone shall take the inheritance, and he shall maintain the others. Having enumerated the *aurasa*, *putrikāsuta* (son of an appointed daughter), *kṣetraja*, *kānīna*, *paunarbhava*, *dattaka* (adopted), *krīta* (bought), *svayamdatta* (self-given), *sahoḍha*, and *apaviddha* sons, Yājñavalkya [2.132] states:
“The giver of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) and the taker of the share among these is each subsequent one in the absence of each preceding one.”

Nārada [16.45–47, 49]: "The legitimate son of the body (aurasa), the son begotten on the wife (kṣetraja), and the son of an appointed daughter (putrikāputra), as well as the maiden-born son (kānīna), the son received with the bride (sahoḍha), and likewise the son secretly born (gūḍhotpanna)..."
The son born again, the abandoned, the given, the purchased, the made,
as well as the one who has come of his own accord— these twelve are proclaimed to be sons.
Among them, six are kinsmen and heirs, and six are kinsmen who are not heirs;
each preceding one is declared superior, while each subsequent one is inferior.
These [heirs] succeed to the father's wealth in succession after his death;
in the absence of each elder, the younger one shall obtain it.
Manu [9.185]: "Neither brothers nor fathers are declared to be heirs to the estate;
likewise [9.184]."
In the absence of a superior [heir], an inferior one is entitled to the inheritance;
however, if there are many of equal status, all are sharers of the estate.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"In the absence of each successive superior heir, the next inferior one is entitled to the inheritance.
Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 26.72–73] says:
The son given, the abandoned, the purchased, the made, and likewise the Śūdra-born—
these sons are considered middling, being pure by birth and pure by their actions.

The son born of the wife (kṣetraja), as well as the son of a remarried woman (paunarbhava), the maiden-born son (kānīna), the son received with the bride (sahoḍha), and likewise the son secretly born (gūḍhotpanna), are all censured by the virtuous.
Hārīta [Bṛhaspati, Vyavahāra 26.74–75]:
Sons born of Śūdra women, those who have given themselves away, and those who are known as purchased—all these are declared to be Kāṇḍapṛṣṭhas, along with their lineage; of this there is no doubt.
He who, having cast his own family behind him, goes instead to another's family, becomes a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha* by that evil conduct; of this there is no doubt.
Yama says: "One who has fallen into calamity, one who has entered [the order] by his own choice, and one who is the son of a Vaiṣṇavī—
all these, as well as the three types of Kāṇḍapṛṣṭhas, have been declared by Manu."
The family is known as the *kāṇḍa*, because the ancestors abandoned it;
whoever among them is the eldest, him indeed one should designate as the *kāṇḍa*.
He who, having cast his own family behind him, goes instead to another's family,
is known as a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha* because of that evil conduct.
The Vaiṣṇavī is a Śūdra woman.
Now, regarding the characteristics of a son:
the legitimate son (aurasa).
Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha [17.12–13] states: "Twelve kinds of sons have been observed; the *aurasa* (legitimate) son is one begotten by oneself upon one's own consecrated wife."

[719] Viṣṇu [15.1–2]: “Now, there are twelve kinds of sons. The first is the legitimate son of the body (aurasa), produced by oneself in one’s own consecrated wife. Manu [9.166]: “But that son whom one may beget oneself in one’s own consecrated wife...”
One should recognize him as the legitimate son of the body (aurasa), the first in the order of sons.
Devala says:
A son who is begotten by oneself upon a consecrated wife is indeed called the *aurasa* (legitimate) son; he is the foremost, for he upholds the father's lineage.

Yājñavalkya [2.128]: “The *aurasa* (legitimate) son is one born of the lawful wife. Āpastamba [2.13.1–2]: “For those who approach a woman of the same caste, not previously married to another, as prescribed by the scriptures, during her fertile season, their sons have a connection through ritual acts; and there is no deviation regarding the inheritance for both. Baudhāyana [2.3.14, 16]: “One should know the *aurasa* son to be one procreated by oneself upon a consecrated woman of the same caste. Now they also cite this:”
"You arise from limb after limb; you are born from the heart.
You are indeed the self (ātman) named 'son' (putra); live for a hundred autumns!"

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “A Brāhmaṇa should take the hand of a woman of his own caste; for in her, the bodies of his ancestors are continued. He consecrates himself with the thought that she is his very self through the care he bestows upon their offspring. Thus it is said: ‘From limb by limb you are produced, from the heart you are born;
you are indeed the self named son—live for a hundred autumns!’”
"O ancestors, bestow the embryo—a boy adorned with a lotus garland.
Thus, here is the self of the man; from that you are born here.
The self is declared to be the son, through the grace of the father and the mother."
Because he protects you from that which is called "demerit," you are designated as his son by that very fact.
Now, regarding the *kṣetraja* son, Vasiṣṭha states immediately after the *aurasa* son [17.18]: “In his absence, the second is the *kṣetraja* son born of a woman authorized [to bear a child].
Viṣṇu [15.2] states: “The second is the *kṣetraja* son begotten by a sapinda or by a man of a higher caste upon a woman who has been authorized.”
Manu [9.167]: He who is born on the bed of one who is deceased, impotent, or diseased,
from a woman appointed according to her own dharma, is known as a *kṣetraja* son.
Yājñavalkya [2.128]:
"The *kṣetraja* is one born in the wife by a man of the same *gotra* or by another.

Baudhāyana [2.3.17–18]: "He who is begotten on a deceased man, or on one who is impotent or diseased, with the consent of another, in his own field—that is the *kṣetraja*. He has two fathers and two *gotras*, and he becomes an heir to the funeral offerings (*svadhā*) and the inheritance of both."
Yājñavalkya [2.127]:
A son begotten through *niyoga* by a childless man upon the wife of another belongs,
according to the law, to the inheritance of both and is the giver of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) for both.
Manu [9.53]: "When this [gift] is given for the sake of the seed by way of an agreement regarding the labor,
both the owner of the seed and the owner of the field are seen here as sharers in it."
Nārada [15.58]:
When seed is sown in another's field with the owner's consent,
the offspring is considered to belong to both— the owner of the seed and the owner of the field.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "The offspring belongs to the one who performed the consecration of the seed; thus says Āṅgirasa. Uśanas says that when seed is sown with the consent of both the owner of the seed and the owner of the field, the harvest belongs to both.
Kātyāyana [859] states: "If one should produce fruit even with the consent of the owner of the field..."
In this world, those two are indeed sharers of it, for there is no fruit without one of them.

Hārīta says: "They say a *kṣetraja* son belongs to the father while he is alive because of his lack of independence; when the father is dead, he belongs to both lineages (*dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*) because no seed was sown [by the deceased]. A field does not bear fruit without seed, nor does a seed sprout without a field; since both are observed [to be necessary], some maintain that the offspring belongs to both. For them, the first funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) belongs to the progenitor. At the offering of the cakes, he should offer two cakes. Or else, at a single cake, he should mention both: the son on the second [cake] and the grandson on the third, while naming the three ancestors who partake of the smearings (*lepin*), up to the seventh generation, according to others."

"While the master of the field (the husband) is alive," they call his son "born of the field" (*kṣetraja*). The reason for this is that a woman lacks independence. However, when the master of the field has died, according to the statement of Manu: "The sonless woman, remaining faithful to her vow, shall protect the bed of her husband. Although the woman's lack of independence remains the same in that state, it does not belong to the owner of the field alone. He states the reason for this: "Because the seed was not sown by the owner of the field. Regarding "in the *nirvāpa*": *nirvāpa* is that in which something is poured out; it refers to the ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛyajña*). As for "two in one *piṇḍa*": the distributive sense "two in each *piṇḍa*" is to be understood. This is in accordance with the statement of Āpastamba: "If there should be two fathers, one should designate two in each *piṇḍa*" [Āp. Śrauta Sūtra 1.9.7]. Regarding "the second [he should begin] with the son," etc.: the meaning is that he should begin with the son in the second [case]. "And pronouncing the three who are smeared (*lepinaḥ*)," the meaning is that he should recite them two by two.
Nārada [16.23]:
Sons belonging to two fathers (dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa) should offer the rice-ball (piṇḍa) and water separately to both [fathers].
Likewise, they should take half of the inheritance from both the biological father (bījika) and the owner of the field (kṣetrika).
Baudhāyana says: "Moreover, they cite this:
'For one who has two fathers, there should be the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍas) for both; on each rice-ball, the names of both should be mentioned.
There should thus be three rice-balls for six ancestors; by acting in this way, one does not go astray.'"

Now, regarding the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*), Vasiṣṭha states at [17.15]: “The third is known as the *putrikā*. For she who has no brother goes toward the ancestors of her male [relative]; she returns to the state of being a son. The word ‘of the male’ (*puṃsaḥ*) means from the husband; ‘returns’ (*pratīcīnam*) means a turning back, that is, facing toward the paternal family.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “According to Pracetas, an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) is like a son. Her offspring—the son of the appointed daughter—is the giver of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) to both the maternal grandfather and the paternal grandfather.
In this world, there is no difference between a son and a daughter’s son in terms of their capacity for showing favor;
therefore, out of doubt, one should not marry a woman who has no brothers.”
Yājñavalkya [2.128] states: "The legitimate son born of the lawful wife, and equal to him is the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*).

Following this, Baudhāyana [2.3.15] continues: "One should know that the son born of a daughter who has been formally accepted is the son of an appointed daughter; [the son] born of her is the *dauhitra* (son of the daughter)."
In this regard, with reference to one who has no biological son, Manu (9.131–32) states:
"The daughter's son alone shall take the entire wealth of one who has no son;
for the daughter's son shall take the whole inheritance of his father who has no son."
Devala says regarding the succession of legitimate sons:
"The son of an appointed daughter (putrikāputra) is equal to him; he may thus be the heir.
He alone shall offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his father and to his maternal grandfather."
In this world, there should be no distinction between a son’s son and a daughter’s son according to the law;
for both of them have brought forth their parents from his own body.
Whether she has been formally appointed or not, whichever son of similar status she may bear,
through him the maternal grandfather becomes the recipient of the *pinda* offerings and shall inherit the wealth.
Regarding the entitlement of a daughter whose marriage has been performed or not yet performed, Bṛhaspati states (Vyavahāra 26.133):
"Just as she has ownership over her father’s wealth even when [paternal] kinsmen are present,
so too does her son have a claim to the wealth of his mother and maternal grandfather."
[726] Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “A daughter receives the woman’s property (strīdhana). That property of her offspring belongs exclusively to the share of the daughter.

By the word “her” (tat-) in the phrase “that offspring” (tadapatyasya), the mother of the appointed daughter (putrikā) is intended. The property of her son—who is born later, who is without other sons, and who has passed away—“belongs exclusively to the share of the daughter,” meaning it belongs exclusively to the share of the appointed daughter. The intention is that he is, in effect, her uterine brother. Now, Manu [9.127–29]:
A sonless man may, by this rite, make a daughter his "appointed daughter" (putrikā), with the agreement:
"Whatever offspring may be born of her shall be the one who performs the ancestral offerings for me."
In accordance with this very procedure, Dakṣa Prajāpati himself formerly created a daughter for the sake of increasing his own lineage.
With a joyful heart, he respectfully gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kāśyapa,
and twenty-seven to King Soma.
Vasiṣṭha [18.17]: "I shall give you this sisterless maiden, adorned with ornaments;
whatever son is born of her, let him be my son."

[727] Gautama [28.18–20]: “A father who has no other offspring may, having performed a sacrifice to Agni and Prajāpati, give away his daughter with the agreement: ‘This child is for our sake. According to some, she becomes an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) by mere intention alone. Because of the uncertainty regarding this, one should not marry a girl who has no brother. Jābāli:
“But in the giving away of an appointed daughter, the knower of Dharma [should perform the rite] with a *sthālīpāka* offering.”
Having worshipped Agni and Prajāpati, and likewise for the granting of a son;
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "And by a sonless man, whatever girl has been mentally adopted as a son,
[that sonship is established] either in the presence of the king, the fire, and kinsmen, or elsewhere."
Whether she has been promised to a suitor by her father before conception or after the payment of a bride-price,
or whether she is given when the father has died, she is to be known as a *putrikā*.
She, being such, receives an equal share from her father's inheritance. [728] Manu [9.140]:
The son of an appointed daughter (putrikā) shall first offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his mother.
The second [offering] is for her father, and the third is for her father's father.
Now, regarding the son born of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*):
on this point, Vasiṣṭha and Viṣṇu state [Va. 17.18; Vi. 14.7]: "The fourth is the son of a remarried woman. Manu [9.175] states:
But he whom a woman, having been abandoned by her husband or being a widow, bears after marrying again of her own accord, is called *paunarbhava*.
Yājñavalkya [2.130]:
A son born to a woman who has been previously married, whether she be unwidowed or widowed, is a *paunarbhava*.
Kātyāyana [860]:
If a woman, having abandoned a eunuch or an outcast husband, takes another husband,
the son born of her from that second husband is clearly the offspring of his biological progenitor.

[729] Now, regarding the *kānīna* son, Vasiṣṭha states at 17.21–23: “The *kānīna* is the fifth. If a girl who has not been consecrated [by marriage] should procreate in her father’s house out of desire, they say that he becomes the son of the maternal grandfather. Furthermore, they cite this example:”

"If an unmarried daughter should obtain a son through a husband of equal status, by that son the maternal grandfather becomes a grandfather-in-law (pautrī); he shall offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) and inherit the wealth. Thus says Nārada [16.18].
But he who has an unknown father and is born of a maiden (kānīna), being secretly begotten by his mother,
shall offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his maternal grandfather and inherit his property from him.
Baudhāyana [2.3.24] states: "He who is born of a woman whom one approaches without having consecrated her and without her being given in marriage is a *kānīna*.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "But he who is born of an unmarried woman (*adattā*) of the same caste in the father's house..."
He is his son born of an unmarried girl (kānīna), to whom she is given once again.
[730] Nārada [16.17]: "The son born of an unmarried girl (kānīna), the son received with the bride (sahoḍha), and he who is born of a concealed woman (gūḍhaja)—
the man who marries them is to be known as their father, and they are recorded as heirs to his property."
Now, regarding one born in secret,
Manu [9.170] states:
"He who is born in a house, but it is not known whose he is— "
He who was born secretly in the house shall belong to him whose wife gave birth to him.

Now, regarding the *sahoḍha* son, Viṣṇu states [14.15–17]: “The seventh is the *sahoḍha*: the son of a woman who is married while pregnant; he belongs to the one who took her hand in marriage. Manu [9.173] says:
If a woman who is pregnant is married, whether her condition be known or unknown, the child belongs to the husband;
such a son is called *sahoḍha* (one taken with the bride).
[731] Now, regarding the adopted son (*dattaka*),
Manu states there (9.168, 141–42):
If a mother or a father should give a son with water in times of distress— one who is similar [in status] and given with affection— he is to be known as the "given" (dattrima) son.
But he whose adopted son is endowed with all good qualities shall indeed inherit that estate, even though he has come from another lineage.
An adopted son shall not inherit the family name or the estate of his biological father;
for the funeral cake follows the family name and the estate, and the ancestral offering (svadhā) ceases for one who gives [the son away].

Vasiṣṭha [15.1–8]: “A person is born from blood and semen, having the mother and father as his cause. Regarding the giving away, selling, or abandoning of such a person, the mother and father have authority. However, one should not give away or receive in adoption an only son; for he is for the sake of the lineage of the ancestors. A woman, however, may neither give away nor receive in adoption a son without the permission of her husband. One intending to adopt a son should summon his kinsmen, inform the king, and having offered the *vyāhṛti* oblations in the middle of the house, he should receive a boy who is not a distant kinsman and who is not too closely related. If a doubt arises, one should treat a distant kinsman as if he were a Śūdra. For it is known from scripture: ‘By means of one, many are saved.’”

‘Not having relatives nearby’ (*adūrebāndhavam*) means having uncles and so forth in close proximity. ‘Only not being closely related’ (*asannikṛṣṭam eva*) means even one whose virtues and faults are unknown; the particle *eva* has the sense of *api* (even). Regarding the phrase ‘in case of doubt,’ etc.—due to the absence of relatives, if there is a doubt concerning caste, one should determine him to be a Śūdra and ‘establish’ him as one devoid of sacraments (*saṃskāra*). The intention is that even a Śūdra may indeed become a son. Now, regarding the purchased son, Manu says [9.174]:
If one should purchase from someone else a son for the sake of his own offspring—
whether he be similar or dissimilar to himself— he is that man’s *krītaka* (bought) son.

Baudhāyana [2.3.26] states: "One who is purchased from the hands of his mother and father, or from those of either one of them, and is taken for the sake of offspring, is a *krītaka* (bought son). Now, regarding one who has come of his own accord, Manu [9.177] says:
He who is bereft of parents, or has been abandoned by them without cause,
and shows himself to someone, is known as one "self-given" (svayaṃdatta).

Now, regarding the *apaviddha* (cast-off son), Viṣṇu [15.24–26] states: “The *apaviddha* is the eleventh; he is one abandoned by both father and mother, and he is taken up by someone. Vasiṣṭha [17.36–37] states: “The *apaviddha* is the fifth; he is one whom a man may take up after he has been cast off by his mother and father.”
[734] Now, regarding that which is artificial, Manu says there (9.169):
He whom the two [parents] might adopt as one who is similar to themselves and discerning of virtues and faults,
a son endowed with the qualities of a son— he is to be known as the *kṛtrima* (adopted) son.
Now, regarding the son of a Śūdra woman, Viṣṇu [15.27] states: “And he who is begotten anywhere [is the twelfth].
Vasiṣṭha [17.38] says: “They say that the son of a Śūdra woman is indeed the sixth.”
"The son whom a Brāhmaṇa may father out of lust upon a Śūdra woman is called a Pāraśava, because he is born as a corpse (śava) even while still alive."
Baudhāyana [2.3.29–30]: "One born from a Śūdra woman through lust by a man of the twice-born castes is a Pāraśava.
Then Manu [9.180–81]:
"These eleven sons, beginning with the Kṣetraja, as they have been described..."
The wise say that these [rites] are substitutes for a son, intended to prevent the omission of sacred duties.
These sons who have been described as born from the seed of another by way of incidental discussion—
belong to him from whose seed they were born, and not to anyone else.
Bṛhaspati (Vyavahāra 26.77–78):
"Thirteen types of sons have been declared by Manu in their proper order;
among them, the legitimate son of the body (*aurasa*) and the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāsuta*) are the causes for the continuity of the lineage."
Just as oil is remembered by the virtuous as a substitute for clarified butter when the latter is unavailable,
so too are the eleven types of sons [considered substitutes] in the absence of both the appointed daughter (*putrikā*) and the legitimate son of the body (*aurasa*).

In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "The adopted son (*dattaka*), the self-given (*svayaṃdatta*), the made (*kṛtrima*), the purchased (*krīta*), and the abandoned (*apaviddha*)— these sons must always indeed be supported."
Those who belong to different lineages (*gotra*), have separate funeral offerings (*piṇḍa*), and likewise establish distinct family lines,
share in the three-day period of impurity (*āśauca*) during both birth and death.
Furthermore, in some places, a Śūdra who is a *pāraśava* slave may exist among Brāhmaṇas who possess clothing, food, wives, fields, and seeds.
But for kings who are consumed by curses, who are constantly subject to decline,
or who are habitually engaged in battle, these [omens] may occasionally occur.

Whether it be a legitimate son (aurasa) or the son of an appointed daughter (putrikāsuta), they exist there; however, among them, the sons born of the wife (kṣetraja) and the others are to be distinguished.
These eleven are of separate lineages, but they merely continue the family line;
all of them constantly perform ancestral rites and other duties for them like servants.
The secret-born, the maiden-born, the one born with the bride, the field-born, and likewise the son of a remarried woman— these also [exist] among Vaiśyas out of fear of royal punishment.
Five [of these] are excluded for the wealthy; all the rest, however, apply even to Śūdras who live as servants and subsist on the food of others.
For those whose bodies are dependent on others, there is no son anywhere;
therefore, from a male slave and a female slave, only a slave is born.
[737] Now follows the investigation into the status of a son.
Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha [18.6] states: “They dispute whether the son belongs to the owner of the field or to the progenitor.”

Āpastamba [2.13.6]: "Guard this lineage with vigilance; let no one sow the seeds of another in your field. In the world beyond, the son belongs to the progenitor; thus the father makes this lineage fruitless. Thus it is said.
"Between the seed and the womb, the seed is said to be superior;
for the offspring of all beings is characterized by the characteristics of the seed."
Whatever kind of seed is sown in a field at the proper time,
that very kind of seed grows therein with its own characteristic marks and qualities.
Thus:
"Therefore, a wise and disciplined man, who understands both theoretical knowledge and practical wisdom and desires long life, must never sow his seed in the wife of another."
[738] The wise have declared that a person is precisely this much: namely, wife, self, and offspring; likewise, he who is the husband is remembered as being the woman herself.
A wife is not released from her husband by means of a ransom or by abandonment;
thus we know the dharma established of old by Prajāpati.

Just as one who is not the biological father of offspring born from mares, camels, female slaves, goats, sheep, or buffaloes does not share in their lineage, so it is likewise with the wives of others.
Those who possess seed but have no field of their own, yet sow it in another's field, never obtain any fruit of the crop that has grown.
If a bull were to sire a hundred calves upon the cows of another, those calves belong only to the owner of the cows; the bull's seed was spent in vain.
In the same way, those who possess no field but sow their seed in another’s field benefit the owner of the field; the owner of the seed does not obtain the fruit.
But when no fruit is intended for either the owner of the field or the sower, the benefit belongs clearly to the owner of the field; for the womb is more important than the seed.
If seed carried by a futile wind should sprout in someone's field, it should be known as belonging to that owner of the field alone; the sower does not receive the fruit.
This law regarding the offspring of cows, horses, female slaves, camels, goats, sheep, birds, and buffaloes should be understood.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "If seed is sown in a field without the knowledge of the owner of the field, it belongs to the owner of the field alone; the owner of the seed does not deserve a share therein. Gautama [18.9–14] states: "The owner of the field who has committed adultery with another's wife does not deserve a share. The offspring of one who has no offspring belongs to the progenitor, unless there is an agreement to the contrary. If born in the field while the husband is alive, it belongs to him; if born from another, it belongs to that other; or it may belong to both. However, if he protects her, it belongs to the protector alone."

“[The rule] ‘the offspring does not belong to the progenitor beyond the second’ means that by means of *niyoga*, the offspring produced beyond the second—that is, the third—is not for the progenitor. ‘Of another, by agreement’: through a convention such as ‘let this offspring be mine,’ it belongs to that other, the seed-giver. And ‘in the field while [the husband] is living’: when an offspring is born in the wife—the ‘field’—of a husband who is living but incapable of procreation, that offspring belongs only to the owner of the field.”

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "The offspring belongs invariably to the owner of the field (*kṣetrin*); this is the Vedic doctrine. Some say the offspring belongs to the mother. Likewise: "When Vasiṣṭha and Kaśyapa, having emerged from their water-dwelling while submerged in the water, one of them procreated offspring unrecognized by the people. Thus, their lineage was twofold. Because, having combined on one side the family duties, the acceptance [of the son], the inheritance, the funeral rice-ball (*piṇḍa*), and the water-offering, they bestow these even upon those born in another's field. Now, the instruction regarding sons and so forth.
Regarding this, Manu says (9.182–83):
"Among brothers born of the same father, if even one should have a son,
Manu has declared that they are all possessed of a son through that son."
If among all the wives of one husband even one should have a son,
Manu has declared that they are all possessed of sons by virtue of that son.
Bṛhaspati (Vyavahāra 26.79–80):
"If there are many brothers born of one father who are uterine siblings,
then upon the birth of a son for even one of them, they are all considered to have sons."
[741] This same rule is prescribed for many wives who have a single husband;
if one among them has sons, he alone shall offer the rice-balls (piṇḍas) for all of them.
Now, regarding the etymology of "son" (*putra*) and related matters, Manu and Viṣṇu state:
"Because a son saves his father from the hell named *put*."
Therefore, he was called "Son" by the Self-existent One himself.
Hārīta says: A hell named Punnāman has been proclaimed, as well as a hell called Chinnatantra;
because he indeed protects one from that, he is remembered as "putra" (son).
Bṛhaspati (Vyavahāra 26.81–82): Since he saves his father from the hell named Put,
he should strive for his birth even by the mere sight of his face.
The grandson and the son of an appointed daughter are both considered equal in their capacity to secure the attainment of heaven through the offering of inheritance and the funeral cake (piṇḍa).
Viṣṇu and Vasiṣṭha [Vi. 15.45; Vas. 17.1]:
"In this son, the father pays off his debt and attains immortality, provided he beholds the face of the born son while still living."
Śaṅkha, Likhita, and Paiṭhīnasi say:
"Wherever he may be born, a son brings joy to his father;
by offering the funeral cakes (piṇḍa), he indeed attains freedom from debt to the ancestors."
Hārīta says: He whose son is pure, capable, virtuous in his early years,
and a restrainer of his own faults, delivers his ancestors.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"The Agnihotra, the three Vedas, and sacrifices accompanied by hundreds of sacrificial fees do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of one who has fathered an eldest son."
For one who is firmly established in sons and grandsons, who has many children, who is alive, and whose Vedic sacrifices have not been spilled— ah, heaven has indeed been attained!
Śaṅkha, Likhita, Viṣṇu, Vasiṣṭha, and Hārīta [state]:
"Through a son one conquers the world; through a grandson one attains infinity;
and through the grandson of a son, one reaches the realm of the Sun."
Yājñavalkya [1.78]:
"Through sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, one attains endless worlds and reaches heaven.

Vasiṣṭha [17.2–4]: "It is heard in the sacred texts that 'endless are the worlds for those who have sons; there is no world for one without a son. 'May offspring be ours, even if we are childless'—this is a curse. Furthermore, there is a Vedic mantra: 'O Agni, through offspring may I attain immortality.'"
Bṛhaspati (Vyavahāra 26.88–90): A man without a son should, with great effort, adopt a son of whatever kind may be available,
for the sake of performing the rites of offering funeral cakes and water, and for the purpose of pronouncing his name.
Ancestors, fearing a fall into hell, long for their sons, thinking:
"Whoever among us shall go to Gayā, he will deliver us."
Just as a man drowning while crossing water with a leaky boat sinks down,
so too does a father sink into blinding darkness because of his wicked sons.
[744] Then, regarding this matter, Manu has been censured there [in the following verses]: [9.143–44].

Both the son born of a woman not authorized [to bear children] and the son obtained from a brother-in-law by a woman who already has a son do not deserve a share; they are born of an adulterer and born of lust.
Even if a man has procreated on an appointed woman,
a son born contrary to the prescribed rule is not entitled to his father's inheritance, for he was begotten by one who has fallen from his status.
Gautama [28.24]: "That which is born of another man in the wife of a god is without a share.
"Those who are born of one man upon an unauthorized woman, as well as those born by many [men], [are not entitled to inheritance]."
All those shares belong to the owner of the seed; they are indeed the sons of the seed-owners alone.
The seeders (the biological fathers) shall offer the funeral cake if the mother was taken for a bride-price;
but if she was obtained without a bride-price, the offering of the cake belongs to the husband alone.
Manu [9.191]: "If two men, born of two different fathers, should dispute over the wealth of a woman, he whose property is inherited from his father shall take that, and not the other."
Now, the division of the estate of one who dies without a son.
Regarding this, Manu [9.190] says:
"For one who has died childless, a kinsman of the same lineage (sagotra) shall carry on the line."
In that regard, whatever property may have been acquired as an inheritance, one should deliver that to him.

‘She should take [a son] from him’ means that she should produce offspring from a man of the same lineage (*sagotra*). Vṛddha-Manu says: “A woman without a son, protecting the bed of her husband and remaining firm in her vow...”
The wife alone should offer that funeral cake, and she shall obtain the entire benefit.
Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 26.92–95, 97–98, 105]: According to the Vedas, the treatises on law, and worldly custom,
the wise have declared that a wife is half of one's body, sharing equally in the fruits of both merit and demerit.
For one whose wife has not passed away, half of his body remains alive;
while half the body still lives, how could another take possession of the wealth?
But when agnatic kinsmen— fathers, brothers, and blood relations— are present,
the wife of one who has died without a son shall take his share.
When her husband has died, a devoted wife shall inherit his wealth, including the previously consecrated *agnihotra* fires; this is the eternal law.
Having taken mobile and immobile property, gold, base metals, grain, liquids, and clothing, one should cause the śrāddha for the monthly, six-monthly, and other rites to be performed.

One should honor paternal uncles, teachers, daughters' sons, the husband's sister's son, maternal uncles, the elderly, the blind, guests, and women with offerings for the ancestors (kavya) and for the gods (pūrta).
The king shall punish with the punishment for a thief those sapindas, kinsmen, or others who might stand as obstacles and seize the property.
[747] Then Nārada said:
"In the absence of a son, however, a daughter [is the heir], because her lineage is seen to be equal [to his].
Both the son and the daughter are the perpetuators of the father's lineage."
Likewise: [Manu 9.130] "As one is oneself, so is a son; a daughter is equal to a son.
While she remains as one's own self, how could another take the wealth?"
Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 26.132]:
A wife who is of equal status, married to an equal, virtuous, and devoted to service—
whether she has borne sons or not, she shall indeed inherit the wealth of her father.
‘Kṛtā’ means one who has been established as an appointed daughter (*putrikā*).
Likewise [Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.135]:
"Of a son who is deceased and destitute of wife and children..."
The mother should be known as the heir to the estate, or else the brother with her permission.
[748] Manu [9.217]: "The mother shall obtain the inheritance of a son who dies without offspring;
and when the mother has also passed away, the father's mother shall take the wealth."
Gautama [27.28]: “The division is without commingling; for the *pretas*, it belongs to the eldest. Manu [9.185–87]:
The father shall take the inheritance of one who has no son, or the brothers themselves.
Water should be offered to three [ancestors], and the funeral cake (piṇḍa) is extended to three.
The fourth among these is the giver; a fifth is not possible.
Beyond that, the inheritance shall go to a *sakulya*, or to a teacher, or even to a pupil.

Paiṭhīnasi: "The property of one who has died without a son goes to his brothers; in their absence, the mother and father shall receive it; or else the wife, provided she is not younger [in seniority], as well as those of the same lineage, pupils, and fellow students."

Furthermore, as for the statement by Viṣṇu [17.4], “The wealth of one who dies without a son goes to the wife,” and so forth, which establishes that even when brothers exist, the wealth of a sonless person goes to the wife—that refers specifically to a wife who possesses qualities such as maintaining the husband’s bed and performing the *śrāddha* rites, as determined by a consideration of the words of Vṛddha-Manu, beginning with “A sonless woman [should protect] the bed of her husband. If such a wife does not exist, or if she is present but lacks these qualities, then that wealth goes to the brother. And as for that which—
And they shall provide for his maintenance until the end of the women's livelihood;
if they preserve their husband’s bed, they shall receive it, but otherwise, that [inheritance] shall be withheld from them.

Thus, what was stated by Śaṅkha refers merely to maintenance, and it concerns only those women who are free from widowhood and are non-adulterous. As for the statement by Yājñavalkya (2.135), “The parents and likewise the brothers,” which assigns the right of inheritance to the parents alone when brothers exist, that refers to property acquired by the father, grandfather, and so forth. Furthermore, that which is acquired without detriment to the paternal estate belongs to the brothers alone, even when the parents are present.
Devala says:
“Then the uterine brothers shall divide the inheritance of one who has no son.”
Or even daughters of noble lineage, or even a father who is still living.
The brothers of the same caste, the mother, or the wife, respectively;
in their absence, the kinsmen or the co-residents shall take [the property].
Yājñavalkya [2.135–36]: The wife, the daughters, the parents, the brothers,
as well as their son, a kinsman of the same lineage (gotraja), a relative, a pupil, and fellow students.
In the absence of these, each subsequent one among them is the heir to the wealth of the deceased who left no son; for this rule applies to all castes.

Viṣṇu (19.4–13): “The wealth of one who has no son goes to his wife; in her absence, it goes to the daughter; in her absence, to the mother; in her absence, to the father; in his absence, to the brothers; in their absence, to the sons of the brothers; in their absence, to the paternal kinsmen (*bandhu*); in their absence, to the *sakulyas*; in their absence, to a fellow student; in their absence, with the exception of the property of a Brāhmaṇa, it goes to the King.
After the daughter and the daughter’s son, Bṛhaspati [Vya. 26.134] states: “In their absence, however, the brothers, as well as the uterine brothers’ sons...”
Sapindas, kinsmen, disciples, and those learned in the Vedas are entitled to the wealth.
If a man dies without offspring, without a wife, and without brothers, father, or mother,
all his *sapiṇḍa* relatives shall divide that inheritance according to their respective shares.
[751] From the wealth that has arisen, one should set aside half; from that half, one should separately set aside another half for the monthly, six-monthly, and annual śrāddhas with great care.
Where there are many kinsmen, as well as members of the same lineage and relatives,
he who is the nearest among them shall take the wealth of one who has no offspring.

Baudhāyana [1.11.15–12]: “The great-grandfather, the grandfather, the father, oneself, uterine brothers, and the sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons of a woman of the same caste—these, while being undivided heirs, are called *sapiṇḍas*. Even those who are divided heirs are called *sakulyas*. For when there are no offspring of the body (*aṅgajas*), the property goes to them. In the absence of *sapiṇḍas*, the *sakulya* [inherits]. In his absence, the father, the teacher, a pupil, or the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) shall take it. In their absence, the king. Nārada [16.51–52]: “And in the absence of daughters, the *sakulyas* and kinsmen likewise [inherit].”
Then, in the absence of all those of the same caste, that property goes to the king.
Except for a Brahmin, however, a king devoted to righteousness shall provide a livelihood for their wives; this is remembered as the rule for inheritance.
Devala says: In all cases, the king shall take the property of one who fails to give, with the exception of the property of a Brahmin;
however, he should cause the property of a Brahmin to be given to those who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*).
Baudhāyana says:
"The property of a Brahmin destroys one's sons and grandsons; poison kills only a single person.
They say that 'poison' is not truly poison; it is the property of a Brahmin that is called poison."
Therefore, a king should never, under any circumstances, seize the property of a Brahmin;
for that which is the property of a Brahmin is indeed the most potent poison.
Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 26.119]:
"Those Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who are childless and deprived of wives and brothers—
the king shall take their wealth, for he is the sovereign lord of all."

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "Property belonging to an assembly or the property of a learned Vedic scholar does not go to the king; it is not to be seized by the king, as it is entrusted to gods and Brahmins. Nor [is seized] that which has come down through the succession of deposits or sealed deposits, nor the wealth of children or women. For thus it is said: 'The wealth of a woman and likewise the wealth of children is not to be seized by the king; the property of women consists of the sixfold income, and the wealth of children is that inherited from their father.'"
Manu [8.27]: But the king shall protect the inheritance obtained by a minor until he has returned from his teacher's house or until he has passed his minority.

Viṣṇu [3.65]: “The king shall protect the property of minors, those without protectors, and women. Śaṅkha and Likhita: “The king shall guard the wealth of minors who have not yet attained legal capacity, as well as that of the wives of Vedic scholars and heroes. Property whose owners have perished reverts to the king. Regarding sons, Baudhāyana [2.3.37]: “He should deposit their shares, along with their increments of interest, under secure custody until they reach legal capacity.”
Kātyāyana [845]: All [the heirs] together shall protect the share of one who has gone abroad;
likewise, when a son dies while still a child, his inheritance must be protected by his kinsmen as his own property.
But after that, those who are *pogaṇḍas* should divide it according to their respective shares.
Regarding the term *bālaputre*: it refers to one whose son is a child (*bāla*). A *pogaṇḍa* is an extremely young person, one who is not yet acquainted with legal affairs.
Viṣṇu [15.40] states: "And he who takes the property is the one who offers the funeral oblation (*piṇḍa*)."
The Smṛti states: "He who takes the wealth shall perform the Śrāddha for him and offer the Piṇḍa for three generations. [754] Vṛddha-Śātātapa and Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 26.139] state:
"A brother, or a brother's son, or a Sapiṇḍa, or even a disciple..."
Having performed the rite of combining the funeral cakes, he should thereafter perform the rite for prosperity.
Vasiṣṭha [Viṣṇu 15.31]: “Even if he has not obtained his father’s wealth, a son should offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa).
Then Viṣṇu [17.15]: “The teacher or the pupil shall take the property of a forest hermit.
Yājñavalkya [2.137].
For forest-dwellers, renunciants, and students, the heirs to their property are, in order:
the preceptor, the virtuous disciple, the spiritual brother, and one who shares the same sacred ford.
Now, the division of reunited property.
Regarding this, Manu [9.210–12] says: "If those who were divided should live together again and then divide once more..."
In that case, the division shall be equal; there, seniority does not exist.
If among them the eldest or the youngest should be deprived of his share at the time of distribution,
or if either of them should die, his portion is not lost.
[755] Those uterine brothers who are reunited, as well as the uterine sisters, shall assemble together and divide that property equally.
Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 26.106]:
"Furthermore, those two who have reunited out of affection shall share in each other's property.
Likewise [Vyavahāra 26.106–08, 112]:
Among brothers who have already divided their inheritance and are living together again out of mutual affection, no seniority exists for the purpose of a subsequent division.
If anyone should die or somehow renounce the world, his share is not lost; it is ordained for his uterine brother.
His sister, however, deserves to receive a share from that [inheritance];
this is the law for one who is childless and lacks both a wife and a father.
But among those who have lived together, whoever acquires more by means of learning, valor, or other such qualities, two shares shall be given to him; the remainder shall have equal shares.
Nārada [16.24]:
But for those who have reunited, the share belongs to them alone;
otherwise, those entitled to a share shall go to the others when there are no offspring.

[756] ‘Otherwise than this,’ in the absence of reunited coparceners (*saṃsṛṣṭin*); ‘among those without seed,’ among those who lack a lineage; ‘the others,’ the heirs to the shares; ‘he shall go to,’ he shall approach.
Śaṅkha says:
“If among brothers someone should die or enter the religious order without offspring...”
The remaining [sons] shall divide his wealth, excluding the woman's property.
They should provide for his maintenance until the end of their lives, provided they preserve the bed of their husband; if they do not, that [duty] shall be withheld from the others.
Regarding his daughter, it is held that her paternal share is for her maintenance:
until her marriage, she shall take her portion; thereafter, her husband shall maintain her.

"In the others," meaning while they do not protect the bed; "until the sacrament" means including the marriage, he shall take that portion by which the completion of the marriage occurs—this is the meaning. Yājñavalkya [2.138]:
"But a reunited coparcener [takes the share] of a reunited coparcener, and a uterine brother [that] of a uterine brother."
One should give a share to one who is born, and likewise take away a share from one who has died.
[757] Immediately thereafter, Yājñavalkya [2.139] states:
"But a uterine brother who is a *saṃsṛṣṭin* (one reunited) shall not take the wealth of one not born of the same womb;
nor shall one not reunited take it, provided he is reunited, even if born of a different mother."
In this context, "associated" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*) refers to one who is connected by the same womb, namely a uterine brother (*sodara*). Kātyāyana states:
"But among those who are associated, the associated inherit; among those who are separate, the separate inherit."
In the absence [of a son], those who share in each other's seedless [property] should be known as takers of the wealth.
‘In the absence’ means in the absence of those who seize the property, such as wives, sons, and others.
Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 26.113]:
“Furthermore, one who was divided by his father or brother and has subsequently lived together again in one place...”
Or, if he is united with his paternal uncle out of affection, he is called a *saṃsṛṣṭin*.
[758] Now, the determination of partition; regarding this, Nārada says [16.36–40]:
In cases of doubt regarding the law of partition among heirs, a decision shall be made by kinsmen based on a written deed of division, as it initiates the separate performance of affairs.
For brothers who have not divided their property, a single religious duty prevails;
once division has occurred, their religious duties also become separate for each of them.

The receipt of gifts, the acceptance of cattle, food, houses, and fields, as well as cooking, religious duties, income, and expenditure, are to be understood as distinct for those who have divided their property.

Brothers who have divided their inheritance may act as witnesses, stand surety for one another, and engage in giving or receiving gifts; those who have not divided may not do so with respect to each other.
One should recognize those among whom these transactions proceed in the world according to their own property as divided, even in the absence of a written document.
Yājñavalkya [2.149]: When there is a denial of partition, the determination of partition is to be known through kinsmen, relatives, witnesses, written documents,
and separate holdings of houses and fields.

Likewise [2.52]: "Indeed, it is recorded in the Smṛti that among brothers, between husband and wife, and between father and son, suretyship, debt, and witness-hood do not exist as long as they have not divided their property."
‘Yautakaiḥ’ means by separate [means].
Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 26.147]:
“When they have separate income, expenditure, and wealth, and lend money to one another...”
And those who establish trade routes shall undoubtedly be divided [in their inheritance].
Now, regarding the duties of those who have separated,
Nārada says:
"If many sons born of one [father] live separately in religious duties and separately in their occupations..."
If they are not esteemed for their tasks, even though they possess distinct skills and qualities.
If they should give away their own shares, or even sell them,
they may do all that as they wish, for they are indeed masters of their own property.
Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 26]:
One should not disturb the share of whatever kind has been enjoyed by someone;
likewise [Vyavahāra 26].
Furthermore, he who makes a division according to his own will and then violates it again shall be made to pay the king’s share and be punished for the offense committed.
Likewise [Vyavahāra 26]:
"Whether divided or undivided, heirs have equal rights to immovable property;
for no single person has authority over it in matters of gift, mortgage, or sale."

Thus ends the section on the Partition of Inheritance in the Vyavahārakāṇḍa of the Kṛtyakalpataru, composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, son of Bhaṭṭa Śrī Hṛdayadhara, who served as the Great Minister for Peace and War (Mahāsāndhivigrahika) to His Majesty, the Emperor of Kings, the illustrious Govindacandradeva.
[761] 75. Now, regarding gambling and betting, Nārada says this: [19.1]
Gambling with dice, sticks, and so forth,
played with deceit, as well as betting games involving animals— this is the category of gambling and betting.
Manu [9.229]: That which is performed with inanimate objects is called "gambling" (dyūta) in the world;
that which is performed with animate beings is to be known as "betting" (samāhvaya).
Kākinyas, vadhrikās, śalākās, lead,
dice with seeds, and kuhakas— these are the six implements of gambling.
Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 28.1]: When birds, rams, deer, and other animals, having been staked upon one another,
strike each other after a wager has been made, they call that *samāhvaya* (challenging match).
[762] Manu [9.221–22, 224, 227–28]: The king shall banish from the kingdom both gambling and betting;
these two vices are the destroyers of the realms of rulers of the earth.
Gambling and betting are open forms of theft;
therefore, the king should always exert effort to suppress them.
The king shall execute all those who engage in gambling or betting, whether they do so themselves or cause others to do so, as well as Śūdras who assume the marks of the twice-born.
In ancient times, this gambling was seen to cause great enmity;
therefore, a wise man should not indulge in gambling, even for the sake of amusement.
Whether it be done secretly or openly, whatever man should practice that [prohibited act],
there shall be a variety of punishments for him at the king's discretion.
Kātyāyana says: One should never indulge in gambling, for it increases anger and greed,
produces wicked people, is cruel, and destroys the wealth of men.
Since strife surely arises from gambling, just as poison comes from the mouth of a serpent,
therefore a king should desist from it, for that is indeed a vice regarding his domain.
If it should appear clearly, even when situated at the door,
one should cause that which bestows its fruit to be made for the purpose of deluding the noble ones.
Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 27.1–2]:
Gambling was prohibited by Manu as it destroys truth, purity, and wealth;
yet it has been practiced by others as well, provided with a share for the king.
For that which is supervised by a master of the assembly is indeed a means for identifying thieves.
Yājñavalkya [2.203]:
Gambling shall be conducted in a single location for the purpose of identifying thieves.
This same rule is to be understood as applicable to gambling with living creatures and to betting matches.
Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 27.3]: "The keeper of the gambling house (sabhika) shall pay to the winner and to the king. Kātyāyana: [764]
The master of the gambling house shall conduct the game and personally pay the stake to the king;
he may take a ten percent interest on the loss sustained by the defeated player.
The winner shall himself pay the stake; the loser's winnings must be recovered within three fortnights, or immediately by the keeper of the gambling house from the gambler—of this there is no doubt.
Nārada [19.2, 8]:
The master of the gaming house shall conduct the gambling and shall collect the stake due in accordance with the facts;
his fee for conducting the gambling shall be ten percent of the hundred.
Alternatively, a gambler, having given the king the share as prescribed, may conduct the gambling openly; in this way, no fault is found.
Yājñavalkya [2.199–200]: In a wager involving interest of one hundred, the keeper of the gambling house shall take five percent from a rogue gambler,
but ten percent from any other.
Having protected it properly, he should give the king the share as prescribed;
he should cause the conquered land to be reclaimed for the victor, being truthful in speech and patient.
Nārada [19.3]:
When the dice fall twice in favor of the stake for a gambler,
they say that victory belongs to the other, the opponent of that cheat.
Kātyāyana [938]: Whether appearing as one form or two forms, victory is seen for that gambler at dice in whom the dice remain settled.
[766] Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 28.2]: "In a duel, however, whoever should suffer defeat,
the wager that was stipulated therein must be paid by his master."
Nārada [19.5]:
An impure person or a gambler shall not resort to another gambling circle. One shall not obstruct a gambler who is paying his own winnings as he pleases.

Yājñavalkya [2.201]: When the king’s share has been received and the gambling circle is well-established, he shall cause the winner to pay that amount to the keeper of the hall; otherwise, however, he shall not do so.
Nārada [19.7]:
But that man who engages in gambling without being authorized by the king shall not obtain his desired object; he deserves punishment.

Whatever was done in jest, and whatever was done without the king's knowledge— in those cases, he shall not incur the desired reward, nor shall there be destruction for both [the king and the minister].
One may live by eating even a small amount of various foods and drinks once out of affection, but one should avoid becoming attached to such habits.
Kātyāyana says: One should compel the payment of what is due in that very place and not otherwise;
for in that case, the decision is won by the presiding officer, as the legal proceeding depends upon his authority.
One who is ignorant, even if defeated, must be released; likewise, one who possesses specialized knowledge (*abhijña*), even if defeated in private, must be released.
Even when all one's possessions have been won, one should not compel the person possessing specialized knowledge to surrender his entire property.

Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 27.6]: One who has lost in secret, one who is ignorant, or one defeated by fraudulent dice or by deceit—such a person should be released even if he is knowledgeable; even if he has lost everything, he shall not be made to pay the entire amount.
Nārada [19.6]:
One should remove wicked gamblers who use fraudulent dice from the gambling circle;
for it is ordained that they be disciplined by placing a rosary around their necks.
Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 27.7]:
"Those who play with false dice, those who are base, those who seize the king's share, and those who deceive in calculation— these gamblers are declared to be punishable."
‘Cheats at counting’ means those who deceive in the act of counting. As it is said [in Vyavahāra 22.11]:
“The stake must be made public; those who play with fraudulent dice shall be banished.”
‘Glahah’ refers to the stake in gambling. Yājñavalkya [2.202]: Those who play with false dice or by means of fraud shall be banished by the king, marked with his insignia.

Viṣṇu [5.134–35]: “In gambling, those who play with fraudulent dice shall have their hands cut off; those who play with fraudulent weights (upadhī) shall have the joint of their thumb and forefinger cut off.
Here, “saṃdaṃśa” refers to the joining of the thumb and forefinger.
Nārada [19.4].
Gamblers themselves should stand for gamblers in matters of doubt;
they alone are the observers there, and they shall be the witnesses in that case.
Kātyāyana states: In a dispute concerning victory, loss, or the fraudulent methods used by gamblers,
the keeper of the gaming house is the authority, provided that the keeper of the gaming house is himself pure.
[769] There is no certainty regarding Mlecchas, dog-cookers, rogues, gamblers, ascetics, or those who violate the customs established by them; however, there is certainty regarding the king.
Bṛhaspati (Vyavahāra 27.9–11):
When both parties are doubtful, gamblers are the investigators;
but when they are hostile, then the king himself should deliberate.
In this manner, the king should daily examine the legal disputes brought by litigants,
as well as other matters related to the state, together with learned Brahmins.
Manu [8.178–80]: By this procedure, the king shall bring to a state of justice the legal cases of men who dispute falsely, as established by the evidence of witnesses.
[770] Thus has been set forth in detail the determination of legal procedure for two parties disputing with one another across the eighteen grounds of litigation.
Acting thus correctly in all his duties, the lord of the earth should seek to acquire territories not yet obtained and protect those already acquired.
Thus ends the section on gambling and betting in the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Lakṣmīdhara.
76. Now, the classification of legal procedures (*kriyābheda*):
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states (Vyavahāra 10.56–59):
"A lawsuit consists of eighteen titles, distinguished by the particulars of the plaint and the reply."
It has now been correctly explained; understand now the various types of ritual actions.
An action that was previously performed must be maintained exactly as it was;
where it is performed otherwise, then there is a deviation in the ritual act.
Having first abandoned the instrument [of proof], the creditor or the debtor may make it less, more, or equal; this is called a "variation in the procedure."
If one who has undertaken two items for a purpose should instead obtain five, the latter gain shall be the authoritative standard; for that is certainly the final determination.
Yājñavalkya [2.23]: In all disputes whatsoever, the subsequent legal act is stronger;
however, in the case of a mortgage, a gift, or a purchase, the prior act is more powerful.
Nārada [4.97]:
Among all the sources of income, such as the performance of rituals and so forth, each subsequent one is more powerful;
among those involving the acceptance of gifts, each preceding one is more significant.
Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 10.61–64]:
In matters such as sale, ownership, and acceptance of gifts, the prior transaction prevails;
however, in cases such as debts and the like, the subsequent one is more authoritative.
By each subsequent bond, the prior bond becomes loosened;
whatever agreement is made later is more powerful than the former.
If one, having made a formal deposit, then takes back the object and creates a pledge or sells it,
the latter transaction therein possesses greater legal force.
If on a single day one has performed both selling and receiving gifts,
and there is doubt regarding all three [transactions], how should the investigation be conducted therein?
For indeed, only the three means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) should be divided according to their respective portions;
and both [the donor and the recipient] should receive [their share] through a division corresponding to the purpose.
Thus ends the classification of ritual actions (kriyābheda).
Now, the miscellaneous topics (prakīrṇaka).
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 29.1] says: "This judicial procedure initiated by litigants has been declared in brief;
I shall now describe the miscellaneous judicial procedure (prakīrṇaka) which rests upon the king."
Nārada [20.1–4]:
Furthermore, the miscellaneous legal proceeding (prakīrṇaka) should be known as that which rests upon the king:
namely, the defiance of the kings' commands and likewise the failure to perform their duties.
The destruction of the city's leaders as well as that of the subjects,
and the subversion of the dharma of heretics, guilds, corporations, and assemblies.
Disputes between father and son, the transgression of penances, the failure to accept gifts, and the neglect of the duties of those in the stages of life;
The fault of the mixing of castes, their harmful livelihoods,
and whatever was not seen among the previous [treatises]— all that shall be included in this miscellaneous section.

Kātyāyana says: That which remains unsaid from what was previously stated, that which has fallen away from its context, that which is brought in from elsewhere, that which is bound to the meaning of another treatise, and that which is inconsistent— [these should be supplied].
That which stands as a repetition at the end of a treatise for the sake of providing an illustration,
or any statement made according to this rule, shall be considered *prakīrṇaka* (scattered or miscellaneous).
The duties of kings, one's own specific duties, the clarification of doubtful points,
what was previously mentioned, and the remainder of what was said— all that constitutes the miscellaneous section (prakīrṇaka).
Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 29.12–15]:
A tax of one-sixth, a marriage fee, and likewise what is to be given at a funeral pit;
as well as deserting an army, betraying a thief, and violating another's wife.
The desire to kill cows or Brahmins, as well as the destruction of crops—
the king himself should investigate these ten offenses.
The failure to perform expiations, the transgression of prohibitions and injunctions,
the neglect of the duties of the castes and stages of life, and the destruction of the caste system through intermixture;
A hidden treasure, wealth that yields no fruit, and the acquisition of riches by a pauper—
the king himself should personally prevent these when they have been thoroughly discovered through spies.
Undeclared duties, the ritual assertions of disputants,
the provocation of the constituent elements, and mutual agreements;
Whatever among his subjects proceeds that is not ordained by the treatises,
the king should pacify those matters through means such as conciliation, sowing dissension, and so forth.
Regarding the establishment of the system of castes and stages of life, Yājñavalkya [1.361] states:
"Families, castes, guilds, as well as assemblies and local communities..."
The king, having disciplined those who have strayed from their own duty, shall establish them upon the right path.
Nārada [20.5–6]:
But the king, being attentive, should protect all the stages of life (āśrama) as well as the constituent elements of the state (prakṛti) by means of the four methods prescribed in the treatises.
Whichever caste should decline and whichever should follow an excess,
