seeing each of them fallen from their own path, one should establish them back upon that path.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"The orderly establishment of the social classes and stages of life, in their proper sequence,
depends upon the king being well-established as the cause for their maintenance."
This kingdom, with the Brahmins and Kshatriyas at its head, has the king as its root;
while the king abides in his duty, people do not engage in misconduct.
"Furthermore, one who lives by the law but has deviated from the covenant of righteousness should be brought back by means of punishment alone, for he has fallen away from his own duty."
One should cause the Vaiśya to practice trade, money-lending, and agriculture;
likewise, the Śūdra [should practice] the tending of cattle and service to the twice-born.
One should cause the Vaiśya and the Śūdra to perform their own duties with diligence; for if they deviate from their respective duties, they would throw this world into turmoil.
Yama said: Whatever a king does, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious,
his servants follow that, just as dancers follow the lead of the dance.
Therefore, for the sake of the prosperity of the Brahmins and Kshatriyas, the king should properly instruct himself in the ancient laws together with his skilled ministers.

Gautama [8.1–3]: “In this world, two uphold the vow: the king and the learned Brāhmaṇa. Upon them depends the livelihood of the fourfold human race—those who possess internal consciousness and are subject to movement, falling, and flowing. Their duty (*dharma*) consists of procreation, protection, and the prevention of intermixture. Vasiṣṭha [1.40–42]: “The three castes should abide under the command of the Brāhmaṇa. The Brāhmaṇa shall proclaim the duties (*dharmas*), and the king shall enforce them.”
Hārīta says: "The king alone is the punisher of all those who act without restraint, who break the bounds of propriety, and who seize the wives and property of others.
He is the teacher of those who possess self-control; the king is the teacher of the wicked;
and Yama, the son of Vivasvat, is the teacher of those whose sins are concealed within."
Those men who, having committed secret sins, are neither corrected by their teachers nor punished by the king, are struck down by the rod of Yama and go to the lowest state.

Āpastamba [2.10.13–16; 2.11.1]: "The punisher shall prescribe atonement for those who have fallen away from the teachings they had acquired due to the weakness of their senses, according to their actions as prescribed. If they should transgress the teaching, he shall send them to the king. The king [shall send them] to the domestic priest who is skilled in dharma and artha. He [the priest] shall employ Brāhmaṇas. According to the degree of their strength, he shall purify them through restrictive penances, with the exception of slavery to others. For the other castes, the king shall inflict punishment after considering their actions, even unto the loss of life."—Uśanas.
If one says, "I spoke thus out of delusion, negligence, excitement, or affection," and adds,
"I shall not speak so again," the judge should impose half the penalty upon him.
This concerns the subject of verbal abuse (*vākpāruṣya*).

Gautama [12.48–49] states: “The application of punishment depends on the recognition of the person’s capacity, the offense, and the persistence [of the habit]; or there may be acquittal based on the testimony of an assembly of those learned in the Vedas.

Vasiṣṭha [19.6] states: “In cases of injury or verbal abuse, the punishment must be determined according to the specificities of place, time, the act, caste, age, learning, and station, as well as from traditional scripture and precedent.”

Following the phrase "by the king," Śaṅkha states: "The punishment should correspond to the strength [of the offender], the nature of the injury, and follow their age, learning, caste, physical characteristics, and virtues.
After the creation of punishment, Manu (7.16) says:
"Having truly considered the place and time, as well as the power and the learning [of the offender],"
One should extend proper courtesy toward men who act unjustly, according to their merit.
Yājñavalkya [1.368]:
Having taken into account the offense, as well as the place, the time, the strength,
the age, the action, and the wealth, the king shall inflict punishment upon those deserving of punishment.
And in cases of other offenses as well, having ascertained the caste, wealth, and age,
the king shall determine the punishment after consulting with Brāhmaṇas.

Furthermore, Viṣṇu [3.91–94] states: “He should inflict punishment upon those deserving of it in accordance with their offense; he should administer punishment correctly. For a second offense, he should not be lenient toward anyone. There is no one who, failing to observe his own duty, is exempt from the king’s punishment. Manu [8.335] says:
“The father, the teacher, the friend, the mother, the wife, the son, and the domestic priest—”
There is no one who does not deserve punishment from the king, should he fail to abide by his own duty.
Yājñavalkya: Officiating priests, family priests, ministers, sons, relatives, and kinsmen who have deviated from dharma should be punished; those who harm the king should be banished.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “The mother and father, the *snātaka* and the family priest, the wandering mendicant and the forest-dweller, and those who possess [exemplary] birth, conduct, Vedic learning, character, purity, and behavior—these are exempt from punishment. For these are the ones who counteract the king’s *dharma*. One should restrain one’s anger toward women, children, the elderly, and ascetics. Kātyāyana says:
“Toward the teacher, the father, the mother, and likewise toward one’s relatives...”
But in the case of an offense committed by these, no punishment whatsoever is ordained.
Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 9.17, 11]:
One should punish teachers, family priests, and those worthy of honor solely with the punishment of speech;
other litigants and offenders one should punish with a fine.
And those who have committed great offenses, he should punish with the penalty of death. Kātyāyana says:
"In the case of friends and others, one should employ the punishment of speech, saying: 'Shame on you, wretched woman!'"
One should perform for him that which has been stated, and even that which is unstated, provided it is well-conceived.
Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 29.2; 9.12–13]:
Having ascertained the nature of the person's fault and his capacity, one should duly impose the fourfold punishment consisting of verbal censure, a fine, and even corporal punishment.

For a very slight offense, there shall be punishment by word or the "fie" punishment; for a previous assault, confinement and a staff-punishment; but for acts of treason against the king, imprisonment.
One who desires his own welfare should carry out the banishment even of those who oppose him;
and all the punishments should be applied to one who has committed a great sin.
Manu [8.123]: One should first apply the punishment of speech, then the punishment of censure;
thirdly, the punishment of fines, and after that, the punishment of corporal chastisement.
Likewise [8.130]:
But when one is unable to restrain him even by execution,
then one should employ all four of these measures against them.
‘Even by killing’ means even by striking. Bṛhaspati [1.91; 29.6, 9]:
“The punishment of speech and the punishment of censure are both traditionally held to depend upon the Brāhmaṇas.”
Both fines and corporal punishments are said to depend entirely upon the king.
One should diligently restrain the unrighteous by three means:
by confinement, by imprisonment, and by various forms of corporal punishment.
And he should place all the fetters upon the left limb of those wicked-doers who appear distressed and deformed.
Manu, the son of the Self-Existent, has declared ten grounds for punishment;
when these exist among the three [lower] castes, a Brāhmaṇa may depart while protecting himself.
The generative organ, the belly, the tongue, the hands, and the feet as the fifth;
the eyes, the nose, the ears, wealth, and likewise the body.
Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 29.4–5]: The hands, feet, private parts, eyes, tongue, ears, nose, neck, half of the foot, the clasp, forehead, lips, anus, and waist;
These fourteen places for punishment have been specified;
for a Brāhmaṇa, a mark on the forehead is ordained, and no other punishment is prescribed.
Yama:
For all castes who have committed offenses against one another,
he shall prescribe a righteous punishment consisting of both corporal and monetary fines.
One might destroy this entire world, yet that is not equal to [the offense against] a Brahmin;
therefore, a king should not even conceive in his mind the thought of killing him.
They say that Brāhmaṇas are not to be slain, even if they are established in every kind of sin;
whatever is beneficial for Brāhmaṇas, that a king should not do himself.
Hārīta says: "The wise do not speak of a physical division of limbs for a Brahmin;
rather, a Brahmin is always purified through austerity and sacrifice."
Manu [8.380–81]: One must never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is guilty of every possible crime;
one should banish him from the kingdom, leaving his property intact and his body uninjured.
No greater unrighteousness exists on earth than the killing of a Brahmin;
therefore, a king should not even contemplate his execution in his mind.

Gautama [8.4–12]: “He alone is one who has heard much (*bahuśruta*): one who knows the *Lokaveda* and the *Vedāṅgas*; one who is skilled in *vākovākya*, *itihāsa*, and *purāṇa*; one who depends on them and subsists by them; one consecrated by the forty sacraments (*saṃskāra*); one devoted to the three [or six] duties; and one well-trained in the rules of customary conduct (*sāmayācārika*). He is exempt from being avoided by the king in six ways: he is not to be killed, nor bound, nor fined, nor banished, nor censured, nor excluded.”

"In three" refers to giving, studying, and sacrificing. "In six" refers to officiating at sacrifices, teaching, receiving gifts, studying, and so forth. Vasiṣṭha [1.45–46] states: "The Brāhmaṇa makes the Veda his first food; the Brāhmaṇa rescues one from calamity. Therefore, the Brāhmaṇa is not to be eaten; he becomes King Soma after death and attains prosperity here—thus it is understood."

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “In all cases involving the three castes, there shall be confiscation of property, imprisonment, corporal punishment, or branding; and for great crimes, there may be exile, the imposition of marks, or purification through penances. For a Brāhmaṇa must not be subjected to suffering. Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 9.10] says:
“Even if he is guilty of a mortal sin (mahāpātaka), a Brāhmaṇa does not deserve corporal punishment.”
The king should cause his head to be shaved, leaving no mark of a dwelling place.
"The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of spirituous liquor, the thief, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—
these are all to be known individually as men who have committed mortal sins (mahāpātakin)."
And for all four of these who do not perform expiation,
the king shall ordain a righteous punishment involving both corporal and monetary fines.
For violating the teacher's bed, the mark of a female organ should be made; for drinking liquor, the sign of a tavern flag;
for theft, the footprint of a dog; and for killing a Brahmin, the figure of a headless man.
Excluded from shared meals, excluded from sacrifices, excluded from Vedic recitation, and excluded from marriage,
they shall wander the earth in misery, cast out from all religious duties.
"But these men, having been branded with the mark, must be abandoned by their kinsmen and relatives;
they shall be without compassion and without salutation—this is the instruction of Manu."
But those of the higher castes who perform the prescribed penance as declared shall not be branded on their foreheads by the king; rather, they should be made to pay the highest fine.
For offenses against a Brāhmaṇa, this middle amercement shall be imposed;
or he may be banished from the kingdom, along with his property and his belongings.
But others who have committed these sins according to the law deserve the forfeiture of all their property; however, if they did so intentionally, they deserve banishment.
In this context, "thief" (*taskara*) refers to one who steals gold.

Baudhāyana [1.18.18] states: “For a Brāhmaṇa who has committed the murder of a learned man (*bhrūṇahatyā*), sexual intercourse with the teacher’s wife, theft of gold, or drinking liquor, one shall brand the forehead with red-hot iron using the emblems of a headless trunk (*kabandha*), a female organ (*bhaga*), a dog’s foot (*śvapada*), or a banner (*dhvaja*), and then banish him from the territory.
Nārada [21.43–45] says:
For four offenses of a Brāhmaṇa, branding is prescribed:
for violating the Guru’s bed, for drinking liquor, for theft, and for the injury of a Brāhmaṇa.
[786] For violating the Guru’s bed, the mark of a female organ should be made; for drinking liquor, the sign of a tavern flag;
but for theft, having fashioned the footprint of a dog, one should fill it with the bile of a peacock.
A man who has killed a twice-born man should be made headless;
furthermore, he must be rendered unfit for social intercourse—this is the ordinance of Manu.
Yama says: For the four offenses of a Brāhmaṇa, this is ordained as punishment:
shaving the head, banishment from the city, and likewise [exile].
For the purpose of proclaiming his sin, the king shall cause him to travel on a donkey and have a mark branded upon his forehead according to the prescribed rule.

Āpastamba [2.27.18–21]: "One should imprison another who violates the rules, or anyone else, in secret, until the offense is completed. If it is not completed, he should be released. A teacher, an officiating priest, a graduate, and a king shall provide protection, except in the case of one deserving death."

"One who transgresses the rules" (*niyamātikramin*) refers to one who fails to perform what is enjoined. "Another" (*anya*) refers to a Brāhmaṇa who commits what is forbidden. One should "bind him in secret" (*rahasi*), that is, in a secluded place. This shall continue "until completion" (*ā samāpteḥ*), until he makes a formal agreement, saying, "I will not do it again. Otherwise, he is "to be destroyed" (*nāśya*), meaning he is to be banished. Teachers and others must provide "protection" (*trāṇa*) for those subject to punishment; they must act as protectors and never adopt an attitude of indifference. Yama says:
"Thieves, drinkers of liquor, slayers of Brahmins, and those who approach the wives of their teachers..."
That king in whose realms these do not exist partakes of the world of Śakra.
[787] Manu [9.243–47]: A righteous king must not take the property of those guilty of mortal sins; for by taking it out of greed, he becomes tainted by that unrighteousness.
Having cast that staff into the waters, he should present it to Varuṇa;
or he should present it to a Brāhmaṇa who is perfected in Vedic learning.
Varuṇa is indeed the lord of punishment for the king, for he is the wielder of the rod;
the Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas is the lord of the entire world.
Wherever a king avoids deriving wealth from evildoers,
there men are born in due time as long-lived.
And crops grow as described, O lord of the people;
children do not die prematurely, nor does any deformity arise.
Yama says: Having confiscated the property of one who has fallen [from his caste], the king should cause it to be given away in an assembly;
he may take the man’s entire estate, leaving only a fourth part remaining.
"One should give food to one's dependents while recollecting the Dharma pertaining to Prajāpati; such is the Vedic revelation."

[788] 78—Now, regarding the ferry-toll (*tara-śulka*), Vasiṣṭha states there (18.17–22): “In a crossing, a boat carrying ten oxen shall pay double the toll. There should be water-stations (*prapā*) for every ten persons. And it should carry half as many men. Women shall pay one and a half times the toll. For a boat of eight *māṣas* that carries reeds, the toll is half a *kārṣāpaṇa*; for one that does not carry reeds, it is a quarter. A boat that does not carry water shall pay one *māṣa*.”

That by which one travels together is a "saṃyāna," namely a river-crossing vessel. In that context, a "vāhinī" is a boat. Those who carry [the load] are "vāhas. Where there are ten men, it is "daśapuruṣavatī"; besides the carriers, there are also ten men mounted upon it. "Prapāḥ syuḥ" means that there should be ten men as protectors for each carrier. "Avarārdhaṃ vāhaṃ vahet" means that the boat should carry half the load—wherein the "avara" (lower) is less than the "ardha" (half)—of whatever burden the boat can carry; one should fill that load with men. "Adhyardhāḥ striyaḥ syuḥ" means that women are one-and-a-half times [the number] of men, because of their extreme timidity. "Taraḥ" is the toll, which is a "māṣa," being the twentieth part of a kārṣāpaṇa. "Śaramadhyāyāḥ" refers to that river into the middle of which an arrow shot by an archer falls. "Aśaramadhyāyāḥ pādaḥ" means where the middle is not reached by an arrow [meaning the arrow passes over it]; "pādaḥ" is a fourth part of a "kārṣāpaṇa. "Nirudakaḥ" means having little water. "Māṣyaḥ" refers to a place where a toll of one māṣa is paid.
One should pay one *paṇa* for crossing by carriage; half a *paṇa* for a man on foot;
a quarter for an animal and a woman; and half a quarter for an empty-handed man.
Vehicles filled with goods shall be made to pay ferry-toll according to their value;
those with empty vessels, as well as men without luggage, shall pay whatever little they can.
On a long journey, one should know that a crossing may be found according to the location and the time on the banks of rivers; however, there is no such certainty in the ocean.
A pregnant woman in her second month or beyond, as well as a wandering ascetic,
a sage, Brāhmaṇas, and those bearing religious marks, shall not be made to pay a ferry-toll when crossing.

Vasiṣṭha [18.23–25]: “A Vedic scholar who has not performed his duties, a king, a man without kin, a wandering ascetic, women who have recently given birth, children, the elderly, young women traveling on foot, and those whose children have died—these must be made to pay a hundredfold if they attempt to cross by swimming with their arms.

‘A man without kin’ means one who is destitute of relatives or afflicted by disease. ‘Women who have recently given birth’ refers to those who have just delivered. ‘Travelers on foot’ refers to those such as letter-carriers who are habituated to constant travel. ‘Those whose children have died’ refers to widows.

Viṣṇu [5.131]: “A ferryman taking land-toll shall be fined ten paṇas; as shall a boatman or a toll-collector taking a toll from a religious student, a forest-dweller, a mendicant, a pregnant woman, or one following a sacred ford (tīrtha). And he shall forfeit that [toll]. The phrase “and [he who] takes” is to be construed with “shall be fined. Manu [8.408–09]:
Whatever may be lost on a ship through the fault of the boatmen,
that must be paid by the boatmen themselves, having assembled together according to their respective shares.
This has been declared as the legal decision regarding those traveling by boat:
in the event of an injury on the water caused by the fault of the boatmen, there is no punishment for a force majeure (divine) accident.
[791] 79— Now, regarding treasure-troves (*nidhi*),
Manu says there (8.35–36):
If one should claim, "This is mine," regarding a treasure on the basis of truth and reason,
the king shall take a sixth part, or even a twelfth part, from him.
But one who speaks falsely shall be made to pay an eighth part of his own wealth,
or a smaller fraction calculated according to the value of that very deposit.

Viṣṇu [3.63–64]: “Except for Brāhmaṇas, those who claim a deposit made by another to be one made by themselves shall pay a twelfth part of its value to the king as a fine; those who claim a deposit made by another to be their own shall likewise incur a fine equal to that amount. Nārada [10.8]:
“Having recovered even one’s own lost property, one should report it to the king.”
One should accept it from that [person] if it is pure; otherwise, it would be impure.

Now, regarding property deposited by another, Vasiṣṭha [3.14–15] states: “If one should discover wealth whose owner is unknown, the king shall recover it after giving a sixth part to the finder. But if a Brāhmaṇa who abides in the six duties should discover it, the king must not take it. The term “whose owner is unknown” (*aprajñāyamāna*) refers to that which has an unknown owner or is ownerless.
Having discovered a treasure deposited by another, one should present it to the king;
for all treasure belongs to the king, with the exception of a Brāhmaṇa.
A Brāhmaṇa, having found a treasure-trove, should also report it to the king immediately;
he may enjoy what is given by him, for if he does not report it, he would be a thief.
Yājñavalkya [2.34–35]:
Upon finding a treasure-trove, a king shall give half to the twice-born;
however, a learned twice-born man may take the whole, since he is the master of all.
When a treasure has been found by another, the king shall take a sixth part;
however, one who discovers it without reporting it shall be made to pay that [sixth part] as well as a fine.

Viṣṇu [3.56–62]: “Having found a treasure-trove, one should give half of it to Brāhmaṇas; having given that, one should deposit the second half in the royal treasury. Having found a treasure-trove, a Brāhmaṇa may take it for himself. A Kṣatriya should give a fourth part to the king, give a fourth part to Brāhmaṇas, and take half for himself. A Vaiśya should give a fourth part to the king, give half a share to Brāhmaṇas, and take half for himself. A Śūdra, however, having divided what he has found into twelve parts, should give the fifth part to the king, give two shares to Brāhmaṇas, and take all the remainder for himself. If a treasure-trove is discovered without having been reported, the king shall confiscate the person’s entire property.”
But whatever ancient treasure the king may discover buried in the earth,
having given half of it to the twice-born, he should deposit the other half in the treasury.
Because he protects ancient treasures, mineral ores, and mines, the king, as the lord of the earth, partakes in merit; for he is its master.

Viṣṇu [3.55]: “One should take everything from the mines. Vasiṣṭha: “However, one should cause the performer of the marriage to swear: ‘With whom and by what means is marriage appropriate for you? Thus, for the sake of establishing the distinction between the social classes (*varṇa*), one should protect the tradition. One should also understand the purification of the mines for the purpose of collecting taxes and the like corresponding thereto; for those who are masters of mines are generally deceitful. [794]
80—Now follows the determination of the infliction of punishment.
Regarding this, Manu [7.14–15, 17–18] says:
For that purpose, [the king should recognize] Dharma, the protector of all beings, who was born from his own self.
In the beginning, the Lord created the staff consisting of the splendor of Brahman.
Out of fear of him, all beings, both stationary and moving, provide sustenance for his enjoyment and do not deviate from their own duties.
That king is the personification of punishment; he is the leader and the ruler, and he has been made the guarantor of the dharma of the four stages of life.
The rod of punishment governs all subjects; the rod alone protects them.
The rod remains awake while others sleep; the wise know the rod to be righteousness itself.
Likewise [7.25]:
Where the dark, red-eyed Punishment stalks, destroying evil,
there the subjects flourish, provided that the leader perceives rightly.
Likewise [7.31, 26, 30, 27–29, 19]: Punishment can be rightly administered by one who is pure, true to his word, follows the scriptures, possesses good assistants, and is wise.
They say that the king who is a speaker of truth,
who acts with circumspection, who is wise, and who is skilled in the matters of dharma, pleasure, and wealth, is the one who should be appointed as its administrator.
One who is without assistance, deluded, greedy,
and of unrefined intellect is not capable of conducting himself rightly regarding wealth and sensual objects.
A king who administers that [punishment] properly prospers through the three aims of life;
but one who is base, whose soul is devoted to sensual pleasure, is destroyed by that very punishment.
For punishment possesses immense power and is difficult to wield by those of undisciplined soul;
it destroys the king himself, along with his kinsmen, if he deviates from righteousness.
Then he would afflict the fortresses, the kingdom, and the world with all its moving and unmoving beings, as well as the ascetics dwelling in the atmosphere and the gods.
A king who is well-supported and acts with thorough deliberation brings joy to all his subjects;
but one who acts without deliberation brings about destruction on every side.
‘Well-maintained’ means maintained according to what is appropriate.
“If the king were not to tirelessly inflict punishment upon those deserving of punishment...”
The stronger would roast the weaker like fish on a spit.
A crow might eat the sacrificial cake, and a dog might lick the oblation;
there would be no ownership over anything, and the social order would be overturned, with the low rising above the high.
Aṅgiras said:
A king who is a teacher and who governs by means of righteousness is joined with merit;
as the agent, he is released from evil and is not defiled by sin.
Yājñavalkya [1.359–60]: That king who punishes those deserving of punishment and duly executes those deserving of death has performed sacrifices completed with the most excellent sacrificial fees.
Having reflected thus, the king, surrounded by his councilors, should personally examine legal cases every day, for they yield a fruit equal to that of a sacrifice.
Likewise:
"In this world, unjust punishment destroys the king's reputation for righteousness;
whereas just punishment brings the king heaven, fame, and victory."
Manu [8.128; 9.247]: A king who punishes those who do not deserve punishment, and fails to punish those who do deserve it, incurs great infamy and goes to hell.
As much demerit is seen for a king in killing one who should not be killed, so much is seen in releasing one who deserves death; but merit belongs to him who restrains [the wicked].

Kātyāyana says: Kings and ministers especially shall attain this [merit] through the punishment of the wicked who do not submit to instruction, and by the wielding of the rod of justice over those who are submissive.
‘Of those who have bowed’ means of those who are disciplined, that is to say, those who are exempt from punishment.

Vasiṣṭha [19.40–43] states: “Upon the failure to inflict punishment, the king shall fast for one night; the domestic priest for three nights. In the case of failing to punish [a guilty person], the domestic priest shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance and the king for three nights.
Now, regarding the increase or decrease of the punishment and so forth, Kātyāyana states:
"Even if a person is guilty of a crime, one should ask for the motive of that crime."
In that manner, one should diligently inflict punishment after having ascribed the fault [to the offender].
But when an improper act has been committed during a life-threatening emergency, there shall be no punishment at all; this is the law as recorded by Bhṛgu.
But when an offense occurs among all those of good conduct,
even if it happens involuntarily through fate, one should not impose punishment in that case.
Kings who administer punishment correctly are worthy of worship even by the gods;
at the commencement [of an offense], one should inflict the first [level of] punishment, while in the case of its continuation, the middle is prescribed.
Whatever punishment has been prescribed for one who is capable, that indeed shall be applied;
whatever punishment has been carefully ordained for a particular offense, that shall be meted out.
The seizure of the coins themselves, or else their value, shall be paid to the king; so say Gārgya and Mānava regarding fixed fines for offenses.
Gautama maintains that he should not be punished first for his negligence,
because virtuous people possess the means [to pay] even the aforementioned fines.
They would not give, nor would they be pacified; therefore, there must be a firm decision in that matter.
Thus, by whatever means evil is unimpeded, one should again [apply] what is auspicious.
They would not do that; rather, it is certain that this alone must be done by them—those lowest of men who, though belonging to a community, are engaged in sinful deeds.
As it has been said: "One should cause each person to pay double the fine.
"Punishment is traditionally held to be of two kinds: corporal punishment and monetary punishment."
The corporeal punishment is declared to be of two kinds, while the monetary fine is also of many types.
The monetary fine begins at one kākiṇī and likewise ends with the confiscation of all property;
the corporal punishment begins with confinement and likewise ends with the taking of life.
The punishment beginning with a *kākiṇī* is traditionally held to culminate in a *māṣa*;
that which is declared to begin with half a *māṣa* culminates in a *kārṣāpaṇa*.
That which is at least one *kārṣāpaṇa* and up to four *kārṣāpaṇas*;
another is at least two *paṇas* and up to eight *paṇas*; and yet another is at least three *paṇas* and up to twelve *paṇas*.
All those [fines] beginning with the *kārṣāpaṇa* that have been mentioned should each be quadrupled;
others should be understood in the same way, provided they fall before the first *sāhasa*.
Manu [8.336]: "Where the fine for an ordinary person would be one kārṣāpaṇa, the fine for kings in that case shall be one thousand; such is the settled rule."
Likewise: "But a king should slay with various means of execution that cause terror— a person of low caste who, out of lust, oppresses Brāhmaṇas."
Kātyāyana states: A Śūdra who has fallen from the life of a renunciant, as well as one devoted to the recitation of mantras and burnt offerings,
should be punished for his sin by execution, or else he should be made to pay a double fine.
[800] For men who are untouchables, rogues, slaves, evildoers,
or born of inverse unions (prātilomya), beating is not a fine that serves as a deterrent.
But those who are dependent, as well as those who exist in a state of servitude, are designated as being without a protector; their punishment, however, is only beating.
Beating, binding, and likewise humiliating—this indeed is the punishment for a slave; there is no monetary fine, O Bṛhaspati.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "Artisans, craftsmen, and Śūdras—even if they commit transgressions—the king shall protect their tools of craft. For merchants, he shall protect the balances, weights, and measures used on the trade routes. For farmers, he shall protect the fields, seeds, food, cattle, carts, and implements for plowing. For those who live by the stage, he shall protect musical instruments, ornaments, and clothing. For courtesans, he shall protect houses, beds, ornaments, and clothing. And for those who live by weapons, he shall protect their arms. A righteous king must not confiscate the tools of production belonging to any of these; for men without property become full of evil and uncontrollable. The king shares in the portion of their sin. Therefore, he should not leave them destitute or without their implements, for livelihood is rooted in those tools, and residence is rooted in livelihood. When they reside there, the kingdom is said to be prosperous."
[801] Bṛhaspati (Vyavahāra 9.19): A man deserving of death shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred gold pieces;
one deserving of the amputation of a limb shall pay half of that, and one deserving of the *saṃdaṃśa* punishment shall pay half of that.
Kātyāyana [964–66]: One who deserves death shall be fined one hundred gold pieces;
for the amputation of a limb, half of that; and for exile, twenty-five.
Toward those who are of noble birth, honorable, or distinguished, as well as toward those who are base, he should act according to their merit;
or, having confiscated all their property, he should swiftly banish them from the city.
Those who are destitute should be placed in confinement; one must never carry out their execution.
This applies to all those guilty of crimes, according to the specific provisions of the scriptures.
Likewise:
"A Brahmin deserving of execution or limb-mutilation shall enter a bondless prison;
then he is freed from that karma, for such is the punishment for one who abides by his duty."
One who gives false testimony should be banished after being publicly proclaimed; one who accepts gifts from the wicked should have his limbs severed;
and one who violates his own dharma should be bound in fetters.
Bhṛgu states that for cutting off the ears, lips, nose, feet, eyes, tongue, penis, or hands, one should pay the highest fine; for piercing them, the middle fine.
In those cases as well, one should apply this same principle to those who have committed equal offenses;
however, for children, the elderly, the sick, women, and the aged, there shall be no corporal punishment—their penalty shall be a beating.

"One deserving of death or limb-mutilation" refers to a Brahmin who, for some offense, would otherwise be subject to the punishment of death or the amputation of a limb for other castes. By the qualification "established in good conduct," he indicates that there is another punishment for one of wicked conduct.
But a Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra of noble birth, being unable to pay a fine, [should perform labor].
A Brahmin should attain freedom from debt through his actions; he should give gradually, little by little.
For women, children, the insane, the elderly, the poor, and the sick,
the king should administer punishment using whips, split bamboo, ropes, and the like.
Kātyāyana [970]: A righteous lord of the earth shall cause the woman's property to be paid as a fine;
however, a woman who is destitute and has committed an offense deserves the punishment of flogging.
A Brahmin is exempt from [the obligation of] rising; the king has a seat of honor at the front.
He is to be seen first in the morning, and he receives salutations before all others.
The first-fruits of the new harvest and the right of way for one passing by are granted;
likewise, entry into another's house for the purpose of begging alms is not forbidden.
Non-stealing consists in not taking firewood, flowers, or *kuśa* grass from what has been appropriated by oneself;
furthermore, one should not provoke others, nor should one converse with another's wife.

On rivers, there shall be free passage for those who lack means, as well as for those who ferry others across; likewise, there shall be exemption from tolls on ferries, provided that this is not his primary trade.
[804] Now follows the rebuttal of the Brahmin's position.

Regarding this, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "In the taking of fuel, water, fire, wood, grass, stones, flowers, roots, fruits, and leaves, there is no offense; likewise, visiting deities and sacred fords, entering one's own house or store-room, carrying weapons on the road, sitting in an unconnected place, not turning back when challenged, and residing with the unworthy. Furthermore, in the case of *śiloñcha* (gleaning), there is no offense in taking from a heap of grain; nor is there offense in passing through the front of a threshing floor, a birth-chamber, a place where interest is being calculated, a mint, a toll-house, or while crossing a river; nor in conversing with another's wife, looking at the king's wife, sitting on the same seat as the king, or even transgressing out of anger—the Brāhmaṇa deserves all these privileges."

Now, concerning the exemptions for the city: regarding this, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "There shall be no tax on those who travel by carriage, those who travel on foot, the removal of field produce, the gathering of flowers and roots, or the entry of goods acquired by oneself; there is no duty on entering or exiting without prior announcement. No customs duty is levied on items carried on the shoulder. The established practices of guilds, corporations, associations, and trade unions are final. Those who recognize the owners are exempt from liability, except in cases of treason against the king. Furthermore, the property of non-Brahmin city-dwellers is protected as long as they are innocent. Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 9.25] states:
One who, having been rightly defeated by means of witnesses, documents, inference, or even by ordeal,
does not pay the debt due, shall be banished from that city.
[Br̥had-Āraṇyaka Prāyaścitta 84] He who causes his own death by means of poison, hanging, or a weapon—
if he dies, he must be smeared with impure matter (amedhya) and is not eligible for any other funeral rite.
Aṅgiras:
He who attempts to kill himself by means such as a rope or other methods—if he dies, he must be smeared with impure matter; if he survives, the fine shall be doubled.
Yājñavalkya [2.307]: A king shall present to Varuṇa any unjust fine he has collected and himself give it to the Brahmins, having multiplied it thirtyfold.
Kātyāyana [971–73]:
One should deposit into the treasury wealth that has been unjustly acquired or placed there;
for the sake of the state's business, one should not cause the ruin of the undertaking, nor should a wise man allow it to perish.
Having given all that wealth arising from fines to the Brahmins,
and having entrusted the kingdom to his son, he should depart for the forest.
Thus, a king should always act with diligence according to the duties of royalty;
he should employ all his servants in ways that are beneficial to the world.

Now, regarding the designation of fines (*daṇḍasaṃjñā*), Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “Twenty-four [paṇas], ninety-one, constitute the first amercement (*prathamasāhasa*); two hundred and five hundred constitute the middle amercement (*madhyamasāhasa*); six hundred and one thousand constitute the highest amercement (*uttamasāhasa*). These apply to all in successive order according to the value of the object and the nature of the injury. Nārada [21.30–31].
The first [type] has twenty-four as the minimum, while the maximum is ninety-six;
the second has five hundred as the minimum, while the middle [type] has two hundred as the minimum.
The highest fine is to be known as one thousand, while the lowest is five hundred;
thus has the threefold punishment for acts of violence been declared by the Self-Existent One.
Regarding this, Manu [8.138] states:
"Two hundred and fifty paṇas are declared to be the first amercement;
five hundred are to be known as the middle, and one thousand as the highest."
Yājñavalkya [1.366]:
A fine of ten thousand eight hundred paṇas is called the highest amercement (uttamasāhasa);
half of that is declared the middle amercement (madhyama), and half of that is recorded as the lowest amercement (adhama).
Now,
regarding the designations of honor, Manu [8.131–37] states: "Those designations which are well-known on earth for the sake of worldly convention..."
I shall describe those [measures] for copper, silver, and gold in their entirety.
When the sun shines through a lattice, that subtle particle of dust which is seen is declared to be the first among all measures of length, known as a *trasareṇu*.
Eight *trasareṇu*s should be known as one *likṣā* by measure;
three of those [likṣās] are a *rājasarṣapa*, and two of those [rājasarṣapas] are a *gaurasarṣapa*.
Six mustard seeds make one medium barley grain; three barley grains make one *kṛṣṇala*;
five *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*; and sixteen of those make one *suvarṇa*.
Four suvarṇas make one pala; ten palas make one dharaṇa;
and two kṛṣṇalas weighed together should be known as one silver māṣaka.
Sixteen of those silver *dharaṇas* constitute one *purāṇa*;
that [purāṇa] is to be known as a *kārṣāpaṇa*, and three of those *kārṣikas* are a *paṇa*.
Ten *dharaṇas* should be known as one *śatamāna* of silver;
furthermore, a *niṣka* should be understood by its measure to consist of four *suvarṇas*.
Yājñavalkya [1.364]:
"Four or even five *plā* are proclaimed as equal to a *suvarṇa*.

Regarding the section on the *māṣa*, Viṣṇu [4.8–9] states: "Twelve of those [make] half an *akṣa*; half an *akṣa* is indeed four *māṣakas*, which is a *suvarṇa*. Bṛhaspati [Vyavahāra 8.8, 10]: [text follows].
For the sake of worldly transaction, this designation has been declared on earth:
a coin made from one karṣa of copper is to be known as a *kārṣika-paṇa*.
That very [weight] is called a *candrikā*; four *dhānakās* make one *māṣa*.
Twelve of those make a *suvarṇa*, which is indeed what is known as a *dīnāra*.
[809] Nārada [21.58–60]: A *māṣa* should be known as the twentieth part of a *kārṣāpaṇa*;
a *kākinī*, however, is the fourth part of both a *māṣa* and a *paṇa*.
In the region of the Five Rivers, however, this is the conventional designation;
its value is fixed here at the measure of one kārṣāpaṇa.
A *kārṣāpaṇa* should be known as four *abdhis*, and four of those make one *dhānaka*.
Twelve of those are a *suvarṇa*, while a *dīnāra* is recorded as being equal to a *citraka*.
Likewise:
"In the southern direction, the silver kārṣāpaṇa circulates;
in the eastern direction, it is fixed at sixteen paṇas."
Kātyāyana [491–92]: Where a fine of one *māṣa*, half a *māṣa*, or two *pādas* is prescribed,
one should calculate that an unspecified amount refers to a gold *māṣaka*.
Where a fine of one māṣaka is prescribed, one should designate that as being in terms of kṛṣṇalas;
this is what has been stated in the determination of fines.
[810] Now, regarding the designations such as "naigama" and so forth, Kātyāyana [states as follows]: [678–82].
A multitude of various citizens is proclaimed as the *naigama*;
a collection of groups bearing various weapons is likewise proclaimed as such when assembled together.
A collection of merchants and the like is celebrated as a *pūga*;
however, a collection of Brāhmaṇas is called a *gaṇa* by the wise.
Those who have settled into the life of renunciation are proclaimed as *pāṣaṇḍas*;
those who subsist by means of crafts are proclaimed as *śilpins*.
The assembly of Arhats and followers of Sugata is called a *saṅgha*;
the assembly of Cāṇḍālas, Śvapacas, and others is designated as a *gulma*.

Bṛhaspati says that *gaṇas*, heretics (*pāṣaṇḍas*), associations (*pūgas*), guilds (*vrātas*), as well as trade unions (*śreṇis*), and whatever other groups exist that are designated as "classes" (*vargas*), are [to be treated] in this manner.
That which is the origin of the four castes, arising from birth, lineage, and so forth—the duties pertaining to it have been fully set forth; that is proclaimed as "jāti" (birth-caste).
Thus ends the section on miscellaneous matters in the Vyavahārakāṇḍa of the Kṛtyakalpataru composed by Śrī Lakṣmīdhara.
81 — Now, regarding the *varṇas* in the direct and inverse order:
on this point, Āpastamba [1.1.4–5] states: “The four *varṇas* are the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra. Among them, each preceding one is superior by birth. Manu [10.3–4] states:
Due to his distinction, the excellence of his origin, his adherence to the rules of discipline, and the particularity of his refinement, the Brāhmaṇa is the lord of the social classes.
The Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya—these three castes are twice-born;
the fourth, however, is once-born, the Śūdra, and there is no fifth.

Bṛhaspati says: Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and the three lowest castes; those born in the inverse order (pratiloma) and the direct order (anuloma)—these constitute the mixed castes (varṇasaṃkara).

Devala said: “The four castes are the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra. There are four *anuloma* (natural-order) offspring: the Savarṇa, Ambaṣṭha, Pāraśava, and Ugra. There are six *pratiloma* (inverse-order) offspring: the Āyogava, Kṣatta, Caṇḍāla, Māgadha, Vaidehaka, and Sūta. There are six *antarāla* (intermediate) offspring: the Kukkuṭa, Pulkasa, Venā, Kuśīlava, Bandi, and Śvapāka. We shall explain the characteristics and regulations for all of them in due order. One born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Brāhmaṇī mother becomes a consecrated Brāhmaṇa.
In the same way, those born from their own respective wombs among the Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are to be understood.”
A son born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Kṣatriya mother is called a Savaṛṇaka;
a son born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Vaiśya mother is known as an Ambaṣṭha.
A Niṣāda, born from a Śūdra woman by a Brāhmaṇa, is also called a Pāraśava;
and one born from a Vaiśya woman by a Kṣatriya is known by the designation Savarṇa.
“The twice-born call one born to a Śūdra woman from a Kṣatriya man an Ugra;
from a Vaiśya man on a Śūdra’s daughter, a Śūdra alone is born.”— Manu [10.6–10].
Sons begotten by twice-born men on women born immediately after them in the caste order are said to be equal [to their fathers], yet they are censured due to the defect of their mothers.
This is the eternal rule regarding those born of women one degree lower;
one should know this righteous rule to apply to those born of women two or three degrees lower.
From a Brāhmaṇa and the daughter of a Vaiśya is born one named Ambaṣṭha;
from a Śūdra daughter is born a Niṣāda, who is called a Pāraśava.
From a Kṣatriya father and a Śūdra mother is born a being named Ugra, who possesses the physical form of both a Kṣatriya and a Śūdra and whose conduct and pastimes are cruel.
These six are declared to be the base-born (apasada): those born from a Brahmin in the [lower] three castes, those from a Kshatriya in two castes, and those from a Vaishya in one caste.
Likewise [10.14]:
"Those sons of the twice-born who are born of women immediately following [their own caste] have been described in order;
however, they are designated by the name of the 'immediate' (anantara) because of the defect of their mothers."
Yājñavalkya [1.90–95]: From men of the same caste, sons of the same caste are born of women of the same caste through blameless marriages; such sons increase the lineage.
For a Mūrdhāvasikta born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Kṣatriya mother, an Ambaṣṭha is born from a Vaiśya woman,
and a Niṣāda or a Pāraśava from a Śūdra woman.
From a Kṣatriya father, a Māhiṣya and an Ugra are born respectively by wives of the Vaiśya and Śūdra castes;
likewise, from a Vaiśya father, a Karaṇa is born by a Śūdra wife, and similarly [an Āyogava] from a Kṣatriya wife by the twice-born [Brahmins].

An Ambaṣṭha is born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Śūdra mother, as is a Pāraśava; however, from a Vaiśya and a Śūdra mother respectively, sons born to a Kṣatriya father are known as Māhiṣyas and Ugras.
From a Vaiśya, however, a Karaṇa is born by a Śūdra woman; this is the rule recorded for women who have been married.
Baudhāyana [1.17.4–6] states: “From a Kṣatriya by a Vaiśya woman, a Kṣatriya is born; by a Śūdra woman, an Ugra; from a Vaiśya by a Śūdra woman, a Rathakāra.”

Uśanas says: "The castes (*varṇas*) are understood through their elevation and degradation. These include the Rathakāra, Ambaṣṭha, Sūta, Ugra, Māgadha, Vaideha, Pukkasa, Kṣattṛ, Kukkuṭa, Cāṇḍāla, Śvapāka, Vrātya, and so forth. Among them, from a man of one caste with a woman of the same caste, the offspring is of that same caste. From a Brāhmaṇa father and a Kṣatriya mother, he who is born is indeed a Brāhmaṇa; from a Vaiśya mother, an Ambaṣṭha; from a Śūdra mother, a Pāraśava—some say a Niṣāda. From a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya mother, a Kṣatriya is born; from a Śūdra mother, an Ugra. From a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother, a Vaiśya is born."
‘He is like a Brāhmaṇa,’ meaning that because he was previously a Kṣatriya, he is superior to a Kṣatriya, just like a Brāhmaṇa.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “In that regard, from a Brāhmaṇa on a Kṣatriya woman, a Kṣatriya alone is born; by a Kṣatriya on a Vaiśya woman, a Vaiśya alone; by a Vaiśya on a Śūdra woman, a Śūdra. By a Brāhmaṇa on a Śūdra woman, a Niṣāda or a Pāraśava is born according to the rule of natural order (ānulomya). In the reverse order (prātilomya), from a Kṣatriya on a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Sūta is born; by a Vaiśya on a Kṣatriya woman, a Māgadha; by a Śūdra on a Vaiśya woman, an Āyogava. And by a Śūdra on a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Caṇḍāla is born. The Ambaṣṭha and Ugra are born from the natural order with one intervening caste; the Kṣattṛ and Vaidehaka from the reverse order with one intervening caste. Because the castes become intermixed, therefore there is a need for purification.”

Gautama [4.16–21]: “Those born in the direct order (*anuloma*) from women one degree, two degrees, three degrees, or four degrees lower are the *savarṇa*, *ambaṣṭha*, *ugra*, *niṣāda*, *daauṣyanta*, and *pāraśava*. Those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*) are the *sūta*, *māgadha*, *āyogava*, *kṣattṛ*, *vaidehaka*, and *caṇḍāla*. From those same [four] castes, a Brāhmaṇa woman gives birth to sons in the direct sequence: a Brāhmaṇa, a *sūta*, a *māgadha*, and a *caṇḍāla*. From those same [four], a Kṣatriya woman gives birth to a *mūrdhāvasikta*, a Kṣatriya, a *dhīvara*, and a *pulkasa*. From those same [four], a Vaiśya woman gives birth to a *bhṛjyakaṇṭha*, a *māhiṣya*, a Vaiśya, and a *vaidehaka*. A Śūdra woman gives birth to a *pāraśava*, a Yavana, a *karaṇa*, and a Śūdra; some say [the last] is a Śūdra.”

Nārada [14.103–04]: A son born from a woman one degree lower is recorded as an *anantara*; likewise, a son born from a woman two degrees lower is an *ekāntara*, and a son born from a woman three degrees lower is a *dvyantara*—this applies both in the direct order (*anuloma*) and likewise in the inverse order (*pratiloma*).
The Ugra, the Pāraśava, and the Niṣāda are proclaimed as the three sons of Śūdra women born from the three highest castes in the direct order of birth.
From a Brāhmaṇa woman as well, the Daṇḍa, Āla-sūta, and Vaidehaka are born;
these three others are to be known as those born in the reverse order (pratiloma).

The Savarṇa and the Māgadha, as well as the Kṣattṛ born of a Kṣatriya woman, are produced in the direct order (ānulomya); among them, one is to be known as born in the natural order and two as born in the inverse order (pratiloma).

The sons of a Vaiśya woman—namely the Ambaṣṭha, Yavana, and Āyogava—are likewise [born] in the reverse order; among them, one and two respectively should be known as born in the natural (anuloma) order.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa from a wife of the same caste is a Savarṇa; from a Kṣatriya wife, he is an Anantara.
Likewise, the Ambaṣṭha and Ugra are the sons of a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya respectively.
But the son of Duṣyanta born of a Vaiśya woman from a Brāhmaṇa is separated by one interval;
likewise, from a Kṣatriya, a son named Niṣāda is born of a Śūdra woman.
A Śūdra woman bears from a Brāhmaṇa a Pāraśava son, who is two castes lower; likewise, there are sons born from the castes in both the direct (ānulomya) and inverse (pratiloma) orders.
The Sūta is declared to be the son born immediately after [the Brāhmaṇa], produced from a Kṣatriya father and a Brāhmaṇa mother;
likewise, the Māgadha and the Āyogava are the two sons born from Vaiśya and Śūdra fathers respectively.
A Brāhmaṇa woman bears a Vaiśya son called a Vaidehaka from a Vaiśya man;
likewise, a Kṣatriya woman bears a Kṣattṛ son, who is one degree lower, from a Śūdra man.
When there is a confusion of castes through inverse union, the most sinful man is born as a Caṇḍāla, occurring where a Brāhmaṇa woman is deluded by a Śūdra.
Devala says: From a Śūdra, the Āyogava, Kṣattṛ, and Caṇḍāla are born in the inverse order (pratiloma),
respectively from a Vaiśya woman, a Kṣatriya woman, and a Brāhmaṇa woman.
In the same way, the Māgadha and the Vaidehaka are born from a Vaiśya father;
and the Sūta is born from a Kṣatriya father upon a Brāhmaṇī mother by birth and by his own specific duty.

Viṣṇu [16.3–6]: “And those born in the inverse order are censured by the noble ones. Among them, the son of a Vaiśya woman by a Śūdra is an Āyogava; the sons of a Kṣatriya woman by Śūdras and Vaiśyas are respectively a Pulkasa and a Māgadha; and the Caṇḍāla, Vaidehaka, and Sūta are the sons of a Brāhmaṇa woman by a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, and a Kṣatriya.”

Vasiṣṭha [18.1–6]: “They say that one born of a Śūdra father and a Brāhmaṇī mother becomes a Caṇḍāla; one born of a Rājanyā mother becomes a Vaiṇa; and one born of a Vaiśyā mother becomes an Antyāvasāyin. They say that one born of a Vaiśya father and a Brāhmaṇī mother becomes a Rāmaka; one born of a Rājanyā mother becomes a Pulkasa. They say that one born of a Rājanya father and a Brāhmaṇī mother becomes a Sūta. Yama states:
“All those born from the four castes who have emerged from the womb of a Caṇḍāla are indeed Caṇḍālas.”
Sūtas, Māgadhas, Caṇḍālas, Śvapacas, Ugras, and Pulkasas.
Of these, the first three have the same origin;
the two immediately following them also have the same origin, while the last one alone is recorded as having a different origin.
From a Kṣatriya, a Sūta is born; from a Vaiśya, a Māgadha is born;
and from a Śūdra, a Caṇḍāla is born—wherever the Brāhmaṇī woman is deluded.
From a Vaiśya father and a Kṣatriya mother, one named a Śvapaca is born;
and from a Śūdra father, when a Kṣatriya woman is deluded, an Ugra is born.
From a Śūdra father and a Vaiśya mother is born one named a Pulkasa;
these [offspring] are distinguished by their seed and womb, and are thus inferior or superior to the [four] social classes (varṇas).

Hārīta states: “From a Brāhmaṇa woman, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—being of inverse status—beget Sūtas, Māgadhas, and Mātaṅgas. From a Kṣatriya woman, a Vaiśya and a Śūdra beget a Bandin and a Niṣāda respectively. From a Vaiśya woman, a Śūdra begets a Pulkasa. Paiṭhīnasi states: “The Sūta, Māgadha, and Caṇḍāla are born from a Brāhmaṇa woman through passion with men of lower castes; the Ambaṣṭha and Āyogava from a Kṣatriya woman; and the Māgadha from a Vaiśya woman. Furthermore, the Pulkasa, Vaiṇa, Rathakāra, Śvapāka, Kaivarta, and Niṣāda are born as offspring of mixed castes.”

Baudhāyana [1.16.6–15]: “From a Śūdra with a Vaiśya woman is born a Māgadha; with a Kṣatriya woman, a Kṣattṛ; and with a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Caṇḍāla. From a Vaiśya with a Kṣatriya woman is born an Āyogava; with a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Vaidehaka. From a Kṣatriya with a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Sūta. Among these, the union of an Ambaṣṭha and an Ugra results in an Anuloma. The union of a Kṣattṛ and a Vaidehaka results in a Pratiloma. Born from an Ugra with a Kṣattṛ woman is a Śvapāka. From a Vaidehaka with an Ambaṣṭha woman is a Vaiṇa. From a Niṣāda with a Śūdra woman is a Pulkasa. From a Śūdra with a Niṣāda woman is a Kukkuṭa. The wise call those born from the intermixture of castes ‘Vrātyas’.”

Paiṭhīnasi states: "From a pratiloma union with a woman of unswerving fidelity, the Sūta, Māgadha, and Āyogava are born. From a Śūdra father and women of the higher castes, the Śvapāka, Caṇḍāla, and Niṣāda are born. From a Brāhmaṇa father and a Kṛṣṇā woman, a Pāraśava is born; from a Pāraśavī woman, a Kṣattṛ. From a Kṣatriya father and a Kṛṣṇā woman, a Bandī is born; from a Vaiśya father, a Vaitāla. From a Pāraśava father and a Kṣatriya woman, an Ambaṣṭha is born; from a Vaiśya woman, a Dundulāda and an Ambaṣṭha. From a Videhā woman, a Vena is born. From a Vaidehaka, Bandī, Niṣāda, or Ambaṣṭha woman, by a Brāhmaṇa father, the Cūcuka, Mudga, Paulkasa, and Kukkuṭaka are born. From a Vaiśya woman, an Āyogava is born. From a Kṣatriya father and women of the Kṣattṛ, Pulkasa, Veṇa, and Ugra castes, the Dūta, Preṣya, Kaivarta, and Āra are born. From an Ugra father and women of the aforementioned castes, the Mauñjiṣṭha, Sautapāṇi, and Vikala are born. From an Ugrā woman and men of the aforementioned castes, the Pauṣṭika, Ḍomba, Bhiñja, and Śiṇḍika are born."

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "From a Kṣatriya woman, through union with an Ugra, a Śvapāka is born; from a Vaidehakī woman, through union with an Ambaṣṭha, a Vena is born; from a Śūdra woman, by a Niṣāda, a Pulkasa is born; and by a Māgadha, a Kukkuṭaka. Baudhāyana [1.13.9] says: "From an Ambaṣṭha on a woman of the first caste, a Śvapāka is born; from an Ugra on a woman of the second caste, a Vena is born; from a Niṣāda on a woman of the third caste, a Pulkasa is born; and in the reverse order, a Kukkuṭaka is born. Devala says:
A son born from an Ugra father and a Niṣāda mother becomes a Kukkuṭa;
one born from a Niṣāda father and a Śūdra mother becomes a Pulkasa.
One born from a Vaidehaka father and an Ambaṣṭhī mother is known as a Vena;
one born from an Ambaṣṭha father and a Vaidehakī mother becomes a Kuśīlava.
Likewise, from a Kṣatriya woman, a son born of a man of a fierce class is called a Śvapāka;
in this manner, these and other intermediate castes arise from mixed unions.

Manu and Viṣṇu [Manu 10.15, 18–19, 25–40; Viṣṇu 16–17]: From a Brāhmaṇa and the daughter of an Ugra is born one named Āvṛta; from the daughter of an Ambaṣṭha is born an Ābhīra; and from the daughter of an Āyogava is born a Dhigvaṇa.
One born from a Niṣāda father and a Śūdra mother is by birth a Pulkasa;
however, one born from a Śūdra father and a Niṣāda mother is known as a Kukkuṭaka.
One born from a Kṣattṛ father and an Ugrā mother is known as a Śvapāka;
however, one produced by a Vaidehaka father and an Ambaṣṭhī mother is called a Vena.
I shall now describe in their entirety those of mixed origin who are born from inverse (pratiloma) and natural (anuloma) unions, as well as those who are mutually intermingled.
The Sūta, the Vaidehaka, and the Caṇḍāla— the lowest of men—
as well as the Māgadha, the Kṣattṛ, and likewise the Āyogava.
These six beget similar castes upon women of their own kind;
they also procreate offspring upon women of superior castes who are like their mothers.
Likewise, for three castes, his offspring is born from two;
from the immediate [caste] and from its own source, and likewise the sequence applies even among those outside [the caste system].
And they also produce many outsiders, even more corrupted than before, who procreate upon one another's wives and are thus censured.
Just as a Śūdra begets an outcast being upon a Brāhmaṇī woman, so too does an outcast beget one even more outcast upon women of the four castes.
Acting in opposition [to their own kind], those who are outsiders beget yet more outsiders;
being inferior, they give birth to fifteen even more inferior castes.

From a Dasyu father and an Ayogava mother is born a Sairandhra, who knows the art of personal adornment and service, yet is not a slave, though he lives by the life of a servant, and subsists by means of snares.
The Vaideha, however, procreates the Maitreyaka,
who praises men incessantly and strikes a bell at the break of dawn.
The Niṣāda begets the Mārgava, a slave who lives by the work of boats;
those dwelling in Āryāvarta call him a Kaivarta.
Among the Āyogavī women— who wear the clothes of the dead, are ignoble, and eat despised food—
these three base-born castes arise separately.
From a Niṣāda father and a Kārāvara mother, a leather-worker (carmakāra) is born;
from a Vaidehaka father, the Andhra and Meda are born, who sleep outside the village.
From a Caṇḍāla and a Vaidehī is born a Pāṇḍusopāka, who deals in bamboo; he is also called an Āhiṇḍika. He is likewise born from a Niṣāda and a Vaidehī.
But from a Caṇḍāla, by a Pulkasī woman, is born a sinful Sopāka who subsists by the occupation of root-digging and is always censured by virtuous people.
But from a Caṇḍāla man and a Niṣāda woman is born a son called Antyāvasāyin,
who frequents cremation grounds and is despised even by those outside the caste system.
These castes resulting from intermixture, as shown by their fathers and mothers,
are to be known— whether they be concealed or manifest— by their respective actions.
Nārada [14.105]:
But those born in the reverse order (pratiloma), such as the Sūta and others who have arisen from the reverse order,
including the Pāka and so forth along with their consecrated castes— their group consists of twenty-one.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "The chariot-maker (rathakāra) is one born from the intermediate union of a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya mother; for him, there are the rites of sacrifice, giving, and initiation (upanayana), as well as the study of the treatises on horses, chariots, and architecture, and his livelihood is [the practice of these crafts]. Vasiṣṭha says: "Some hold that the chariot-maker is born from the intermediate union of a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya mother. For him, the study of the Vedas, sacrifice, the establishment of the sacred fires (adhāna), and the rite of initiation are not prohibited; and his livelihood consists of the study of the treatises on chariots and architecture. Yājñavalkya [1.95] states: [823] Śaṅkha and Likhita: "The chariot-maker is one born from the intermediate union of a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya mother; for him, there are the ritual acts of sacrifice, giving, and initiation, as well as the study of the treatises on horses, chariots, and architecture, and his mode of livelihood. Vasiṣṭha: "Some say that the chariot-maker is born from the intermediate union of a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya mother. For him, the study [of the Vedas], sacrifice, the establishment of the sacred fires, and the rite of initiation are not forbidden; and his livelihood is the study of the treatises on chariots and architecture. Yājñavalkya [1.95]: [823] Śaṅkha and Likhita: "The chariot-maker is one born from the intermediate union of a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya mother; for him, there are the ritual acts of sacrifice, giving, and initiation, as well as the study of the treatises on horses, chariots, and architecture, and his mode of livelihood. Vasiṣṭha: "Some say that the chariot-maker is born from the intermediate union of a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya mother. For him, the study [of the Vedas], sacrifice, the establishment of the sacred fires, and the rite of initiation are not forbidden; and his livelihood is the study of the treatises on chariots and architecture. Yājñavalkya [1.95]: [823] Śaṅkha and Likhita: "The chariot-maker is one born from the intermediate union of a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya mother; for him, there are the ritual acts of sacrifice, giving, and initiation, as well as the study of the treatises on horses, chariots, and architecture, and his mode of livelihood. Vasiṣṭha: "Some say that the chariot-maker is born from the intermediate union of a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya mother. For him, the study [of the Vedas], sacrifice, the establishment of the sacred fires, and the rite of initiation are not forbidden; and his livelihood is the study of the treatises on chariots and architecture. Yājñavalkya [1.95]: [823] Śaṅkha and Likhita: "The chariot-maker is one born from the intermediate union of a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya mother; for him, there are the ritual acts of sacrifice, giving, and initiation, as well as the study of the treatises on horses, chariots, and architecture, and his mode of livelihood. From a Māhiṣya father and a Karaṇī mother, a Rathakāra is born.
Yama says: Through the violation of the established order, a mixture of castes (varṇasaṃkara) arises.
But those who have fallen from their lineage become outcasts and are deprived of right conduct.
Furthermore, Yama says: "Understand the virtues and faults according to the direct and inverse orders;
through the direct order one attains the status of a caste, while through the inverse order there is a downfall."
Manu [10.66–72]: "If it should be asked, 'Wherein lies the superiority' between one born by chance from a Brāhmaṇa to a non-Aryan woman, and one born from a non-Aryan man to a Brāhmaṇa woman?"
One born of a noble man from a non-noble woman may become noble through his qualities;
however, one born even from a noble man to a non-noble woman is certainly non-noble—this is the settled rule.
But both of these are unfit for sacramental rites; such is the established rule of dharma:
the former because of the deficiency of his birth, and the latter because of being born in the inverse order.
Just as a good seed, when grown in a fertile field, reaches fulfillment,
so too one born of a noble father from a noble mother is worthy of every refinement.

Some wise men praise the seed, others the field; still others praise both the seed and the field. In this matter, however, the established rule is as follows: The seed sown in a bad field perishes along with the field; but the seed sown in a good field flourishes according to its own nature. Even a small seed, when planted in a well-prepared field, grows into a great tree and yields abundant fruit. Therefore, one should always strive to cultivate a virtuous field, for it is the field that brings forth the harvest. Even a tiny seed, when sown in a fertile field, becomes a great tree and produces many fruits. Thus, the wise should always endeavor to prepare their own fields through the cultivation of virtue. Just as a seed sown in a bad field perishes, so too does merit perish when placed in an unworthy person. But merit bestowed upon a worthy recipient increases manifold, like a drop of water falling into the ocean. Therefore, one should always bestow gifts upon those who are worthy, for a gift given to an unworthy person is lost, while one given to a worthy person bears great fruit. Just as a seed sown in a bad field perishes, so too does a gift given to an unworthy person go to waste. But a gift given to a worthy person is never lost; it grows and yields inexhaustible results. Therefore, one should always seek out a worthy field and sow the seeds of charity there. For a gift given to a worthy person is like a seed sown in a fertile field—it thrives and brings forth an abundant harvest. Seed sown in a non-field perishes right there within;
even a field without seed becomes merely a barren plot of ground.
Since sages born of animal species became honored and praised through the power of their seed, therefore the seed is preeminent.
Likewise [10.41–42]:
"The six sons born of women of their own caste and those born immediately after are of the nature of the twice-born;
however, all those born of degradation from the Śūdra caste are recorded as being of the same nature as Śūdras."
And by the power of the seeds of their asceticism,
they undergo increase and decrease among human beings here, birth after birth, in age after age.
Likewise [10.64–65]:
"If one born of a Śūdra woman from a Brāhmaṇa father procreates with someone of superior status,
he attains the higher caste by the seventh generation."
A Śūdra attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa, and a Brāhmaṇa likewise attains the status of a Śūdra;
one should know that this is exactly the same for those born from a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya.

Baudhāyana [1.16.13–14]: "One born from a Niṣāda father and a Niṣāda mother uproots the status of a Śūdra up to the fifth generation. One should initiate him; at the sixth generation one may cause him to sacrifice; at the seventh he becomes unaltered. These designations—Jīva, Saṃjīvaka, and Kara—fall in sequence upon them. Yājñavalkya [1.96]:
"The elevation of caste is to be known as occurring in the fifth or even the seventh generation."
Upon the reversal of actions, there is equilibrium, and as before, there is the state of higher and lower.

Āpastamba [2.11.10–11]: “Through the practice of dharma, a lower caste attains each successive higher caste in the transformation of birth; through the practice of adharma, a higher caste falls to each successive lower caste in the transformation of birth. Manu [10.73]:
“One who is non-Aryan but performs the actions of an Aryan, and one who is Aryan but performs the actions of a non-Aryan...”
Having reflected, the Creator said: "They are neither equal nor unequal."
Likewise [10.20–23]:
Those whom twice-born men beget upon women of their own caste, but who are devoid of vows—
one should designate them as *vrātyas*, fallen away from the *Sāvitrī*.
From a Vratya Brahmin is born the evil-natured Bhṛjjakaṇṭaka,
as well as the Āvantya, the Vāṭadhāna, the Puṣpadha, and the Śaikha.
From the Vrātya of the Rājanya caste are born the Jhalla, the Malla, and the Licchivi;
as well as the Naṭa, the Karaṇa, the Khasa, and the Draviḍa.
From a Vrātya Vaiśya are born the Sudhanvan, the Ācārya, the Kāruṣa,
the Vijanman, the Maitra, and the Sātvata.
Devala says:
Furthermore, those who have been procreated by men lacking vows and lacking sacraments, even upon women of their own caste, shall be excluded like Vratyas.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "A Brahmin who has been born from an uninitiated woman within the three [upper] castes, who is known by his age, is one whose Sāvitrī has fallen.
Yama says:
"He who is born of a female ascetic, and he who has lapsed from the ascetic life..."
To both of them—the Brahmin and the Caṇḍāla—Yama, the son of Vivasvat, said:
"He who has fallen from his station after having ascended it, and he who was born as one already fallen—
Manu, the son of the Self-Existent, declared these two to be *brahma-caṇḍālas*."
But he who is born of a woman of the Brāhmaṇa caste by one who has entered the religious order, and he who is born of a Śūdra woman by a Brāhmaṇa—
Manu, the son of Svayambhū, declared these two to be "Brahma-chaṇḍālas."
Aṅgiras says:

Know that both he who is the son of one who has gone forth (a renunciant) born of a Brāhmaṇī woman, and he who is born of a Śūdra woman, as well as he who is born of a woman of the same lineage (sagotra), are Caṇḍālas.
But these Kṣatriya castes gradually attained the state of Śūdras in the world through their neglect of ritual acts and through the absence of Brāhmaṇas.
The Pauṇḍrakas, Auḍras, Draviḍas, Kāmbojas, Yavanas, Śakas,
Pāradas, Pallavas, Cīnas, Kirātas, Daradas, and Khaśas.
Likewise [10.57–61]: One should discern by their own actions a man who is devoid of caste, unrecognizable, born of a defiled womb, and who, though appearing noble in form, is actually ignoble.
Lack of nobility, harshness, cruelty,
and a disposition toward inaction reveal in this world a man born of a defiled womb.
A child inherits the character of the father, or the mother, or perhaps both;
however, no offspring can ever suppress its own innate nature.
Even for one born into a preeminent family, if there should be a confusion of birth,
that person surely adopts the conduct of those [of mixed origin], whether to a small or great extent.
But in that place where these corrupters of the social orders are born through promiscuity,
that kingdom, together with its inhabitants, perishes very quickly.
Nārada [14.113]:
From the king’s failure to provide protection, the intermixture of castes arises;
therefore, women must be protected by the king specifically from such intermixture.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “Thus there is a distinction in the castes. However, due to negligence or weakness, the king shall cause the offender to pay the penalty; furthermore, the king must provide for their respective occupations.
Now, regarding their occupations, Manu says [10.46–50]:
Those who are considered the outcasts among the twice-born, as well as those born of degraded unions,
should subsist by means of those very occupations of the twice-born that are held in contempt.
The management of horses and charioteering for the Sūtas; medical practice for the Ambaṣṭhas;
the service of women for the Vaidehakas; and the trade of merchants for the Māgadhas.
The killing of fish is the occupation of Niṣādas; that of Tvaṣṭṛs and Āyogavas is [the same];
and for Medas, Andhras, Cuñcus, and Madgus, it is the slaughter of wild animals.
For the Kṣattrus, Ugras, and Pulkasas, however, there shall be dwelling in holes and the killing and binding [of animals];
for the Dhigvaṇas, the work of leather; and for the Veṇas, the playing of drums.
These known [offenders] shall dwell at sacred shrines, near trees, in cremation grounds, and in the groves of actors, subsisting by their own labor.

‘Born of degradation’ (apadhvaṃsajāḥ) means those born from inverse unions (pratilomajāḥ). ‘By censured [means]’ refers to trade and so forth prescribed for the twice-born in times of distress; ‘by services useful to the twice-born, such as menial labor,’ says Medhātithi [on MDh 10.46].

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "The duties of Sūtas are the preparation of food, the shaving of hair, beards, nails, and body hair, bathing, anointing, ornamentation, training horses, and the management of vehicles and spectacles. The duties of Kṣattṛs are serving as doorkeepers and messengers. The duties of Māgadhas are playing the mṛdaṅga drum, flute, and lute; performing dances, songs, and the rites of the Puṣpamāṇavakas; the accomplishment of magical feats; attendance upon royalty; and the recitation of gāthās, ślokas, and morning awakenings. The duties of Ambaṣṭhas—due to their specific caste—are the extraction of bodily arrows, the application of probes and elixirs, the treatment of poisoning, insanity, impotence, fever, epilepsy, and childhood ailments, as well as the nourishment of the body and similar tasks. The duties of Vaidehakas are the cutting of leaves, sewing, dyeing, cleaning, and the clearing of refuse from ponds, tanks, gardens, groves, and waste heaps. The duties of Ugras are the capturing of elephants, holding the royal parasol, running ahead [of the king], and the confinement and restraint of prisoners. The duties of Veṇas are leaping, forest sports, wrestling, the employment of magic and the arts of Indra (illusion), and the wielding of weapons. The duties of Kukkuṭas are the use of weapons such as the discus, the tomara-club, the bhindipāla-sling, the noose, the sword, the axe, the cudgel, and iron nets, as well as the maintenance of battle arrays. The duties of Āyogavas are the clearing of refuse, pottery-making, the crafting of gold, silver, gems, and metals, and working in leather. The duties of Pulkasas are the guarding of city streets, keeping watch, the removal of the dead and the destitute, and the work of painting, leaf-cutting, and garland-making. The duties of Niṣādas are the setting of snares and traps, the hunting and killing of deer, cattle, birds, and fish, the distillation of honey-wine, and the carving of meat."

[831] ‘The attendance upon the king for the purpose of instructing on the accomplishment of rites by means of being a *puṣpamāṇavaka* (a flower-boy) and an expert in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*)’: this refers to attending in the presence of the king for the sake of teaching the successful performance of rituals as a *puṣpamāṇavaka*, according to Śabarasvāmin.

Viṣṇu [16.7–13]: “Entering the arena is for the *āyogavas*; hunting is for the *pulkasas*; the act of praising is for the *māgadhas*; execution is for the *caṇḍālas*; protecting women and living thereby is for the *vaidehakas*; and charioteering of horses is for the *sūtas*.”

Hārīta says: "We shall describe their occupations: for the Sūta, the driving of horses and chariots; for the Māgadha, subsistence by playing the mṛdaṅga drum; for the Caṇḍāla, subsistence by [handling] the equipment for the dead at cremation grounds; for the Bandin, reciting after an actor; for the Niṣāda, subsistence by piloting boats; and for the Pulakasa, playing musical instruments, [working on] streets and stages, and washing sites.
Yama says: "For the Sūtas, the driving of horses; for the Māgadhas, medical practice."
The execution of those condemned to death is the wage of the Caṇḍālas and the Cuñcupas.
And there shall be a proclamation for the Madgus and the Pulkasas crossing over.
But the dwelling place for Caṇḍālas and Śvapacas shall be outside the village.
They should be rendered outcasts, and their wealth shall consist of dogs and donkeys.
Their garments shall be the clothes of the dead, their food from broken vessels,
their ornament iron, and they shall always lead a life of wandering mendicancy.
These recognized individuals shall dwell at shrines, near sacred trees, in cremation grounds, and in forests or groves, subsisting by their own prescribed duties.
A man practicing dharma should not seek association with them;
their mutual dealings and marriages are with their own equals.
Their food, which must be given by others, should be provided in a separate vessel;
they shall not wander at night through villages or cities.
They should move about during the day for the sake of their business, marked by royal edicts; and it is ordained that they shall carry out the funeral of a corpse that has no kinsmen.
They shall constantly execute those deserving of death according to the scriptures upon the king's command;
they shall also take the garments, beds, and ornaments of those condemned to death.
Yama says:
Their ornaments shall be of black iron, their food shall be eaten from vessels made of that same metal,
they shall dwell outside the village, and their wealth shall be a donkey.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “The occupations of Caṇḍālas are dwelling in a secluded place, guarding cemeteries, running about with packs of dogs, and executing those condemned to death; the same applies to Śvapacas. The occupations of the bands of Dasyus and Mlecchas are living by the use of weapons. The women of all these classes shall be of their own kind, and they shall be superior to all others. Viṣṇu (16.14–16) states: “The specific rules for Caṇḍālas are that they must dwell outside the village and wear the clothes of the dead. For all of them, however, there is residence among those of their own caste, as well as the inheritance of their fathers’ property. Devala says:
In that regard, one should separately establish for those born in the intermediate castes, according to both the inverse and the natural orders,
their respective connections with their own origins.
In that same way, he should establish the four castes each in their own duty;
thus the king's prosperity, fame, contentment, and righteousness increase.
Manu [10.62–63]: "Sacrificing one's body without expectation of reward for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa or for the sake of a cow,
and for the protection of women and children, is the cause of liberation for those outside [the fold]."
[834] Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, and restraint of the senses—
Manu declared this to be the summary of the Dharma for the four castes.

Devala states: "Living according to one's own caste, endurance of all authorities, conducting worldly affairs according to the authority of others, supporting one's own dependents, and the avoidance of improper actions—these are the duties of a Caṇḍāla.
Thus ends the section on the characteristics and livelihoods of the anuloma and pratiloma castes within the section on legal procedure (*vyavahārakāṇḍa*).

Thus ends the section on Judicial Procedure (*vyavahārakāṇḍa*) in the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara, the Great Minister for Peace and War (*mahāsāndhivigrahika*) of His Majesty the Emperor (*mahārājādhirāja*), the illustrious Govindacandradeva.
